To Sierra Isley, the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.”
Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville.
It was a blessing in disguise. One month later, while Sierra and Jamie were still unpacking boxes and building furniture, the remnants of Hurricane Helene turned Asheville into a disaster zone. The basement of their apartment flooded, but they were luckier than some of their neighbors, whose homes had been destroyed.
Owning a home has long been seen as a cornerstone of the American Dream—a way to build wealth that you could use one day to pay for your children’s education and fund your retirement. That arrangement was always more precarious than it was made out to be. But as fires and floods damage homes and drive up insurance rates, pouring your life savings into a house has become riskier than ever. In a report called “Property Prices in Peril,” the firm First Street projected last year that climate risks could knock nearly $1.5 trillion off the value of American homes by 2055. For some people, the sociologist Rebecca Elliott wrote, “the American dream of homeownership may become a nightmare.”
Americans are beginning to grasp the threat that climate change poses to their aspirations. According to exclusive polling for Grist from the think tank Data for Progress, 58 percent of likely U.S. voters believe that climate change will hinder their ability to achieve the American Dream over the next 20 years, including 42 percent of Republicans. The survey suggests that people are worried that climate change will increase the cost of living, and such widespread concern very likely played a role in the major gains for Democrats last Tuesday.
The irony is that fossil fuels have long been promoted as necessary ingredients for the American “way of life.” Starting a century ago, oil and gas companies led extensive campaigns to tie their products to comfort and prosperity, a narrative that has been repeatedly deployed by politicians and oil industry executives to thwart climate action. President Donald Trump’s administration has often said that efforts to rein in fossil fuels threaten the American Dream. Earlier this year, when the administration scrapped Biden-era rules to cut emissions from cars, along with the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority to regulate climate change, it touted the effort as “restoring the American Dream.”
But the fossil-fueled American Dream is in the process of destroying itself. Greenhouse gas emissions from burning coal, oil, and gas have ushered in a new period of precarity, undermining the promise that each generation can expect a better life than the last. Scientific reports warn that climate change “imperil[s] the quality of life” for communities in the United States, disrupting livelihoods and cultural traditions.
Either Americans decide to reimagine what makes up the American Dream and abandon that oil-soaked version of prosperity, or climate change will dismantle it for them.
The memories of living through Hurricane Helene are still fresh in Isley’s mind. Hauling water from their flooded basement up to the toilet to flush it when the water ran out. Driving to Jamie’s parents’ house in Atlanta, holed up in a room with both of their cats until they couldn’t take it anymore. Coming back to Asheville and cooking meals in the Crock-Pot with disposable liners because even when the water was running again, it wasn’t safe to wash dishes with.
Two years later, Isley browses Zillow for fun, but she looks at homes through a post-disaster lens. “Now I have that fear in the back of my mind—anywhere near a river, or even a stream, if there’s a little bit of water on the map, I’m like, ‘Oh, no,’” she said. Jamie is trans, and after Trump was elected in 2024, the two of them briefly entertained the idea of moving somewhere with more protective policies, like California. But Isley’s mind immediately went to wildfires. Out of the question.
Isley had fled from hurricanes before, when she lived in Florida during college. She thought she’d be safe from them tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville was supposed to be a “climate haven,” somewhere that would fare better than the rest of the country as the world warmed. Those promises were shattered when almost 14 inches of rain fell on Asheville over three days in September 2024. The French Broad River overflowed its banks, flooding homes and destroying parts of the town’s River Arts District. In western North Carolina, more than 74,000 homes were damaged and only about 4 percent had flood insurance, resulting in $9.5 billion in uninsured residential property losses.
Home values in western North Carolina have declined since the storm, especially in the hardest-hit counties. Asheville’s average home price shrunk 5 percent over the past year, while the national average increased 1.2 percent.
To some degree, housing markets are already pricing in the risk of increased environmental hazards. Homes within FEMA’s high-risk flood zones sell for 2.8 percent less, on average, than what they would otherwise sell for, according to a 2023 study published in the journal Nature Climate Change. The researchers found that homes exposed to flood risk were still overvalued by between $121 billion and $237 billion, though—and they identified Appalachia as a hot spot of overvaluation, one year before Helene hit. The devaluation of homes in high-risk zones is unfolding unevenly and causing “tremendous social harm,” said Elliott, a sociology professor at The London School of Economics and Political Science.
Homes are billed as a way for people to build wealth, but they can turn into a trap. After Superstorm Sandy devastated New York City and the New Jersey coast in 2012, many homeowners couldn’t sell their houses for enough money to buy a new place, leaving them stranded. Even homes that haven’t seen any kind of devastation are at risk of losing value as more people become wary of living in floodplains, coastal places exposed to storms, and wildfire-prone areas. “Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable,” Elliott wrote in a study about property values and climate change.
Insurance is meant to offer a measure of safety when taking on a huge debt for a mortgage on a house. Douglas Heller, the director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, called it “the safety net for the American Dream.” But insurance rates are part of what’s making homeownership unaffordable for so many. Since 2020, property insurance costs have ballooned almost 80 percent, with the average single-family mortgage holder now paying $209 per month. Homeowners in the riskiest areas are paying substantially more, and many in California have been dropped by their insurers. Home insurance rates are rising faster in the Midwest than any other region, driven by the costs of severe storms.
“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace,” Heller said. The more extreme weather we’re seeing is only part of the story: He argues that the insurance industry has become a “climate opportunist,” using climate change as an excuse to justify excessive rate increases.
People relying on Social Security benefits who own condos around Lake Tahoe are particularly vulnerable to rising rates, said Andrew Engler, the founder and CEO of Rock Rose Risk, who helps people in California protect their homes against wildfire and get their insurance premiums down. They’re facing ballooning homeowners association payments, to share the cost of insurance in a risky wildfire area, on a limited paycheck. If they try to move, their properties are worth significantly less because of the huge HOA bills, Engler said. Economists estimate that rising insurance costs linked to disaster risk have reduced the growth of home prices by more than $40,000 in the most hurricane- and wildfire-prone ZIP codes.
Renting might make you more nimble, but it doesn’t insulate you from these costs. One reason rents are going up is because landlords’ property insurance rates are increasing. “Whether you are a homeowner or a renter, we’re all paying for living under the increased risks of climate change,” said Caroline Nagy, the associate director of housing policy at Americans for Financial Reform. That makes it harder for people to save for a home—if that’s even a good idea anymore.
When Sierra Isley walks around her neighborhood these days, she sees the evidence of Helene all around her—in the form of banners with the slogan “Asheville Strong” and shirts that say “WNC Strong.”
One of the most surprising things about disasters might be the way that people who live through them rise to the occasion and come together. In the aftermath of the Helene, with the power and cell service knocked out, Sierra and Jamie walked all around town, talking to their neighbors to try to learn what had happened. People started congregating at the fire station where there was fresh water.
“It’s hard to put into words what that experience was like, but I’ve never felt more of a community, and really having to lean on my neighbors and feeling like my neighbors were leaning on me,” Isley said.
While the American Dream is usually all about independence and personal freedom, living through a disaster has a way of revealing how people depend on each other. The experience can prompt people to hold tightly to what they have, doubling down on protecting their communities, said Nick Tinoco, a sociology researcher in a doctoral program at the University of California, Los Angeles, who interviewed survivors of the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Los Angeles County. Some of the residents he talked to have taken things into their own hands and organized volunteer fire brigades and plan to stay behind to defend their neighborhoods during future fires.
As supposedly safe “climate havens” like Asheville experience more disasters, the idea that people can simply move out of harm’s way is losing its grip. “I think we have to just reckon with the fact that we’re going to have to make people secure in the places that they live,” Elliott said.
She thinks it’s time to rethink the bargain of the American Dream—the expectation that so much of a person’s economic future depends on the fate of a single structure. Many young people have begun to define success differently. A poll from Ipsos last year showed that 46 percent of baby boomers associate homeownership with the American Dream but only 13 percent of Gen Zers do, suggesting that there’s room for its defining features to change.
Sierra and Jamie couldn’t help but wonder what happened to the house they’d almost bought, and they drove over to check it out soon after Hurricane Helene hit. It was still standing, but they couldn’t see if there was any damage hidden inside. “Who knows if it flooded or anything like that, what kind of storm damage it took, and that would have immediately been our problem,” Isley said.
Living through Hurricane Helene didn’t just make Isley relieved she hadn’t bought a house in Asheville. It has shaped what she wants for her life, helping her discover a passion for public health and pushing her to want to work in emergency preparedness. Now she’s applying to schools to pursue a master’s degree in public health.
“I think I owe it to people like me, people in other rural communities who are going to face the same kind of climate change emergencies, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters,” Isley said. “I just feel such a calling.”

In November 2026, a screenshot (archived) circulated online that social media users claimed authentically showed a Truth Social post by U.S. President Donald Trump accusing Democrats of using "WITCHCRAFT AND SATANISM" to win the 2026 midterm elections.
For example, one version of the screenshot on Threads read:
I was told not to say this but we all know the truth, The Democrats and lunatic left have engaged in WITCHCRAFT AND SATANISM to interfere in our elections on a spiritual level!!
America is ONE NATION UNDER GOD and we WILL FIGHT these results!
President DONALD J TRUMP
The screenshot also circulated on Facebook and X (archived). Snopes readers wrote in, asking if the alleged post was real.
The post was fake. A search of the term "WITCHCRAFT AND SATANISM" on Trump's Truth, a site that archives the president's Truth Social posts, returned no results.
Additionally, the screenshot of the fake post listed the date as "11/4/2026." Real Truth Social posts use the date format "Nov 04, 2026." Therefore, the screenshot did not come from Truth Social.
We contacted the White House Press Office for additional confirmation that Trump did not write or publish the post in question and await a reply.
Trump reportedly told the New York Times on Nov. 3 that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results of the election. By contrast, the fake post claimed Trump would "fight" the results.
Trump reportedly told the Times he would "look forward" to working with the incoming Democrats.
Democrats wrested power from Republicans in both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. The 120th Congress, which will include the winners from November's election, will be sworn in in January 2027.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the 2026 U.S. elections.

Lando Norris put his McLaren on pole position for the third year in a row at the Sao Paulo Formula One Grand Prix on Saturday in tough conditions after a long delay caused by torrential rain at Interlagos.
George Russell qualified second fastest for Mercedes,. 0.204 slower, but dropped down the grid due to a five-place penalty, with his newly-crowned world champion teammate Kimi Antonelli replacing him alongside last year’s race winner and champion.
Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc was fourth fastest but has a 10-place grid drop due to power unit changes, which meant Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson will start third and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg fourth.
READ | Ayrton Senna: The most valuable deceased athlete in sport
With the rain getting heavier and leaving no chance for anyone to improve on their times in the final phase, the clock ticked down for the last five minutes without a car on track.
“Today is about getting on pole. It doesn’t really matter how you do it, so very pleased with that,” said Norris after a qualifying that started and was then halted for nearly an hour and a half.
RUSSELL ANGRY AFTER ABORTED LAP
Russell was furious not to be fastest, wanting to make a statement despite knowing he had a penalty but having to abort his quick lap when he came up behind Williams’ Alex Albon.
“Mate, you told me to back off! What the hell?,” he shouted over team radio after realising his day was done. “P2. I don’t want to be P2. I want to be P1.”
Isack Hadjar will line up fifth for Red Bull, with Oliver Bearman sixth for Haas. Russell will start seventh and Fernando Alonso judging the conditions to finish eighth as Aston Martin reached the final phase for the first time this season.
Albon qualified ninth and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri 10th.
Red Bull’s four-time champion Max Verstappen, with a 30 place grid penalty due to power unit changes, sat out the second phase that was red-flagged when Haas debutant Rafael Camara crashed.
Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who will also be starting at the back of the grid due to engine penalties amounting to an impossible 65 place drop, also went out.
There was then a further delay to clear debris before the decisive third phase.
Conditions had eased in Q2, with double world champion Alonso leaning on his experience and the first to switch to intermediates.
Camara earlier had the home crowd roaring when he reached the second phase but fellow-Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto had a nightmare for the second year running when he went off and qualified last.
Bortoleto slid into the tyre wall with seven minutes to go but returned to the track and made his way back to the pits where the damage proved too extensive to fix in the time available.
Both Alpines also went out at the first hurdle along with the two Cadillacs and Aston Martin’s Lance Stroll.

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a message on his Instagram handle ahead of a protest in Kerala's Kochi on Saturday demanding the cancellation of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying that “it is not over until we say it is over”.

Bengaluru-based biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 Mn (around ₹25.5 Cr) in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. The startup, spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), combines venom biology, AI and experimental screening to identify and develop venom-derived molecules into potential therapeutic leads. The fresh capital will be used to expand ‘Venom Atlas’, a molecular dataset of venom-derived compounds, and strengthen its AI and laboratory screening capabilities. The startup also plans to expand its team across venom biology, computational science and drug discovery, while supporting the validation and optimisation of promising molecules. Founded in 2026 by Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, Venomics AI is working to tap the largely unexplored molecular diversity found in animal venoms to identify potential drug candidates. Animal venoms contain complex molecules that have evolved over millions of years to interact with specific biological targets. Some of these compounds have already inspired medicines. However, a large part of the molecular diversity across venomous species remains unexplored, presenting an opportunity for drug discovery. Venomics AI is building a platform that combines molecular sequencing and venom biology to map this diversity through its Venom Atlas. It then uses AI to prioritise promising molecular candidates and validates its predictions through functional laboratory screening. “Animal venoms represent one of nature’s richest yet least explored sources of potential medicines, and at Venomics AI, we are combining cutting-edge experimental science with artificial intelligence to unlock this extraordinary potential,” Sunagar said. India's bioeconomy is on track to reach $300 Bn by 2030, with the country's rapid emergence as a global biotechnology hub, based on IBEF data. Notably, the biotech sector in the country has been booming in recent years. The country is home to more than 11,000 biotech startups. Also, as part of the Budget 2027, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced a new ‘Biopharma SHAKTI’ scheme with an outlay of ₹10,000 Cr. Meanwhile, investor interest in this space has been gradually seeing an uptick, where earlier this year, Cellogen Therapeutics secured ₹20 Cr in funding from Kotak Alternate Asset Managers (Kotak Alts), while StrainX Bioworks has raised $13 Mn in a funding round led by Prime Venture Partners and Leo Capital.

Why managers can learn a lot from leaders like Napoleon - Pulis
- Published
The November international break is almost upon us, which always means one thing - the managerial merry-go-round is about to properly get into gear.
It's known as 'sacking season' for a reason - the new campaign has started to take shape and I know from experience that any manager who is not winning games will always be sleeping with just one eye closed, and the other one open.
At any club on a poor run of results, the owners and supporters will be questioning whether the manager is the right fit to continue.
This two-week break from domestic games is the ideal opportunity to blood the new incumbent and give them a period of getting to know everyone before the games start up again.
That means it is 'hiring season' too, but there are always far more out-of-work managers than vacant positions.
Since the start of last season, 60 different managers have resigned or been sacked by teams in the Premier League and Football League. Three of them left to take up offers from other clubs but, in total, 37 of them - or 62% - are not currently in management.
For most managers, it's rarely the case where you walk into a new club within a few weeks of leaving your last one, so what do out-of-work managers do between jobs to make sure they are ready to take the next opportunity that fits?
'Get your backside off the sofa'
It is more than 32 years since I received my marching orders from my first job at Bournemouth, who were in what is now known as League One. I was devastated.
I had - as I always did - given everything I could do to benefit the club, and with it being my first sacking I honestly did not know where my next step would take me.
But, on the second day of me being out of work, my home phone rang and at the end of the line was Jim Smith, who was in charge of Portsmouth, a few miles down the south coast.
I knew Jim then, but not really well. I'd been a manager for two years, but by then he had already spent 25 years in the dugout, at eight different clubs.
He asked how I was and, before I could even reply, recited these immortal words, which always stuck with me - "son, you're not a real manager until you get sacked at least three times - so get your backside off the sofa and get on with getting another job" - then he put the phone down!
I've used that sentence myself many times since to managers who have lost their job and are struggling to come to terms with it.
That can happen a lot. People outside the game maybe don't realise how difficult it can be when you are sacked, and how it affects certain individuals differently - you can easily fall off the merry-go-round and, as a manager, you never know for sure whether you will get another chance.
'When you are out of work, you can still learn a lot'
Someone else who phoned me up in the summer of 1994 was another great name in the game as a player and manager, Bruce Rioch.
At the time, Bruce was having a lot of success as manager of Bolton - he would get the Arsenal job a few months later - and he asked me if I would scout for him while I was trying to find my next manager's post.
He was very keen to get me involved and very helpful in keeping me busy watching games.
I was equally keen on helping Bruce and ended up scouting for him for that entire season. To this day, I owe him so much in respect of what he asked me to do, because of what I learned during that time.
Football is the best team sport in the world and the fundamental thing I picked up that season is that its 'product', the players, were the secret to success.
By that, I mean that I realised that at all levels there are good players, and at all levels there are managers working on budgets. I learned that knowing the level you were at, and placing the right players at that level who you could afford, would be an enormous factor in your chances of success, or failure.
Yes, there is more to it than that - you then also had to pick good characters, coach them well and motivate them with a driving force they could handle and enjoy - but you have to start by getting the right players for the level you are at.
The following summer, I was appointed manager of Gillingham, who had just finished 89th out of the 92 clubs across the top four divisions.
I was lucky enough to inherit a club who had quite a few players out of contract, so it enabled me to reset the first team with several players I had watched during my time scouting for Bruce and Bolton.
All the hours and miles I travelled that year paid off, with Gillingham finishing second in what is now League Two and gaining promotion in my first season. Those players who we recruited kick-started four years of my managerial career in Kent, and left me with some fantastic on-field memories.
'Napoleon Bonaparte kept me busy'
My time and success at Priestfield opened up an ever-revolving door of work and rest.
Whenever I was out of work in the years that followed, watching games still occupied my midweeks and weekends for the same reasons as before - I wanted to watch players who I might end up signing.
Lots of games I went to were watched from the terraces with either home or away supporters, which was always interesting and illuminating - I've always valued the views of match-going fans on different players.
Down the years, I was also invited to spend a few weeks coaching abroad, in Kuwait and the United States, by friends I had in the game.
Whatever I was doing, I always felt like I was learning, and not just by watching football around the world. I became an avid reader of sports books and also finding out about great leaders of men through history.
So, as well as visiting Bayer Leverkusen, Athletic Bilbao and RB Leipzig - who back then had only just started their rise from the bottom tier of German football - I would analyse and investigate historic battles or events.
Napoleon Bonaparte really kept me busy. His attention to detail and his command of his generals was only superseded by his troop's loyalty to him - they would literally die for him!
His 250th birthday was celebrated in Corsica in the summer of 2019, and a French newspaper invited me to go along and give a British perspective on how we see Napoleon as a leader and a person.
I was delighted to accept and was amazed by how many people from all over Europe turned up too.
Hated by many countries, but still adored by his followers, Napoleon also produced the Napoleonic Code, which is still the foundation of French civil law today.
'It's better to be in a job than out of football full-stop'
As well as great military triumphs, I studied defeats too - they are as much a part of football management as victories, after all - and you can compare the organisational brilliance of Napoleon to the disaster of the Battle of Balaclava and the Charge of the Light Brigade.
One summer, I travelled out to Crimea to witness the scene of that tragic charge by the bravest of brave men.
Lord Raglan, the British commander-in-chief, was based on the high ground and could see everything in the Russian positions and the brigades.
His order to attack was ambiguous and although Lord Cardigan, who led the charge, questioned it, he still followed it through - leading to one of the most infamous military disasters in history.
It should never have happened but, just as in football, leadership and communication from the top was key. The instructions were passed down from Raglan to Lord Lucan to Cardigan and became garbled - too many cooks, in my opinion!
The last book which really stuck with me, in terms of inspiring me as a leader, was the story of HMS Endurance - disaster strikes during a journey through the ice fields of the southern hemisphere when the ship becomes stuck.
I cannot do justice to the deeds of Sir Ernest Shackleton in this column but his leadership of his men, along with his number two Frank Worsley, was extraordinary.
Both dovetailed in a way that gave their men the energy, desire and determination to believe and follow instructions in the most appalling conditions, never once questioning their leaders' abilities to help them survive.
Over the years, I've never stopped reading about, or watching, great leaders like that - there is so much that young coaches can learn from other sports or history that will benefit then, the same way it did me.
Going to games was still the most important thing when I was between jobs, because I would always believe my own eyes when watching players.
There were times when that became more of a challenge, especially at the back end of my career, but times change and if you are not in tune with what is happening in the game then you can get dropped very quickly.
But I am sure that most of my managerial compatriots would also agree with me that experience in all walks of life can be invaluable.
I learned so much when I was out of work, about all aspects of leadership, individually and collectively.
My advice to managers out of work now is the same that I received from Jim, all those years ago - pick yourselves up and get off the sofa to get back in work as quickly as possible.
You should never be afraid of dropping down a level the way I did, too. It is better to get a job, any job, than be out of football full-stop. That hasn't changed since my day, either.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Images purportedly showing U.S. soldiers practicing digging mass battlefield graves circulated on social media in late October.
According to several posts, the purpose of the supposed grave-digging rehearsal was to prepare soldiers for large-scale temporary burial until bodies could be identified and returned home in the case of mass casualties as the U.S. war on Iran stretched on.
"DISTURBING: The U.S. Army is now training soldiers to dig MASS BATTLEFIELD GRAVES for American troops as the war continues," one Facebook post read (archived).
Both the image and the claim were real. The images were originally distributed (archived) on Oct. 22 by the Department of Defense's media distribution service.
It wasn't clear precisely what the exercise was in preparation for, though it appears that conclusions drawn about an imminent or specific threat originated on social media, not the Army's report. We reached out to the Army for comment and a spokesperson responded: "XVIII Airborne Corps conducts rigorous training exercises to ensure constant readiness for any national mission."
According to the photo credit, they were taken by Capt. Thomas McCarty on Oct. 21. The caption called the operation a "simulated temporary interment trench," meaning that soldiers were practicing digging 15-foot-wide trenches for temporary burial of bodies so that they could later be identified and relocated. The full caption read:
A U.S. Army D6 bulldozer, operated by horizontal construction engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, backfills a simulated temporary interment trench during Phase II of Operation Dragon Covenant near the St. Mere Eglise Drop Zone, Oct. 21, 2026. The test-of-concept exercise, executed by the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, evaluated the structural impact of heavy earthmoving equipment on remains by placing simulated skeletal models and sealed water containers inside burial bags. Operators practiced casting dirt inward from a 15-foot-wide trench to verify that the gravity fall of displaced soil preserves remains intact for future forensic identification and repatriation, while refining spatial standards for future Army fatality management doctrine. (U.S. Army photo by Capt. Thomas McCarty)
McCarty later wrote a report on the training exercise that both the Defense Department and the Army website published. (The article on the Army website appeared to no longer be available, as of this writing.)
According to McCarty, the exercise was "an operational reality the U.S. Army has not executed at scale since the Korean War."
The report detailed how in a 24-hour period of continuous operations, a crew could bury up to 2,400 bodies.
"Backfilling without desecrating the remains is where the real skill lies," one engineering officer reportedly said.

- After Democrats swept up the legislatures and governorships of five U.S. states in November, a rumor spread they were in a position to abolish the Electoral College — the group of 538 electors who can cast votes for U.S. president.
- While this system is enshrined in the U.S. Constitution, it has allowed the election of five presidents who lost the popular vote (in 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000 and 2016). Critics have panned the Electoral College as a form of minority rule that undermines democracy.
- The five states in question are Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. It is true that, combined, they have enough electors to join and enact an agreement between states — a "compact" — to bypass the Electoral College, but not abolish it altogether.
- Instead, the states that joined the compact would grant their Electoral College votes to whichever candidate won the popular vote in a presidential election. In other words, the Electoral College would still exist, but it would defer to the result of the national vote.
- However, some experts say legal hurdles may stop this plan. The Compact Clause of the U.S. Constitution says Congress would have to approve the plan.
After Democrats swept up the legislatures and governorships of five U.S. states in the November midterm elections, a rumor spread they were now in a position to abolish the Electoral College — the group of 538 electors who cast votes for the U.S. president on behalf of their states.
Several social media posts made the claim, including on Instagram and X. One X post said "Dems now have the power to pass the National Voter Compact to effectively abolish the Electoral College" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers reached out, seeking to confirm the veracity of the rumor.
It is true that Democrats swept the legislatures and governorships of five states (Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin). It is also true that, combined, they have enough electors to join and enact an existing agreement between 18 states and Washington, D.C. — a "compact" — to bypass the Electoral College.
However, the compact would not abolish the Electoral College altogether. In addition, as we outline below, some experts say the move would require congressional approval.
We contacted the Democratic leadership of all five states and a constitutional law expert seeking more clarity. We will update this report should we receive responses.
The Electoral College
In the United States, voters do not elect the president directly. Instead, they vote for electors in each state who, for the most part, cast their ballots for the presidential candidate who wins a majority in that state (Maine and Nebraska cast two electoral votes to the statewide winner, then they allow each congressional district to cast its vote for that district's winner). There are currently 538 electors in the Electoral College; presidents win with a simple majority of 270 electors.
This system has led to five instances where the elected president lost the national popular vote. For example in 2016, Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton won the popular vote, but her Republican opponent, Donald Trump, became president. In 2000, George W. Bush, a Republican, was elected despite earning fewer votes than Democrat Al Gore. The same thing happened in 1824, 1876 and 1888.
In practice, critics say, the Electoral College gives way to a minority rule — a system in which less-populated states have disproportionate political power. This, they argue, undermines democracy, which on principle allows the majority to decide.
There has long been a battle to restore balance by abolishing the Electoral College, which is enshrined in the 12th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. This fact sets a high bar for abolition. Per Article 5, any change in the Constitution requires an amendment proposal by two-thirds of both chambers of Congress, which must then be ratified by three-quarters of the states.
Bypassing the Electoral College
How elections are run is the prerogative of each state. Nothing in federal law compels a state to give its electors' votes to the statewide winner. This freedom has led to an effort, called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, that aims at electing the presidential winner of the nationwide popular vote while bypassing the constitutional amendment process.
An interstate compact is an agreement between two or more states. The states that joined the NPVIC agreed to give all their electors' votes to the winner of the popular vote in a presidential election. Eighteen states and Washington, D.C. have joined the compact since its 2006 launch, for a total of 222 electors.
In order for the compact to become effective, the total number of electors for all of the states that adopt it must reach or surpass 270 — the simple majority. This, its supporters say, has become more likely now that Democrats have won both state houses and the governorship in five states during the 2026 midterms: Pennsylvania (19 Electoral College votes), Michigan (15 votes), Arizona (11 votes), Wisconsin (10 votes) and Nevada (6 votes). Should they adopt the NPVIC, these states would bring the total of electors above 270.
Legal challenges to the compact
But others say that even if the five states agree to join the compact, legal challenges lie ahead. One such challenge is that the compact may need Congress' approval, University of Notre Dame Law Professor Derek Muller wrote in a 2023 blog post, citing two U.S. Supreme Court decisions. We reached out to Muller asking for more details.
It is true that the Compact Clause of the Constitution says states may not agree to anything without congressional approval (emphasis ours):
No State shall, without the Consent of Congress, lay any Duty of Tonnage, keep Troops, or Ships of War in time of Peace, enter into any Agreement or Compact with another State, or with a foreign Power, or engage in War, unless actually invaded, or in such imminent Danger as will not admit of delay.
In other words, it is possible that these states may consider joining the NPVIC. However, the path to enacting it may not be straightforward.
For further reading, Snopes has covered several claims related to the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections, including a rumor that Trump is considering a nuclear strike on Iran.

The young politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
- Published
"JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".
It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.
Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.
The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations.
"My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.
El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.
The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.
But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.
The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.
At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.
Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.
Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.
Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.
Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.
She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests.
Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".
She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.
Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.
The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.
Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.
His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.
In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.
Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.
Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.
Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.
Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House.
Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.
For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.
On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who will be next PM?
Votes are being counted in New Zealand, with incumbent PM Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party and Chris Hipkins' centre-left Labour Party currently neck-and-neck. Both parties are calling for compromise to find common ground as the vote tallies show the election is too close to call.
The latest electoral commission data suggests a slight lead for National in overall votes, but New Zealand's electoral system often forces parties into coalition - which means Hipkins' Labour Party may still take power.
Meanwhile, the centrist Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time. The party, led by Qiulae Wong, may hold the power in future coalition negotiations.
The BBC's Tiffanie Turnbull reports from Wellington after an inconclusive night for New Zealand.

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) seized drugs and cosmetics worth ₹34.51 lakh, cancelled 122 licences and suspended 422 others following enforcement action across the State in October 2026, according to a press note issued by the department on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The FDA conducted 1,986 inspections of drug manufacturing, sales and other regulated establishments during the month and issued 674 notices. Of these, 1,694 inspections were conducted at drug sales establishments and 292 at manufacturing and other regulated establishments. The department cancelled 105 licences and suspended 367 licences of sales establishments, while 17 licences were cancelled and 55 suspended in the manufacturing and other categories.
The department also carried out 11 search and seizure operations involving alleged violations related to the manufacture, storage and sale of drugs and cosmetics. Two FIRs were registered, and four persons were arrested under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act in connection with the illegal sale of narcotic drugs.
Among the major seizures, FDA officials recovered allopathic drugs worth ₹22.03 lakh from the premises of Phoenix Medicorp in Nagpur on October 7. According to the department, the establishment had stored drugs at unlicensed premises despite surrendering its licences.
In Mumbai, FDA officials seized spurious drugs identified as Empirime tablets and Cardiurex 2 ml, worth ₹1.01 lakh, from INHS Asvini in Colaba on October 29, according to the department.
In separate operations in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on October 14 and 25, officials seized 199 Nitrosun 10 tablets containing Nitrazepam. Four persons were arrested in connection with their alleged illegal sale.
The FDA also seized cosmetic soaps worth ₹4.05 lakh from Vedas Herbals Mahila Gruh Udyog in Baramati, Pune district, on October 14, for alleged manufacturing without a licence. In Vasai East, officials seized raw materials, packaging materials and machinery worth ₹1.83 lakh from G.B. Cosmetics on October 10 in connection with alleged unlicensed manufacture and sale of nail polish.
The Konkan division recorded the highest number of inspections in October at 556, followed by Pune with 375 and Greater Mumbai with 322. Konkan also accounted for the highest number of regulatory actions at 156, followed by Greater Mumbai with 105 and Pune with 77.
Between April 1 and October 31, the FDA conducted 7,950 inspections across Maharashtra, issued 2,888 notices, cancelled 555 licences and suspended 2,074 licences. The department recorded 2,629 regulatory actions, comprising licence cancellations and suspensions, during the seven-month period.
The FDA urged citizens to report instances of illegal drug manufacturing or sales, as well as suspected substandard drugs, medical devices and cosmetics, to its commissioner’s office or the nearest district office.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

Red gold from purple flowers: saffron harvest in Kashmir – in pictures

Defence minister Rajnath Singh reviews battle readiness, infra push along LAC in Sikkim
Singh asked the armed forces to strengthen cyber resilience, information integrity and domain awareness to boost combat readiness and tackle emerging threats.
Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday reviewed the army’s operational preparedness along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Sikkim, focusing on border infrastructure development and the deployment of advanced military equipment and emerging technologies to sharpen combat effectiveness.
He was briefed at the Sukna-headquartered 33 Corps, near Siliguri.
“Sukna and its surrounding region is a critical hub for the movement of supplies, weaponry, food, medical provisions and personnel to forward locations. Its geographical sensitivity necessitates round-the-clock operational readiness,” Singh said.
Deep Dive
Army chief General Dhiraj Seth, Eastern Army commander Lieutenant General VMB Krishnan, and corps commander Lieutenant General Man Raj Singh Mann were present.
The defence minister is scheduled to visit the Sherathang war memorial in Sikkim on Diwali to pay tribute to Indian soldiers killed in the 1967 Nathu La and Cho La clashes with China. The battles ended in a decisive Indian victory, with one account putting Indian casualties at 88, against 340 on the Chinese side.
In Bagdogra, also near Siliguri, Singh asked the armed forces to strengthen cyber resilience, information integrity and domain awareness to boost combat readiness and tackle emerging threats. Security landscape has become more complex, with warfare stretching beyond conventional engagements along the borders to include “asymmetric warfare, proxy wars, cyber-attacks, drone swarms, information operations and narrative management,” he said while interacting with air warriors at Air Force Station, Bagdogra.
“Often, the adversary avoids direct confrontation and instead seeks to exploit our vulnerabilities. Through social media, the adversary may attempt to sow doubt in the minds of the local population and our soldiers by spreading misleading information. In such a scenario, your role extends beyond that of an ordinary soldier,” Singh said.
IAF chief Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit was also present.
Singh described Bagdogra as a strategically important region and a crucial link in India’s security framework, particularly for the North-east.
A December 2025 report of the parliamentary committee on external affairs contained pointed mentions about Chinese activities in areas surrounding the so-called “chicken’s neck,” or the Siliguri Corridor—the territory linking India’s strategic northeastern states to the rest of the country.
The report on “Future of India-Bangladesh relationship” said China’s increasing footprint in Bangladesh, especially through infrastructure and port development and military cooperation, is a concern though the government is taking all measures to safeguard India’s national interests.
Singh said that the air warriors deployed in the region serve as a robust shield for the security of the eastern sector, and their preparedness is fundamental to maintaining stability in the region. “The more you engage with the local community, the weaker the adversary’s conspiracies will become.”
He described the revamped Agnipath scheme as a Diwali gift for Agniveers, while reiterating the government’s commitment to the welfare of military personnel and their families. The new Agnipath framework will apply only to existing Agniveers who miss out on retention, giving them two more years in uniform and another shot at becoming permanent soldiers, as first reported by Hindustan Times. Essentially, all current Agniveers will become permanent after this two year extended service, subject to meeting specific eligibility criteria and individual consent
The government will revisit the scheme’s provisions for those who begin their military training after December 31. The Agnipath reboot was announced by Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani on November 4, weeks before the three services were set to release 75% of Agniveers from their first batch after four years of service, retaining only the 25% selected on merit for another 15 years under the scheme’s earlier provisions.

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Mumbai: In a major relief to farmers facing severe losses due to drought, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Sunday announced an extension of the deadline for borewell drilling in areas where fruit orchards are at risk. Farmers in such areas will be allowed to drill borewells until December 15, while the blanket ban on drilling elsewhere will continue.
Government Allows Borewell Drilling To Protect Fruit Orchards
Fadnavis said the decision was taken as a special measure to protect fruit orchards, which take nearly 10 to 12 years to mature and start yielding produce. Failure to provide adequate water at this critical stage could cause irreparable losses to farmers.
"If we fail to save these orchards now, farmers will suffer huge losses. Therefore, we have decided to temporarily lift the ban on borewell drilling in selected areas where fruit orchards need protection. However, the ban will not be lifted across the state," Fadnavis said.
Government Aims To Ensure Water Supply For Orchards Till May 2027
He stressed that the government aims to ensure water availability for these orchards until May next year. He also clarified that there is no ban on flashing, while restrictions on deepening existing borewells will remain and require permission.
The Chief Minister said he had interacted with farmers on Saturday night and subsequently held discussions with sarpanches from the taluka to understand local issues concerning agriculture, roads, lakes and other infrastructure. Several demands and suggestions were submitted, and the government would examine them and initiate necessary action. He added that some of the demands were already covered under announced government schemes.
Drought Severely Affects Orange Orchards, Cotton And Soybean Crops
Referring to his visit to a farmer's family, Fadnavis said the drought had severely affected their orange orchards, cotton and soybean crops. The family had three landholders, all of whom had benefited from the farm loan waiver scheme.
He said the family's determination to overcome the crisis had given him confidence and valuable lessons about the resilience of farmers despite difficult circumstances.
Fadnavis also thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi for appreciating his interaction with the farmer's family, saying the Prime Minister's concern for farmers, women and persons with disabilities inspired the government to prioritise their issues.
On irrigation, the Chief Minister said the government had completed 97 pending irrigation projects and approved the remaining ones. The state plans to raise a loan of Rs 15,000 crore to complete the balance work, which would significantly benefit farmers in Vidarbha and Marathwada.
He also said the government was considering expanding solar fencing arrangements to protect farmers living near forests from attacks by wild animals, including gaurs.

Tarmo Peltokoski begins HK Phil tenure with Mahler’s monumental Symphony No 8
Ambitious performance at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre involved nearly 600 musicians and singers from six choirs

Gustav Mahler’s rarely performed Symphony No 8, a work requiring such a large orchestra and choir it is known as “Symphony of a Thousand”, finally received its Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra premiere on Saturday, heralding an ambitious new chapter as the 26-year-old Finnish conductor Tarmo Peltokoski officially took the podium as music director.
The 5pm performance at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre involved nearly 600 musicians and singers from six choirs: the Hong Kong Philharmonic Chorus; the Learners Chorus; the London Philharmonic Choir; St Paul’s Co-educational College Senior Mixed-Voice Choir; Ying Wa College Choir; and the Hong Kong Children’s Choir.
The monumental 85-minute piece, with performers pushing the stage to the limit and the choir occupying about a third of the seats on the balcony, formalised the start of the youthful maestro’s four-year contract as the ensemble’s ninth music director.

The defeat did not stop East Bengal from making history, as the ‘Moshal Girls’ qualified to the knockout stage as the second-best third-placed team among the three groups in the continental club competition.

The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
- Published
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.

One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'
Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.
In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.
Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.
Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.
In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.
Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."
