Will China’s slow and steady moon landing plan be a safer bet than the US’?
China’s planned trial run ahead of its crewed moon landing will see the Lanyue lander and Mengzhou spacecraft dock in lunar orbit
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Ling Xinin Ohio
China’s full dress rehearsal for its crewed moon landing would be tougher on schedule but safer than Nasa’s cheaper bet on commercial landers, a US space policy analyst said after the rival powers updated their lunar plans within a week of each other.
Wang Xiang, deputy chief designer of China’s crewed space programme, said in Beijing on October 31 that, before sending any astronauts, China would dock the Lanyue lander and Mengzhou spacecraft in lunar orbit, and Lanyue would touch down, lift off and redock.
Nasa would instead have its crews practise docking with commercial landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin in Earth orbit in 2027, then try to reach the lunar surface in 2028, Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman said at a briefing on October 23.

The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.
The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.
He added that Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.
More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.
He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.
Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US where he is now living.
Remulla said: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.”
He added: “We will know in the next few days.”
Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.
Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.
Markle Jr reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.
Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.
Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.
In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియోలో చెప్పిన విషయాలు నిజం కాదని, వాస్తవానికి ఆ ఫుటేజ్ ఒక టెలివిజన్ సిరీస్కు చెందినదని నిర్ధారించవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, ఉనికిలో లేని “టొరెంజో” దేశం నుండి ఒక మహిళ వచ్చిందంటూ, ఒక అమెరికన్ టెలివిజన్ సిరీస్కు చెందిన దృశ్యాలను తప్పుగా ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు.

What does Apple One Family come with and which subscription is best for you?
The answer comes down to how many of Apple's services you use regularly.
This year, several of Apple's subscriptions saw serious price upticks, so much so that even students had to pay a bit more. Apple Music prices rose by $1 a month for individual plans and $3 for the Family plan. A few weeks later, monthly Apple TV subscriptions went up from $13 to 15, while annual ones saw a $20 total jump.
If you use many Apple services, you might have looked to Apple One to bundle them and reduce the hurt from these increases. Unfortunately, the package subscription didn't get by unscathed either. The Individual tier climbed from $20 to $22 a month, though it's still cheaper than subscribing to Apple Music ($12/month) and Apple TV ($15/month) separately.
While the Apple One Family plan is now $28/month, you can share it with five other people, which drastically brings down the cost per person. There's also a higher-cost shareable Premier tier at $40/month. But before you ask friends and family to group up with you, you need to figure out which of the three Apple One subscriptions is most worth your while. That mostly depends on how many Apple services you already use.
Which Apple One tier makes the most sense for you?
Getting the cheapest tier out of the way: Individual subscribers get Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Arcade and 50GB of iCloud storage for $22 per month; that's about $13 less than it would be to subscribe to each one on its own.
Moving on, the Family tier is a great choice if you're providing for multiple people or want to split the monthly cost with up to five other members. At $28 per month, you get a shared 200GB pool of iCloud storage, the Apple Music Family plan (which costs $20 by itself), plus Apple TV and Apple Arcade. Combined, the Family plan saves you about $17 per month, which can stretch even further if you split the bill. With six people paying their own way, each person pays less than $5/month. Unlike some family plans, Apple doesn't require everyone to live in the same household.
The final step up is Apple One Premier, which offers the full suite of Apple services and $35 in monthly savings compared to joining each one individually. Along with everything included in the Family plan, you also get Apple Fitness+ ($10 per month), Apple News+ ($13/month) and 2TB of shared iCloud storage ($10 per month). On their own, these would total $75, so it's a good value at $40 per month.
Before deciding, you need to narrow down what you'll use, what you won't and how much storage you need. When I was subscribed to the Individual plan, I could have skated by with the 50GB of iCloud storage, but paying an additional $13 per month for Apple News+ was a pain. Before upgrading to Premier, I was paying about $38 per month when accounting for News+ and 200GB of iCloud Storage. At that rate, switching over to upgrade to 2TB of storage was well worth it, and it even included Apple Fitness+.
In case you weren't aware, every Apple subscription within Apple One is already shareable with a Family Sharing group — with the exception of Apple Music, which requires the Family plan for multi-person access. But if your family only cares about playing the best Apple Arcade games, for example, you could pay $7/month for that and make it available to your Family Sharing group. Apple One makes the most sense when you'll use everything.
What if I need more iCloud storage?
You can always tack on extra iCloud storage by subscribing to iCloud+, letting you max out at 14TB of storage if you get the 12TB iCloud+ plan for $60 per month alongside Apple One Premier. While you share the pool of storage, your files are not visible to other family plan members unless you so choose.
If you're already subscribed to iCloud+ with a plan that has less storage than your chosen Apple One plan, the former will be canceled, keeping any stored data intact, and you'll get a pro-rated refund. Meanwhile, if your active iCloud+ plan has more storage than your Apple One tier offers, you can keep your current plan alongside the storage Apple One provides. In case you don't need all that space, you can cancel iCloud+.
When you jump to Apple One, if you're subscribed to individual Apple services, don't worry about getting charged twice. You'll stop being billed for any individual services included in whichever Apple One plan you choose.

Over the last few years, the kratom plant and supplements made from it have garnered increasing attention from public health leaders. This broad category of products, which largely skirts any regulation, has seen major surges in potency, while becoming omnipresent on smoke shop and gas station shelves. Health officials have warned that concentrated compounds like 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) are an emerging public health threat, and federal policies to limit their availability are pending. In the meantime, multiple states and smaller localities have issued emergency bans on 7-OH, and in some cases, on all kratom products.
Despite the messaging and rising use, few Americans are familiar with kratom or the newer derivative products. They’re made with compounds that have scientific names like 7-OH, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI) and dihydro-7-hydroxy mitragynine (MGM-15) but are often sold on shelves with names like Dozo Perks, Roxy, and UltraOhmz Pseudo Supreme. New survey data from the Annenberg Public Policy Center show about two-thirds (66%) of Americans have never heard of kratom. Among those who had at least some familiarity, few understood the difference between its natural leaf form and more synthetic products.
That confusion carries over to the associated risks. In the survey of nearly 2,000 people, 66% were unsure if kratom products posed a serious public safety hazard. And most people didn’t understand health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s stance on regulation — a question that’s become complicated by repeated reports of kratom industry lobbying influence on the DEA’s proposed action.
STAT spoke with researchers and people who use or have used kratom and 7-OH to get a full picture of what these products are, along with their potential risks and benefits.
What is kratom?
To an untrained eye, a kratom leaf might resemble a bay leaf. It grows on evergreen trees indigenous to Southeast Asian countries, including Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. For centuries, people there have chewed the leaf or brewed it into tea for its stimulant-like effects.
Kratom (pronounce it with a hard or soft “a,” your choice) contains dozens of alkaloids, but mitragynine is the most abundant and the best understood. It acts as a partial agonist that binds to mu-opioid receptors in the nervous system. (Partial agonists produce less of a response from the receptor than full agonists, such as fentanyl or oxycodone.)
The first kratom products to arrive in the U.S. were made by drying and grinding up those leaves to create a matcha-like powder often used as a tea or swallowed in a capsule. In low quantities, it acts as a mild stimulant that can appear similar to coffee. In higher doses, people have used kratom to stave off chronic pain and even to help ease withdrawal from opioids. (There are no evidence-based dose recommendations, and there’s a lot of variation in both product potency and personal preference.)
“We call it swamp water, so that should give you a good visual,” said Madalyn Sklar, who uses kratom to ease chronic pain caused by degenerative disc disease, and hosts two podcasts on kratom. The first time Sklar drank the bitter tea made from kratom powder, she added orange juice as a sweetener, but still “it was so gross that I almost puked.” She’s taken it nearly every day since 2019, and says the results are better than when she was on meds like OxyContin and gabapentin.
She takes two teaspoons of powder — which works out to about 70-75 milligrams of mitragynine — every six hours. For her, there’s no high or euphoria. But she can do simple tasks that she couldn’t before, such as walk her dog and bend down to pick up its poop.
Sklar hasn’t experienced withdrawal symptoms when she’s occasionally stopped taking kratom and returned to more traditional pain medication. Research is limited, but has found that up to around 38% of kratom users may develop use disorders. In studies, withdrawal from kratom has appeared mild on a scale that measures clinical opioid withdrawal, with symptoms like anxiety, fatigue, gastrointestinal issues, and restlessness.
Before semi-synthetic products came onto the scene, most public health concern around kratom was directed at extracts and tinctures, recalled Sklar. Many of these products still tout mitragynine as the active ingredient, but in much more concentrated volumes than the whole leaf powder — think 100 to 300 milligrams of mitragynine in a bottle of liquid the size of a 5-hour Energy. (There are currently no federal proposals that aim to regulate concentrated mitragynine products.)
“But people got really interested in the other alkaloids over time,” said Katherine Hill, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health who has studied kratom. “And specifically they got interested in 7-hydroxymitrogynine.”
What is 7-OH?
The alkaloid 7-OH does not appear in the fresh kratom leaf that people in Southeast Asia chew, according to Hill. It shows up in the dried leaf powder products, in small amounts. It’s also a metabolite, meaning that when the body absorbs mitragynine, some of it turns it into 7-OH. Once inside the body, 7-OH, like mitragynine, is a partial agonist to the mu-opioid receptor.
The products made with 7-OH — including tablets, gummies, shots, and drink powders — are semi-synthetic; they contain artificially concentrated amounts of the compound. When the products first started popping up, they were often sold in tablets containing 12-14 milligrams, users said. Those can offer sedative effects and pain relief. But now, tablets containing 25, 50, and even 100 milligrams of 7-OH are available.
“The first time I heard of 7-OH, it was very negative,” said Twinkle VanFleet, who co-hosts a kratom podcast with Sklar.
While natural kratom products carry a risk of dependence and what’s thought to be mild withdrawal at low doses, there’s growing concern that concentrated 7-OH products are even more addictive, and that withdrawal can be as bad as coming off a traditional opioid. Hill is working on a study of 7-OH users that will look at both tolerance and withdrawal. But for now, the risks are mainly documented in case reports, series, and other anecdotal accounts.
VanFleet suffers from intense pain from an injury that led to complex regional pain syndrome, and she has a deep mistrust of the medical system. Kratom didn’t ease her symptoms, so she eventually tried 7-OH, and found comfort in what she calls “nibbles” of smaller tablets. She currently takes around 12 milligrams per day and worries about a ban by the Drug Enforcement Administration. Still, she shares concerns about the availability of higher-dose products.
“I do see both sides of a lot of this,” VanFleet said. “In my perfect world, there would be 3, 5, and 10 milligram tablets, period. If even that.”
Greg Kiesow had been sober from alcohol for nearly 20 years and retired for three days when he went into a smoke shop that was promoting 7-OH products. The shopkeeper had heard it was some sort of natural energy supplement, like coffee, and gave Kiesow a free sample of tablets. “I took it home, and I took it. And 10 to 15 minutes later, it wasn’t coffee. It was a very powerful opioid,” Kiesow said.
Kiesow said he quickly developed an addiction. After 10 months, which he described as an extremely isolated period spent sitting on his back porch watching the birds at his bird feeder, he began to taper himself off the products. A few weeks later, he formed Kratom Anonymous, which has 15 virtual meetings per week for people looking to quit.
What about MGPI?
As 7-OH gained popularity, newer synthetic products have continued to crop up, including some with concentrated levels of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI), another metabolite of mitragynine. Over the summer, the DEA proposed a ban of MGPI at any quantity. But an updated proposal in October, pushed by a lobbyist for the American Kratom Association, would allow small amounts of the compound to show up in products. Instead of an outright ban, the DEA now proposes limiting both MGPI and 7-OH based on the ratio of those compounds to mitragynine in any given product.
The reason for the change, according to the DEA, is that trace amounts of MGPI could appear in natural kratom. But the safety of small amounts is unclear. Test results presented in recent wrongful death lawsuits suggest that a natural kratom powder product, used by somebody who died after taking it, was likely contaminated with MGPI.
Kratom, 7-OH, and MGPI: What are the risks?
As more people use kratom and other associated products, there’s a growing recognition of the potential risk for addiction. Over 10 years, the National Poison Data Center found a 1,200% increase in kratom-related exposure reports — from 258 in 2015 to 3,434 in 2025. That includes all types of products. Clinicians who run addiction treatment centers say, over the last year, they’ve seen a rise in patients seeking help to get off 7-OH in particular.
But data on the most serious risks — overdose and death — are murky. The poison center data showed 233 deaths over the decade, most of which involved other substances like opioids, benzodiazepines, stimulants, and alcohol. (Researchers believe kratom can exacerbate the danger of a drug like fentanyl, and even more common medications like certain antidepressants.) A 2023 investigation by the Tampa Bay Times found that, over nearly 10 years, more than 580 people in Florida alone died from overdoses that involved kratom products.
Because both 7-OH and MGPI are metabolites of mitragynine, it can be difficult to draw conclusions about a given death, even with toxicology data. Complicating the matter even further: When tested, many kratom products — natural and synthetic — are found to have different concentration levels than the labels advertise, and some have been found to contain compounds that were not on the label at all.
Sklar and VanFleet are both proponents of regulations, not bans, on all types of kratom-related products. Others who advocate for natural kratom are working hard to distance themselves from the more synthetic products.
“Any who unwittingly support every concentrated 7-OH product are not defending the natural kratom plant. It may be helping to destroy it,” Mac Haddow, the American Kratom Association’s lobbyist, said in a recent video. “The solution is not to defend everything. The solution is to draw a clear, bright line.”
But others said they’ve suffered from taking natural kratom products, too. Danelle Kawasaki first tried kratom at a dry bar in her Montana town. It came at room temperature, and was advertised as a natural, herbal tea. The concoction eased her anxiety, making her feel both calm and energetic, able to speak with anyone she wanted. At first it was a weekly treat, then a few times a week. After a few months, she was having two drinks per day. She’d wake up with a jolt of anxiety, which she attributes to the tea not being in her system overnight. Without more, she’d be sick, crawling to the bathroom to puke.
It frustrates Kawasaki when people try to tell her that 7-OH, not natural kratom, is the problem. “This argument comes up all the time and it drives me nuts,” she said. “I know what was going on — it was the actual kratom tea powder. It wasn’t a concentrated form.”
At one point, she was drinking nearly 140 ounces of the tea per day. When she finally stopped, cold turkey, the withdrawal was its own dayslong nightmare.
Now, she advocates that the Fort Peck tribe, of which she’s a member, ban kratom on the reservation. For Kawasaki, “the risks outweigh the remedy that people are searching for.”

The GTA series has fundamentally always been about stealing cars, robbing stores, escaping the cops, and killing people with minimal consequences. You rob another car, the cops catch you, and you do it all over again without a care in the world.
No sleep, no food, just endless chaos in an open-world sandbox. However, the more I learn about GTA 6’s in-depth mechanics, the more I feel like Rockstar is trying to make me live inside the game with its life-sim elements, rather than play it.
With new systems like maintaining Jason and Lucia’s relationship, tracking their calorie intake and weight, registering vehicles under your name, and even depositing money in the bank, Rockstar seems to be going all-in on immersion.
But this obsession with making GTA 6 feel hyperrealistic and immersive could end up taking away what makes the series so much fun in the first place, and here’s why.
I Want to Play as Jason and Lucia in GTA 6, Not Manage Them
In my opinion, there’s a clear conflict between immersion and fun in GTA 6. For the first time, I feel like I’ll have to consciously take care of both Jason and Lucia instead of playing GTA 6 however I want, as I did in previous GTA games. I had similar issues in Red Dead Redemption 2’s life-sim elements, but they were negligible since it’s a Red Dead title.
For a GTA title, this is completely new. Now, I have to maintain Jason and Lucia’s relationship by doing different activities in GTA 6 together, texting each other, working out to keep their stats and attributes in check, and even getting enough sleep to avoid exhaustion.
There’s a lot more to these life-sim and roleplay elements in GTA 6. While these details make the characters feel more alive, it also starts to feel like I’m managing their lives rather than playing as them. I always did take care of Michael, Franklin, and Trevor in GTA 5, but it didn’t feel like something you had to do.
In GTA 6, I feel like the moment I open my save file, I have to wonder what I’ve neglected. Did Jason and Lucia sleep well? Are they well fed? Have I spent enough time with each other? Are they angry at one another? What can I do to fix it?
Sure, it’s immersive, extremely, if I’m being honest, but is it convenient? I do want the best for the characters I play with, as long as it’s fun and doesn’t feel forced.
GTA 6’s Immersion Is Starting to Feel Like a Second Life
With Jason and Lucia out of the way, let’s discuss some features I personally think shouldn’t be in a GTA game. For example, GTA 6’s refueling mechanic. I never stopped to think about how much fuel I have left in a GTA game when running from the cops, chasing an NPC, or in any other situation.
It feels more like an evolution of the horse’s stamina mechanic from Red Dead Redemption 2 than a genuinely meaningful addition. Is it immersive? Absolutely. But I can also see it getting repetitive pretty quickly. Next up in the coterie of life-sim roleplay elements is how GTA 6’s cash acts like the real thing.
You now have to deposit your cash, earn specific amounts of money to progress certain GTA 6 missions, and even worry about other robbers stealing the money you’re carrying. When it comes to stealing cars, there’s a tiered security system and specialized tools to steal one, as the Slim Jim showcased in the GTA 6 Extended Look.
So, you can no longer steal exotic rides the moment you start your GTA 6 playthrough. You’ll need to earn your way up to it, and later register it under your name if you want to own it. This is where GTA 6’s fully functional public transport system chimes in. As I said, it’s all extremely immersive.
You can even doomscroll with your in-game phone and the apps in GTA 6, making it feel more like living a second life than simply playing a game.
Rockstar is clearly building on the foundations they’ve set with Red Dead Redemption 2, and that’s what worries me. It’s all incredibly immersive, but I can’t help feeling these life-sim systems could come at the cost of the classic GTA fun we’ve always loved.
GTA 6 Is Replacing the Series’ Power Fantasy with Real Consequences
In previous GTA outings like San Andreas, Vice City, or even 5, you were borderline overpowered. Play how you want, shoot whoever you want, launch a missile straight into the Los Santos Police Department, and you could still come out of the entire fiasco alive, without losing anything (except maybe your life if you mess up).
On the other hand, GTA 6’s Criminal Profile brings in new consequences for Jason and Lucia’s actions. It’s another life-sim element I’m worried about. For those unaware, the Criminal Profile will limit how you approach and play certain situations, and in most cases, killing everyone will be a no-no.
The cleaner you pull off your crimes, the better your Criminal Profile gets. But you can also permanently shatter it if you reach the “Irredeemable” state, and honestly, I’d hate to mess up my entire playthrough for a little fun and possibly end up with a worse ending.
Additionally, the cops in GTA 6 are far smarter than in previous entries. They can remember your clothes, your appearance, your vehicle, and even whether you were with Jason or Lucia when the crime happened.
These life-sim and roleplay elements in GTA 6 may hinder the series’ power fantasy, with Rockstar taking a more believable and consequential approach. It’s for immersion, I know, and players can tailor their experience to their own liking, but how immersive is too immersive?
Because it looks like I’ll need a separate manual save to have the traditional GTA fun, because Jason and Lucia will have too much to lose in my main GTA 6 playthrough. To me, it feels like Rockstar was so preoccupied with adding these life-sim elements to GTA 6 that they didn’t stop to think about whether they should.
However, despite it all, I have secured my GTA 6 pre-order and am very much looking forward to testing these roleplaying systems myself. I’d love to be wrong, and I genuinely hope these realistic life-sim mechanics enhance the overall experience without taking away from the chaotic, unpredictable GTA gameplay that made me fall in love with the series in the first place.

Italian chef fired after refusing to put pineapple on pizza
- Published
An Italian chef sacked from a Brisbane restaurant had refused to put pineapple on a pizza because it was an "insult to his culture".
Davide Tamburella was fired from the now-closed La Costa restaurant in May, a fortnight after a meeting with management who had a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function. At the time, the chef had stated that any direction from management "need not be followed when it is offensive to his culture".
The details came to light after the chef went to Australia's Fair Work Commission claiming he had been unfairly dismissed.
In its ruling released on Tuesday, the commission noted that Tamburella's refusal to put pineapple on the pizzas was because "he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture".
It also noted that it was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
He had previously requested his boss to "check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza".
The state of Queensland, where the restaurant is located, is considered Australia's pineapple heartland and produces all of the country's commercially-grown pineapples.
On the Sunshine Coast, visitors regularly stop to take photos next to The Big Pineapple, a heritage-listed 16m-tall fibreglass model of the fruit, which has become a local landmark.
Other concerns were raised about Tamburella using foul language, his communication style and "escalation of frustration in the workplace".
The ruling also detailed an incident at work in April this year where Tamburella fractured bones in his right hand when he struck a metal hand rail.
Tamburella had been hoping the restaurant would sponsor a visa for him that allows skilled workers to be permanent residents.
However after his sacking, the restaurant ended that process, the tribunal heard.
He lost his unfair dismissal claim on the grounds that the application had been filed too late, according to the ruling.
The restaurant's managing director, Elliot Ingram, told the Daily Mail there was "more to this story than a pizza topping".
The BBC has approached Tamburella for comment.
On the chef's LinkedIn profile, he describes himself as someone who, throughout his career, has focused on "delivering exceptional food" and "improving business performance".
Three months ago he posted a "letter for chefs" with the theme "respecting the ingredients".
The LinkedIn profile states he now works at another Brisbane restaurant. A BBC check has found that pineapple is not on that restaurant's menu.

Regina councillor shared great replacement conspiracy theory with colleagues during mosque broadcast debate
Experts say it's concerning to see city councillor share Islamophobic conspiracy theory
As Regina debated a mosque's decision to broadcast a call to prayer, Ward 1 Coun. Dan Rashovich forwarded an email to his colleagues that contained what experts say is the "great replacement" conspiracy theory, which falsely suggests immigrants are attempting to replace a country's white population.
The email, obtained by CBC News through a freedom of information request, says the Islamic call to prayer or adhan is a "strategic tactic" to expand Islam in Canada through changing demographics.
"Thank You for your email. You nailed it!" Rashovich wrote in an email CC'd to every member of Regina city council, as well as Regina police Chief Lorilee Davies, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and provincial Justice Minister Tim McLeod.
Rashovich declined multiple requests for an on-camera interview. Instead, in a series of emailed statements, Rashovich said he did not not see the email's entire contents before sharing it.
The city councillor said his "You nailed it!" response was referring to a different email from the same sender — an email that doesn't refer to the great replacement conspiracy theory. That email was redacted when provided to CBC.
But one of Rashovich's colleagues did not interpret Rashovich's comment as reacting to a different email.
Ward 6 Coun. Victoria Flores pushed back on the email containing the Islamophobic screed, saying the City of Regina needed to call the email "exactly what it is."
"This unnamed person is explicitly calling for violence and the destruction of places of worship in our city," Flores wrote.
Rashovich told CBC he could not comment on the "accuracy of religious interpretations," and that he did not respond or agree with the email that contains the passage with the conspiracy theory in it.
Amin Asfari, a professor and researcher at the University of Regina, says the email promotes fears that Europeans or Canadians with European heritage are being replaced through a so-called "white genocide."
Jasmin Zine, a professor of sociology and religion at Wilfred Laurier University who has studied Islamophobia, says the conspiracy theory is prominent among white supremacists, nationalists and neo-nazis.
This example, which hinges on Islamophobia, preys on fears of replacement.
"It assumes there's kind of a nefarious intention by people who are immigrants," Asfari said.
'A glaring hypocrisy': professor
Rashovich made his own views on the broadcast of the adhan clear in an email dated July 6, 2026.
The email shows Rashovich responding to an email that is entirely redacted. Rashovich's response is CC'd to the rest of council.
"I agree this should not be happening," Rashovich said, saying he believes in freedom of worship but not at the "expense of publicly expressing this on everybody."
Rashovich says the country was founded on "Judeo Christian values" and that "Religion and Politics should not mix."
"Every religion has the right to worship who and how they want and this should be done within their church besides some outdoor events or marches that happen," Rashovich said.
He goes on to say that the city's noise bylaw allows the broadcast of the adhan "when it should not be allowed."
"We do not need others religious messages being broadcasted. That is for every Religion," Rashovich wrote.
When asked whether he stands by this email, Rashovich said that it must be read in context.
Asfari said the email is an example of hypocrisy from Rashovich.
The University of Regina professor said the email shows Rashovich acknowledging that religious freedom is a central concept to the Canadian identity, while also stating that certain aspects of faith should be relegated away from the general public.
Asfari said religions often use a call to prayer. In Christianity there is the ringing of church bells, in Judaism the shofar horn is used and Islam uses the adhan.
"There's a glaring hypocrisy, and it comes across rather consistently, when people like this speak about what they believe to be the kind of supreme or dominant narrative that must be there, and then the other, which is foreign, must be tucked away," Asfari said.
The email
Rashovich's email that CC's the Islamophic conspiracy theory was sent on the evening of July 14, 2026. CBC obtained it through a freedom of information request filed with the City of Regina.
At that time, the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque had recently paused its plans to broadcast the adhan over the noon hour on Fridays.
The mosque had obtained a permit from the Regina Police Service allowing it to broadcast the three-minute call over rooftop speakers once a week, under the city's noise bylaw.
M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid, told media that he later decided to pause broadcasts because the mosque had received threats after the first broadcast.
M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque in downtown Regina, poses for a photo outside of the centre on July 17. (Randi LaRocque/CBC)
The email containing the Islamophic message — including who sent it — is redacted in the emails disclosed by the city, but it is partially quoted by Flores in a later email.
The message says the adhan directs adherents to spread the religion in "non-Muslim lands" through "public assertion" and "demographic presence," according to Flores' quotation.
Zine said the message references the great replacement conspiracy theory and the civilizational jihad conspiracy theory, which falsely claims that Muslims immigrants are attempting to establish social, cultural and political strongholds in nations that they are "infiltrating."
The tying of two different conspiracy theories together in one message paints a picture of a grand Islamophobic plan, he said.
"The idea is that Muslims are a Trojan horse that will unleash these invaders who will infiltrate Western societies. They will install themselves politically as a fifth column and then start installing Sharia law," Zine said.
Asfari said Islamophobic conspiracy theories can be precursor to violence, saying it "does tend to plant seeds in more nefarious circles where the propensity for violence is greater."
Zine and Asfari point to the 2017 Quebec City mosque shooting and the 2021 London truck attack as examples of rhetoric becoming action in Canada.
Asfari and Zine said it's particularly concerning that a municipal politician — rather than a random person online — is sharing the conspiracy theory.
Zine said municipal leaders and politicians are looked to as trusted sources of information. When they share conspiracy theories that are otherwise circulating in white nationalist echo chambers, it helps to legitimize beliefs that are otherwise clearly false and harmful.
"It does give average people more licence to share those stories. And maybe they believe that those are bona fide," Zine said.
A person within an institution, or an institution itself, sharing a conspiracy theory can help give it more weight, Asfari said.
"When we talk about institutionalized Islamophobia, this is precisely the kind of thing that we're talking about," Asfari said.
Asfari commended other councillors for pushing back against the rhetoric in the email.
In one example, Flores directly confronts Rashovich for sharing it.
"...Differentiate between a noise bylaw concern and someone who is using this opportunity to spread misinformation and hate," Flores wrote.

As my family of four began our descent to Puerto Rico, I made the announcement. There would be no more English for the duration of our trip.
My kids, 9 and 11, who had been learning Spanish in immersion school since preschool, would get an opportunity to put it to good use. I thought this trip would be the perfect crash course for them before school started back up in the fall.
When we landed in Puerto Rico and headed to our hotel, I realized I was going to have my work cut out. The driver spoke English, as did the workers at the front desk, restaurant waiters, and other staff. Turns out, they were just as bilingual as I was.
Our no-English rule didn't last long
At first, the kids were happy to skip the intense Spanish practice I had envisioned, but I still wanted us to try. Then, before I knew it, I was catching myself slipping into English, too.
My husband doesn't speak Spanish, and with Duolingo as his only teacher, we often defaulted to English so he could follow the conversation. Before long, we were all speaking our own version of Spanglish, mixing languages to get our point across. My no-English rule was harder to enforce than I'd expected.
Even I had a lot to learn
I grew up speaking Spanish in the US, but it isn't my dominant language. Our kids being able to speak another language is important to my husband and me, so we decided to enroll them in Spanish immersion schools, starting in preschool.
The Spanish language varies across countries and regions, but hearing Puerto Rican Spanish reminded me of how different the language can be. Some familiar words sounded unfamiliar, and I kept having to ask locals to describe the word they were using so I could connect it to the one I knew from Mexico, where my mother is from.
The cadence and speed of conversations were different too, which made me listen more closely to what was being said. Instead of being the one helping my family navigate the language, I was the one asking questions and learning at the same time.
I wanted my kids to see that Spanish isn't the same everywhere
On the surface, I wanted my kids to practice their Spanish, become more confident speakers, and immerse themselves in another Latin culture, but it became more than that.
As a Mexican Spanish-speaker and a parent, there was something meaningful about recognizing familiar words, trying to understand unfamiliar ones, and explaining how people could express the same idea differently. In their schools, they have Spanish teachers from different countries — including Spain, Mexico, Colombia, and Peru — all with their own different dialects, words, and intonation.
Rather than correcting my kids or testing their vocabulary, we ended up all figuring out how to communicate in a place where the Spanish we knew wasn't necessarily the Spanish we heard.
I came home with a different idea of language learning
When we landed in Puerto Rico, I had only one rule: to practice our Spanish before school started back up. Instead, we all slipped into English, mixed languages, and learned to navigate unfamiliar words.
I realized that fluency isn't the same as knowing every word, and learning doesn't stop when the lesson ends or the school bell rings. Sometimes it means asking questions, listening, and discovering a little more about the world along the way.

Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV has arrived in South America for a 12-day, three-country journey that will be his longest and most far-reaching trip yet, and his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.
Along the way Leo will take 12 flights, including two helicopter rides, give 36 speeches and visit 10 cities including Cusco, Peru, which sits more than 11,000 feet above sea level. Even the heartiest of travelers can experience altitude sickness there and may require supplemental oxygen.
Last month, Leo underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Vatican officials say he has completed his two-week recovery period and requires no further treatment.
The Vatican's new communications chief Maria Montserrat Alvarado said the pontiff was eager to begin his journey. "His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen," she said.
First stop Uruguay
It's a puzzling choice for the first leg of the pope's anticipated return to South America, where he spent two decades in Peru, first as a missionary then as Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. Uruguay, a small nation of around 3.5 million people, where adoring crowds will be small, is famously Latin America's most secular nation.
When asked why go to Uruguay at all, given the high rate of atheists and strict separation of church and state, communications chief Alvarado answered simply, "Why Not?" Adding, "the Gospel is meant to go everywhere."
Few welcome banners are seen throughout the capital Montevideo, except for large posters of a waving Pope Leo adorning city churches. A huge banner drapes down the facade of the Blessed Sacrament Church, in Montevideo's upscale Pocitos neighborhood, where 70-year old retiree Ana Maria Saprissa was heading for quiet prayer.
We are thankful, agradecida, she says that the pontiff is coming to visit. "His visit gives us such joy because … he remembered us all here in this tiny country that has so many needs," she says.
Uruguay's tradition of separating religion from government and public life dates back more than a century. Christmas has long been officially referred to as Family Day, while Easter week is given the vacation-friendly name Tourism Week.
Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholics and even less say they practice the religion, according to political analyst Mariana Pomiés , director of the public polling firm CIFRA.
But as a practicing Catholic, Pomiés says sometimes Uruguayan and especially officials misinterpret what secularism is. "Secularism is not anti-religion, it's the neutrality of the state in religious matters. But here the neutrality se convirtió en un absoluto … it became an absolute."
Pope celebrates "positive secularism"
Dozens of volunteers cleaned streets, mowed lawns and erected a simple stage outside the tiny brick Our Lady of Guadalupe Church. It's the focal spot for many in the Casavalle neighborhood, a working-class city about a half hour north of Montevideo, where the pope is scheduled to visit on Saturday.
"I am very happy, very glad, very grateful … that eyes have been set here," where many are forgotten and stigmatized, said Father Pablo Coimbra who's served as the community's pastoral leader for the past six years
"For the first time many people who live their lives always on the margins, on the margins of opportunities, of possibilities, of the future, on the margins of a loving gaze ... well, today they are in the heart, in the center," he said.
A proposed papal address to the parliament triggered a swift rebuke from the public and politicos alike and was quickly scrapped. However, Uruguay's left-wing President Yamandú Orsi is overseeing a welcome ceremony outside Montevideo's main cathedral, where Leo is celebrating evening prayers, vespers with church leaders and laypeople.
Sunday mass will take place in Florida, about an hour outside the capital, a town replete with Catholic and national pride. Every Nov. 8, church goers commemorate the Virgin of the Thirty-five, a symbol of Uruguay's independence movement from the Brazilian empire in 1825.
A long awaited Papal return to Argentina
By Sunday, Pope Leo will be in neighboring Argentina, fulfilling a wish of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who had hoped to return to his homeland but never made the trip.
Before his death, Francis had said he didn't want a papal visit to become entangled in Argentina's intensely polarized politics.
Pope Leo's visit to Argentina offers an early test of how he will address the Catholic Church's differences with right-wing populist leaders gaining ground across Latin America. Those tensions have also surfaced in the U.S., where Leo has clashed with President Trump over immigration and the treatment of migrants.
Far-right President Javier Milei's sweeping austerity measures, which have pushed millions of Argentines into poverty, could put him at odds with Leo, who has long championed the poor.
Milei has also embraced data centers and a largely unfettered approach to artificial intelligence regulation, while Pope Leo's inaugural encyclical called for ethical caution and safeguards to protect human dignity in the age of AI.
Saving the best for last?
The final leg of the trip will take Leo back to Peru in what has been billed as a homecoming.
As a missionary priest and later appointed Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo, Pope Leo spent two decades in the country. He became a naturalized Peruvian in 2015, and has said the country shaped his life more than anything else.
He will visit several cities and towns where he lived and will meet with President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of former Peruvian dictator Alberto Fujimori.
As a priest during the Fujimori dictatorship, Leo was openly critical of military violence and human rights abuses and supported efforts leading to Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission following the return to democracy.
But for many Uruguayans Pope Leo is not very well known. Walking past the huge stage set up for Leo's welcoming ceremony, Juan Martin Guerreiro said he wasn't sure he would attend the pope's speeches.
"He doesn't feel as influential to me … as Pope Francis," said Guerreiro. But he said he's willing to give the new pope a chance because he is South American.
When reminded that Pope Leo was born in Chicago, Guerreiro said he wouldn't hold that against him.

A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

Book Box: Diwali and the books we give each other
A reflection on parent-child bonds, nostalgic reading, and recommended books for the festive season.
Dear Reader,
It is Diwali morning in Mumbai. Four days ago we left the new home we are still making. The carpenters caught a bus home to Mandi, the masons to Bajaura, the polisher to Bilaspur. The Other Reader and I drove down to the plains, to Chandigarh, and flew to Mumbai to spend Diwali with my parents and my siblings.
In Mumbai, my mother needs containers for her kitchen. Little jars for cardamom, cinnamon, cumin. We go together to the neighbourhood market. The shop down the road is crammed with containers of every kind. My mother finds what she wants. Flushed with the hunter-gatherer thrill of a successful expedition, we go for cold coffee at Poetry and Cheesecake. We share a frappe and talk about how to parent adult children.
The waitress, a friendly young woman in her twenties, brings us the bill inside an anthology of poetry.
My mother pays. Then she opens the book. “’There was a ship,” quoth he,” she begins, and we are both gone. Back to a bungalow in Jamshedpur. Back to the evenings when she read to us, sometimes The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, sometimes The Highwayman.
“It’s been so long,” she says, “since I read aloud.”
She asks if she can buy the book. The waitress smiles and says no. They don’t sell these. It is the only copy, kept for bringing bills to customers. Then she looks at our faces and says, “You can borrow it.”
I want to tell her how much this means to me. My mother has been a little sad and overwhelmed of late, and these poems are just what she needs. I want her to know that this small gesture has made my mother very happy.
Instead, I say, “Thank you, thank you. I live just down the road. I’ll leave my number.”
“That’s okay,” she says. “Just drop it back.”
In the car my mother worries. “I hope she doesn’t get into trouble.” But she is already turning pages, finding her favourites one by one. “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” she reads.
“These are the poems I really love. And this print is large enough for my eyes,” she says.
Tonight, after the diyas, we will read them aloud. Tomorrow morning I will take the book back. I hope the young woman is there. I want to tell her what it meant to my mother.
Yesterday the book club met, and it was different. We came dressed in saris. We swapped books, which seemed apt for Diwali. We laughed and joked and squabbled a little. Everyone wanted Leftovers:A History of Food Waste and Preservation by Dr. Eleanor Barnett. Everyone wanted Prayers for Rain, a murder mystery by Dennis Lehane. Nobody wanted Swallowing the Sun by Lakshmi Murdeshwar Puri, a striking hardback with a beautiful cover and a slow-moving story inside.
If you are still looking for books to give this Diwali, here are a few possibilities.
· The one everyone’s talking about: Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, a satirical suspense novel about a tradwife influencer.
· Feel-good novels about human relationships : Whistler by Ann Patchett or The Correspondent by Virginia Evans.
· Poetry for the shelf: Glass, Irony and God by this year’s Nobel laureate Anne Carson, which includes the extraordinary The Glass Essay. And perhaps an anthology of the fifty greatest poets : something to dip into, and something to read aloud.
· Non-fiction: London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe, a true story about a London teenager’s death set against an extraordinary landscape of crime in the city. Or Marginlands by Arati Kumar-Rao, a book that explores India’s vulnerable landscapes and the people who live in them.
Our borrowed poetry anthology is on the table by the door, to be read aloud and then given back.
Happy Diwali and happy reading. I’d love to know: is there a poem someone read to you as a child that you still remember?
Sonya Dutta Choudhury is a Mumbai-based journalist, Founder of Sonya’s Book Box, and a teacher of Storytelling in Business. Got a knot in your life, a dilemma at work, or a reading slump you can’t shake? Send your questions and book requests to sonyasbookbox@gmail.com, and she promises to give each one her most earnest consideration.

While you might be pondering whether to replace a smartphone with one that has a slightly better camera or a second screen, the Federal Aviation Administration is planning a much bigger leap in technology for the country’s air traffic control system.
The FAA said yesterday that it will stop using floppy disks as part of a long-awaited upgrade that will give air traffic controllers faster access to data needed for crucial safety alerts. The new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) will be installed in 435 facilities, replacing several information display systems dating to the 1980s.
The FAA “is continuing its historic modernization of America’s air traffic control system by replacing outdated floppy disks that contain vital weather and other critical information with a streamlined, 21st-century system,” the agency said. E-IDS will be “deployed to operational control positions at more than 400 facilities across all air traffic control domains,” and “provide operationally essential information for controlling aircraft,” the FAA said.
The change has been in the works for over six years. “No more floppy disks or paper strips,” then-Acting FAA Administrator Chris Rocheleau told the House Appropriations Committee last year.
The FAA said E-IDS will replace older tools that have “technical end-of-life issues” and address two of the aviation agency’s top safety concerns: distribution of weather alerts to pilots (known as PIREP for Pilot Report); and timely distribution of Notices to Airmen (NOTAM), which include information on abnormal statuses and hazards.
“E-IDS gives air traffic controllers the information they need to make timely decisions and keep the flying public safe,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports across the National Airspace System.”
Upgrades will take a year
It’ll take a year or so to make the upgrades at every facility. The first sites to get E-IDS will be Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. The FAA said it plans to complete the upgrade at 435 sites by the end of 2028.

A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.
Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5), indicating a “moderate” brain injury, just one point above “mild.” He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).
In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.
“Pull-and-see”
The blade was entirely through the right eye socket and eyeball. It traversed the left frontal and temporal lobes of his brain, passing through in front of—and without apparently injuring—the corpus callosum, which connects the two sides of the brain and is full of nerve fibers. The blade also missed the left internal capsule, which holds another bundle of nerve fibers.
In terms of damage to major blood vessels, doctors found that the blade was close to the left internal carotid artery, a major blood vessel, but didn’t seem to have damaged it. Doctors did find, however, that a branch of the middle cerebral artery looked to be indented by the knife.
After consulting with various medical specialties, the man’s doctors moved to emergency neurosurgery. They opted to remove part of his skull to directly see into the brain, but used a conservative “pull-and-see” method to slide the blade out rather than invasively excavate it. After it was out, the doctors saw no signs of significant hemorrhaging. The brain wound was cleaned and drained before surgeons patched up his skull. His right eye, however, couldn’t be saved. Given its extensive damage, it was removed.

Tesla will end production of the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory next year.
It’s a uniquely toxic electric vehicle, between its divisive design and Elon Musk’s embrace of you name it. That toxicity certainly contributed to subpar sales, along with a number of recalls.
But the end of the Cybertruck is also another sign that the era of big EVs—particularly big trucks—is waning. That’s great news for pedestrian and biker safety, but also for the battery supply chain at a time when more people need to get behind the electric wheel.
The Cybertruck uses a massive 123 kilowatt-hour battery that clocks in at around 1,600 pounds, or around a quarter of its weight. That’s on par with the battery that powered Ford’s F-150 Lightning, another electric truck that was canceled late last year. (The company also killed a three-row EV in 2024.) Ford’s behemoth batteries ranged from 98 kilowatt-hours up to 131 kilowatt-hours.
Seeing both trucks canceled within a year of each other, while automakers have announced a bevy of smaller EVs and gas-powered autos with electric motors that can extend range, indicates there may be a shift afoot. Ford is planning to launch the Fathom next year. The sub-$30,000 electric pickup is expected to be about the size of the automaker’s compact gas-powered Maverick pickup. Though Ford hasn’t announced the battery sizes available in various trims, it’s a safe bet they won’t be anywhere near the size of the F-150 Lightning or Cybertruck. The company is also planning to relaunch the Lightning as an extended-range model.
Startup Slate is also launching a tiny electric pickup that can be converted to an SUV, with a bare-bones base model starting below $25,000. It also features a svelte battery and has seen a massive surge in preorders—though, to be fair, so did the Cybertruck, and we saw that turned out.
Then there’s the Rivian R2, which launched this year. While the SUV isn’t as tiny or cheap as Ford and Slate’s vehicles—its battery has 88 kilowatt-hours of capacity and weighs in at around 1,200 pounds—it’s still smaller than the company’s flagship R1S. Rivian has also teased the R3, an even more-slimmed down SUV, in the coming years.
That’s not to say big EVs are dead. The Kia EV9, for example, is among the top 10 EVs by sales in the US, as is the R1S. There’s also a torrid resale market for the F-150 Lightning. But the rest of the top 10 new EV sales are all crossovers, sedans, or mid-sized SUVs with moderately sized batteries, and a number of newly announced EVs are trending on the smaller side or function as extended range vehicles.
Building smaller vehicles is, of course, one way to make EVs cheaper. With less weight to propel, you can rely on a smaller battery. And given that the battery pack is the most costly component of an EV, that can in turn help automakers offer more affordable vehicles at a time when the price of so many other consumer goods is skyrocketing. That includes the current crop of EVs: The average transaction price for a new model is now $55,800, according to Cox Automotive.
Going small—or smaller, anyway—also means making the most of a limited battery supply chain. The vast majority of Cybertruck drivers are doing the same thing with their vehicles as Hyundai Ioniq 5 drivers: getting groceries, commuting, and driving kids to soccer games. But a standard range Ioniq 5 driver is doing it with a battery about half the size.
After President Donald Trump’s administration killed EV incentives last year, sales plummeted. The Iran War and rising gas prices have led to an uptick in interest, though sales still lag behind the global average. (Used hybrid sales have also picked up, reflecting the pain people have been feeling at the pump.) Even with a Democratic-controlled Congress, EV incentives coming back under Trump are about as likely as defense secretary Pete Hegseth putting pronouns in his email signature. But should Democrats take the White House in 2028, marking the culmination of Woke 2.0, support for would-be EV buyers becomes much more likely.
Automakers pivoting to smaller cars could be much better-positioned to meet pent-up demand if that happens, while also lowering the risks of delivery delays.
Even Elon’s announcement killing the Cybertruck points to where the market is heading: He claims Tesla is ending production to make room for cranking out more Cybercabs. The battery size in those vehicles? Just 48 kilowatt-hours.

The 57th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu explores how researchers are using advanced imaging and reconstruction techniques to create detailed, three-dimensional maps of the human brain.
Zubeda Hamid, senior assistant editor, The Hindu, speaks to Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam, Head of the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras, about the technology, how the maps are created and what they could reveal about the human brain.
The episode looks at C-STROKE, a recently released three-dimensional atlas of a stroke-affected brain. Unlike conventional MRI scans, which provide images of the brain at a particular resolution, the new approach allows researchers to examine brain structures in greater detail and build comprehensive 3D maps.
The discussion explains how researchers prepare brain tissue, use imaging techniques and reconstruct the data to create these maps. It also looks at the different scientific and technological disciplines involved in the process and how detailed mapping could help researchers study the brain’s structure and changes associated with neurological conditions.
Another focus is the Centre’s plan to map more than 100 human brains across different stages of life. The project aims to build a larger collection of brain maps that could help researchers understand variations in brain structure, study neurological conditions and expand the available resources for brain research.
The episode also examines the potential applications of these atlases in clinical research and healthcare, including how they could contribute to a better understanding of stroke and other brain conditions. It discusses the possibilities as well as the work needed before such maps can be translated into clinical applications.
