Amid a sweep of Democratic victories in Tuesday’s midterms, some online commentators jokingly declared “Woke is back.”
There was little congressional pushback over the past two years as the Trump administration terminated hundreds of grants meant to chronicle and remedy medical inequities, shuttered programs intended to diversify the science workforce, and opened investigations into universities and medical schools it accused of discriminating against white and Asian applicants. Will that change now that the Democratic Party has won control of the 120th Congress?
Two newly elected candidates with science credentials told STAT they hope to change that: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former health disparities researcher, and incoming Rep. Jasmine Clark of Georgia, a microbiologist who will be the first Black woman with a STEM Ph.D. in Congress.
Democrats have a long list of priorities, and with President Trump still wielding his veto power, passing bills related to health equity will still be an uphill battle. The White House posted on X Thursday, “FYI: DEI is still dead.” But, the introduction of at least two lawmakers with personal connections to health equity work could offer a counterweight to such policies for the rest of the second Trump administration.
“I know firsthand what DEI initiatives can do for students who are trying to find their way, and they don’t actually quite know all of the options that are available to them,” Clark told STAT in an interview Wednesday. A former professor, she said such programs have opened up opportunities for her students in the sciences.
El-Sayed, interviewed a few days before the election, said, “The war on diversity, equity, and inclusion is about a vision of an America that doesn’t include certain kinds of people. I will always stand for an America where everybody is included and empowered, and I think that’s critical for us as we move to the future.” During his time in academia, he did research on disparities in maternal health and within the Arab American community. He added, “we need to be able to document the ways in which our systems are allowing for and, in some respects, creating the differences in the ability for people to live long, healthy lives. It’s important work, and it should help guide where public policy gaps are and where we need to fill them.”
The second Trump administration has seen unprecedented changes to the scientific ecosystem. Some of the most major have drawn forceful responses from Congress. Proposals to cut the National Institutes of Health’s budget, cap funding for overhead costs at universities, and exert more political control over federal funding have all been rebuked by Congress. With the Democrats taking control of both chambers, further pushback may be coming.
The NIH did not respond to a request for comment.
A number of physicians and scientists who won their races have noted that accountability for health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is high on their list of priorities. Part of that accountability should be understanding which communities and researchers were affected by policies like grant terminations over the past two years, said Jennifer Jones, who directs the Center for Science and Democracy at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “I want to know who was most harmed by this because there’s absolutely a justice and equity issue at play when you clearly attack issues of diversity, equity, and inclusion,” she said.
While equity work is sometimes portrayed as controversial, Philip Alberti, the founding director of the Association of American Medical Colleges Center for Health Justice, said polling he has done has shown broad support for health equity initiatives across ideological groups. “Three-quarters of U.S. adults support the goal of ‘all communities having a fair and just opportunity to be healthy,’ and 65% of adults who have ever heard the term ‘health equity’ support it, too,” he said. “This was true across all subgroups, including across groups defined by self-identified ideology. This is not controversial.”
Clark trained as a microbiologist before taking to politics during the first Trump administration. She said she would seek an assignment on the House oversight committee and has a number of questions she’d like to pose to appointees like Kennedy. For one, she would like to understand why the administration has repeatedly pushed for a controversial hepatitis B vaccine study in Guinea-Bissau. Clark likened that trial to the Tuskegee syphilis experiment, an unethical study conducted by the U.S. Public Health Service and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that withheld treatment for syphilis from nearly 400 African American men from 1932 to 1972.
Another way she has seen the fallout of the administration is that her former lab, which studies HIV transmission, had to pause some of its longitudinal studies in Africa because of restrictions on international collaborations. Even if the lab is able to find more funding, “you basically have to start from scratch, or you just have a big hole in your data. That’s not what we need to be doing if we want to actually do things like end the HIV epidemic,” she said.
She also lamented the process of grants for federal funding being screened for certain terms and phrases to determine if they are related to “DEI.” This process has particularly affected researchers studying health disparities, and has made it difficult for some to apply for new funding. In September, a handful of researchers sued the agency, arguing this process infringed on their first amendment rights.
“Having the ability to write in your research grant that you’re looking at the disproportionate impact without having to dance around those words because any grant that has the word ‘disproportionate,’ or ‘woman,’ or ‘Black,’ or ‘gender,’ or anything like that all of a sudden gets flagged,” she said. “That’s not the environment we should be operating under if we actually want to answer real-life questions. So I look forward to being a part of a Congress that will prioritize moving toward and not immediately dismissing research because they are trying to answer questions about why one group is impacted more than another.”

This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
- Published
In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.
He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.
Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.
As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.
But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.
The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.
A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.
His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.
Isaac - who his twin brother Jacob Valdez describes as an intelligent man who loved volunteering and helping the elderly - died on 26 August 2026 when doctors turned off his life support.
Just 23 days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a seismic change in teaching that would, in effect, have given Isaac the religious green light to have the life-saving treatment he had refused.
The change suddenly means the vast majority of medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited to followers. Now, decisions on whether to accept such treatments are to be left to individuals.
Jacob, already dealing with the death of his twin, was angered at the Jehovah's Witnesses' leadership for not coming to their conclusion sooner. He told BBC News he believes Isaac could well still be alive if they had.
The original rule on blood transfusions dates back to 1945, towards the very end of a war during which the use of blood transfusions had been increasingly widespread. The leaders of Jehovah's Witnesses announced that their believers were not permitted to accept transfusions.
This was based on their interpretation of Bible verses from both the Old and New Testaments prohibiting the consumption of blood, including one from the Book of Acts that instructs believers to abstain from blood, from food offered to idols, and from things that had been strangled.
So, why has the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body, based in New York state, now decided to change the rules, 81 years after introducing them?
It comes after years of pressure from both within and outside the faith, but that is not how leaders of the faith describe the decision.
"The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," says the Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, who described it as both a fresh look at scripture and at medical advances.
We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.
He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.
The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.
Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".
He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.
But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.
Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.
These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.
Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.
He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".
Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.
This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.
"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.
It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.
"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.
But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.
"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.
And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.
He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.
Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.
"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."
With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.
More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.
It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.
Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.
They also cost her her marriage too, with her husband of 10 years leaving the faith and divorcing her after it came to light that he had had a blood transfusion as a child, something that was looked down upon in her Witness community.
"Since the blood policy change, I have not been myself," she says. "It left me in a sort of depressed mode."
"How many houses did I go to trying to convince people about the blood doctrine? And you're coming now and it's something totally different," Elisha says.
Elisha says her beliefs as a whole have been shaken, yet she feels reluctant to leave the faith, partly because it is what provides her with her community and she fears isolation.
In the past, those who disagreed with "blood doctrine" were ostracised or felt like they needed to leave the faith. Will they now be able to come back?
"Any individual that wants to come back to the faith is warmly welcomed," says Gillies, speaking of those who had left the faith because they had accepted a transfusion for themselves or a relative.
"If they would like to become one of Jehovah's Witnesses again and would like to speak to the elders, then they're very welcome to do so."

The lobbying group for the U.S. pharmaceutical industry spent an estimated $59 million on search advertising over a recent seven-year period to influence how Americans view the highly charged issue of prescription drug costs, according to a new analysis that used data to model the spending.
Of that, the Pharmaceutical Research & Manufacturers of America spent roughly $32 million on ads linked to insurance and health plan searches, while $28 million was spent directing people to its web pages and domains criticizing pharmacy benefit managers, which drugmakers argue are the true culprits behind the rising prices for many medicines.
Spending also surged around well-publicized legislative and regulatory actions, such as when Medicare began drug price negotiations in 2023. In all, PhRMA used more than 283,500 distinct keywords to generate 17.1 million paid visits from 2019 through 2025, according to an analysis published in Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to immediately suspend the manufacturing licences of drugs declared Not of Standard Quality (NSQ) on specified critical quality parameters.
The government said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that the proposed amendments seek to enable prompt regulatory intervention upon detection of substandard medicines, prevent their continued manufacture and distribution, and strengthen the mechanism for ensuring compliance with prescribed quality standards, in the interest of patient safety and public health.
Under the existing provisions of the Drugs Rules, 1945, suspension or cancellation of a manufacturing licence is preceded by the prescribed regulatory procedure, including issuance of a show-cause notice. This may result in a time gap between the declaration of a drug as NSQ and the initiation of regulatory action. During this period, the drug may remain in circulation, posing potential risks to public health and making effective recall more challenging.
To address this regulatory concern, the Ministry has proposed a provision for immediate suspension of the manufacturing licence of the drug by the Central Licensing Approving Authority or the State Licensing Authority upon receipt of a government analyst’s report declaring the drug as NSQ with respect to assay, dissolution, related substances, impurities or sterility.
“These parameters are critical to determining the quality of medicines. The proposed provision aims to ensure that instances of non-compliance involving these specified parameters are met with prompt regulatory action, thereby minimising potential risks to patients,’’ the Ministry said.
The proposed amendment provides for mandatory corrective measures before revocation of the suspension. The suspension shall continue until the manufacturer undertakes an effective root cause analysis to identify the reasons for the quality failure and implements appropriate Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) to the satisfaction of the licensing authority.
Suspension can be revoked after the requisite corrective and preventive measures are implemented and then verified by the licensing authority. This mechanism will ensure that identified quality deficiencies are adequately addressed and necessary safeguards are put in place to prevent their recurrence.
“To further strengthen regulatory coordination and facilitate timely action, consequential amendments have also been proposed to Form 13, relating to the test report of the Government Analyst. Under the proposed mechanism, the Government Analyst’s report would be endorsed to the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), the concerned State/UT Licensing Authority under whose jurisdiction the manufacturing site is located, as well as the manufacturer and marketer of the concerned drug,’’ the government said.
It added that the proposed arrangement is aimed at ensuring timely communication of NSQ findings to the relevant authorities and stakeholders, thereby facilitating coordinated regulatory action and strengthening accountability across the drug manufacturing and marketing chain.
The proposed amendments follow deliberations at the 65th meeting of the Drugs Consultative Committee, held on December 20, 2024, and recommendations of the 92nd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board, held on April 24, 2025.
The amendments are expected to strengthen post-marketing regulatory surveillance, facilitate timely action against substandard medicines, promote greater accountability among manufacturers and marketers, and reinforce public confidence in the quality of medicines available in the country.
The draft amendments have been notified for public consultation, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days from the date on which copies of the Gazette of India containing the draft rules are made available to the public.

Anthropic is holding firm on the pledge made in its Super Bowl commercial this year to keep Claude ad-free. The company’s recent IPO filing didn’t even mention the possibility of selling ads to make money from the AI chatbot. It’s easy to maintain the high ground with about $112 billion in investor cash.
The chatbot industry, though, may find selling ads necessary to defray the high costs of generating AI responses. OpenAI is all in, with over 100,000 customers advertising in ChatGPT since ads debuted there in February. Last week, Google expanded ads in its search chatbot AI Mode to 10 more countries beyond the US and declared that users “find them highly relevant.” Advertisers are far from satisfied with the experience, but they expect it to improve.
Ads stand to be particularly vital for the long-term viability of niche chatbot platforms, which can’t rely on the same degree of venture capital largesse as the top AI labs or the massive revenues of tech giants. I recently spoke with Koah Labs, one of a number of new ad technology companies focused on AI experiences. The San Francisco startup markets itself as bringing ads to over 200 apps, such as DeepAI, which offers tools for creative queries, and Liner, which focuses on providing citations in AI answers. It works with brands like telehealth giant Hims and flower delivery service UrbanStems.
Koah has attracted just a tenth of the advertisers OpenAI has, but CEO Nic Baird still believes he’s getting a good sense of what’s working and what’s fuzzy as chatbots take over from traditional search engines—and what their rise will mean for your AI experiences.
Machine-Crafted
Ads composed partly by AI rather than fully by a human generate double the clicks, Baird says. It’s difficult to assess exactly why, but AI-generated marketing copy likely feels more natural next to the output of an AI model.
Because ads shown by Koah are grounded in product details and imagery supplied by the advertiser, users don’t seem to be encountering AI-hallucinated, erroneous information. But some advertisers, such as drugmakers, face government requirements on what they must—or cannot—say in ads, Baird says. These companies default to more human control over their ads, generating weaker results, according to Baird.
Since ads with dull messages or that feel like clutter could drive users away, the onus is on ad tech companies to find a middle ground that’s engaging to users without triggering risk-averse brands. That balance might be harder to strike when a human is out of the loop.
Creative Targeting
Google searches for “help with stress” are likely to bring up ads for therapists. Chatbots can get more creative, in Baird’s view. For instance, ads for spas have performed well within Koah’s network when shown after users’ prompts related to “stress,” he says.
The key difference, according to Baird, is that Koah can select and customize the ad based on “not only the prompt, or the Google search, but also the response from the AI platform, which brings context from the rest of the conversation thus far.” In addition, chatbot prompts tend to be at least double the length of Google queries, giving Koah more information to determine a relevant ad.
Baird claims users are accustomed to navigating through multiple topics within a chatbot conversation, which could make them more receptive to adjacent marketing than they are in traditional search. Koah says users are clicking on about 3 percent of ads, about on par with the performance of the more mature Google ads system.
All the Context
When called on to show an ad, Koah generally receives a user’s entire conversation up to that point to help inform what it displays. While traditional search queries generally look for specific information, people often use chatbots as not just conversation partners but confidants. It’s unclear whether users will accept the privacy trade-offs that come with personalized chatbot ads as they begin to proliferate.
Baird says Koah anonymizes the queries it receives and stores them in a de-identified way, but he declined to comment any further on the data collection and storage. While acknowledging that personalization can become intrusive, he argues that there are benefits for users and advertisers alike as the tech matures. Nonsensitive information about chatbot discussions, for instance, could inform personalized content on the page that loads after an ad click. Perhaps someone expressed interest in a specific feature, or the AI model didn’t highlight a particular downside of a competing product. The advertiser could fill in the gap.
Koah doesn’t have data on whether people actually want these customized pages, but the tech industry has long argued that people prefer when ad experiences feel relevant. Having the conversation history also could benefit advertisers when Koah enables retargeting, or repeating, an ad to the same user.
Negative Triggers
By Koah’s estimate, one out of every four chatbot queries about a retailer or brand concerns a return, exchange, or other support issue. Baird believes chatbots provide an opportunity not replicated easily elsewhere for advertisers to address what they might politely call a “customer success” matter.
He expects manufacturers and retailers will eventually target disappointed customers to remind them about warranties, engage them in an AI-intermediated support, and potentially steer them away from a more costly customer service interaction. It’s possible that the AI chatbot’s response may provide users with similar help, but buying an ad guarantees companies get their message across.
The ideal outcome is users reaching resolution they can live with more swiftly than through other means. In the worst case, it's a wasted ad buy and a more irate consumer.
Great Unknown
None of the apps Koah currently serves ads in offer users AI agents that can shop on their own. However, apps like Instinct and Meta’s Muse are starting to take over shopping chores for some users. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said Muse could become the company’s biggest source of revenue but suggested it would come from transaction fees rather than ads.
That doesn’t mean advertising will be entirely cut out from bot-dominated ecommerce, with initial studies suggesting that ads could influence AI agents.
Baird expects an opportunity to give “the user's agent the best possible recommendation, and that’s going to be a combination of a great discount, a really relevant product,” and an easy digital path to make the purchase. The chatbot must make “abundantly clear” to the agent what content is sponsored or else risk losing user trust, Baird says.
It’s also possible the chatbot ad market fizzles out before agents take hold if more AI developers adopt Anthropic’s stance. Kevin Baragona, CEO of DeepAI, says while ad revenue has been meaningful, he’s not committed to it because the experience just doesn’t feel right yet in terms of privacy, design, and more.
“I don’t think the ads are working terribly well for anyone,” he says.

Ukrainian forces have reportedly targeted an oil refinery as fires and explosions were reported across southern Russia, according to the Kyiv Independent citing the Ukrainian channel Exilenova Plus.
It follows statements made by President Volodymyr Zelensky that every Ukrainian power plant has been damaged by Russian attacks.
“The Russians use Shaheds and missiles to strike even the energy equipment that our nuclear power plants depend on. Every power plant in Ukraine has suffered from Russian attacks in one way or another,” he said in an address to participants of the 30th Ibero-American Summit on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Donald Trump has claimed that Russia's war on Ukraine was close to being settled and that ending it might involve all of Europe.
Trump said he met privately with Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House as first lady, Melania Trump, hosted representatives from Kyiv and Moscow.
"It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine ... I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled," Trump said.
Russia's military intelligence chief to attend talks with US and Ukraine
Igor Kostyukov, the chief of Russia's military intelligence agency, will join talks with the US and Ukraine next week, the Russian news agency Interfax reported.
Russia's delegation will also include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, as well as deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin.
The trilateral meeting is set to take place in Abu Dhabi from 10 to 11 November.
Zelensky warns Trump-Russia negotiations could be 'dangerous'
US president Donald Trump’s proposed security agreement with Russia, potentially covering all of Europe, "can be dangerous", Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said yesterday.
Zelensky's warning comes a day after Trump met Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev and predicted a major agreement extending beyond Ukraine.
“It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe,” Trump said on Thursday.
Zelensky said negotiations must first focus on ending Russia’s war, and then assuring security guarantees for Ukraine, before considering any broader arrangements between Europe and Moscow.
“For me, it’s not simple, and it can be dangerous,” he said.
“We don’t want to have Yalta 2.0,” the Ukrainian president said, referring to the 1945 conference at which Allied leaders of World War II discussed Europe’s postwar order.
Poland demands 'ceasefire first' before Kremlin raises concerns in peace discussions
Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski called for a ceasefire before initiating any peace negotiations discussing Russia's concerns.
“First, a ceasefire, then negotiations on lasting peace, and only afterwards possible discussions on restoring Europe’s security architecture and arms control arrangements,” Sikorski said yesterday after a meeting of the Council of the Baltic Sea States in Warsaw.
“No solution can be imposed on Ukraine without its consent and participation at the table. Likewise, Europe’s security cannot be discussed without our involvement," he said, adding that Russia's continued aggression "will carry increasing costs and consequences".
Ukraine strikes oil refinery in mass attack across Russia: report
Ukraine has reportedly struck an oil refinery in major overnight attacks on Russian regions, including Oryol, Saratov, and Rostov.
The attacks set the Saratov Oil Refinery ablaze and led to fires breaking out at the Almaz military factory in the southern Russian city of Rostov, according to the Kyiv Independent.
An electronic components factory was targeted in the western city of Oryol, reports say.
Ukraine reportedly used Flamingo missiles in some of the attacks.
Ukraine approves new process to identify bodies of personnel
Ukraine has approved a new process to speed up the identification of deceased military personnel, which usually takes several months.
The new process requires all regional teams to follow the same rules at every stage, from the initial inspection of remains to the collection of DNA samples.
A single coding system has also been approved for storing case records to prevent the loss of data.
“This will help eliminate unnecessary delays, improve the quality of the investigations, and ensure smoother coordination between teams at every stage,” Ukrainian prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
Ukraine's drones completed record 30,000 missions in October, report says
Kyiv's unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) completed a record 31,398 missions in October, the Ukrainian defence ministry said yesterday.
This number is four times the 7,511 missions recorded in January 2026.
The record indicates that UGVs have become crucial for the operation of Ukraine's brigades, including for logistics and evacuation missions.
UGVs are being widely used for strike missions, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance, mining and demining, as well as for launching aerial drones.
"UGVs are the technology that makes it possible to minimise the risk to humans on the front," the Ukrainian defence ministry said.
US midterm results ‘double’ Ukraine’s chances of getting aid, official says

The Democrats gaining control of both houses of the US Congress shifts the balance of power in Washington, dealing a blow to president Donald Trump’s political agenda for the next two years.
Given Trump’s recent pro-Russian moves and Washington slashing aid to Ukraine, he added, the midterm election results were seen as a promising sign for Kyiv.
“It’s my personal estimate, but the chances for us to get better U.S. support in terms of both financially and militarily at least doubled,” Arakhamia said.
“This is my feeling. But it’s going to happen next year, most probably, you know, like the first quarter.”
Musk reshares X post calling Starlink service for Ukraine ‘a mistake’
SpaceX chief Elon Musk reshared a post on X, the social media platform he owns, calling it a “mistake” to give Ukraine access to Starlink terminals to aid its war effort against Russia.
“In hindsight, it was a mistake for SpaceX to send (Ukraine) thousands of free Starlink dishes and millions of dollars a month in free service at the beginning of the war,” the post amplified by Musk read.
The multibillionaire reshared the post after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky criticised Musk’s oversized political influence.
“There is too much power in the hands of one very wealthy person. Such a concentration of power is dangerous,” Zelensky said in an interview on Thursday.

Srinagar, Nov 8: Thousands of lamps illuminated the iconic clock tower at Srinagar's Lal Chowk as tourists and locals celebrated Diwali here on Sunday.
Dozens of tourists assembled at the clock tower, popularly known as Ghanta Ghar, in the evening and lit earthen lamps, turning the area around the city's iconic tourist spot luminous.

How much is too much to pay for a smartphone? Prices have climbed globally—IDC forecasts a nearly 30 percent rise this year alone amid ongoing memory supply crunches—but would you pay $1,600 for a Motorola?
That kind of money typically buys a folding phone with a bendable screen—where steep manufacturing costs justify the markup—or a maxed-out “candy bar” slab from an established premium brand like Apple or Samsung with gobs of internal storage. Motorola hasn't pushed into this price bracket outside of its latest Razr Fold or Razr Ultra folding devices, but that's changing with the new Motorola Signature 27.
It marks Motorola’s first unapologetic, ultra-premium candy bar in the US in six years, harking back to the Edge+ from 2020. And this time, rather than settling into the comfortable value-flagship tier, Motorola is taking direct aim at the highest-end Galaxies and iPhones on hardware alone. Preorders open on November 19, and the phone goes on sale November 26.
Top Shelf
So what exactly do you get for $1,600? The Signature 27 has contoured edges, a thin design, and an “integrated” camera plane—similar to the iPhone 18 Pro’s Camera Plateau—finished in ceramic and brushed aluminum. It comes in two colors: Pantone Capulet Olive with a textile-inspired finish and Pantone Coal Smoke with a tactical-weave finish. The front glass is Corning's Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3, and the phone has an IP68/69 rating for top-of-the-line dust and water resistance.
Most notable is the 6.8-inch screen. Motorola claims its “Extreme AMOLED Duo” panel is the brightest smartphone display on the market, peaking at an eye-searing 12,000 nits. Underneath, it uses tandem OLED tech—stacking two panels on top of each other—similar to what Apple debuted on its iPad Pro and touchscreen MacBook.
Even so, Apple's new display peaks at around 2,000 nits, and most smartphones today top out around 3,600 nits, which is more than enough nits to read the screen in harsh sunlight. Chinese phone brands like Honor and Huawei have recently touted 10,000-plus max nits of brightness, but those ratings rarely apply outside of tiny slivers of the display during HDR playback. Treat Moto’s brightness statement as pure spec-sheet marketing.
The tech does deliver better energy efficiency, meaning the display uses less power and could improve battery life, plus a 121 percent longer lifespan than normal AMOLED panels. The screen also has a 1.5K resolution, Dolby Vision support, and “Pantone Validated” color calibration for accurate colors.
Once a handicap, the company's camera tech has become more competitive in recent years, and Motorola hopes the Signature 27 will stand out with its top-end image sensors. There's a 50-megapixel Sony Lytia L910 main camera—Sony's first sensor with LOFIC (Lateral Overflow Integration Capacitor) technology, which can dramatically improve dynamic range in a single exposure. Basically, it should perform better in challenging lighting conditions, with fewer crushed blacks and blown-out skies.
Next up is a 200-megapixel periscope 3X telephoto camera with up to 100X digital zoom, enhanced with generative AI, similar to what Google and Samsung offer on their respective devices. Rounding things out is a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 50-megapixel selfie camera with 4K video support. Speaking of video, Motorola says its new video enhancement engine uses AI to optimize color, contrast, and dynamic range, and improved stabilization should make footage look smoother.
But wait, isn't there a fourth camera on the back? No, that's actually a dedicated “Event-Based Vision Sensor” (EVS), which Motorola claims is a first on a smartphone. It works with Motorola's Action Shot mode, freezing motion so photos of moving subjects look perfectly crisp and sharp with no motion blur.
The Signature 27 is among the first phones to use the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip, announced in September, the top-end processor you can expect to see in most flagship Android smartphones in 2027. Motorola cites better cooling performance with a 40 percent larger thermal chamber to keep the processor running longer. It comes with 12 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage.
It's one of the first phones with Wi-Fi 8. (Yes, you'll need a Wi-Fi 8 router to take advantage, and those barely exist on the market right now.)
A massive 7,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery sits inside—relatively new technology that enables denser yet slim batteries. That size should get you around 66 hours of battery life—more than two days. It supports 90-watt TurboPower fast charging—the company claims 12 minutes of charging will get you 12 hours of use—and wireless charging (but still no Qi2 magnetic wireless charging).
To help justify that $1,600 price, Motorola is partnering with premium audio brand Bang & Olufsen for the phone's speaker system, with a new speaker architecture promising the kind of “deep bass” and “clear vocals” every phone maker claims in their latest and greatest.
On software, Motorola promises 7 years of software updates. Motorola has historically lagged in updates, but it is changing its tune with higher-priced devices like the Razr Fold and now the Signature 27. This is also Motorola's first smartphone to support GrapheneOS—a de-Googled version of Android that focuses on protecting your privacy. (You can just stick with stock Android if you want.)
The Signature also gets a few Gemini Intelligence features that Google introduced this year with Android 17. You can ask Gemini to tackle tasks on your behalf, like booking an Uber or ordering food through DoorDash; create widgets using generative AI; and translate American Sign Language into English in real time with Google's Gboard and Live Transcribe apps. Google is also lending Motorola its Rambler feature that until now was exclusive to the Pixel 11. Rambler dramatically improves speech-to-text dictation.
Lifestyle Chops
Will all of that be enough to convince someone to part with $1,600? Motorola's Nicole Hagen, head of global product marketing, thinks so. She tells WIRED that Motorola has positioned itself as a lifestyle company for the last few years by leaning into luxury partnerships with brands like Pantone and Swarovski and pushing into the premium tier.
She points out that revenue is up 15 percent year over year in the second quarter of 2026, with a third of that coming from the “premium” category. She also says that the Signature model launched outside the US earlier this year alongside the Razr Fold saw the highest net promoter scores in the company's history, suggesting greater customer satisfaction and brand loyalty.
“Historically for Motorola, higher pricing has been tied to the foldable form factor, but we wanted to offer that set of consumers seeking the highest-quality smartphone where no technical specification has been overlooked,” Hagen says. And if the price is off-putting? Hagen points to Motorola's entire portfolio, from the budget and midrange Moto G series to the upper-midrange Motorola Edge phones.
Nabila Popal, senior research director at research and consulting firm IDC, isn't convinced that Motorola can successfully command such high prices. In the US, Apple captured 80 percent of the premium smartphone market in the second quarter of 2026, with Samsung sitting at 16 percent. Lenovo, Motorola's parent company, had just one percent.
“The average consumer—even the premium consumer—is not seeing which phone wins on a spec sheet,” Popal says. “Regardless of how great this phone is, it's going to be quite hard for Motorola to compete.”
Still, Motorola has seen success in this bracket. Its pricey folding phones are the most popular in the US, leading with 78 percent of the folding market. (Apple is expected to dramatically chip away at Motorola's lead with the new iPhone Duo.)
Motorola’s new handset does fall in line with the current “premiumization” trend in the hardware industry, though, where devices get a glow-up so companies can charge higher prices and preserve profitability in the memory-crisis era. Amazon's slate of October announcements is a good example—its new tablets, Echo devices, and Kindles all have higher starting prices but are made with nicer materials and more powerful components.
If the premiumization playbook works, Motorola will have proved that luxury doesn't have to bend. But it’s an uphill climb in this economic climate—especially when $500 can still buy you a fantastic phone.

Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
- Published
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.
Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.
Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.
Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).
But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.
Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.
Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.
Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.
Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.
Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.
In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.
Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.
Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.
The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.
- Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat 
  - Published24 October
Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.
"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.
That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."
The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.
But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.
Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.
"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.
Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.
"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.
Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".
Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.
Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".
"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.
Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.
With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.
A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.
In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.
The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.
But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.
As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

Why is CM silent? Akhilesh raises Ram Temple theft after Yogi's apology demand
An apology demand over the 1990 firing on kar sevaks drew a counter from Akhilesh Yadav on temple donation theft and land compensation, setting off a war of words with Yogi Adityanath ahead of his Ayodhya visit.
Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Sunday accused the Uttar Pradesh government of failing to act in the Ram Temple donation theft case and questioned Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s silence.
Yadav asked who had protected those involved despite an SIT investigation into the matter. “Why has the Chief Minister remained silent? Who will take responsibility?” he asked.
The former chief minister also alleged that Ayodhya residents had been humiliated and denied fair compensation for land acquired in the name of development.
His remarks came a day after Adityanath demanded an apology over the 1990 firing on kar sevaks, following the announcement that Yadav would visit the Ram Temple on December 12.
Though Adityanath did not name Yadav or the SP, he invoked the police firing that took place when Yadav’s father, Mulayam Singh Yadav, was chief minister.
YOGI SEEKS APOLOGY BEFORE TEMPLE VISIT
Speaking at Ayodhya’s Deepotsav on Saturday, Adityanath accused previous governments of neglecting the city and acting against Ram devotees and saints.
“Those who had neglected and insulted (Ayodhya), who opened fire on Ram devotees and subjected saints to lathicharge, should certainly come to Ayodhya, but only after apologising,” he said.
“Let them apologise once to Ram devotees and once to the saints. Let them repent for their actions," he added.
Adityanath, without naming Yadav or the SP, also appeared to target Yadav’s recent attendance at a religious discourse, questioning whether some visitors understood the decorum of a “katha”.
He described Lord Ram as central to India’s culture and national consciousness, credited devotees and saints for Ayodhya’s revival, and highlighted its roads, airport and railway facilities.
HOW THE DONATION THEFT CASE UNFOLDED
While Yadav alleged a lack of action, the donation theft case has seen eight arrests and the filing of a chargesheet.
The allegations concern cash offerings being diverted during counting at the Ram Temple. After the temple trust sought an investigation, the state government constituted a three-member SIT.
The team submitted its preliminary report in June, and eight accused were arrested that month. The state government later sent the SIT’s final report to the temple trust.
The SIT filed its chargesheet before an Ayodhya court on September 23. According to reported findings, investigators identified 105 instances of unauthorised removal or concealment of cash from the counting room.
Police recovered Rs 79.85 lakh allegedly linked to the suspected embezzlement from seven of the eight accused. Investigators also examined bank accounts, transactions and assets allegedly acquired with the diverted money.
On November 2, the Supreme Court disposed of petitions seeking a CBI investigation after the state confirmed that the SIT had filed its chargesheet.

Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
- Published
The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.
The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.
"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."
There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.
"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.
Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.
Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.
He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."
He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."

Can a hacker really do anything with your IP address?
An IP address won’t hand over your passwords, but it can give attackers somewhere to aim
In November 2021, Twitch streamer xQc lost his internet connection shortly after playing "Crab Game." The game's developer then warned streamers to avoid public lobbies after discovering that the game could expose players' IP addresses to distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. Although xQc couldn't confirm an attack caused that specific outage, the developer soon switched to newer Steam networking to hide IP addresses.
IP addresses basically help route data to and from websites and games. Now, most home routers let multiple devices share one public IPv4 address, while IPv6 can give each device its own public-facing address. But before you pull out the tinfoil hat, understand that neither type of IP address gives someone access to your passwords or personal data. However, both can give a hacker a target to aim at, and that's enough to raise an eyebrow.
What can a hacker actually do with your IP address?
An IP lookup is a quick way to reveal your internet service provider and approximate city or region. Back in 2016, a Kansas family sued MaxMind after its database mapped approximately 650 million unrelated IP addresses to their farm, prompting repeated law enforcement visits over incidents involving people elsewhere.
A typical DDoS attack floods a target with traffic from multiple sources. It's the same kind of attack Bluesky blamed for its server outages, and on a smaller scale, it could interrupt gaming sessions, video calls, or even an entire household internet connection. A firewall may offer little help once the internet connection is overwhelmed.
To access a device, an attacker needs a way in, such as an exposed security camera, remote-access software with a security flaw, or a home server with weak password protection. IPv4 port forwarding or permissive IPv6 firewall settings can expose those services.
Some IPv6 addresses are used only within local or private networks. Temporary IPv6 addresses can change over time, making individual devices harder to track, although devices on the same home network may still share a recognizable address prefix.
Is IPv6 riskier than IPv4 if a hacker has your IP address?
IPv6 can give devices their own public IP addresses, which sounds riskier than it is. A properly configured router firewall can still block unsolicited connections while allowing responses to traffic initiated from inside your network.
An OpenWrt user on Reddit turned on IPv6, tested their home server remotely, and discovered that their remote-access and file-sharing ports were reachable from outside the network. Their firewall had been set to allow forwarding, and changing that setting to reject closed the opening.
In October 2026, Microsoft disclosed CVE-2026-105016, a critical vulnerability in its QUIC implementation. It could allow specially crafted IPv6 traffic to execute code in affected .NET applications on Windows. Microsoft's advisory hasn't mentioned whether attackers had exploited the flaw.
So rather than disabling IPv6 altogether, check your router's firewall settings for both protocols, remove unnecessary remote-access rules, and install security updates. Microsoft mentions that turning off IPv6 could result in problems with some of the Windows components. And while a VPN can hide your usual public IP address from websites if it handles both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic correctly, it isn't going to patch vulnerable software. It's also worth checking that your VPN is working before you rely on it.

A video circulating on social media purportedly shows External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar recounting how a Russian minister mocked him over the India-China border dispute, questioning India’s position on China before he advised Russia on its conflict with Ukraine. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar recounting how a Russian minister mocked him over the India-China border dispute.
Fact: The viral video is manipulated. It features an actual video of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar speaking in Atlanta, US, about discussions on the Russia-Ukraine conflict at the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting. The original audio has been replaced with fabricated remarks. The MEA Fact Check also flagged the viral video as fake. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements confirming the claim.
We also reviewed the official social media accounts of the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) (here, here, and here) and S Jaishankar (here, here, and here) but found no mention of the alleged exchange or the remarks attributed to him.
We noticed that the viral video carries a watermark from the news agency ANI. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 01 November 2026, featuring the same footage of Jaishankar, wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, his actual remarks in the original video were entirely different. He was speaking in Atlanta, US, about the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and discussions on the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The viral clip has been manipulated, with fabricated audio added to the original footage.
Suspecting the video was doctored, we analysed it with multiple AI detection tools, including Hive AI and NVIDIA’s Synthetic Video Detector. Hive AI gave an aggregate score of 99.4%, indicating a high likelihood of AI-generated or manipulated content. NVIDIA’s detector also classified the footage as synthetic media.
The MEA Fact Check also debunked the claim in an X post (archived) dated 3 November 2026, flagging the viral video as fake and cautioning against the circulation of such malicious posts on social media.
To sum up, this viral video of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar allegedly saying a Russian minister mocked him over the India-China border dispute is a deepfake.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.
A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.
The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.
The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.
Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.
In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”
Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.
British health authorities say the risk to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.
There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, according to the UK Health Security Agency.

Two Australians have survived a helicopter crash after it nosedived into an Indonesian river while fighting fires on the island of Borneo.
Video shows the helicopter collecting water for water-bombing operations from a river in Indonesia's South Kalimantan province.

Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
- Published
David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.
It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.
David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.
"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".
Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".
David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.
Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.
"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.
By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.
For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.
But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.
"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."
Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.
"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.
"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired – they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.
During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

The opening film this evening at Camerimage was Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI origin story Artificial, starring Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as key creative Ilya Sutskever. “I’ve been interested and kind of curious about the personalities of what they call tech oligarchs or tech bros for a while,” Guadagnino said. “And when I got the script that Simon Rich wrote, the world he was describing was an immediate hook for me because there was a lot in that that could be told about the dynamics of power and narcissism but at the same time it was an unprecedented setup for showing how very few people control societies.”
When pressed about whether there were constraints from a legal perspective when making a film featuring real people like Altman and Sutskever, Guadagnino said: “The only constraints we gave ourselves were facts. We wanted it to be factual, and we didn’t want to dramatize anything.”

- The claim that every calf birthed on a Texas ranch has been stillborn following the construction of a nearby artificial intelligence data center is unproven.
- The rumor has spread since at least May 2026. It appears to be based on an account shared by Clayton Tucker — the Democratic incoming Texas agriculture commissioner — who described a rancher in the state allegedly experiencing repeated cattle stillbirths after such a facility was built nearby.
- None of the versions of the story contain enough verifiable details to identify the rancher or the nearby facility. The accounts also differ regarding whether the plant is an AI data center or a battery energy storage system. The Texas Animal Health Commission said via email that it has not received any complaints or reports matching the account and has found no related investigations.
- It was not possible to find any scientific evidence linking noise or electromagnetic fields from data centers to cattle stillbirths.
- Snopes has reached out to Tucker — as well as veterinary and scientific experts specializing in cattle reproduction, noise and electromagnetic fields — for more information. We await replies to our inquiries and will update this article if additional information surfaces.
Throughout 2026, a claim circulated that every calf birthed on an unnamed Texas ranch has been stillborn following the construction of a nearby artificial intelligence data center.
For instance, one popular Instagram post (archived) from October features an image with text that says:
A Texas rancher says every calf born on his ranch has been stillborn since a data center was built next door.
They will call it anecdotal. A man burying calf after calf does not need a peer-reviewed study to know the building next door changed something.
(Instagram user @wonderzofthewild)
The caption attributes the story to Clayton Tucker — the Democratic candidate who won the 2026 midterms race to become the next Texas agriculture commissioner — and suggests "noise or vibrations" from the facility could be affecting the cattle.
Iterations of the rumor have spread widely on X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit and TikTok. One Instagram user posted about it in early June 2026 without mentioning any identifying details. Snopes readers also contacted us to ask whether the story is true.
In short, it was not possible to find evidence confirming the rumor. None of the posts identify the rancher or the facility, while different versions of the story describe the facility as either a data center or a battery energy storage system. A spokesperson for the Texas Animal Health Commission said via email the agency has not received any reports or complaints about cattle stillbirths near data centers or battery storage facilities.
It was also not possible to find evidence that noise or electromagnetic fields from data centers cause cattle stillbirths.
Given the above and the lack of verifiable information, we have left this claim unrated.
Origin of rumor
The source of the claim, and the origin of the story at the heart of it, is unclear. Some of the earliest accounts come from Tucker, though it was not possible to establish when he first heard the alleged story.
Tucker discussed the supposed issue in a YouTube video posted on May 18, in which he said a farmer told him they had "not had a new calf in about two years" because of "ultra-low-frequency" noise and vibrations originating from a nearby AI data center.
He then told the story during a June 1 meeting of the Bell County Commissioners Court, at a July 7 Lubbock City Council meeting (around 1:33:51) — on that occasion citing numerous farmers — and during an August interview, in which he said a retired man bought a ranch in Fannin County, north of Dallas, but had to sell it for a loss due to a nearby data center causing multiple calf stillbirths.
Tucker's descriptions of the facility have, at times, differed. For instance, during an Aug. 24 podcast interview, he described the plant at the center of the story as a battery energy storage system (BESS), rather than an AI data center.
Local reporting confirms that a battery energy storage facility was built near Savoy, Fannin County. Meanwhile, reports from March describe plans for a data center in the area, but it was not possible to confirm that one was operating when Tucker began sharing the story. We also could not establish whether either one was the facility Tucker described.
Tucker shared posts repeating the allegation on Oct. 17 and Oct. 25. His captions acknowledge that "no veterinarian has confirmed the stillbirths" and that "no study has tied data center noise to livestock deaths," but still suggest data centers are to blame.
Separately, in April 2026 testimony (Page 42) to Texas lawmakers, Fannin County resident Cindy Tronzano reported that her cattle stopped grazing near a BESS facility and that her family had moved because of the noise. She did not mention stillbirths and it is unclear whether her account is connected to Tucker's story.
Snopes has contacted Tucker seeking more details about the stories he has repeatedly told. We will update this article if we receive a response.
A spokesperson for the Texas Animal Health Commission said via email that it has not received any reports or complaints about cattle stillbirths near data centers or battery storage facilities. The agency also said it has not found any investigations matching those circumstances.
Potential effects of data center noise on cattle
Data centers can produce continuous noise from cooling systems and other equipment, but it was not possible to locate evidence that such noise causes calf stillbirths, like the ones Tucker has discussed.
A 2023 scientific review published in "Annals of Animal Science" found that noise can cause stress in cattle and affect their behavior and health. It did not establish a connection between noise and stillbirths.
In early September 2026, French news agency Agence France-Presse investigated similar claims about data centers causing health problems and deaths among animals, including cattle and honeybees. Researcher Said Benaissa reportedly told AFP that studies do not support claims that electromagnetic fields from data centers cause cattle stillbirths. He reportedly said some studies have found small changes in fertility cycles and milk production.
It should be noted that electromagnetic fields and noise are different things. Therefore, these findings do not directly address the claims about low-frequency noise that social media posts cited.
What a September 2026 noise survey found
Some social media posts cite a survey that two nonprofit organizations, Quiet Communities and Science for Georgia, published in September 2026. Out of 103 people surveyed near data centers or cryptomining facilities, 83% reported hearing the noise they produce inside their homes. The organizations also note that some equipment can produce noise above 80 decibels.
The survey involved a small group and includes no reference to measuring noise at a Texas ranch. Only about 20% of respondents could answer questions about livestock, which was too little data to analyze. Therefore, the survey did not provide evidence linking data center noise to cattle stillbirths.
Snopes contacted experts in cattle reproduction, acoustics and electromagnetic fields for comment on the rumor about the calf stillbirths in Texas. We are awaiting their responses.
For further reading, we have previously investigated numerous other claims about data centers.

This week on Uncanny Valley, Hugo Lowell, David Gilbert, and Vittoria Elliott from WIRED’s politics team join Leah Feiger to break down how Democrats flipped both the House and the Senate, and why the MAGA base is pinning the losses on Trump and the Iran war.
