The US Food and Drug Administration has approved an India-made generic version of the world's only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV -- a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organisations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir.
The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy's Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
The drug is expected to cost USD 40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they're needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk.
People don't always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Perez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organisation Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.”
Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS -- and deaths. According to the WHO, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.
With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV programme for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organisation.
“And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.”
Generic lenacapavir can't be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is USD 28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that's similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA's standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent.
Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.
“We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.”
Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection.
“For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.”
Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by FDA.
“The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.”
Casa said she's optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV.
“Now,” she said, “we have the tools.”

Voters approved Question 1, which places protections for first- and second-trimester abortions in the state constitution. However, it also gives the state Legislature the power to pass some restrictions on abortions in the third trimester.
As the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections rolled in, posts on social media suggested that Virginia voters had approved an amendment to the state's constitution that would allow, as one X post put it, "the abortion of babies who are minutes from being born."
Snopes readers also contacted us looking for more information about the supposed vote.
The claim is false.
The posts used common anti-abortion framing to create a misleading description of a real proposal on the ballot, Question 1. The measure, which voters overwhelmingly approved, does enshrine in Virginia's constitution an individual's right to receive an abortion.
However, the measure explicitly contains an exception allowing the state Legislature to pass laws that restrict access to some abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy. Because this exception exists, Virginia voters did not approve "abortions up to birth."
It's also worth reviewing basic facts about abortions — doing so reveals that the anti-abortion posts are using dramatic language to attack a strawman argument they created.
The strawman argument
The misleading posts do not mention how far into their pregnancies women generally receive abortions. That's because the language of the claim relies on the idea that late-term abortions are a common practice, while the medical data shows they are quite uncommon.
According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the premier professional association for OB/GYNs in the U.S., less than 1% of abortions in the country are performed in the third trimester, and about 1% of abortions are performed after the woman has reached 21 weeks of pregnancy. The nonprofit Guttmacher Institute, a highly reputable source of information on abortion data, estimated that doctors performed 1.13 million abortion procedures throughout the country in 2025. Therefore, only about 11,300 abortions total were performed after the 21-week mark, still seven weeks shy of the third trimester.
In sum, late-term abortions are incredibly rare. The ACOG lists the following reasons why they are performed:
- As a result of a fetal diagnosis received later in pregnancy that may have a profound impact on the pregnancy's prognosis
- As a result of a diagnosis related to risks to their own health during pregnancy that did not present until later in pregnancy
- Not recognizing that they were pregnant until later in the pregnancy, which may delay them in presenting to start care
- Barriers to obtaining care earlier in pregnancy, including limited financial means, inability to travel, or work or childcare obligations
- A combination of any of the above
To put it another way, doctors, who take an oath to do no harm, perform late-term abortions because the baby is "life-limiting," the mother may not survive the pregnancy or the mother couldn't have the procedure earlier, even if she wanted to.
Question 1, explained
Question 1 enshrines the right to an abortion without any limitations through the first and second trimesters of pregnancy, amongst other reproductive care. This language reinforces the access currently available under Virginia law, according to reproductive healthcare nonprofit Planned Parenthood.
The amendment specifically permits the state Legislature to enact laws restricting abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy, with caveats. Those laws may not restrict abortions if "the patient's health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive," according to the wording on the ballot.
The following paragraph is the actual language of that caveat that will be added to the state constitution, according to Ballotpedia:
Notwithstanding the above, the Commonwealth may regulate the provision of abortion care in the third trimester, provided that in no circumstance shall the Commonwealth prohibit an abortion (i) that in the professional judgment of a physician is medically indicated to protect the life or physical or mental health of the pregnant individual or (ii) when in the professional judgment of a physician the fetus is not viable.
In addition, Question 1 also protects both patients and medical providers from punishment for providing or receiving abortion care.

Resource group for Education and Advocacy for Community Health (REACH), a not-for-profit organisation working to strengthen the tuberculosis (TB) response in India, has been awarded the Kochon Prize 2026, becoming the first civil society, non-profit organisation from India to receive this prestigious global recognition for its contributions to combating TB, a press release said.
Presented by the Kochon Foundation, an independent Korean non-profit foundation, in partnership with the Stop TB Partnership, the Kochon Prize recognises individuals and organisations that have made significant contributions to the fight against TB. The 2026 Kochon Prize is shared by REACH, the Centre for Health Solutions, Kenya, and the Marshall Islands TB Control Program. Previous winners from India include L.S. Chauhan (2006), head of the Revised National TB Control Programme, the Indian Council of Medical Research (2017) and Molbio Diagnostics (2024). The award was presented at the Stop TB Partnership Board Meeting held in Indonesia on November 5, 2026.
“Treat the person, not the disease - our journey with TB communities has been just that. We realised early on that overcoming barriers to care means addressing more than clinical needs - it means recognising social, community, family, mental health and situational challenges. That is the essence of integrated care: seeing the whole person, understanding their realities, and doing whatever it takes to ensure that no one is left behind,” said Nalini Krishnan, chairperson and co-founder, REACH.
“REACH is a remarkable and rare organisation that has been consistently ahead of the curve in terms of public health action, and particularly in the field of TB. A women-led organisation, they genuinely care about the people they’re supporting, beyond the numbers, data and reports to donor. However, they combine this with a robust scientific and technical approach and a shrewd understanding of the public health landscape in the country,” said Soumya Swaminathan, chairperson, M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation and former chief scientist, WHO, who nominated REACH for the award.
“This recognition is testimony to the dedication of the community health workers, TB Nanbans and TB Champions who work alongside us, and to the families affected by TB and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) who have placed their trust in us. We are deeply grateful to their unwavering commitment and fortitude, and are energised to do more to help facilitate equitable access to health,” said Ramya Ananthakrishnan, director, REACH.

An Indian Air Force (IAF) IL-76MD heavy-lift transport aircraft has landed at the Nyoma airbase in eastern Ladakh at an altitude of 13,629 feet, setting a world record for the highest-altitude landing by an aircraft of its class. The achievement marks a significant milestone in India's strategic airlift capabilities, demonstrating the IAF's ability to operate heavy military transport aircraft in some of the world's most challenging high-altitude terrain. It also strengthens India's logistical reach close to the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. The Russian-origin four-engine aircraft, known as the 'Gajraj', landed at the airbase on Friday. Located approximately 25 km from the LAC, Nyoma is emerging as a key military infrastructure asset for India's forward deployment and logistical operations in eastern Ladakh. The development comes amid continued military sensitivities along the India-China border. Although the two countries have completed disengagement at several friction points and resumed patrolling arrangements since October 2024, a complete de-escalation of troops in eastern Ladakh remains a broader strategic concern. The successful landing demonstrates the IAF's ability to operate a heavy strategic transport aircraft at an altitude where thin air, reduced engine performance and difficult terrain pose considerable operational challenges. The IL-76MD can transport approximately 40–45 tonnes of cargo, depending on its configuration and operating conditions. This includes heavy military equipment and platforms such as infantry combat vehicles and other armoured assets. Its ability to land at Nyoma could significantly improve the movement of troops, equipment and supplies to forward areas, reducing dependence on airfields located farther from the China border, including Leh and Thoise. The aircraft also played an important role during the 2020 India-China military standoff in eastern Ladakh, when the IAF used its heavy-lift capabilities to transport military equipment and other essential assets to the region, according to an Indian Express report. The IAF announced the latest achievement in a post on X, describing it as a "remarkable demonstration of the aircraft's enduring capability", backed by the skill, precision and professionalism of its crew. It added that the landing was a milestone reinforcing India's strategic capabilities. The landing also highlights the growing operational importance of the Nyoma airbase, which has been developed as a strategic military facility close to the LAC. The airfield, located in the Nyoma subdivision of Leh district, was originally constructed in 1962 as a mud-paved landing ground but remained largely inactive for several decades. It was reactivated in 2009 after an AN-32 aircraft successfully landed there, demonstrating its potential for military operations. Following the 2020 border standoff with China, the airstrip supported the operations of several IAF aircraft, including the C-130J and AN-32 transport aircraft, as well as Apache attack helicopters and Chinook heavy-lift helicopters. The airbase was subsequently upgraded under a Border Roads Organisation (BRO) project estimated at around ₹214–218 crore, as per Indian Express. Its approximately 2.7–3-km runway, built with a rigid pavement surface, is designed to support the operations of military transport aircraft and fighter jets. Nyoma's proximity to the LAC makes it particularly important for rapid mobilisation. The ability to move heavy equipment and personnel directly to a forward airbase could reduce logistical turnaround times and strengthen India's capacity to sustain troops deployed in eastern Ladakh. The facility is especially valuable given the region's difficult geography and extreme weather conditions. Situated in the cold-desert terrain of the Changthang plateau, Nyoma experiences temperatures that can fall to around –30°C. Its high altitude and rugged mountainous surroundings also make infrastructure construction and aircraft operations challenging, with the construction window limited to a few months each year. The IAF has demonstrated its ability to operate military transport aircraft at extreme altitudes in eastern Ladakh before. In 2013, an IAF C-130J Super Hercules successfully landed at the Daulat Beg Oldie (DBO) airstrip, situated at an altitude of approximately 16,614 feet. That landing demonstrated the IAF's ability to operate transport aircraft at even higher elevations. However, the latest Nyoma landing is significant because of the aircraft involved. Unlike the C-130J, the IL-76MD is a much heavier strategic transport aircraft, with a substantially larger payload capacity. Operating an aircraft of this size at high altitude presents additional challenges because thinner air reduces lift and engine performance, requiring careful calculations of payload, runway requirements and operating conditions. The successful landing therefore demonstrates a different dimension of India's strategic airlift capability, particularly its ability to transport heavier military equipment closer to forward deployment areas. Despite the achievement, the landing also draws attention to the challenges facing India's ageing strategic transport fleet. India acquired 17 IL-76 aircraft between 1985 and 1989, making the Gajraj fleet one of the IAF's oldest heavy-lift assets. The aircraft have faced serviceability challenges over the years, particularly because of difficulties in sourcing spare parts following the collapse of the Soviet Union. These challenges have been further complicated by the Russia-Ukraine war. There have been discussions about extending the technical service life of around a dozen IL-76 aircraft. At the same time, the IAF is pursuing its Medium Transport Aircraft (MTA) programme, which is intended to replace both the IL-76 and AN-32 fleets. The latest landing at Nyoma is significant not only as an aviation milestone but also as a demonstration of the capabilities India continues to rely on to maintain military readiness along its disputed border with China. Often derided as a “B-class” cuisine, Japanese curry was adapted from the British navy in the late 19th century but has grown to be its own paradigm.
Mildly spiced, usually store-bought bases are bulked up with meat and vegetables before being infused at home with ingredients akin to family secrets: apple, honey, soy sauce and miso are all common kakushi aji (literally, “hidden flavors”) — components that may not register overtly but elevate a dish overall.
Making curry roux cubes, complete with your own kakushi aji, is surprisingly simple. When mixed with water, each cube from this recipe will make approximately 550 milliliters of curry, a generous portion for four adults when combined with other fillings. There is no chile whatsoever in the base recipe, but there is room for adaptation. Feel free to incorporate as much or little heat as you like, adding or subtracting other spices or kakushi aji as you like.
Makes 6 125-gram cubes
Cook time: 45 minutes
Ingredients:
Whole spices for toasting
- 7 1/2 grams cumin seeds
- 7 1/2 grams coriander seeds
- 7 1/2 grams fennel seeds
- 7 1/2 grams cinnamon stick
- 7 1/2 grams black peppercorns
- 5 grams cardamom pods
- 5 grams fenugreek seeds
- 2 1/2 grams cloves
- 2 1/2 grams allspice
- 2 bay leaves
Powders and kakushi aji:
- 10 grams dried kombu (I used shaved tororo kombu)
- 5 grams dried shiitake
- 5 grams dried mandarin peel
- 10 grams salt
- 10 grams cocoa powder
- 5 grams ground turmeric
- 5 grams powdered ginger
Roux:
- 350 grams butter
- 275 grams all-purpose flour
- 50 grams honey
Directions:
- In a small pan, add all of your whole spices and toast over medium heat for about one to two minutes or until fragrant. If you use powdered spices, skip the toasting.
- Place everything in a spice grinder or mortar and pestle in batches with the kombu, shiitake and mandarin peel. Pulse to grind until it reaches the consistency of a powder. Once done, mix in your salt, turmeric, ginger and cocoa to form a curry powder.
- In a medium pot, melt your butter over medium heat. When the butter begins to lightly brown, add the flour and stir constantly until the roux turns dark brown. This could take up to 10 minutes. A richer color equals more flavor, but do not allow it to burn or stick to the pan. Remove from heat and add the curry powder. Stir until completely combined, then add in the honey.
- Carefully pour out the hot mixture into six silicone muffin molds or freezer containers. You can also leave the mixture to set as a single piece, then carefully divide it later. Place it in the refrigerator to harden.
- Once completely solid, remove the roux pieces from the mold or container and place them in an airtight container. They will last a month or more refrigerated or six months in the freezer.

Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
- Published
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past 
  - Published31 October 2025
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.
"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.
The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.
Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.
Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.
Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.
And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.
And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.
"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.
When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Healthcare of last resort
Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.
But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)
Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.
Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.
"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."
And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.
Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.
Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.
For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.
"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."
Training elite clinicians
This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.
Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.
"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.
When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.
Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.
On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.
Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."
His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.
"What happened to you?" Horne asks.
"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.
A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.
Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.
Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.
Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.
Experiments
Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.
Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.
EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.
"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.
That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.
"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."
About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."
Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.
Today's trip
The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.
Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.
But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.
Merklin serves on a peer support team.
"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."
If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."
As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.
Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.
Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

An ex-New York City police officer who was kicked off the force after being deemed psychologically unfit has been arrested in the fatal stabbing of a Brooklyn jogger.
Sayed Mohassib, 27, was charged with second-degree murder, tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon Saturday in the October 30 killing of Katie Suarez. The 28-year-old was fatally stabbed in the neck while running along the Shore Parkway Greenway near her home.
Mohassib, who was working as an elementary school aide at the time of his arrest, allegedly told investigators he had no memory of the attack but woke up covered in blood and holding a knife, according to police sources cited by the New York Post.
Investigators tracked Mohassib to his Bensonhurst home after surveillance footage allegedly showed him leaving the park around the time Suarez was attacked. Police believe he disposed of the weapon in the garbage, which was taken to a Staten Island landfill before eventually ending up at a New Jersey dump, the outlet reports.
Suarez, a TD Bank teller training for an upcoming race, was following her usual waterfront running route after work on October 30. She planned to meet her parents afterward.
She spoke to her dad on the phone around 7:56 p.m., telling him she was about half a mile away and would meet him shortly, according to NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny. When she never arrived, her dad went looking for her and found her unconscious beneath a tree along the waterfront path around 8:16 p.m.
Suarez was taken to the hospital with serious neck injuries. She was later declared brain dead but remained on life support so her organs could be donated. She died three days after the attack.
The circumstances surrounding Mohassib's arrest prompted interest in his previous time in law enforcement and the military.
Mohassib initially worked as a paraprofessional for the NYC Department of Education before joining the NYPD in 2022. However, he spent only about six weeks on the force before leaving to enlist in the Marines, according to the Post.
The military later discharged him after determining he was psychologically unfit for service, police sources told the outlet. Mohassib subsequently attempted to rejoin the NYPD but was denied and returned to working for the city's education department.
He was employed as a paraprofessional at PS 200 in Bensonhurst, just blocks from the waterfront area where Suarez was attacked.
Mohassib returned to the elementary school in the days after the stabbing, but colleagues reportedly became concerned by his erratic behavior and incoherent speech. They alerted police, although those reports were not what ultimately led investigators to him, according to the Post.
Resurfaced photographs of Mohassib also show him wearing an NYPD dress uniform and posing in a Brooklyn College basketball uniform. He attended Brooklyn College during the same period as Suarez, although investigators have not established whether the two knew each other, according to the outlet.
Police believe the attack was random, according to ABC7. The investigation remains ongoing.

Dozens of global health and environmental organisations called on the World Health Organization on Tuesday to revise decades-old standards for nitrate levels in drinking water, arguing they do not reflect recent scientific evidence about potential health risks.
In an open letter, 85 organisations, including Greenpeace International and the World Organization of Family Doctors (WONCA), called on the United Nations health agency to include nitrate in an upcoming review of its drinking water guidelines.
The toxic effects of nitrates -- a residue left behind by intensive farming -- are widely recognised as particularly dangerous for children and pregnant women.
But the current WHO guidelines -- which set the maximum acceptable nitrate level in drinking water at 50 milligrammes per litre as nitrate or 11.3 milligrammes per litre as nitrate-nitrogen -- date back to 1958 and are "outdated", the organisations warned.
That level was set specifically to prevent so-called "blue-baby syndrome" -- a deadly blood disorder in which the blood's capacity for carrying oxygen is reduced.
But the limit "has not been updated in response to robust epidemiological evidence linking chronic, low-level nitrate exposure to long-term human health risks", Tuesday's letter said, pointing in particular to "colorectal cancer and adverse birth outcomes".
"Studies now link nitrate in drinking water, at levels well below the current WHO limit, to bowel cancer and premature birth," WONCA chair Pratyush Kumar said in a joint statement.
Decisive action
The letter was sent to coincide with WHO's annual One Health Day, which aims to raise awareness about the interconnected health of humans, animals, plants and shared ecosystems.
Surface water models indicate that hundreds of millions of people globally are exposed to elevated nitrate levels, the letter warned.
"Water should be life-giving, not life-threatening," Amanda Larsson, the global project lead for agriculture at Greenpeace, said in the statement.
"We cannot protect human health without protecting the groundwater and rivers that sustain us," she insisted.
"Governments must take decisive action to curb the growth of intensive livestock farming and actively support producers in transitioning to ecological farming practices -- ensuring that clean, safe drinking water isn't a luxury but a guarantee."
The organisations pointed to findings published last year by an expert panel commissioned by the Danish government indicating that the current international standard was insufficient to protect public health.
That expert panel recommended reducing the nitrate limit to 6.0 mg/L -- nearly 10 times below the current WHO benchmark -- something Denmark committed to earlier this year.
But most national governments base their drinking water standards on WHO guidelines, the organisations said, stressing that updating those guidelines was "vital for global policy reform".

A video circulating on X, bearing the logo of M World, purports to show Russian foreign minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov saying that India is merely an oil-trading partner to Russia and that the two countries share only a commercial relationship. In the video, Lavrov is also heard claiming that India has no right to interfere in Russia’s foreign policy or advise Moscow on matters concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States or any other country.
Supreme Court advocate and activist Prashant Bhushan shared the video on his X account (@pbhushan1), which he later deleted. In his post, he criticized the Indian government and questioned what kind of advice external affairs minister S Jaishankar gave to Russia.
Another X account, Diya Kapoor, also shared the video with the similar claim of Sergey Lavrov drawing clear boundaries about the relationship with India.
🚨🇷🇺🇮🇳 RUSSIA DRAWS A CLEAR LINE!
“India is a trading partner, nothing more. We supply oil, and India pays for it. This commercial relationship does not give New Delhi the right to dictate or interfere in Russia’s foreign policy.”
Sergey Viktorovich ⚠️🌍 https://t.co/uX1x0adl0G
— Diya kapoor (@DiyaKapoor113) November 2, 2026
Some X accounts also shared this video with the claim of Sergey Lavrov dismissing India.
Fact Check
After a closer examination of the video, the movements of Sergey Lavrov while speaking appear unnatural and seem out of sync with the audio. This suggests that the clip may have been edited or manipulated. Using this as a lead, we performed a Google reverse image search on several keyframes from the video and found a video with the same background and clothing uploaded by M WORLD on October 31.
A comparison of the two videos shows that Sergey Lavrov’s clothing, background, head movements, and hand gestures are the same, with only the audio being different. Even the ‘M World’ YouTube channel logo appeared in both videos, confirming that the original video had been digitally manipulated. Both videos also feature the exact same glitch at the same moment.
In the original video, Sergey Lavrov is seen refusing the reports from Ukrainian officials claiming that Russian President Vladimir Putin refused to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and stating if Zelenskyy wants a direct meeting, he must travel to Moscow, where Russia will guarantee his safety and security.
Media outlet DW News posted the original video on October 31 showing the conversation about President Putin and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy meeting.
Furthermore, the official X account of the Russian Embassy in India, Russia in India (@RusEmbIndia) has also debunked the video. “Please stop copying silly AI fakes,” it said in a comment to the X post by Diya Kapoor.
@DiyaKapoor113 Please stop copying silly AI fakes
— Russia in India 🇷🇺 (@RusEmbIndia) November 3, 2026
Union government’s official MEA fact check account, too, flagged the post as fake.
Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨
The video of the Russian Foreign Minister being used in this post is fake! https://t.co/jpEX6qu19p
— MEA FactCheck (@MEAFactCheck) November 3, 2026
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov publicly dismissed India’s diplomatic standing is completely false and an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage contains a briefing regarding Russia-Ukraine relations, and there is no mention of India.
Twinkle Shrivastav is an intern at Alt News.

The parents of a 13-year-old girl have sued Google claiming she planned a potential suicide and funeral using its AI technology on a school-issued computer.
Filed Monday in a California court, the complaint is the first known case accusing Google of negligence related to AI integrations on Chromebooks, the tech giant's low-cost laptops used by millions of students in the United States and around the world.
The teenager was not able to access Google's Gemini app, nor OpenAI's ChatGPT, because they were blocked by her school. She was nonetheless still able to use Google's search engine, which contains AI-powered tools.
Those features were notably not among the tools that Google announced this week will be disabled by default for students.
"Schools should turn search off and keep it off until Google removes AI mode from search or ensures that every single student is always safe when they're interacting with AI," Andrew Liddell, one of the family's attorneys, told AFP on Thursday.
The complaint alleges that the child had been a "happy 13-year-old girl" in North Carolina who received great grades, played music and participated in Girl Scouts.
Despite "no history" of mental illness, within months of using Google's AI-powered search on her school laptop, she began a "quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis" according to the complaint.
On March 17, the school's monitoring software flagged a document titled "Funeral," and the school notified her parents.
Her mother then saw the child writing a farewell letter in real-time after logging into her daughter's account, and her father intervened.
"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told AFP.
Google argues that AI mode includes safeguards against self-harm and attempts to bypass them.
But the child "was able to keep going back over and over and over again," Liddle said. "Whatever safeguards they think they put in place were obviously insufficient."
Developers of fast-evolving AI technology are facing a litany of similar lawsuits in the US.
OpenAI faces several wrongful death suits, including from the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, a teenager who committed suicide allegedly using methods advised by ChatGPT.
Google and the startup Character.AI agreed in January to settle several lawsuits filed by families of teenagers out of court.
On Wednesday, Google, TikTok and Meta each separately sued California to block a law that prohibits social media companies from providing addictive features to users under 16.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law in September, and it goes into effect on January 1, 2027.

Old powers reign again as Australia crushes Samoa to make Rugby League World Cup final
They say you can't fight city hall, but sometimes against Australia, it feels like you're flat out breaking a few windows.
The Kangaroos cruised into the World Cup final by turning Samoa's dream into a recurring nightmare via their 44-12 win in Sydney on Sunday night.
As New Zealand did the night before, Australia won this on the finer margins.
Spirit filled the night through the anthems, where tears again flowed freely, and the Siva Tau, which ended with Brian To'o and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui sharing a moment more powerful than words can say.
Moments like that are the big things, the reason these matches matter in the first place. And it's what makes them feel like more than a game but through the blinding emotion there is still a game to be won.
To do it when it really matters, you need to do all the little things and Australia proved it's the little things that make up life right from the start as, not for the first time, its science defeated Samoa's magic on the big stage.
Against any other team, it might not matter that Francis Manuleleua and Jazz Tevaga, two middle forwards, found themselves defend together off a scrum. It's not the done thing, but you can get away with it.
But the Kangaroo punished Samoa for that lapse when Tom Dearden took them and threw a dummy everyone knows is coming but nobody seems to know how to stop for the first try of the night.
Like the hardest teachers, Australia stressed the same lesson over and over again and Samoa's inability to change the course meant frustration took hold, which only made things worse.
Three times in the first half alone, Samoa conceded a penalty, a set restart and a try in quick sequence. For the final 19 minutes of the half, they got to their kick just twice.
Give Australia that much ball and field position and you're asking for punishment.
The Kangaroos ran up the tries and carried a 26-2 lead into the break that killed off the game as a contest and robbed the blue wave in the stands of their power.
The harder the Samoans tried and the more venom they played with, the more it turned to a choking bile in their throats.
Spencer Leniu dropped the ball with his first touch, got sin-binned for dissent, then dropped the ball with his first touch on return.
They did what they could to the end, and twice had tries chalked off by the barest of margins. But in the end Australia were too clinical, too clever, too willing and able to exploit every little edge on offer until it all added up to a comfortable win.
Samoa's poor discipline — Adam Gee pinged them for a combined 12 restarts and penalties in the end — and errors would have been much to overcome against most sides and most sides aren't packing Australia's heat.
Reece Walsh, raced in a brilliant hat-trick to continue his dazzling tournament and put himself right in the frame to be awarded the Golden Boot on Thursday as the best international player of the year.
The Broncos firecracker was the explosion and the fuse was lit by Cameron Munster and Harry Grant, who were in total control of every aspect of the match throughout.
Pat Carrigan and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui were both strong in the middle in a performance that should help restore a little of the Australian forwards battered reputation.
The win would have been a personal triumph for Fa'asuamaleaui given the Samoa international copped plenty from the crowd.
The Pacific nations have given this World Cup so much and they feel like the future of Test football. But this game was a reminder of the power of old money and that the most dangerous creatures in these waters are still Kangaroos.
There is a reason, for all the improvement Samoa and Tonga have made in recent years, they only have one win over Australia from a combined 10 attempts.
It's the same reason Australia has only lost one game from 18 starts in the set restart era, which is the same reason they haven't lost a game on home soil in 11 years.
To climb the green and gold mountain, you need to be as close as perfect as reality can allow because need a way to douse their firepower and blunt their smarts while getting just about everything right yourself.
New Zealand have the team to do it, to the point they should be favourites for the final. But it's no guarantee they will because team as fierce and skilled as Samoa, for all their might and power, couldn't really get themselves in the fight.
After all their growth, it is the last step they need to take but perhaps the longest of all.
The Kangaroos are as ruthless as they are well-drilled, as fast as they are merciless.
That is why, even as the Davids have gotten bigger, Goliath still reigns.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.
The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.
Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region’s undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
One cable under construction, the 2Africa cable, is owned by a tech consortium that includes the US company Meta. That was one of the major cable corridors visited by the drifting Iran-linked ships.
Windward used both ship-tracking data and satellite images to track the vessels as they slowed down and looped around near multiple cables, with some ships then “going dark” by switching off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders that normally broadcast their location and other information.
Such movement and behavioral patterns suggest the Iran-linked ships may be “mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark,” Windward told the Financial Times.
Windward highlighted the examples of two sanctioned tankers linked to Iran that spent days drifting “directly over regional cable corridors… both with no commercial reason to stop” in a blog post on October 26. Both ships carried no commercial cargo.

Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has collected approximately Rs. 176 crores nett at the Indian box office in its first three days. While the mythological epic has generated substantial business across the country, a detailed state-wise analysis reveals several fascinating trends. Maharashtra has emerged as the film's highest-grossing market, narrowly beating Karnataka. However, the bigger surprise is that Karnataka has sold more tickets than Maharashtra despite generating lower revenue.
According to the detailed box office data for November 5, 6 and 7, Maharashtra leads with Rs. 32.96 crores nett, followed closely by Karnataka at Rs. 30.29 crores. The National Capital Region (NCR) occupies the third position with Rs. 17.95 crores, while Telangana and Gujarat complete the top five.
Maharashtra No. 1 in revenue, but Karnataka wins the footfall battle
Maharashtra has emerged as Ramayana's biggest revenue-generating market, contributing approximately 18.73% of the film's nationwide nett collections.
The state collected Rs. 10.12 crores on Thursday, followed by Rs. 8.55 crores on Friday and a substantial Rs. 14.28 crores on Saturday. Interestingly, Maharashtra witnessed a massive 67.05% jump on Saturday compared with Friday, helping it consolidate its lead over Karnataka. Karnataka, meanwhile, has collected Rs. 30.29 crores over three days, accounting for approximately 17.22% of the nationwide total.
However, the ticket-sales figures tell a different story. Karnataka has sold 7.95 lakh tickets, compared with Maharashtra's 7.47 lakh tickets. In other words, Karnataka has attracted approximately 47,600 more admissions despite earning Rs. 2.66 crores less.
Maharashtra and Karnataka account for 36% of nationwide business
Together, Maharashtra and Karnataka have generated Rs. 63.25 crores nett over the first three days. This means that just two states account for nearly 36% of Ramayana's entire domestic collections. Interestingly, Karnataka led Maharashtra on Thursday, collecting Rs. 11.37 crores against Maharashtra's Rs. 10.12 crores. However, Maharashtra overtook Karnataka on Friday and widened the gap further on Saturday. This indicates that while Karnataka delivered a particularly strong opening, Maharashtra demonstrated greater momentum as the weekend progressed.
NCR takes third position; Telangana beats Gujarat
The National Capital Region (NCR) occupies the third position with Rs. 17.95 crores nett. The territory contributed Rs. 6.06 crores on Thursday, Rs. 4.88 crores on Friday and Rs. 7.01 crores on Saturday, registering a healthy recovery over the weekend. Telangana follows in fourth position with Rs. 13.28 crores, narrowly beating Gujarat's Rs. 12.78 crores. However, the ticket-sales figures reveal another interesting contrast. Telangana has sold approximately 6.39 lakh tickets, while Gujarat has registered 3.65 lakh admissions. Despite selling roughly 75% more tickets, Telangana's revenue lead over Gujarat is just Rs. 50 lakh.
Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh complete the next three positions
Tamil Nadu occupies sixth position with Rs. 7.81 crores nett, followed by West Bengal at Rs. 7.43 crores and Uttar Pradesh at Rs. 7.29 crores. Andhra Pradesh ranks ninth with Rs. 7.09 crores, while Kerala completes the top ten with Rs. 6.84 crores. Andhra Pradesh provides another fascinating example of the difference between revenue and admissions. The state has sold approximately 5.45 lakh tickets, substantially more than Gujarat, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, yet ranks below all three in revenue.

In the Israeli legislative elections held in late October 2026, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority required to govern. The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, alongside other opposition factions, captured 48 seats. Notably, Arab-led parties made historic gains by winning 19 seats, elevating them to a potential “kingmaker” role. Following the vote, President Isaac Herzog formally accepted the results and opened a two-day consultation window with party leaders to determine who is best positioned to assemble a stable coalition.
In this context, a video (here, here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that Muslim MPs are performing Namaz together in the Israeli parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of Muslim MPs performing Namaz together inside the Israeli parliament.
Fact: The video shows Jordanian MPs performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the Jordanian parliament in Amman on 03 November 2026. There are no reports of Muslim MPs performing namaz in the Israeli parliament. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we searched for reports of any such act happening in the Israeli Knesset recently but couldn’t find any credible reports to support it. Moreover, the parliament announced that Israel’s newly elected Knesset will hold its inaugural session on 10 November 2026, during which lawmakers will be sworn in, and the speaker will be elected.
Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same visuals published by BBC News Arabic and Jordanian media outlets (here, here & here). These reports state that the footage shows members of parliament performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the House of Representatives of Jordan (the Jordanian Parliament) in Amman on 03 November 2026.
The prayer was reportedly led by MP Dr. Ahmad Al-Raqab right before a scheduled legislative session to elect members of the parliament’s permanent bureau. He can be seen leading the prayer in the extended video published by some media outlets.
Furthermore, the presence of Jordan’s national emblem in the viral video, along with matching interior visuals, conclusively proves that the footage is from the Jordanian parliament and not the Israeli parliament.
To sum it up, the video from Jordan’s parliament is being falsely shared with the claim that it shows Muslim MPs performing Namaz in the Israeli parliament.

Victorian premier vows to make 'whatever changes' after delivery driver fatal stabbing
In short:
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says community safety is his top priority, after a deadly attack involving two delivery riders in Melbourne's CBD.
Jianming Feng, 47, was fatally stabbed on Friday night while making a delivery for Hungry Panda.
A 51-year-old man has been arrested over the incident.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has vowed to make "whatever changes are necessary" following the fatal stabbing attack of a delivery driver in Melbourne's CBD.
Chinese national and father of two, Jianming Feng, was fatally stabbed on Friday night while making a delivery run for Hungry Panda near the Queen Victoria Market.
Another food deliver rider, aged 34, was injured in the alleged altercation.
On Sunday, Mr Carroll said he would continue to work with the Transport Workers Union and other representatives to ensure the safety of gig economy workers.
"As premier I will ensure I do everything I can with the Chief Commissioner of Victoria Police that, no matter where you work, no matter where you shop, no matter where you live, that you are safe," he said.
"We do know that often people in the gig economy, people who are doing transit deliveries, are some of the most vulnerable Victorians and they do need proper protections in place and workplace safety."
Homicide Squad detectives have arrested a 51-year-old Footscray man over the incident.
Safety concerns on the rise
Last night hundreds of people attended a vigil for Mr Feng, with many raising concerns about safety in the city.
"This is not how we're picturing Melbourne would be like," international student Xi Ip said, who was among those at the vigil.
"We were expecting a safer community. We don't want anything like this to ever happen again. That's a 47-year-old man who has a family to support.
"This is a pure tragedy … We want police to protect not just citizens but all of the community in the city."
Another student Xenith Yen said she was considering moving back home to Shanghai.
"I feel so unsafe in this city and I am paying a very high rate of tax but I don't get anything back from this city. I want to go back home."
Student Casper Ge called on the state's leaders to do more.
"It's everyone's right to have a safe city when they're doing their job. I feel very bad for this poor man."
Ria Li, who lives next to the scene, said she had lived in Melbourne for two years and was concerned about her safety because of drug use in the CBD.
She said she wanted to see steps taken by the government and Hungry Panda, which she said was a well-used delivery service among the Chinese student community, to improve driver safety.
"In Melbourne's CBD, international students are not a small group," she said.
"It's very depressing, it's very unfair that … someone's husband, someone's son and someone's dad got killed. It's really depressing as a Chinese to see such tragedy happen right next to my apartment."
Hungry Panda and the Chinese consulate in Melbourne have been contacted for comment.

The Republicans' defeat in the U.S. midterm elections was watched closely in Russia, where some observers are predicting it could herald more support for Ukraine when the Democrats take over Congress in January.
But if the Kremlin is hearing the ticking of a clock on its nearly 5-year-old full-scale invasion of its neighbour, it seemingly remains unperturbed.
Asked if the election's outcome could stymie U.S. attempts to help negotiate a settlement between Moscow and Kyiv, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov voiced hope that U.S. President Donald Trump will continue to pursue his peace efforts.
“There is groundwork already in place, and another round of trilateral negotiations is set to take place very soon,” Mr. Peskov said of talks planned for Tuesday (November 10, 2026) and Wednesday (November 11) involving Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. representatives in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.
He also praised the “successful humanitarian peace-building efforts” by first lady Melania Trump, adding that “we hope that all of this will continue.”
Last week's limited ceasefire around the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky, brokered with her help, allowed for the delivery of humanitarian aid and the evacuation of some residents.
Mr. Peskov shrugged off a question from reporters on whether the new Congress would challenge Mr. Trump's stance on Russia and Ukraine. He called it an “internal matter” for the U.S.
Trump's recent moves have appeared to favour Moscow
Trump’s recent moves appear to favour Moscow
In recent months, Mr. Trump's actions appeared to favour Moscow
Last month, he struck a diesel fuel import deal with Russia in a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on the Kremlin, to the dismay of Ukraine and its European allies. He also claimed that Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil refineries caused a spike in diesel prices in the U.S. He urged Kyiv to halt the strikes, even though rising global energy prices were largely driven by the Iran war.
Mr. Trump also issued an executive order to put on hold sweeping new sanctions that clamped down on the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. Lawmakers from both parties blasted Mr. Trump's move as benefiting Russian President Vladimir Putin.
At the same time, Ukraine reported a throttling of Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Mr. Trump denied being behind the brief slowing of Starshield, but the move to limit the system that serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and battlefield communications was widely seen as part of Washington's efforts to pressure Kyiv.
The diesel deal appeared to falter this week after U.S. federal and state officials warned that handling any shipments could bring legal consequences, and two U.S.-bound tankers changed course. The Kremlin sought to play down the development, saying deliveries will continue.
Kyiv desperately needs to replenish its supplies of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors to fend off Russia's ballistic missile attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made repeated requests for Washington to speed up delivery of the defensive systems, but U.S. stockpiles have been exhausted by the Iran war, and the U.S. has prioritised replenishing its own arsenals.
On October 30, the Trump administration said it has approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot interceptors for Ukraine after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying delivery.
Mr. Trump also appeared to echo the Kremlin's view that Mr. Zelenskyy was an obstacle to peace while saying Mr. Putin was more open to a deal.
Mr. Trump on Thursday (November 5) conferred with Mr. Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who attended a White House ceremony with the first lady recognising last week's humanitarian truce. The President didn't meet any of the Ukrainian officials also at the event but hinted that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works.
Many in Russia argue that the Democrats' victory could put congressional pressure on Mr. Trump to tread more carefully and toughen his stand on Russia.
Dmitry Medvedev, who served as Russian President in 2008-12, predicted that Mr. Trump would be less inclined to press Ukraine when a new Congress is seated.
"He doesn't need an extra confrontation with Democrats,” said Mr. Medvedev, who now serves as deputy head of Russia's Security Council.
New House and Senate could boost aid to Ukraine
There has been strong bipartisan support for Ukraine, raising the prospect of veto-proof passage of more aid to Kyiv or tough new sanctions on Moscow.
On Wednesday (November 4), Mr. Zelenskyy told German broadcaster ZDF that while there has been backing for Kyiv from both parties, the Democrats “speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine."
In other remarks on Thursday (November 5), the Ukrainian leader also noted the midterm elections could have a positive effect on U.S. assistance, including speedier delivery of the Patriot interceptors. “I believe our chances of getting additional assistance from the United States may now grow,” he said.
Abbas Gallyamov, a former Putin speechwriter-turned-political analyst who lives abroad, argued that his old boss had missed a chance of striking a deal on Ukraine before the Democrats won and now could face a less cooperative Washington.
“Putin's prospects have significantly worsened,” Mr. Gallyamov wrote in a commentary. “He thought that the time was on his side and wasn't in a hurry to use the window of opportunity that had opened after Trump's victory, and now this window is starting to close.”
Some policy experts, however, cautioned against expectations of a dramatic shift.
The Democrats could put more funding for Ukraine on the agenda and increase pressure on Mr. Trump over the diesel deal or Russia sanctions waivers, but hard limits on the President's power are unlikely, said Jorn Fleck, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Europe Center.
“Even with a strong majority in both chambers of Congress, Democrats will struggle to impose meaningful limits on Trump's conduct of foreign policy, given his constitutional powers and willingness to push the envelope,” Mr. Fleck said in a commentary.
“Unshackled from having to face voters at the ballot box again, Trump may shift into deal-making overdrive to cement his legacy.”
Some expect a more hard-lined Trump
Konstantin Kosachev, a Deputy Speaker of the upper house of the Russian parliament, argued that Mr. Trump's executive powers in the foreign policy sphere would allow him to pursue his course regardless of congressional opposition.
He said if authorities in Kyiv believed that the Republicans' defeat would make the Trump administration more receptive to Ukraine's requests, they could be mistaken.
“They will not find a more pliable or constrained Trump," Mr. Kosachev said. “Rather, they will face a more resolute one, who is no longer looking over his shoulder at upcoming elections.”
For all the importance of Congress, "the U.S. President's role in foreign policy remains paramount — a fact Trump understands better than anyone else,” he said.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna struck a similar tone in an interview on Thursday (November 5) with The Associated Press, saying "the President is President Trump,” and he has the ability to dictate foreign and security policy. “Unpredictability” should be expected, he added.
Mr. Kosachev said that by pinning their hopes on a victory by the Democrats, Kyiv and its allies in London, Brussels and other capitals in Europe have sided with Mr. Trump's domestic political adversaries.
"Consequently, they are all but guaranteed two years of a hard-line Trump,” he said.
