Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
- Published
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

The Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) and its partners have invested in 27 projects, backed by NT$5.64 billion ($180 million) in total, including NT$740 million ($23.7 million) from the agency and NT$4.9 billion ($157 million) in private capital, TAICCA chair Sue Wang said at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF).
TAICCA brought together its four joint ventures – Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund, Enjoy Entertainment Limited Partnership, momomini Kids Content Fund and Joint Journey Creative – to present their slates. The partnerships span nine countries, and Wang said the joint-venture model allows for more professional and precise investment assessments.
Enjoy Entertainment, a partnership between TAICCA and Taiwanese telecom Far EasTone, said it had invested in 15 projects in its first 10 months: eight in film and TV and seven in music and live events. They include horror film “The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak,” which took NT$80 million ($2.6 million) at the Taiwanese box office, a franchise record, and VMTheatre Company’s “Don’t Cry, Dancing Girls the Musical,” billed at the event as the first Taiwanese musical to reach Off-Broadway.
On the music side, Enjoy developed the ID. Music Festival with Spotify, which brought 14 Taiwanese acts to two stages in the streamer’s first collaboration with a Taiwanese music event. It also highlighted “Her Voice,” a concert featuring five female performers from Taiwan and South Korea, and indie band Shallow Levée’s “Speak in Silence” project, which pairs the band’s 10th-anniversary album with collaborations with Japanese and Korean musicians and a planned tour of about 50 shows across Taiwan and eight other Asian countries.
Enjoy is also behind an immersive project marking 25 years of work by Taiwanese picture-book artist Jimmy Liao.
Gary Tsai, general manager of Enjoy Entertainment and COO of Far EasTone’s FET Entertainment Service, said the company aims to take Taiwanese original content to international audiences while adapting international IP for local viewers. Through Far EasTone’s streaming service friDay Video, investment and cross-border partnerships, it hopes to help Taiwanese productions expand overseas and create more opportunities for local talent.
Launched in December 2025, momomini Kids Content Fund has made six investments: three in animation, two in live-action and one in drama. COO Phoebe Tsai said the fund weighs each project’s potential impact on the industry alongside content production, talent development and commercial viability. It focuses on children’s content, which Phoebe Tsai said had not previously been treated as a distinct investment category in Taiwan.
Its projects include “Who’s Our Sub Today?,” a comedy-adventure series for children ages 8 to 12; “Feifei,” a picture-book adaptation in development as an animated children’s sitcom; and “Mogu & Perol,” which pairs a French IP with Taiwanese talent. The 39-episode series includes six or seven episodes featuring the culture of Taiwan’s Hakka people, one of the island’s main ethnic groups.
The fund also backed “Mountain Adventure Squad 2,” a children’s outdoor reality show slated to launch in the first quarter of 2027, and “Hello, Mr. President!,” which received an Excellent Screenplay Award from Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture.
Joint Journey Creative’s slate includes Taiwanese films “The Damp,” “All Money Back My Home” and “Suffocation,” as well as Season 6 of Japanese series “Midnight Diner,” an international production it is participating in.
The Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund totals NT$1 billion ($32 million). Chunghwa Telecom holds 64%, TAICCA 30% through the National Development Fund, E.Sun Financial Holding 5% and fund manager CDCC Capital 1%.
The fund backs film, TV and other programs at the project level. It also takes equity stakes in companies working in content development and production, international distribution and business integration, and new uses for IP across cultural technology, games and music.
Its equity investments include DaMou Entertainment, the production company behind “The World Between Us,” and Horiza Creations, which focuses on international IP operations, data-driven business models and crowdfunding. Its project slate includes “Call of Lobster,” an action comedy spanning Taiwan and South Korea that won the Chunghwa Telecom Award at TCCF’s 2024 pitching competition, and “C’est la Vie,” an eight-episode drama executive produced by and starring Esther Liu, with Tu Cheng-che as screenwriter and director. The fund is also an investor in Shallow Levée’s “Speak in Silence.”
Enjoy Entertainment’s slate also includes “Our Blues,” a Taiwanese remake of the 2022 Korean series, which launches globally on Netflix on Dec. 3.

On 02 November 2026, Union Home Minister Amit Shah participated in the BJP’s ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha Padayatra in Hyderabad. Organised by the Telangana unit of the BJP, the march began near the Dr Babu Jagjivan Ram statue in Basheerbagh and concluded at Moazzam Jahi Market. Shah was accompanied by Union Ministers G Kishan Reddy and Bandi Sanjay Kumar, Telangana BJP president N Ramchander Rao, and other party leaders and workers. The march was organised as part of the BJP’s campaign against the INDIA bloc’s allegations concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls (here, here, and here).
Amid this incident, a video is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming it shows people protesting against Union Home Minister Amit Shah and chasing him away during the BJP’s Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha padayatra in Telangana on 02 November 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows people chasing Union Home Minister Amit Shah away during his Telangana padayatra on 02 November 2026.
Fact: The video dates back to July 2023 and shows Rahul Gandhi travelling in a car amid a crowd waving Congress flags in Khammam, Telangana. Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha’ in Khammam on 02 July 2023. On the same day, Amit Shah attended a programme in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, after virtually inaugurating the Akshar River Cruise in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. We found no reports of him visiting Hyderabad that day. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an X post (archived) dated 4 July 2023, featuring a clearer version of the same video. Rahul Gandhi is clearly visible inside the VIP car, with people waving Congress flags. The post’s caption identifies the location as Khammam district in Telangana and states that Rahul Gandhi was returning after delivering a speech. This suggests that the video is from a Congress event held in Telangana.
On 02 July 2023, Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha‘ in Khammam, Telangana, as part of the Congress party’s campaign ahead of the Telangana Assembly elections. Rahul Gandhi also shared videos from the event on his official YouTube channel, while the Congress party issued a press release about the programme.
To verify whether Amit Shah was in Hyderabad on 2 July 2023, we conducted a Google search and found that he was scheduled to attend the ‘Jan-Swabhiman Divas‘ programme at the Indira Gandhi Pratishthan in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, organised to mark the 74th birth anniversary of Dr Sonelal Patel. He attended the event as the chief guest and addressed the gathering between 2:30 pm and 4:30 pm. Earlier that day, he had virtually inaugurated the Akshar River Cruise at the Sabarmati Riverfront in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, through video conferencing. These reports indicate that Amit Shah was engaged in public programmes in Ahmedabad and Lucknow on 2 July 2023; However, we found no reports indicating that he visited Hyderabad that day.
To sum up, this viral video does not show Union Home Minister Amit Shah being chased away during the Hyderabad padayatra on 02 November 2026.

Delivery of various services in government hospitals and health centres across Keralam are likely to get affected in the coming days as the job contracts of 1,495 temporary staff working under the National Health Mission (NHM) have been terminated from October 31.
According to sources, those who lost their jobs include doctors, nurses, pharmacists, accountants, physiotherapists, lab technicians, and the staff who coordinate the activities of Accredited Social Health Activists. The services of special newborn units in district hospitals and activities of ‘Ashadhara’ project, the digital and decentralised healthcare initiative launched by the government through the NHM to manage haemophilia and other rare genetic bleeding and coagulation disorders, may be hit. Functioning of urban health centres and labs and pharmacies in many hospitals and other healthcare institutions too may get affected.
Leaders of the Centre of Indian Trade Unions-affiliated NHM Employees Federation say that the highest number of the affected staff are in Ernakulam and Thrissur districts, 183 and 180, respectively. Ninety-nine people have lost their jobs in Kozhikode district alone.
Assembly elections
Meera Nimeesh, State general secretary of the federation, says that the contract staff are appointed for a one-year period from April to March. However, this year, the contract was extended till May, because of the model code of conduct for the Assembly elections. After the new government assumed office, their tenure was extended twice, till October 31. Ms. Nimeesh adds that though the staff had earlier undergone one round of performance appraisal in May, they were asked to do it again in October. Following this, their services were terminated.
Ms. Nimeesh claims that even those with close to 20 years of experience, who have consistently recorded good performance, found themselves jobless one fine morning. She alleges that the government’s action is politically motivated as those who don’t align themselves with the United Democratic Front government have been singled out and terminated.
In a statement, the federation says that the services provided by NHM staff—spanning areas such as immunisation, maternal and child care, communicable disease control, management of lifestyle diseases, palliative care, laboratory services, day-to-day operations of hospitals, and field-level health activities—constitute an integral part of the healthcare system. Meanwhile, it is learnt that the Health department has issued a notification for the appointment of new staff.

Armed Maoists eliminated, but ‘dimagi Naxals’ remain a threat: PM Modi
He described the elimination of armed Maoists as a victory for the government’s policies and strong political will
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday warned that the threat of Naxalism persists despite the elimination of armed Maoists, alleging that ideological supporters of the movement, whom he described as “dimagi Naxals”, have infiltrated political parties and various organisations to instigate people against the Constitution and democracy.
Addressing security personnel during Diwali celebrations at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) camp in Karanpur in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar district, Modi said identifying and defeating such elements was essential to securing the country.
He described the elimination of armed Maoists as a victory for the government’s policies and strong political will, but cautioned against complacency.
“Amid the successes, we must remember one more thing. Naxalites have been eliminated, but the threat is not over yet. Armed Naxalites have disappeared from the forests, but ‘dimagi Naxals’ have taken control of several organisations,” he said.
Also Read:‘First Diwali when India is free from Naxalism’: PM Modi marks festival in Bastar
He alleged that such elements continued to instigate people against the country’s Constitution and democratic institutions and had infiltrated several political parties and organisations.
“We must identify and defeat them and secure the country,” the Prime Minister said.
Modi said his government had taken several decisions to deal a major blow to the funding networks of Naxalites and separatists. He alleged that previous governments had restricted the operational freedom of security forces, preventing them from responding effectively to Maoist attacks.
“We gave security forces the freedom to take all necessary decisions,” he said.
He also said his government had worked to dismantle the support system that Left-Wing Extremism allegedly enjoyed from certain sections of the government and administration.
Modi said the government’s objective was to ensure that no mother lost her child, no family was pushed into devastation, no child took up arms and no young person’s future was destroyed.
Also Read: History of Diwali celebrations at White House, and Indian diaspora’s political profile in US
“We remained committed to this resolve until the goal was achieved. Without publicity or showmanship, we worked with sensitivity and broke the backbone of Maoist terrorists. We transformed the lives of people in Naxal-affected areas through a spirit of service, which led those suffering from Naxalism to stand firmly with the government and security forces,” he said.
Modi said government action had destroyed counterfeit currency networks and disrupted the supply lines of Naxalites and separatists.
Describing the fight against Maoist violence as a major challenge, he said more than 230 districts across nearly 20 states were once affected by Naxalism.
“To take the country forward, its enemies must be crushed with unwavering determination and a well-planned strategy,” he said.
Modi said the lack of political will to tackle the menace had been addressed in 2014, when people gave him an opportunity to serve the country.
He also said that, for the first time in 47 years, not a single Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel had been killed in the line of duty during the preceding year.
Bastar, once considered the epicentre of Left-Wing Extremism in Chhattisgarh, has witnessed significant change in recent years following intensified anti-Maoist operations, large-scale surrenders and the expansion of development initiatives.

The best laptop display ever made, bar none. The notch is gone! Having a touchscreen is occasionally useful. Much lighter to carry. Somehow, even better speakers. Glowing Apple logo returns.
TIRED
Touchscreen implementation feels half-baked. High price for the same performance as last year’s model.
Apple doesn’t change its mind very often. Its history is one of sticking to its guns, even when pressed on certain design or technology decisions. And yet, I’ve been working on a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen for the past few days—a device I never thought would come into being.
Ignoring the (very reasonable) arguments about the poor ergonomics of touchscreen laptops made in the past, Apple has brought such a display to the MacBook Pro in the most un-Apple way I could have imagined. I’m not sure why it’s here, but it is.
I do know, though, that I love the new “PROLED XDR” screen. Combine that with a hole-punch cutout for the webcam and the return of the light-up Apple logo on the lid—and it's enough improvements to call this a big upgrade over the rest of the MacBook lineup. But compared to a similarly specced MacBook Pro from a year ago, the OLED model costs almost $1,000 more by comparison.
Small Touches Add Up
Photograph: Luke Larsen
With the arrival of the OLED MacBook Pro, Apple now offers two flavors of its flagship premium laptop. The standard Mini-LED option now comes with the M6 processor with improved graphics and battery life, but otherwise looks largely the same as before.
The OLED MacBook Pro, however, is the biggest change since 2021. You won’t notice it immediately on the outside. Color options are still just Silver and Space Black. You still have a choice between 14- and 16-inch. Ports are the same. Open it up, and you’ll see the familiar keyboard and trackpad. It’s all there as you’d expect.
The only visual indication that you’re using something different is the glowing Apple logo on the lid. As a feature only available in the very expensive OLED MacBook Pro, it’s a pure, unabashed status symbol. And I love it. It even matches the display’s brightness, so it doesn’t distract in a dark room.
Another discernible difference in the OLED MacBook Pro is something you’ll notice with your hands rather than your eyes. The 16-inch model I tested now weighs just 4 pounds, well over half a pound lighter than the non-OLED equivalent. Most of the weight savings come from OLED, which uses much thinner, lighter layers (more on OLED later). This is a very large laptop, but the weight reduction makes it much easier to carry around in a bag.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
And the notch is gone! No Apple design feature has bothered me more than this large cutout at the top of the screen, which houses the webcam and sensors (it remains in the non-OLED model). The punch-hole camera is a huge improvement. As someone who found the notch a complete eyesore since it was introduced, this might be the change I’ve been most excited about. Like on newer iPhones, the MacBook Pro is also getting Dynamic Island, which makes the punch-hole camera more useful. It can show interactive Live Activities, such as timers or currently-playing music. I imagine it won’t be used too often, though it does its job by hiding the punch-hole and showing off those narrow bezels.
There are some subtler tweaks. The rubber feet on the bottom have softer, rounded edges. The bezels around the screen are slightly smaller.
Even Brighter OLED
It’s been over two years since Apple first brought its tandem OLED displays to the iPad Pro. In that time, MacBook Pro users have been patiently using the same Mini-LED display. Nevertheless, the OLED MacBook Pro has finally arrived, and Apple has pushed the tandem OLED panel further than ever before. This is the brightest laptop display I’ve ever tested, capable of reaching up to 1,000 nits in SDR. That’s on everyday content throughout the operating system and across all apps. The screen can, however, crank out 2,000 nits of brightness—but only in specific circumstances.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
For example, under very bright light or outdoors, the ambient light sensor built into the webcam module will detect those conditions and tune the display beyond the 1,000-nit upper limit. Combine that with the optional nano-texture screen, and you have what is undoubtedly the best laptop for working outside. That’s especially impressive considering glare is a big problem with typical OLED laptop screens. (You’ll need to turn on the “Automatically adjust brightness” setting, which I typically don’t.) Apple sent me the OLED with standard glass for testing, which comes with an antireflective coating that the company calls “groundbreaking." Next to the non-OLED M6 MacBook Pro, it looks about as reflective. If you really want to use this thing outside, the nano-texture upgrade is well worth it.
HDR content is the second situation in which the screen can be cranked up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness. Here, the idea isn’t to blast your eyes with brightness; it’s about details. In HDR-rendered photos, videos, movies, and games, 2,000 nits would be bright enough to deliver incredible depth of detail and color. I’ve never seen HDR like this on a laptop, and you really have to experience it to truly get it. In my HDR testing, my OLED MacBook Pro never quite reached 2,000 nits, maxing out at 1,849 nits. But amazingly, it can even produce this in a 25 percent window, and 1,025 nits with every pixel lit up. The only place you’ll find brighter OLED is in the very latest OLED TVs.
Now, this is actually only 12 percent brighter than the Mini-LED MacBook Pro, which I retested to make this comparison. But when you pair a brighter OLED screen with the deep blacks it can produce, you have absolutely stellar HDR, giving the content a range of depth never before seen on a laptop.
I watched a number of professional HDR footage, side-by-side with the Mini-LED MacBook Pro. That difference is very noticeable. Is it something only TV nerds and videographers will care about? Maybe. The Mini-LED MacBook Pro is already a great laptop for watching movies on. All I can say is the OLED model is noticeably better. And for those who work professionally with HDR footage, this should open up new possibilities. My hope is that, as these HDR-capable devices proliferate, we’ll see more HDR video produced—even just for the web.
The speakers also make the OLED MacBook Pro an ever better movie-watching device. Apple says the six-speaker sound system has “50 percent deeper bass.” That’s hard to measure, but like the screen, you notice a difference when you compare it side-by-side with the previous-gen model. The bass really does stand out more, giving you a fuller sound both for music-listening and movie-watching. And just to be clear: Apple already had the best speakers in the game.
Like an iPad
Photograph: Luke Larsen
In the time I’ve had with the touchscreen MacBook Pro so far, I tried to remind myself of its new powers. But when I’m deep in work, I completely forget the touchscreen. It just has no place in my workflows. That doesn’t mean it’s not ever useful, though. Sometimes, swiping away a notification with a finger feels intuitive. Or if you’re lounging on the couch and use your thumb to scroll through your Instagram feed as you would on an iPad, it works. But those times are few and far between. I’m certainly not going to be poking three fingers up at the screen to swipe between Spaces when I could do that on a trackpad without even lifting my hand.
I’ve noticed the same tendency when I use an iPad Air or iPad Pro connected to the Magic Keyboard. It’s just easier and faster to keep your hands where they are. The difference here on the MacBook Pro is the software. The interface doesn’t exactly draw you in to touch it. Everything that could click you can now touch, but tapping tiny icons and controls with your finger feels clumsy, as it always has. It’s the same problem in Windows 11. To be fair, Apple has put in more effort than Microsoft ever has, tweaking macOS to optimize for touch—not unlike iPadOS.
One of my favorite optimizations happens when you tap on the window controls (the three buttons to close, minimize, or fullscreen). After you tap, it pops out and lets you select one of the three more precisely. The drop-downs in the menu bar are also more spaced out, and you can tap and drag your finger to select options more easily. These visual touches are handy, and some of Apple’s apps have found ways to make certain tasks touch-based.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
I admit I don’t benefit much from a touchscreen laptop, but Apple also hasn’t made any hardware changes to make touching the screen feel more natural. Would Apple ever put a 180- or 360-degree hinge on a MacBook? I would have thought no—then again, I never thought a MacBook would have a touchscreen in the first place. Not even the Apple Pencil is supported here (not that it would ever be comfortable to use at an angle).
The bigger problem is that third-party apps have to optimize for touch. Even though click-to-touch will work in all apps right out of the box, not all developers will put in the effort. Also, I’ve noticed some apps translated through Rosetta (which lets Intel-based software run on Apple silicon, such as Steam) don’t support some features, like the zoom-in window controls. I can’t see myself adjusting my behavior when you can’t reliably expect consistency across these apps.
Apple has been selling the OLED MacBook Pro’s touch capabilities to creative pros—the kind of user who would use this laptop. The ideas are mildly interesting, whether it’s drawing directly on the screen with Pixelmator Pro or applying brush textures onto 3D models in ZBrush. I’m not an artist, but I use Logic Pro. You can now touch the screen to play drums right on the screen or draw automations into Remix FX. But that’s where I started to think these are more gimmicks than real features creatives will actually benefit from. Even amateur musicians will always have a physical MIDI keyboard, and playing musical instruments on the laptop keyboard (a Logic feature that’s been around forever) feels more natural than tapping the screen. I’ll wait for Adobe to prove me wrong.
Here’s the thing: In all my discussions with Apple about the touchscreen, I never got the impression that touch was supposed to replace the keyboard and trackpad as the primary input method. That’s a safe, smart play if the goal is to not rock the boat too much. For so many years, Apple sat back and watched Microsoft fumble its own touch implementation through the disaster that was Windows 8. It’s certainly true that in today’s world, it feels strange that you can’t control a MacBook screen with your fingers. As someone with kids, my MacBook is safe from their fingerprints. This feels more like a “catch-up” feature we’ve long been without, but I hope Apple commits more to touch and engineers a more unique way to integrate it.
The Same M5 Max
The 2026 OLED MacBook Pro uses the same chips as the previous generation: the M5 Pro and M5 Max. This is the first time Apple has done this since introducing Apple Silicon in 2020. Each new version of any Mac has always come with an updated chip. Either Apple’s pace is slowing down, or the company thinks the OLED touchscreen will be a strong enough draw to convince buyers to refresh.
To be fair, the M5 Max and M5 Pro were already at the top of their game. Even compared to new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops like the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, the M5 Max dominates in overall power. Time to rest on their laurels, I suppose. Rumor has it that Apple will skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max altogether, saving those more powerful configurations for the M7 generation. Again, that would be a first for Apple Silicon since its introduction.
On the other hand, Apple claims the OLED MacBook Pro internals have been completely redesigned to support the PROLED XDR display. The goal is performance parity with the non-OLED M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro—nothing more. And in my testing, that’s precisely what I saw. Scores were very similar to the previous-gen MacBook Pro in Cinebench 2026, as well as in the games I tested. I won’t go too in-depth here—check out my review of the previous M5 Max MacBook Pro if you want more performance analysis.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
If you already own an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro, it’s very difficult to justify upgrading to the OLED version, even if you’re able to sell it for a decent price. Unless you have a specific use case for the OLED display, I can see many people wanting to wait until next year for the performance upgrade. On the flip side, if you want to upgrade from an M1 Max or M2 Max, you face a tricky decision between the OLED and non-OLED MacBook Pro. For now, Apple is still selling both models in its lineup.
The OLED model costs $400 more, which is steep for a display upgrade. This is on top of the price increase from earlier this year, which already added an extra $500 to the M5 Max MacBook Pro. The 14-inch OLED MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, while its 16-inch sibling starts at $3,399—startling pricing to be sure.
For my review, Apple sent me a souped-up 16-inch model with the M5 Max with an 18-core CPU and 32-core GPU, a standard glass OLED (nano-texture is an optional $150), 128 GB of unified memory, and 2 TB of storage. This configuration costs $7,399, and it’s not even the most expensive!
There’s little hope prices will come down anytime soon, as the memory shortage continues to tighten. If the OLED touchscreen is what draws you to these devices, the 14-inch M5 Pro is the way to go. Just know that you’re leaving a decent amount of performance on the table by not choosing the M5 Max.
Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. Israel is not finished with Iran, its Defence Minister said Sunday (November 8, 2026), as he also warned Tehran's Lebanese ally Hezbollah to hold fire in any resumption of war.

Defence Minister Israel Katz renewed charges that Iran — attacked twice since last year in major Israeli-U.S. bombing campaigns — is pursuing nuclear weapons, a claim that Tehran denies.
"Concerning Iran, the mission is still not complete. Iran is trying to renew its efforts to obtain nuclear weapons — alongside other grave efforts that place the State of Israel in real danger," Mr. Katz said.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political life, has repeatedly threatened new strikes against Iran in recent weeks.

"We will not withdraw from the security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and if the terrorist organisation Hezbollah chooses to join Iran in an attack on Israel, it will suffer extremely severe blows," Mr. Katz said.
Mr. Netanyahu suffered losses in the October 27 election, with his rival Gadi Eisenkot tasked with forming a new government.
Eisenkot has warned Israel's military that Mr. Netanyahu has no mandate and that it should not go to war for his "political needs", although the former army chief has largely supported Mr. Netanyahu's war decisions.
"We may argue, and we may disagree, but when the security of the state is at stake, we must know how to rise above our disputes," said Mr. Katz, who was speaking at a ceremony for Israeli troops who died in a 1956 attack on Egypt.

My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.
His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.
Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.
Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.
After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.
Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.
In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.
While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.
After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.
Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.
“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.
As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.
Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.
“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.
“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

What do Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, South Carolina senator-elect Annie Andrews, Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton, and North Carolina representative-elect Jamie Ager have in common, beyond their victories in this week’s midterm elections?
Each is either a doctor or a scientist. And each had the backing of the political action committee 314 Action Fund, which focuses on electing pro-science voices to public office.
“We really benefit by having those data-driven, fact-based decisionmakers actually in a position at the governing table,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, a chemist and former congressional candidate who founded 314 Action after losing her race in 2016. This cycle, the PAC spent above $30 million donating to and supporting various campaigns, including fundraising for specific races. It raised $3.6 million for pediatrician Andrews in the fight over what had been Lindsay Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina, for example, and another $3 million for physician Acton’s campaign in the hotly contested Ohio governor race, according to Naughton.
The organization’s success rate topped 80 percent this cycle for congressional candidates, with 14 of 17 of its candidates in the US House of Representatives winning their races and hundreds of successful down-ballot candidates. Nine of these races flipped seats from Republican to Democrat. Victorious congressional candidates who flipped their districts this year include an oncology nurse-practitioner, a mathematician, a microbiologist, a nuclear engineer, and an agricultural scientist. “It did turn out to be a health care election,” Naughton says.
Richard Frank, the director of the Brookings Institute’s Center on Health Policy, notes that health care workers and scientists have always been part of the makeup of Congress, but not to this degree. “What is unusual,” he says, “is just how many came in one wave.” He sees the spike in this type of candidate as a direct result of the hostility toward medical and technical expertise from the Trump administration. “Science has been under attack,” Frank says. “It’s not surprising that scientists have recognized that, and some of them went out and ran for Congress.”
The rise of the science candidate has several causes, according to historian Kristoffer Shields, who runs Rutgers University’s Eagleton Institute of Politics. “Some of it certainly is a reaction to what's been happening at the federal level, the defunding of a lot of laboratories and scientific exploration,” he says. But he also sees this as a legacy of the pandemic, when many health care workers started thinking about how politics impacts public health.
Earlier this year, El-Sayed emphasized to WIRED that his candidacy was focused on public health, noting that the cyclospora outbreak that sickened Americans over the summer likely stemmed from the Trump administration’s choices. “We DOGE’d our whole service that keeps the lettuce safe,” he said at the time, referencing the so-called Department of Government Efficiency directing mass layoffs at the Food and Drug Administration.
In 2024, 314 Action’s past acceptance of funding from groups with ties to the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC came under scrutiny. The organization no longer accepts AIPAC funding and supported candidates like El-Sayed who were vocally critical of the Israeli government. Unlike some other political committees that aim to put doctors in office, like the American Medical Association’s PAC, 314 Action specifically focuses on electing Democratic health and science experts; it is forthright about its opposition to the Trump administration’s approach to public health.
That so many of these politicians are advocates for the importance of public health and scientific expertise suggests that the election was, in part, a rejection of current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA movement, which promotes medical misinformation, including anti-vaccine sentiment. Many of the winning candidates with scientific and technical backgrounds have explicitly discussed how their concerns about the state of health care policy drove them to enter the race. “I am appalled seeing infectious diseases spreading through our communities that we had once declared eradicated,” microbiologist Jasmine Clark, the incoming representative from Georgia, told The Guardian earlier this year.
Clark was first supported by 314 Action when she ran for Georgia’s House of Representatives eight years ago. “She was in the first class of scientists that we helped elect in that 2018 cycle and now has made that move up to the federal level,” says Naughton.
Shields sees the straightforward communication style favored by doctors and scientists as another asset that has made them strong candidates. Some of this year’s winners are especially direct. In recent interviews, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews has referred to RFK Jr. as her “archnemesis” and promised to hold him accountable.
314 Action has also been clear that rebuking RFK Jr.’s agenda is a core part of its goals. In 2025, it launched its Guardians of Public Health initiative to recruit health care experts to run for public office. “We thought it was important to speak directly to doctors and people in public health, like nurses, to say that we have this program and we need you to step up to run, because we have a madman running the Health and Human Services cabinet,” Naughton says.
The push for pro-science public servants isn’t over; 314 Action is starting its next recruitment round later this month.

Cosmoserve Space has raised $6 Mn in a seed funding round led by Japan-based Rebright Partners. While Aranya Holdings and Naandi Ventures also participated in the round, existing investors AUM Ventures and Shakti VC doubled down on their erstwhile bet. The startup shared plans to utilise the fresh capital to support tech demonstrations, fuel two upcoming missions, as well enhance the operations of its recently unveiled Hyderabad facility. Cosmoserve has now raised over $9 Mn since inception last year. The startup has doubled its valuation since it raised pre-seed funding in September, founder Chiranjeevi Phanindra told Inc42. The exact valuation is yet to be discerned. For context, the startup is building tech to remove defunct satellites and orbital debris from space and reduce the collision risks for operational spacecraft in a cost effective manner. It plans on optimising costs by setting up features within its craft that will allow it to refuel in-orbit and remove multiple pieces of debris in a single mission. The startup made its first tech demonstration, Mission Embrace-1, aboard Skyroot Aerospace’s Vikram-1 rocket. The mission was designed to test the startup’s soft robotic capture system that removes space debris, but the system’s robotic petals failed to deploy as intended. Cosmoserve claims to have now identified and addressed potential issues with the thermal mechanism used to release the petals and the impact of low temperatures on the system, according to Phanindra. The startup is now gearing up for Embrace-2, an upgraded version of the mission to validate its upgraded robotic capture mechanism, which is expected to launch in the coming months. It is also planning a full-scale demonstration of its debris-removal capabilities, aiming to break a world record by approaching within 10 m of a dead satellite. Phanindra, who served close to 15 years with the ISRO before setting up Cosmoserve in June 2025, believes that the startup would be able to complete all tech demos by 2027 and start commercial operations by 2028. “We have several letters of intent from satellite constellation operators – one from the US, one from Europe and two from India. They have to abide by the regulation for removing the dead satellite from space … so we are aiming to get one paid customer before actual commercial operations begin,” he added. Cosmoserve’s Base 1 Alongside the funding announcement, Cosmoserve inaugurated its new space debris removal facility in Hyderabad named Base 1 today, in an event attended by union minister of state Dr Jitendra Singh and Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu. Phanindra says that Base 1 is India’s first private and the world’s sixth facility equipped with space vision effects and microgravity simulation. In simpler terms, Base 1 can recreate conditions that spacecraft and equipment encounter in space, allowing companies to test how their tech will perform before an actual mission. This includes simulating how objects behave in microgravity (near-weightlessness) and how they appear or function under space-like visual conditions. This costs around ₹6 Cr to construct, per Phanindra. Base 1 houses infrastructure for designing, building and testing satellite servicing and space debris recovery missions. This includes an orbital rendezvous and capture lab, an ISO Class 8 clean room for satellite integration, a mission control centre and a microgravity simulation platform. The facility will also support the development of in-orbit satellite repair and refuelling technologies. Besides, the startup plans to use Base 1 to develop more critical technologies in-house in order to increase its share of local manufacturing from 60% and reduce dependence on imported components such as optics, avionics and space-grade electronics. “Primarily, the core technology we are building is a soft robotic capture system. We have a space robotics innovation lab where the R&D is happening. Then the next technology we are working on is a vision-based navigation system,” the founder told Inc42.

At least four people were killed and 88 injured after two trains crashed into each other in Egypt on Sunday.
Several carriages derailed in Giza province after one train rammed into the back of another, according to the Transportation Ministry.
One of the train drivers was among those killed in the collision, the health ministry said, adding that as many as 72 ambulances had been deployed to evacuate the injured to three different hospitals.
It was not immediately clear what had caused the crash. President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said authorities had been told to investigate the circumstances of the tragedy and to “hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence”.
“I am following the aftermath of the train collision with great concern and extend my deepest condolences to the families of those who lost their lives, along with my sincere wishes for a speedy recovery for the injured,” he said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo, between a train heading for the southwestern Fayoum province and another heading to the southern province of Aswan.
It was not immediately clear which had derailed.
Emergency teams and cranes were on hand to clear the wreckage and restore the service as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.
The ministry of health said in a statement it would continue to monitor the casualties and provide them with full medical care.
All health facilities in Giza and Beni Suef governorates were ordered to raise their level of alertness and to provide all necessary medical and emergency support to the injured, the ministry said.
The trains crashed on the Cairo–Aswan agricultural road near the Gerza junction in Giza Governorate, the ministry added.
Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

The Best Wireless Chargers to Refuel Your Phone
Featured in this article
Wireless charging has been around for more than a decade, yet many people still plug in the old-fashioned way. But trust me: Once you free yourself from fishing for and fumbling with cables in the dark, you’ll never want to go back. Dropping your phone on a pad or stand at the end of the day and waking up to a fully charged battery in the morning is easy and convenient. Yes, it’s slower than wired charging—but at night that hardly matters anyways.
After testing more than 100 wireless chargers over the past decade, sorting the good from the bad (there are certainly bad ones), I have identified the best wireless chargers. You will find many pads and stands in different styles, shapes, and build materials with spots for other devices, alongside your phone.
Check out our other buying guides, including the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, Best 3-in-1 Apple Wireless Chargers, Best MagSafe and Qi2 Chargers, and Best MagSafe Power Banks.
Updated November 2026: I added wireless chargers from Peak Design, UGreen, and Mophie, removed some older devices, and updated prices.
Other Wireless Chargers We Tested
There are a lot of wireless chargers. Here are a few more we like, but for one reason or another don’t warrant a place above.
Peak Design Mobile Wireless Charging Stand for $80: This slim, aluminum, hinged Qi2 wireless charging stand folds flat, but Peak Design also offers magnetic cases for Samsung, Google, and Apple phones. I tested with the Pixel 8 case ($30), and it stuck on the stand in portrait or landscape orientation. It charges phones at up to 15 watts and comes with a 6.6-foot USB-C cable and three adhesive clips to keep it neat. You need a 20-watt power adapter (I like this teeny tiny Anker charger). Peak Design has a whole ecosystem of magnetic accessories, including a stand wallet, a tripod for mobile photography, and wall, bike, and car mounts. Everything I tried is top quality and comes with a lifetime guarantee.
Krafted Couch Wireless Charger for $52: I thought this wireless charger, designed to drape over the arm of your couch, was a great idea when I saw it, but the ridges failed to keep it in place on my velvety couch, so it kept slipping down the side. The silicone finish with the Krafted logo is also a bit ugly. It’s basically a silicone mat with a magnetic charger inside, though it includes a fairly generous 6.6-foot (2-meter) cable and is Qi2-rated. If you’re always rooting around for a charger and one of the colors blends well with your furniture, it might be a good fit.
Nimble Apollo Wireless Pad for $18: The silicone surface of this wireless charger easily picks up dust and lint, but that might not matter if you’re shopping for the most eco-friendly charger. It’s made of recycled silicone, and its texture helps keep phones from sliding off the surface. The rest of it is made with post-consumer plastic and alloy, and even the packaging is plastic-free. Better yet, if you have an iPhone 12 or newer with MagSafe, the magnets inside the Apollo keep your iPhone aligned for more efficient charging, even if they’re not as strong as standard MagSafe wireless chargers.
Einova Eggtronic Charging Stone for $70: Made with 100 percent solid marble or stone—you can choose from a variety. Every pick in this guide looks a lot like a wireless charger, but visiting friends have asked if this one is a drink coaster. (I’m still figuring out whether that’s a good or bad thing.) It has zero LEDs, perfect for bedrooms; just try to hide the cable to truly make it blend into your home. We recommend putting a case on your phone when using it with this charger, as there’s a risk of scuffing up the back with these harder surfaces. —Julian Chokkattu
Rapport London Formula Wireless Charging Tray for $495: Yes, this is an obscene price for a Qi wireless charger. You can probably make a version for a fraction of the cost. But Rapport’s build quality is quite nice, with a lacquered grey box and a soft-touch fabric to keep your watches and phone scratch-free. It reliably recharged several Android phones without making them too warm, all while offering storage for a few watches. It’s attractive, but you’ll need cash to burn at this price. —Julian Chokkattu
iOttie iOS Wireless Duo for $50: This dual-charging system looks pretty—I like the fabric-wrapped stand—and you can charge another device on the rubberized charging pad next to it. The stand can be used in portrait or landscape, though in the latter orientation it’ll block the pad. I use the pad to top up my wireless earbuds, but I wouldn’t use this iOttie on a nightstand because the front LED can be glaring. A cable and adapter are included, which makes it a good value. It can charge Pixel phones at up to 15 watts, iPhones at 7.5 watts, and other Android phones at 10 watts. —Julian Chokkattu
Journey Alti Play Performance Desk Mat for $120: This desk mat doubles as a wireless charging pad. On the left side is a plasticky rectangle with a Qi2 magnetic puck for your smartphone. Above it is a little area to charge wireless earbuds (5 watts). Naturally, there’s RGB all over, and two buttons let you cycle through patterns and colors. It’s a smart-looking system, but the mat’s quality leaves a bit to be desired. I didn’t have issues gliding my mouse on it, and it stays put thanks to the rubber underside, but I just didn’t like the look and feel of the Lycra surface. Journey has some other versions of this mat that use different materials, so take a look if you like the overall aesthetic. —Julian Chokkattu
Zens Liberty Wireless Charger for $150: I tested the Glass Edition of this wireless charging pad, and it looks stunning with the 16 overlapping copper coils on display (the standard version has a woolen fabric top). It can charge two devices simultaneously at up to 15 watts apiece. As stylish as it is, the price is too high. Because you can see the coils, placement is never an issue, but it’s bulky; the fan is audible at times, and while I had no problem charging my iPhone or AirPods, my Pixel 6 Pro got very warm on this pad.
Xiaomi Mi 80-W Wireless Charging Stand for $80: By far the fastest wireless charger we have tested, this stand is only worth considering for Xiaomi phones (it seems to charge most other phones at 10 watts or below). I tested with the Xiaomi 13 Ultra, which tops out at 50 watts (some Xiaomi models can go higher). The unusual sail shape combines a white triangular section with a clear acrylic base that has a subtle groove to hold your phone in place and a gap underneath for the exhaust grill from the noisy fan. The USB-C port and LED indicator are on the back.
Does My Phone Support Wireless Charging?
Not all phones support wireless charging, but most brands have models that do, so look up your phone model first. You’ll usually see “Qi wireless charging” (the default standard) or simply “wireless charging” if it does on the product page or specs list.
Phones that support the latest Qi2 standard bear the Qi2 logo and have a ring of magnets for easy alignment (just like Apple’s MagSafe). Qi2 is backward compatible, so Qi phones can charge on Qi2 chargers, though they may charge more slowly. Sadly, this does not always apply the other way round, as we discovered with the HMD Skyline (the first Qi2 Android phone), which cannot be charged with all Qi chargers.
Some phones are also Qi2 Ready, like Samsung’s Galaxy S25 series. This means they have the necessary internal components to enable Qi2 functionality—faster charging and more efficient energy transfer—but they don’t have built-in magnets. To enable full Qi2 magnetic wireless charging, you need to pair the phone with a Qi2 Ready case with magnets inside. The latest update, Qi2 25W, allows for a faster maximum charging rate of 25 watts, up from 15 watts. Supported phones include the iPhone 17 range and Google’s Pixel 10 Pro XL.
Do Wireless Chargers Work With Phone Cases?
Yes, most wireless chargers can charge through cases, unless the case is particularly thick. Check the product listing—there’s usually a case thickness limit in millimeters. Phones can get hot when charging wirelessly, so don’t worry if your phone is really warm when you pick it up. Most smartphones have limits that stop charging if they get too hot.
If you have a MagSafe charger or a Qi2 charger with magnets, you can use a magnetic case even if your phone doesn’t support those standards. You may not be able to take advantage of all the features, but it should deliver basic wireless charging that’s more precise thanks to the magnets.
Yes, Cords Will Charge Your Phone Faster
Some manufacturers like Apple make wireless chargers that recharge their respective phones faster than others, but if you want the fastest phone charger, you're better off sticking with a cord. Wireless charging works best on desks or nightstands when you're not using your phone or in a rush to recharge it. Check out our Best USB-C Cables guide if you need one, though the cable that comes with your phone should be sufficient.
What’s a Fast Wireless Charging Speed?
Most MagSafe and Qi2 chargers can go up to 15 watts, and a handful of proprietary wireless chargers for specific phone models can charge even faster. The latest Qi2 25W standard allows for charging up to 25 watts. It's worth noting that, even where phones support them, the maximum charging rates are only reached some of the time (the charging rate is automatically adjusted to preserve battery health). Many older iPhones are capped at 7.5 watts for wireless charging and many older Android phones are capped at 10 watts. We have included the maximum wireless charging rate in the specs table for each entry. Remember that the charger also requires the correct cable and power adapter to charge at its maximum rate.
Is Wireless Charging Safe?
There’s no definitive evidence that it’s harmful. You may worry the phone’s battery might degrade faster with wireless charging, but manufacturers set safe limits for phone batteries, stipulating how much a battery can be charged and how far it can discharge. Regardless of the charging source you use, whether you plug into a wall adapter or use a wireless charging pad, these limits can’t be overridden. You won’t overcharge your phone by leaving it on a wireless charger all night.
How Do I Keep My Phone’s Battery Healthy?
Try to keep your battery between 50 and 80 percent for optimum battery health. Keeping your phone fully charged or fully discharged will degrade it slightly faster, and regularly swinging between full and empty will shorten its life. Battery technology has improved in recent years, and phone batteries are more reliable than ever. If you switch phones every two to three years or don’t mind paying a modest fee for a battery replacement on that timescale, it’s not worth worrying too much about how often or when you charge your phone.
What Is the Downside of Wireless Charging?
The main downside is that wireless charging is slower than wired charging. Wireless charging is less efficient because some of the power is lost as heat. Original Qi chargers are only around 60 to 75 percent efficient. Qi2 chargers manage 75 to 80 percent efficiency, but wired charging is typically 85 to 95 percent efficient.
How I Test Wireless Chargers
I test every wireless charger for at least a week, using it to charge both my Pixel 11 Pro XL and iPhone 16. I also test with an older iPhone 12 and Pixel 9. I live with most chargers on my nightstand or work desk. When possible, I check the charging rate and note how long it takes to charge my phone. I assess the design’s usability and the magnets' strength, test any additional charging ports or pads, and try out any special features.

President Donald Trump is set to appear on Sunday’s edition of “60 Minutes” for his first in-depth interview since Republicans suffered sweeping losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
The president is scheduled to sit down with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat on Friday, with the interview slated to air Nov. 8. According to CNN, CBS News sources confirmed the plans, while the White House’s Friday schedule listed a pre-taped interview for 10:30 a.m. ET. The best way for cable-cutters to stream the interview online is on Paramount+ Premium. Essential subscribers can stream the full episode on demand beginning Monday, Nov. 9.
You can also access CBS live streams on services on DirecTV and Hulu+ Live TV.
The appearance comes just days after Democrats seized control of both the House and Senate, dealing a major blow to Trump’s second-term agenda. The election saw Democrats flip seats in traditionally Republican strongholds, with voters expressing growing frustration over the cost of living and the administration’s war with Iran.
Douthat, a longtime conservative columnist for The New York Times who joined “60 Minutes” earlier this year, has been a frequent critic of Trump. In a column published earlier this week, he described the midterm results as a failure of the “New Right.” The interview will mark one of Douthat’s highest-profile assignments since joining the newsmagazine as part of its revamped correspondent lineup.
The president has a complicated history with “60 Minutes,” having sued CBS and its parent company over the editing of a 2024 interview with his then-presidential opponent Kamala Harris. Paramount ultimately agreed to a $16 million settlement in 2025.
Since Skydance’s takeover of Paramount, CBS News has undergone a sweeping leadership overhaul under editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, including the departure of several longtime “60 Minutes” journalists and the appointment of Nick Bilton as executive producer.
Trump most recently appeared on the newsmagazine in April, when a contentious exchange with correspondent Norah O’Donnell saw the president call her a “disgrace.”
“60 Minutes” airs Sundays at 7 p.m. ET on CBS and streams on Paramount+.

No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
- Published
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announce the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Hipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.

The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

An employee has sparked an online debate after claiming that their employer eliminated their role following the automation of most of their daily responsibilities, only to ask them to train the person hired to replace them.
The employee is now refusing to help with the handover, raising questions about workplace loyalty, the growing role of automation, job security and whether workers should be expected to train their replacements after being made redundant.
The issue gained traction on social media after a user shared a screenshot of what appeared to be a Reddit discussion titled, "My employer is asking me to train the person replacing me after I automated most of my daily tasks. Am I wrong for refusing?"
The post has prompted contrasting reactions, with some users backing the employee's decision not to help the company after losing their job, while others argued that completing a handover is part of professional responsibility, particularly if the employee continues to receive a salary or severance benefits.
According to the Reddit discussion shared, the employee automated most of their routine daily tasks, apparently making their work more efficient.
However, the employer subsequently decided to eliminate the employee's role and asked them to train the person who would take over their responsibilities.
The request has reportedly not gone down well with the employee, who questioned why they should help the organisation transition to a replacement after the company decided to dispense with their services.
The situation has raised a larger question about whether employees who automate their work risk making their own positions redundant, only to be expected to transfer the efficiencies and knowledge they developed to someone else.
The employee's refusal has also triggered a discussion about whether a company can reasonably expect workers to cooperate with a transition after deciding to let them go.
The discussion has divided Reddit users, with several arguing that employees should not be expected to train someone who is taking over their job without receiving additional compensation.
One user questioned the logic of helping an employer replace them, while another suggested that the decision ultimately came down to whether the employee wanted to maintain a professional relationship with the organisation.
"You're getting fired either way, so the question is so you keep the bridge or burn it?" one comment read.
Another user argued that employees should consider the financial implications before refusing the handover.
"Usually layoffs where they ask you to train your replacement offer an incentive. At the very least training someone will give you a few more weeks of paychecks while you look," the user commented.
A similar view was expressed by another Redditor, who said that continuing to work during the transition could provide additional time to search for another job while still receiving a salary.
"Because it lets you keep your job for that much longer," another comment read.
Some users also pointed out that refusing to cooperate could mean losing out on severance benefits or other financial incentives offered as part of a layoff arrangement.
One Redditor shared their personal experience of being laid off and receiving six months of salary and insurance premiums, arguing that such benefits could make a short handover period worthwhile.
Others took a different position, arguing that training colleagues and transferring knowledge are normal workplace responsibilities.
One user said that managers and leaders are expected to develop people with similar or better skills, adding that sharing expertise can multiply an employee's contribution.
"Training people to have a similar skill set and talent as you or better is what managers and leaders are supposed to do. That's how you really multiply your efforts and impact," the user wrote.
Another Redditor said employees should consider the colleagues who would continue working with the replacement.
"There are people that you still care about who will be working with your replacement. Do what you can for them, take a clear conscience with you," the comment read.
One commenter suggested that employees could limit the handover to essential information rather than sharing every efficiency or shortcut they had developed.
"Train them enough to get the job done. Keep to yourself any shortcuts or workflows that you created," the user suggested.
Several users also shared experiences of being asked to recruit or train their replacements before leaving their organisations.
One Redditor said they had hired their own replacement and trained people who would take over their entire department after the company decided to outsource the team to India.
The user said the transition lasted three months and that they eventually left with an exit package.
"It's just business. It made economic sense for the business to move the team overseas. If I hadn't trained them it wouldn't have changed the facts of the situation. I made the transition as smooth as possible and I got a nice exit package as a result," the user wrote.
