On Tuesday, president Donald Trump made the bombshell announcement that Washington - Israel’s most powerful and longest-standing ally - would end military aid to the country by the end of 2026.
The decision concerns a 10-year pact made during Barack Obama’s administration in 2026 to provide $3.8bn in military aid to Israel every year. This consists of $3.3bn in foreign military financing primarily to purchase US weapons and an additional $500m for annual missile defence.
The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) starting from 2019 was due to expire in 2028, but the Trump administration made the shocking decision to cut the provision, with almost immediate effect, just two days before America went to the polls to vote in the midterm elections. The Republicans went on to suffer a crushing defeat to the Democrats.
Since Israel’s founding it has been the largest cumulative recipient of US foreign aid, receiving over $300bn in both economic and military support, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.
Many have interpreted the change as a seismic shift in the relationship between the US and Israel, but experts told The Independent that the picture is a little more complicated.
A ‘bolt from the blue’ or a smart strategic decision by Netanyahu?
While the move has been interpreted by some as a sign of America’s shifting priorities with a population increasingly unsympathetic to Israel following its war in Gaza, experts say that it is all part of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s plan.
In May, he told CBS’s 60 Minutes that he wanted to wean Israel off US military support. He even appeared impatient to make the shift saying: “I don’t want to wait for the next Congress. I want to start now.”
Netanyahu said that his goal was to “draw down to zero the American financial support, the financial component of the military cooperation that we have” in an attempt to create a image of Israel as self-reliant and independent. This will be of particular importance with Netanyahu losing his majority in the Knesset.
Making his announcement, Trump confirmed that the Israeli leader had come to him with the idea months ago and that they had collectively agreed to cut off support by the end of the year. Netanyahu’s office said on Friday that the end of aid shows the “strength” of the US-Israeli relationship.
“It is his [Netanyahu’s] idea,” says Gregg Roman, executive director of the Middle East Forum. “Ending aid gives Israel full control over what it buys and where it builds it, and it removes the main argument US critics use against the alliance.”
He says that the decision “moves from aid to partnership, with arms sales, co-production, intelligence sharing, and joint operations like the war against Iran.”
Nevertheless, president Isaac Herzog says that the announcement came like a “bolt from the blue” and Israeli media report that there is still considerable confusion around the agreement.
“Nobody knows anything, except that Bibi promised him he would give it up without making a fuss,” one senior Israeli official told Ynet.
How would the cuts impact Israel’s military capacity?
A gap in funding
The suddenness of the announcement means that the economic impact on both Israelis and Americans could be powerful.
Around 17 per cent of Israel’s spending is allocated to defence. Without US aid this burden is likely to increase and the effects could be felt by the country’s taxpayers.
It could also affect US citizens, with Ynet citing Israeli assessments that around one million American households whose livelihoods depend on the the production of weapons and ammunitions purchased by Israel, could be impacted.
“Israel will need to draw from its own sources to purchase these weapons,” says Dr Julie Norman, an associate fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House.
“That puts a lot of pressure on Israel to figure out where that money - which is significant for Israel - is going to to come from. In order to sustain the current capabilities you need to find $3.8bn in your budget, either by pulling from other parts of defence or from pulling from other parts of your broader ministerial government budget, or from increasing your borrowing and your broader economic debt.
“This does put economic pressure on Israel, crucially, I would say at a time when Israel is also facing increasing economic pressure from the announcement of at least some targeted sanctions from the UK, from European states and from others.”
Effect on Israel’s weapons
While Israel will have to find its own money to purchase the American weapons it buys back using US aid with the bulk of the $3.3bn allocated for military financing, this will not end joint missile defence and development, where the rest of the annual funding tends to go.
”My expectation is that there will be some sort of carve out to allow for that cooperation to continue,” says Dr Norman. “That’s something that I think many American politicians, even in this different political landscape with Israel will see as important for both US and Israeli defence.”
Mr Roman agrees and says that the $500 million line co-funds the Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and Arrow, so missile defence could be what to watch.
Nevertheless, analysis by the Wall Street Journal reveals that billions of dollars worth of orders for US military hardware means that getting out of the agreement so quickly could be more complicated than it appears.
Because the US has already pledged around $7bn in aid over the next two years, Israel will have to find $10bn to pay for outstanding orders, according to a State Department document sent to Congress, reviewed by the WSJ.
Mr Roman says that the impact operationally is likely to be small initially but larger over a decade.
“Nearly all of the military financing funding buys the American platforms the Israeli Air Force flies: F-15s, F-16s, F-35s, and KC-46 tankers. Planes keep flying. The defence ministry has to find shekels for those deliveries or stretch them out,” he explains.
“The larger effect is industrial. Israel has moved more munitions production home since Washington held back 2,000-pound bombs in 2024, and ending aid speeds that shift.
“Israeli firms built US production lines partly to win aid-funded contracts, and one major firm told Calcalist it will now reassess its American production.”
What does this mean for the US-Israeli relationship?
The larger significance of the decision could be what it implies about the state of the political relationship between the US and Israel.
”Politically this is an incredibly important statement,” says Dr Norman.“For years, even predating this current arrangement, the idea of giving direct military aid without a traditional contract and traditional procurement process has been part of the political posturing for Washington towards Israel.
”So this marks something very different. It’s also extremely significant that it is not just coming from one party, it is coming from both. It would have been just unthinkable a couple of years ago that the parties would in fact be jockeying to get ahead of each other to announce a drawdown of military aid to Israel.”
She suggests that Netanyahu could have read the “writing on the wall” when it comes to US sentiment and sought to get ahead of the situation. But she says that the speed with which the funding is to be cut would have likely been unexpected.
Mr Roman adds that “the test comes on 3 January when the new Congress takes the purse”. With Israeli elections last week culminating in an undecided outcome meaning that a government is yet to be formed, it is possible that Congress could shift its position depending on whether Netanyahu or opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot are in power.

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.

Relative newcomer emerges as kingmaker after New Zealand election yields deadlock
Neither the ruling National Party nor the opposition Labour are likely to secure decisive victory

New Zealand may need to wait for weeks to find out who can form the next government as neither the left nor the right has secured a decisive victory in the general election.
The ruling centre-right National Party and the main opposition Labour remain in a deadlock even after the counting of over 99 per cent of the ballots, with the relative newcomer Opportunity Party shaping up to be a key decider in the incredibly tight race.
The election, which began on 26 October and ended on Saturday, was defined by voter disillusionment with the two main contenders.
Prime minister Christopher Luxon’s National won just 29.21 per cent of the preferred party vote, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races.
Mr Luxon, who faced two separate confidence votes from his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.
However, Labour also won just 29.36 per cent of the party vote, suggesting a second election defeat for its leader Chris Hipkins.
In spite of winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour secured only 36 seats on numbers because they won fewer local races.
Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The Greens won 16 seats and the Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.
The total number of seats in New Zealand's parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats needed for a majority.
Mr Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties.
However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.
Even if the final tally boosted the left’s seats slightly, Mr Hipkins would apparently need support from Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity Party to govern.
Before the election, Mr Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Ms Wong. On Sunday, however, he sidestepped questions about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.
"Tonight New Zealand has spoken,” Mr Hipkins said, addressing supporters on Saturday. “It may take us a little bit longer to figure out what exactly it is that you've said.”
In the lead-up to the election, it was clear from polls that voters had lost faith in the two major parties amid frustrations over a sluggish economy and ageing infrastructure.
Household budgets remained strained and unemployment rose to about 6 per cent in the third quarter, the highest it had been in New Zealand in over a decade.
The tight deadlock means the country's smaller parties can potentially participate more in a governing coalition.
“I think it’s going to take some time before that becomes clear,” ACT leader David Seymour said when asked if the coalition led by the National Party would return to power.
The new government will be formed only after official final results are released on 27 November.
Special ballots, including from overseas voters, will not be included in the final count until this date.
Overseas voters have historically favoured the left, meaning their votes will be crucial in races that remain tight between Labour and National candidates.
It appears that parties won’t begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on 27 November, when their exact number of seats can be confirmed.
Mr Luxon on Sunday urged people to “calm down” and enjoy a break from politics. “I think everyone's over politics, so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks,” he told reporters.

People will realise electoral Hindus: Ravi Kishan's dig at Akhilesh over Ram Mandir visit
Akhilesh Yadav is set to visit the Ram Mandir on December 12, his first visit to the shrine since its consecration in January 2024. BJP asked him to apologise first.
BJP MP Ravi Kishan on Sunday took a pointed swipe at Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav over his proposed visit to the Ram Temple in Ayodhya, saying he should take Congress leader Rahul Gandhi along and apologise to the kar sevaks before entering the temple.
Taking a dig at the Opposition, the Gorakhpur MP said people would be watching those whom he described as "electoral Hindus", suggesting that the Opposition's renewed engagement with religious symbolism was driven by political calculations. Akhilesh Yadav's first visit to the Ram Mandi is scheduled for mid-December, just months ahead of the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.
"I just heard that Akhilesh Yadav is going to visit the Ram Temple. When he goes, he should take his elder brother Rahul Gandhi along. The Congress's mother believed that Lord Shri Ram was imaginary. You should apologise to the kar sevaks before leaving. You should go with emotions, not for elections," Kishan said.
The BJP leader further criticised the Opposition, questioning its commitment to Lord Ram and accusing it of approaching the temple visit with electoral considerations.
His remarks came amid a fresh political exchange between the BJP and the Samajwadi Party over Akhilesh Yadav's proposed visit to Ayodhya on December 12.
According to former SP MLA Pawan Pandey, Akhilesh Yadav and his wife, Dimple Yadav, will visit the Ram Temple and Hanumangarhi temple during their trip. The visit will be Akhilesh's first to the Ram Temple since its consecration in January 2024.
The announcement has triggered a political debate in Uttar Pradesh, where the BJP has repeatedly questioned why the former chief minister has not visited the temple since its inauguration. The proposed visit is being viewed as part of the Samajwadi Party's attempt to counter the BJP's political narrative around Hindu identity.
The BJP has frequently targeted Akhilesh over the police firing on kar sevaks in Ayodhya in 1990, when his father, Mulayam Singh Yadav, was the Uttar Pradesh chief minister. The incident remains a major political flashpoint between the two parties.
Kishan's remarks came amid a similar attack by Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, who said Akhilesh should apologise to Ram devotees and saints before visiting Ayodhya.
Speaking at AajTak Panchayat during a conversation with Aaj Tak Senior Managing Editor Sweta Singh, Adityanath said everyone had the right to visit the temple town but insisted that the Samajwadi Party chief should first acknowledge his party's past actions.
"Everyone has the right to come to Ayodhya. But if the Samajwadi Party chief wants to visit, he should first apologise to Ram devotees for his actions and deeds. He should also apologise for neglecting Ayodhya," the Chief Minister said.
The Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) has also criticised Akhilesh's proposed visit. The outfit's national spokesperson, Vinod Bansal, asked the SP chief to seek forgiveness for his alleged remarks against Lord Ram, the Ram Temple and Hindu religious beliefs.
AKHILESH HITS BACK CITING TEMPLE DONATION THEFT
SP chief Akhilesh Yadav shot back at the BJP, questioning the Uttar Pradesh government's handling of the alleged donation case in Ayodhya and raised concerns over the compensation paid to residents whose land was acquired for development projects.
"When will the truth behind the donation case come out? Who were involved, who protected them and why has no action been taken despite an SIT investigation? Why has the Chief Minister remained silent? Who will take responsibility?" the Samajwadi Party chief said.
He added, "People of Ayodhya were humiliated and denied fair compensation for their land in the name of development."
The exchange comes amid an intensifying political contest over Ayodhya, with the BJP and the Samajwadi Party trading allegations over religious identity, the Ram Temple and the treatment of local residents.

Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:
The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.
Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.
What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.
Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

After Democrats flipped the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, an image (archived) spread online purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump being carried out of the White House by Secret Service agents after fainting in response to Republican losses.
The image in question has signs of being edited or created using artificial intelligence tools. The White House also denied that fainted in response to the midterm election results. As a result, rate this image as fake.
A White House official told Snopes over email, "This is completely false and an unserious question."
The night of the election, Trump told The New York Times over the phone that he would accept all the results. In the aftermath, on Nov. 4, Trump appeared before the media speaking about his White House ballroom and other Washington, D.C., construction projects. There was no indication he had suffered any health event the evening prior.
The image had strong indications of being AI-generated. The soles of Trump's shoes are too small. One version of the image shows cameras taking photographs of Trump being carried. If there were so many cameras present, the images would almost certainly have appeared in reliable media outlets like Reuters or The Associated Press. The lighting in this version of the image is also incongruous with the flashing cameras. 
However, other versions of the image on X and Threads don't show any cameras. An X post (archived) shared by the Iranian embassy in India shows a video version with Trump being carried out by agents and thrown into a bin labeled "Hazardous waste." Other indications of AI generation include Trump's tie, which appears to have three separate sections hanging from the knot, and disembodied hand appearing under Trump's right thigh.
The story also appears on a site named USALOD, which publishes unverified content including articles with the headline: "Meghan Markle, 45, is looking stunning in New Look, raising big questions as she was recently spotted enjoying some quality time with a mysterious man."
In an apparent contradiction to the headline, the article in question states:
Any genuine medical emergency involving an American president would require clear communication from the White House and reliable confirmation from medical officials.
At present, there is no verified confirmation that Trump fainted, was rushed out of the White House, or received a new medical diagnosis.
Snopes has previously debunked false rumors about Trump, including fake quotes attributed to him.

In September, the Gallup-Pivotal Women’s Health Survey reported that 34% of U.S. women strongly or somewhat agreed that a health care provider minimized or dismissed their symptoms in the past five years. Thirty-three percent reported being misdiagnosed or unable to get a diagnosis, compared with 21% of men reporting these experiences.
Medical records tell a different story. An epidemiologist and a sociologist, we recently released a study where we paired electronic medical records with detailed interviews with 87 women. We talked to these women about their pain and illnesses, work, family, poverty, violence, and encounters with the health care system.
Fifty-three of the women described a trust-breaking encounter with a health system, but only seven of them had medical records that documented mistrust. Thirty-two women reported experiencing a misdiagnosis, but misdiagnosis was only documented for eight of these women. Thirty women reported that they felt that clinicians treated them with disrespect, but this was not documented in the records anywhere.
Consider Kate (not a real name).
For more than a decade, Kate lived with debilitating pelvic pain. Her doctors repeatedly attributed her symptoms to obesity. Her medical record reflected these assumptions.
“She can’t control what she is eating.”
“She admits to poor eating habits.”
When Kate underwent bariatric surgery and lost a significant amount of weight, her clinical notes became optimistic.
“Ran ½ marathon in October!!!!”
However, her symptoms persisted. Medical records pivoted from linking symptoms from obesity to mental health factors.
“Gastrointestinal malfunctions arising from mental factors.”
The turning point came only after Kate attended an appointment with her new husband. In the clinical notes, the provider documented Kate’s husband’s concerns:
“Painful intercourse for the past year.”
“Pain makes pt stop having intercourse.”
“Pt’s husband had very good questions.”
For the first time in 10 years, doctors conducted the exams needed to finally diagnose Kate with endometriosis.
Kate’s medical record accurately documented years of conversations about weight and mental health. What it failed to capture was equally important: the cost of years spent with an undiagnosed disease, the frustration of not being believed, and the erosion of trust that occurs when symptoms are repeatedly explained away rather than investigated. Kate told us, “If I was tired, it was because I was overweight. If I had cramps, it was because I was overweight. Migraines, I was overweight. … They’re not hearing what you’re saying, and that compounded the issues that were going on.”
We often think of medical records as objective accounts of a patient’s health. They are not. Medical records are narratives, shaped by the questions clinicians ask and the assumptions they bring into the room. Medical record data reflect clinical decisions as well as biology. The language clinicians use and the details they choose to record can reinforce stereotypes that follow patients from one encounter to the next, influencing how future clinicians interpret symptoms, assess credibility, and make treatment decisions.
Medical record data also reflect what patients feel comfortable disclosing. What women share with their doctors depends on how much they trust them and how safe they feel. When people fear judgment, dismissal, or not being believed, important parts of their stories may remain unspoken, and thus, undocumented.
This fear may why 53 women in our data described a trust-breaking clinical encounter in their interview, while only seven of their medical records noted their mistrust. This is particularly a problem for women, who feel the pressure to be pleasant and pliant with doctors for fear of not being taken seriously.
Across the country, clinics and hospitals are adopting AI scribes that transcribe recorded interactions between doctor and patient and produce a clinical note. AI tools can be used to search and synthesize medical records to help with diagnostics and treatment plans, some with great success.
However, these tools are only as good as the data in the medical record. If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.
For AI to achieve its full potential in women’s health, medical records need to tell the complete story. Health care settings must be safe spaces where women can tell their stories; clinicians need to listen to women, even when their experiences do not fit clinical expectations; and clinicians need to document in the medical record when diagnoses are delayed or incorrect, without fear of being penalized.
Armed with these data, AI has the potential to do more than replicate biases of the past. AI could help identify patterns of missed diagnoses, reduce disparities in care, and ensure that more women are heard.
Annemarie G. Hirsch, Ph.D., M.P.H., and Jennifer Silva, Ph.D., are authors of “Seen But Not Heard: What Medical Records Don’t Tell Us About Women’s Lives.”

The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.
The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.
Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”
Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”
Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”
But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.
The summit will have a notable absentee, with the US refusing to send a delegation for the second year in a row. The Trump administration wants no part of “extremist climate policies” embraced by other countries, according to a White House spokesperson.
Donald Trump expressed glee shortly before the US midterm elections about the huge profits made by oil and gas companies due to the Iran war, which he started and has caused an increase in living costs around the world. “I don’t give a damn,” the president said at a recent rally in Georgia. “I’m going to say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune.”
However, a group of 20 Democratic members of Congress have made the trip to Antalya, buoyed by their party’s stunning success in the US midterms last week that will enable them to stymie Trump’s attempts to dismantle pollution rules and withhold financial support for clean energy.
Developing countries and civil society will seek to put climate finance and justice at the heart of the Cop31 talks. Rukiya Khamis, the east Africa programme manager at the 350.org campaigning group, said: “Across east Africa, people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. From prolonged droughts to destructive floods, we are losing homes, livelihoods and access to food and water. Yet the money needed to respond to these impacts remains out of reach for many of the countries and communities most affected. It is fundamentally unjust that those least responsible are being left to carry the greatest costs.”
This summer more than 50,000 people died in Europe due to heatwaves, severe wildfire smoke shrouded swathes of North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal triggered a landslide that caused more than 1,500 deaths, while the El Niño weather event, described as “staggering” by scientists and still to reach its peak, is gathering strength.
However, while the pace of progress on cutting global emissions has been slow, the Iran war has spurred many countries to see fossil fuels as expensive and vulnerable to shocks, while renewables continue to plummet in price.
Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said before the talks: “Climate impacts hit every population and every economy harder each year. [But] almost every major economy, and many medium-sized and smaller economies, now see climate action as a central driver of economic growth, jobs, and affordable and secure energy.”
Cop host Turkey also wants more countries to switch to electric technologies, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, as these are many times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts. A target for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035 will be on the table, but faces opposition from some.
Both presidency countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Australia is one of the world’s leading exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas. The centre-left Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and have more than 80% of its electricity generated by solar and wind by 2030, but is off track to meet them.
Labor also faces a political threat from the resurgent rightwing One Nation party, which dismisses climate science. One Nation and the Liberal and National party coalition want to scrap the net zero goal.
The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “This summer, we all felt it: climate change is here, in Britain, now. No country can tackle it alone, which is why Cop31 matters. The answer to high bills and climate change is the same – more clean, homegrown power, creating good jobs and warmer homes. Cop31 is about Britain’s national interest.”

Apoorv Shankar believes that in the very near future, humans will interact with technology through a series of approvals and rejections. AI agents will proactively come to us to complete tasks, and humans will say, “Yes, order that Uber,” or “No, don't get lunch from that spot.”
But if you get multiple pings from an AI agent throughout the day, taking out your phone to say yes or no every single time will be a “bottleneck,” he says. That's why he made the Aina Ring. It has a small display and a joystick-like button that lets you quickly accept or reject an AI agent's actions with your hands. Your phone can stay in your pocket.
Aina has been in stealth for the last 15 months, though the company debuted a few experimental products at CES 2026 under a different name: Project Mirage. One was called Dune—think of it as the precursor to the Aina Ring. Connect it to your Mac and the three buttons become context-aware controls based on what you're doing. In a meeting? The buttons can turn into shortcuts for mute, camera off, or record.
Aina studied how people used Dune and developed the Aina Ring, which it’s announcing today. Preorders are live now, and the ring costs $399 for a limited time before the retail price rises to $499 when it starts shipping in January 2027.
“Approvals are going to be the future of interfaces and interaction, and we wanted to build a device that just made it easy to approve stuff,” Shankar says.
This isn't Shankar's first time with a smart ring—he previously was the vice president of hardware at Ultrahuman, a fitness- and health-tracking ring that competed with Oura. (Ultrahuman was briefly banned in the US after a patent dispute with Oura.)
The team explored other gadgets like smart glasses and pendants, but ultimately decided the ring was the most convenient way to interact with agents. The titanium Aina Ring connects to Macs or iPhones, and at any moment, the onboard assistant is looking for the three things you need next. It learns your routines from your personal data, like location, calendar, and email, and after you connect various third-party services in the Aina app, like Uber or Spotify.
If you usually go for a run at 6 am, as soon as you put on your running shoes, it will suggest continuing the podcast you started last night, or play music—the ring's joystick doubles as a music-playback controller. If it's 8:30 am and you usually take an Uber to work, it'll suggest the ride—flick yes on the ring, and it'll handle the task right away. If you're running late for a Zoom meeting, Aina will ask if you want the assistant to send an email saying you'll be late. Shankar calls these “Aina Cues,” powered by the ring's Context Aware Operating System.
Many of these actions will likely be limited based on what apps and features are supported, though Shankar says users can create their own Cues using natural language. So if you want the ring to prompt you about turning on the coffee machine every morning at 8 am, you can configure that. If your favorite app or service doesn't work through Aina, you can connect your preferred AI agent—like Muse or Instinct—to Aina, and they will handle the task through virtual browsers.
The display is crucial to make sure the user knows whether an action went through. “Agents today don't respond immediately,” Shankar says. “For us to trust these devices—that what I said actually just happened—you need display confirmation.”
These Cues aren't the only capability on the Aina Ring. Aina Voice lets you quickly talk to your AI agents by pressing the center button, or ask Aina to take notes, similar to smart rings like the Sandbar Stream or Pebble Index 01. The ring also has a tiny speaker, so you can take phone calls—initiate the call with a voice command, then bring your hand to your ear, like you're James Bond talking through an earpiece. (Bond would strongly advise against the gesture.)
Like the experimental Dune gadget, the ring also turns into a context-aware remote based on what you're doing. If it knows you're in a Zoom call on your Mac, it will offer up Zoom controls on the ring. If you're watching TV and can connect your TV system to Aina, it can act as a TV remote.
Many companies have tried and failed to be the next gadget for the AI revolution. Humane and Rabbit are two notable examples, but nothing has stuck so far. OpenAI is developing such a product with ex-Apple designer Jony Ive. But many of these devices claimed to replace your phone, and some, like the Rabbit, just felt awkward to carry around alongside the smartphone.
The Aina Ring isn't trying to replace anything—Shankar says phones are “too perfect.” Instead, it's just a means to stop you from being a bottleneck, so your AI agents can keep working on your behalf.
“We are seeing a major shift in how we operate with things—agents are able to do so much, and everything is waiting on us," he says. "I don't have an easy way to approve—we're going to see that a lot more once we see what the potential of proactive AI is.”

Trump says he will become ‘Mr Veto’ after losing Congress. But what will he be able to do?
The US president retains the power to block legislation which is likely create deadlock in government, Daniel Keane reports

Donald Trump has responded to his disastrous defeat in the US midterm elections by threatening to use one of his most significant remaining powers: the presidential veto.
In a major setback to the President, the Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House on Wednesday after scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds, including Kansas and Texas.
The results will severely hamper Trump’s efforts to deliver his legislative agenda for the remainder of his presidency, following two years in which Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in the President.
As the scale of the Republican defeat became clear, Trump posted a picture of one of his iconic red baseball caps on his Truth Social account featuring one word: “Veto”.
On Sunday, Trump said he expected to issue vetoes for “a month or two” before reaching compromises with the Democrats. “I guess I’ll become Mr Veto,” Trump told the New York Post’s Pod Force One podcast. “And then at some point, we’ll probably make deals.”
The White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress and will seek to advance Trump’s agenda on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending through executive power.
The Independent looks at what veto powers Trump will have – and what he will find difficult to do in government after the results.
What is the veto?
Despite the Democrats winning both chambers, Trump retains veto power and broad executive authority, limiting the ability of his rivals to enact major legislation.
Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution states that the President can veto bills passed by Congress before they become law. Congress can override the veto, but it requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
The veto does not allow the President to change the content of the legislation. But by threatening a veto, they can seek to influence and shape a bill before it is proposed.
A “pocket veto” happens if the President does not sign a bill within 10days of it being passed to their desk by Congress. If Congress is adjourned before the 10days are up and the legislation is not returned by the President, the bill effectively dies. This type of veto is particularly powerful because Congress cannot override it, as it is not able to vote whilst in adjournment.
Has Trump used the veto before?
Trump used the presidential veto 10 times during his first term, according to the American Presidency Project at UC Santa Barbara.
In his second term, he has used it twice. This compares with 13 vetoes during the Biden administration and 12 during Barack Obama’s two terms.
In December last year, Trump vetoed two bills that passed Congress with bipartisan support. One had aimed to cut the amount that communities in Colorado were paying toward a new water pipeline, proposed by one of Trump’s MAGA allies Rep. Lauren Boebert.
The other would have supported a flooding mitigation project for a Native American tribe in Florida.
Under the legislation, the Miccosukee tribe would have been given more control of their tribal lands. But Trump claimed that the tribe had “actively sought to obstruct reasonable immigration policies that the American people decisively voted for when I was elected”.
The tribe was among groups suing the Trump administration over an immigration detention center built in the Everglades known as “Alligator Alcatraz”, which has now been shut down.
Trump has previously invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.
What will be difficult for Trump to do?
The results are likely to usher in deadlock in Washington.
Once seated in January, the Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation.
A Democratic Senate can also block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.
But there are still a number of areas that Trump can influence without congressional approval. He will still retain significant authority to pursue foreign policy and implement tariffs, two areas that have been a focus during his second term.
For example, Trump can continue to order new airstrikes on Iran, impose economic sanctions and directly negotiate with world leaders, including Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.
However, new treaties with other countries cannot be ratified without congressional approval. And Trump will not be able to declare war on another country – only Congress has the constitutional power to do so.
Will the veto force Trump and the Democrats to compromise?
During both of his presidential terms, Trump has shown little appetite for seeking congressional approval for many of his key policies. This includes his deeply unpopular war in Iran, which began in late February with the assassination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
In an interview with the New York Times on Tuesday, Trump offered a surprisingly conciliatory message to the Democrats and said he’s “willing to accept the results” of the midterms.
"We’ll work with the Democrats and we’ll look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out," he said.
For anything to be accomplished, Trump and the Democrats will need to strike a compromise.
There is past precedent for this. In 1995-96, the then Democrat President Bill Clinton was forced to negotiate with a Republican-controlled House and Senate to pass a federal budget. Clinton vetoed the initial Republican legislation in December 1995 and the government was shut down for nearly a month.
Negotiations between Democrats and Republicans eventually led to the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which contained compromises on both sides on taxes and spending cuts.
But many experts say that Trump will likely continue to govern as he always has done – without the approval of Congress.
“President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. “I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities.”
Past history also suggests that while the Democrats are likely to bombard Trump with new legislation, he is unlikely to give most of it his backing.
“They can send over 50 different great bills that they are all excited about, and I send them back with a nice stamp,” he told FOX News.
Dr Rebecca Stone, associate professor of US History at the University of Warwick, told The Independent that a gridlock caused by constant vetoes could ultimately harm the Republicans’ chances at the next presidential election.
“Unlike Trump, members of his party will face re-election in just two years’ time and, after yesterday’s blue wave, can ill afford a political landscape in which nothing has changed,” she explained.
“A bipartisan effort to get the country moving again would likely prove popular with moderate voters, and the Republican Party may come to see a stern repudiation of its leader as the boost it needs.”

Past White House adviser Raj Panjabi has written a playbook for 'living room' crises
Dr. Raj Panjabi's new book has a simple title: Safer: A Playbook.
Yes, a playbook like the kind sports managers use to firm up a winning strategy. But playbooks aren't just for games.
"In the intensive care unit, we have a playbook when someone's heart stops beating," And when he was a White House health adviser during the COVID emergency, he says, "In the Situation Room, we had a playbook for pandemic preparedness."
Then there was his own family's situation — at age 1, his daughter was diagnosed with heart failure.
That experience inspired Panjabi to write a different kind of playbook. "I was frustrated that we didn't have a playbook for crises that appear in our own living room."
What he wrote is actually three books in one: The story of how he and his wife addressed their daughter's life-threatening condition; an exploration of public health issues that beset the globe – and straightforward advice for anyone with a living-room crisis. The book's chapter titles telegraph his philosophy: "Turn Denial Into Action." "Don't Go It Alone." "Get Ready to Pivot." "Embrace Uncertainty."
Panjabi was born to Indian parents in Liberia; his family immigrated to the United States when he was 9. He became a physician and went on to found the award-winning humanitarian group Last Mile Health, which employs community workers to bring health information to people in remote areas.
We interviewed Raj Panjabi at NPR headquarters on October 30. He had just flown in from meetings in Boston, wearing a sharp-looking sports jacket he'd bought at the airport — because his mother, who sells men's clothing, is a tough critic of his fashion choices.
So one thing that happens in a crisis — and that a playbook can help address — is denial. You and your wife both dismissed early concerns about your daughter — thinking at first that her extremely low weight was because she was a picky eater.
I was wrought with the guilt of being a dad and missing this illness — and being a doctor and missing this illness in my own daughter. I thought it was a character flaw. What I learned is that it's not. Denial is the first stage of almost every crisis. It could be a medical emergency, like in the case of my daughter. It could be job loss, that layoff you never thought would affect you.
And what I learned in researching the book — it turns out we have a hard time detecting slow moving threats until they reach a tipping point.
Psychologists call it normalcy bias — the idea that tomorrow will look a lot like yesterday. Until, of course, it doesn't. The good news is that there are ways we can overcome that.
Such as …
In the case of a slow-moving crisis like my daughter's illness, the very first thing you might do is set an if/then threshold. If I see a warning sign, I will act in X or Y way.
Your daughter is 9 now and has recovered. How do you deal with any lingering uncertainty about her heart health?
Every couple of years, she goes to the cardiologist and she gets an ultrasound of the heart. The trigger we're looking for is whether the heart's ability to squeeze is at a normal level or not. We'll see that well before we see any major heart failure. Allowing a trigger to do the monitoring for you allows you to feel some agency and allows you to control what you can control.
Health crises can be very personal — but also societal. In the United States, measles — eradicated 36 years ago, is back because parents are opting not to vaccinate their kids. What's the playbook for talking to those parents?
It's much easier to ask a blame-oriented question when someone's not protecting themselves or their community, such as "Why aren't you following the guidelines?"
And you say in a family crisis or a crisis like the measles outbreak, it's important to ask a different kind of question to move ahead.
When you meet face-to-face, you ask not a blame-oriented question but a barrier-oriented question. What's in the way of you following the guidelines? And that starts to open up potential barriers that you can solve for.
Such as …
Often you start to hear some practical barriers — I can't take time off work because I work multiple shifts in a day. I can't find enough money to get a bus ticket to come to the clinic to get a vaccine.
You may also hear, "I heard that this vaccine might lead to a side effect." Or, you know, in parts of the world I've worked in, people assume vaccines can lead to sterility or infertility.
What I've found Is in almost every scenario, if you meet face-to-face, if you ask a barrier- oriented question not a blame-oriented question, you start to understand people's beliefs and their behaviors. And you don't have to change someone's beliefs for their behaviors to be more protective.
You stress that a bond of trust is essential in this type of situation.
One of the most important messages, as we have measles spreading in many parts of the country, is to ask: Where is trust still present? And what I found again and again is it's not in Washington. It comes from your local faith leader, your local physician, your local healthcare provider, your local school. It turns out even in polling now, 80 to 90% of Americans still trust their healthcare provider. I argue in the book that our greatest protection is connection. If we build those relationships before a crisis, we're more likely to weather it.
Arguably we are experiencing an artificial intelligence crisis now. Is it good … or will it doom us? You currently do work involving AI. What's your take?
I do medical research now with scientists who are using AI to develop the next medicine to defeat cancer or the next vaccine to stop a supervirus. The same tools we're using in our labs can be used by a terrorist to design a virus and make it more capable of evading our vaccines, [of] unleashing a super virus on humanity.
How do you address that dichotomy?
Psychologists have come up [a strategy] with when we face tremendous uncertainty — draw a circle on a piece of paper. Outside of that circle are actions you can't control, such as whether or not a terrorist tomorrow decides they're going to use this or not. But within the circle, I can control whether or not the scientists I work with are minimizing the risks of the way they use AI so that we can maximize its benefit for humanity.
And there is a simple point to keep in mind. You have to grow a virus in a lab. You have to have DNA to do it. AI has not yet been able to dissolve the barrier between the screen and the freezer, as it were. But that doesn't give us permission to relax. We should be setting those warning signs, articulating them now and acting before that barrier gets dissolved.
I had to laugh at a note in your book's closing comments. You mention making "legendary" peanut butter and jelly sandwiches to woo your wife-to-be. What made them legendary?
I had been rejected about three or four times by this young woman named Amisha Raja when I was a freshman at Chapel Hill. And I was a terrible cook. So I made peanut butter and jelly sandwiches, took her out for a lunch, surprised her. It was our first date. I don't think the peanut butter and jelly sandwiches had a whole lot to do with her deciding to go on that date, but I'm grateful she did. Because 25 years later and then some were still together.
What's your jelly of choice?
Oh, I am a big, big strawberry jam guy. And you gotta layer so it's two thirds jelly, one third peanut butter.
That's … sweet!

Horrific mass shooting in Krakow as gunman kills six in Polish tourist spot
A British national is among the six killed in the shooting in Krakow on Saturday afternoon

A British national is among six people who were shot dead in Krakow on Saturday by a gunman authorities believe was inspired by far-right ideologies.
Poland’s defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz described the horrific attack in the city’s main market square as an “act of terror”.
Following the attack, the bodies of two women and a man were later discovered at the suspect’s home.
Police said the gunman drove into the Krakow’s historic quarter and began randomly firing at people, killing four women and two men. One is a British citizen, and at least three of the women are Polish, authorities said.
At least 16 people were also injured, including another British national.
The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish man, was shot and detained by armed officers during a gunfight which left one officer critically injured.
Later on Saturday, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk announced the discovery of three bodies at the home of the suspect almost 100 miles from Krakow. They were likely the man’s family members, Mr Tusk said.
The Polish interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said the attacker held “very radical views” and “was fascinated by far-right ideologies”.
In a press conference, Polish police commander-in-chief Marek Boron said: “There are 16 people injured including two police officers and the perpetrator himself – 11 of those are Polish citizens, five citizens of foreign countries.
“There are six fatalities, four women and two men – three Polish persons, one citizen of Great Britain and two persons who are not yet identified.”
“We are undertaking activities at the place where the perpetrator lived, so I think we will know more what those investigations bring.”
As it emerged that a British citizen was among the dead, prime minister Andy Burnham paid tribute to the victims of the attack.
Mr Burnham said: “I’m shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Krakow today.
“My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland.”
The gunman opened fire in Krakow’s Main Square, in the centre of the old town, at around 3.30pm with an automatic weapon.
Police said the suspect wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and used a military-type long gun.
After being subdued by police, he was taken to hospital for surgery.
Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy. “The square will belong to us again,” Gibała said in a video posted to X.
Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims.
In one video, a police officer was seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse himself to the ground.
The FCDO is advising British nationals in Krakow to “follow the advice of local authorities and monitor local media”.
In a statement, foreign secretary Ed Miliband said: “The UK Government deeply mourns the British national and other victims who have died after the appalling attack in Krakow.
“All of my deepest condolences go to the families of the victims. The UK stands resolutely in solidarity with the people of Poland.”

How does this fluoride-free toothpaste compare when it comes to oral health?
How you brush your teeth — and what you use to do it — matters.
Recently, dentist Dr. Jin-Ho Phark says he's noticed patients asking about fluoride-free toothpaste options. Phark is an associate professor of clinical dentistry at the Herman Ostrow School of Dentistry of University of Southern California.
"There's a lot of interest from the patients," Phark says. "I hear that also regularly from students."
One product that patients are asking about in particular is a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite. Many patients, Phark says, may have seen the products on social media, "being pushed by influencers and other people quite intensively."
The traditional fluoride toothpaste became common in the late 1950s, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, when Procter & Gamble Co. released Crest nationally. Over the next few decades, oral care products with fluoride as their active ingredient became widely available around the world. These products help protect the outer layer of teeth from cavity-causing bacteria.
And dental health is important because it's related to so many systems in your body, from your heart to digestion.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
"There are these connections made between your oral health, and the bugs that you have in your mouth, and systemic health and even the composition of your gut microbiome," says Dr. Livia Tenuta, a dentist who specializes in preventing tooth decay and associate professor at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry.
The claim
The promise of hydroxyapatite? Many of the things you care about when it comes to toothpaste: cavity protection, whitening, enamel-strengthening. But without fluoride.
Health experts widely agree that fluoride — a naturally occurring mineral — is beneficial to health. But curiosity is growing about fluoride-free options.
"There is an increasing number of people who are refusing fluoride totally, or hesitant to take it, especially for their children," says Bennett Amaechi, a professor of dentistry at the University of Texas at San Antonio.
That hesitancy stems from a history of skepticism about fluoride. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has blamed the fluoridation of water for a number of health problems, including arthritis, bone fractures, bone cancer, IQ loss, neurodevelopmental disorders and thyroid disease.
Low levels of fluoride are generally considered safe and key to preventing cavities. Amaechi says there's no concrete evidence about potential harms of fluoride when it comes to children's IQ. And research that has found associations between fluoride and IQ has looked at very high levels of fluoride — over twice what's recommended in the U.S. water supply. The CDC previously named the addition of fluoride to public drinking water one of the top 10 great public health achievements of the 20th century, alongside vaccinations and family planning. They also say fluoride in water reduces cavities by 25%.
Still, Kennedy's criticism of fluoride seems to have made its way to toothpaste — and opened up space for products that use hydroxyapatite instead.
So what is hydroxyapatite?
The hype around hydroxyapatite is, in part, due to its similarity to tooth enamel. There's also some research that suggests hydroxyapatite can help with tooth sensitivity.
Tooth enamel is mostly made of calcium and phosphate. Those minerals form the outer layer of your teeth, which protects the internal layers of tissues, nerves and blood vessels, from damage.
Your enamel is stronger than your bones, but still susceptible to damage over time from things like sugary foods and dental plaque. Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugars, and produce acids that eat away at the outer layer of your teeth. Tenuta says over time, that process sets the stage for tooth decay, often referred to as caries, or eventually cavities (a hole in a tooth that comes from this decay).
She says fluoride toothpaste helps protect teeth by "remineralizing" them with calcium and phosphate.
"When [fluoride is] available in our saliva, in the dental plaque that we were not very perfect in brushing, that fluoride that is left over after brushing with the fluoride toothpaste will actually bring minerals back to the tooth," Tenuta says.
Fluoride works with those minerals to form a new compound that protects teeth. It acts like a shield for your enamel. But you need to brush with fluoride toothpaste consistently. Dentists recommend twice daily to keep those minerals around in our mouths.
Hydroxyapatite is thought to work in a slightly different way. These products seem to get into tiny crevices in the tooth enamel.
Many hydroxyapatite products use a form called nano-hydroxyapatite, which has smaller particles that, in theory, can more easily penetrate pores in enamel, though research data is limited.
The evidence
Amaechi, who studies hydroxyapatite use, says fluoride is extensively researched, especially in long-term studies. But he says early research on hydroxyapatite is positive.
"When it comes to remineralization and preventing caries manifestation, it is as effective as fluoride," Amaechi says.
Amaechi was an author on a 2021 study in the journal Scientific Reports, that followed 177 children for almost one year, and compared hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste. The researchers tracked tooth decay in each group, and found that both groups had similar outcomes. That study included funding from Dr. Wolff Group, a German company that owns two brands that make hydroxyapatite toothpastes.
That company contributed funding to another study, published two years later in the journal Frontiers in Public Health. Researchers found similar results after tracking 171 adults, comparing tooth decay in participants using a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to those using a fluoride toothpaste for 18 months. Both groups showed similar outcomes, suggesting that hydroxyapatite worked as well as fluoride in the study. However, the participants in the study were mostly healthy young adults without any severe oral health problems.
Tenuta says she'd want to see more long-term studies, especially in people with high risk of tooth decay.
"There are very few studies and they recruited participants of low caries risk," she says.
One shorter-term study in 2019, published in the Journal of Investigative and Clinical Dentistry, did compare a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste in 133 people who were at higher risk of caries. After a little over five months, the researchers found both toothpastes performed similarly.
The bottom line
Hydroxyapatite toothpastes tend to be more expensive than fluoride ones — some over a dollar more expensive per ounce.
For patients who are open to both options, "I will advise them to use fluoride because fluoride has more evidence supporting its efficacy," Amaechi says.
Tenuta agrees.
"I would recommend as a best option to stick to a fluoride toothpaste because that's what we have a lot of evidence behind," she says.
The American Dental Association, a professional group for dentists, said in an email to NPR they acknowledge more people are using products with forms of hydroxyapatite and that some evidence suggests those products can contribute to remineralization.
However, research on the ingredient is new, "and evidence regarding its clinical effectiveness remains limited and ambiguous, especially regarding clinical indications," wrote ADA Consumer Advisor spokesperson Dr. Ada Cooper.
Instead, the ADA recommends you brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste, floss daily and regularly visit a dentist.

Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has registered advance ticket sales worth Rs. 10.48 crores nett for its sixth day, Tuesday, November 10, across all language versions and formats. As of 10 AM on Sunday, November 8, the much-awaited mythological epic has sold approximately 2.56 lakh tickets across 17,600 shows, indicating continued advance demand beyond its extended opening weekend.
The Hindi version continues to be the biggest revenue driver for Ramayana. Of the total Rs. 10.48 crores nett in advance sales, Hindi alone has contributed Rs. 8.93 crores, accounting for approximately 85.15% of the nationwide total. Kannada occupies the second position with Rs. 66.26 lakh, representing 6.32% of the advance business. Telugu follows with Rs. 44.43 lakh, while Tamil has generated Rs. 35.89 lakh and Malayalam Rs. 9.14 lakh. The substantial Hindi contribution is particularly interesting considering that the language accounted for approximately 74.62% of the film's cumulative domestic box office collections during its first three days.
Collectively, the four South Indian language versions have contributed approximately Rs. 1.56 crores, representing just 14.85% of the advance-booking revenue.
Perhaps the most fascinating aspect of the Day 6 advance bookings is the overwhelming contribution from 3D screenings. All 3D formats collectively account for Rs. 7.68 crores nett, representing approximately 73.30% of the total advance revenue. In comparison, 2D formats have contributed Rs. 2.80 crores, or 26.70%.
Standard 3D is the single biggest revenue generator, collecting Rs. 4.84 crores nett, approximately 46.14% of the overall advance business. Standard 2D follows with Rs. 2.73 crores, while IMAX 3D has generated an impressive Rs. 2.38 crores. Premium 3D formats, excluding standard 3D, have collectively contributed approximately Rs. 2.85 crores, highlighting the importance of premium-priced screenings to the film's revenue.
Maharashtra and Karnataka have emerged as the two leading states in terms of Day 6 advance-booking revenue. At the city level, Bengaluru and Mumbai occupy the top two positions.

The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) has conducted search and seizure operations at five premises linked to persons and entities allegedly involved in a counterfeit medicines racket in Karnataka. The agency has also frozen a bank account containing approximately ₹9 lakh belonging to one of the accused.
The searches were conducted under Section 17 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, as part of an ongoing money-laundering investigation arising from an FIR registered at Tavarekere police station on August 18, 2026.
The case originated from a joint raid conducted by the Drug Controlling Authority and police personnel at a residential property in C.K. Tandya village on August 18. During the raid, the accused were allegedly found storing medicines and pharmaceutical drugs without valid licences, permits or authorisations and replacing labels on the stored medicines. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) led by Vamsi Krishna, Joint Commissioner (West), Bengaluru is probing the case.
The FIR was registered under Section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, and Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957. Since these offences are scheduled offences under the PMLA, the ED registered an Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR) and initiated a money-laundering investigation.
According to the ED investigation, a man identified as R. Prashanth allegedly arranged a farmhouse near Bidadi to manufacture, repackage and relabel medicines without the requisite drug licence or permit.
Cheap bulk pharmaceutical formulations allegedly sourced from manufacturing centres in various States were repackaged into new vials and fraudulently labelled as expensive Pfizer antibiotics, including Zavicefta and Emblaveo. Although the vials allegedly contained generic medicines, they carried labels bearing the Pfizer brand name.
The counterfeit medicines were allegedly distributed through M/s DM Pharmaceuticals and supplied to M/s Krupa Healthcare. The latter subsequently supplied the medicines to other pharmaceutical entities and hospitals, mixing them with genuine medicines to avoid detection, the ED said.
During the searches, the agency froze bank accounts belonging to Veeresh Kumar containing approximately ₹9 lakh. Digital devices, records and other incriminating documents belonging to various persons were also seized.
Further investigation is underway to identify the extent of the alleged money-laundering network and trace the proceeds of crime.

How the Democrats' midterm wave shows a path back to the presidency
Pocketbook populism that worked in red and swing states could be message in 2028 post-Trump election
Although thrilled by their sweeping defeat of U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the midterms, Democrats remain cautious about jumping to conclusions of what it could mean for the next presidential election campaign.
Still, the dramatic scale of the victory has some seeing a potential path back to the White House in 2028.
The Democrats won the popular vote for House districts by 13 percentage points, the biggest margin for either party in 50 years.
They ousted Republicans in Senate races in the red states of South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, which haven't sent a Democratic senator to Washington since 1998, 1988 and 1932, respectively.
Strategists are busy analyzing both what went so wrong for the Republicans and what went right for the Democrats. If there's one consistent thread in this midterm post-mortem, it's that cost of living concerns made all the difference.
That's why leading Democrats believe the pocketbook populism that worked at the midterms in both swing states and red states is a message that could work in the next presidential election.
Mo Elleithee, former spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee (DNC), says his party "isn't always the best at message discipline," but its candidates stayed solidly on-message in the midterm campaign.
"Candidate after candidate, the most progressive to the most moderate, from Kansas and Texas to Maine and Michigan, every Democratic candidate was talking about cost of living and corruption, and, in many cases, tying those two things together," Elleithee told PBS News Hour.
'What the future looks like'
Democrats who want to run for president will need to show voters their vision for the post-Trump era, Elleithee said.
"For the past decade, what we have mainly been doing is playing opposition to Donald Trump," he said. "Now we can paint a picture of what the future looks like."
For a decade, Democrats have been searching for ways to win back the many working-class voters who had abandoned them in favour of Trump.
Their winning candidates in the midterms in red and swing states focused relentlessly on pocketbook issues in a way that could seize the terrain of economic populism back from the Trump GOP.
"The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right. It's top versus bottom," the Texas Democrat senator-elect James Talarico said frequently from the very launch of his campaign.
James Talarico, the Democratic senator-elect for Texas, thanked supporters in Austin after his win on Tuesday. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)
DNC chairman Ken Martin says the midterm victories were in part a repudiation of Trump, but also a consequence of Democrats talking about affordability.
"Our candidates across the board ran for something, not against something," he told NPR. "They gave people a sense of a positive vision of what Democrats would do while we're in power."
The three priorities that Democrat leaders have said they intend to pursue immediately once the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3 are all aimed at bringing down costs for Americans: repealing Trump's tariffs, restoring health insurance subsidies cut by the Republicans and ending the war in Iran that triggered big jumps in fuel prices.
Midterm results shift electoral college map
Midterm wins at the state level mean next year will see Democrat governors in power in all seven swing states that Trump won in 2024: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
Democrats also now envision Ohio, which has voted solidly for Trump in three straight elections, to be a potential target in 2028 after midterm wins for both governor and Senate.
Some are even dreaming that Texas, with its shifting demographics and its 38 electoral college votes, may no be longer a lost cause, after a Democrat sweep of statewide races.
It remains to be seen how long the Democratic Party's midterm-fuelled unity will last once the fight for the 2028 nomination begins.
That could start as soon as next spring, given the track record of would-be presidential candidates announcing their intentions roughly a year and a half before election day.
- Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles after midterm defeat
- Analysis JD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?
The dominant theme in the nomination race could be the competing visions of centrist and progressive Democrats.
Progressive icon Bernie Sanders — the independent U.S. senator from Vermont who the Democratic Party spurned in 2016 as presidential nominee in favour of establishment candidate Hillary Clinton — argues the midterm results show there's only one route to victory.
"We can win over millions of Republicans and independents who are struggling economically if we focus on the issues that are important," Sanders told Politico Playbook this week.
Sen. Bernie Sanders campaigned for the Michigan Democrat Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, at a rally in Grand Rapids on Oct. 25. (Kristen Norman/The Associated Press)
Sanders said Democrats need to have the courage to tell big-money donors, "Thank you very much for your help, but right now we are going to focus on the needs of the working families of this country, whether you like it or not."
Warnings abound for the Democrats about what lessons they should and shouldn't draw from the midterm result and how it may apply to 2028.
David Plouffe, who served as Barack Obama's campaign manager in 2008 and advised Kamala Harris in 2024, says the Democrats can't count on voter sentiment in this year's midterms being the same in the next presidential election.
"I would say this was a vote against Trump more than a vote for the Democratic Party. Our brand is still quite weak," Plouffe told a post-midterm forum at Harvard University's Institute of Politics.
- U.S. midterm results won't deter Trump from 'bombastic, over-the-top' style, says strategist
- Analysis Ohio and Texas went from red to blue in the midterms but may not stay that way in 2028
Mark Leibovich, a journalist who has extensively covered the party's Trump-era struggles, has a message similar to Plouffe's.
"Democrats should avoid the obvious trap of thinking that their victory means they've magically solved their 'brand problem,' 'trust problem,' or 'working-class-voter problem,' among various others," Leibovich wrote in the Atlantic this week.

A special court in Maharashtra's Thane district has sentenced a 35-year-old man to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment for repeatedly raping a minor girl after promising to marry her.
Additional Sessions Judge Premal S. Vithalani convicted the accused, Shrinivas Ashok Yelgonda, a painter, under relevant sections of the Indian Penal Code and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, noting that while the absence of violence and premeditation was a mitigating factor, the law mandated a minimum 20-year term.
According to the prosecution, the victim resided in the same housing society in Diva East as the accused, and the two became acquainted in June 2020 and subsequently developed a romantic relationship through phone chats.
Special public prosecutor Rekha Hiwrale stated that the accused first sexually assaulted the minor in November 2020 inside a neighbour's vacant apartment by promising to marry her, and later raped her on several occasions. The abuse came to light in February 2022 when a dispute arose after the accused reneged on his promise to marry her.
Four prosecution witnesses, including the survivor, her mother and neighbour, were examined to prove the charges against the accused.
The defence argued that there was an unexplained delay in registering the FIR in 2022, and that exact dates of the recurring assaults were missing. However, relying on the survivor's birth certificate and school leaving certificate, the court verified that she was a "child" under 18 years of age during the major part of the abuse timeline, rendering her legal consent immaterial.
"The evidence on record clearly establishes that the victim was under the bona fide impression that the accused would solemnise marriage with her, which led her to keep the relationship and the repeated physical intimacies concealed from her parents," the judge observed.
The subsequent deliberation by the family before approaching the police is both natural and understandable given the social stigma, honour, and future of an unmarried girl, the court said.
It also noted that there was no evidence of brutal force, physical injury or premeditated sexual predation.
"While the victim's minority under the age of 18 renders her consent legally ineffective and makes the conviction unavoidable, the romantic backdrop remains a vital and compelling mitigating factor in sentencing," it stated.
The court sentenced the convict to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment and imposed a fine of ₹5,000.

Argentina football association (AFA) announced on Saturday that it had appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) against the sanctions FIFA imposed on it over World Cup final incidents.

The AFA was fined $321,000 for breaches of FIFA’s disciplinary code relating to using a sports event for making demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters.
