The midterm elections were great for Democrats everywhere, but some triumphed even more decisively than others: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, for example, cruised to reelection with roughly 63 percent of the vote.
How Democrats can make good on their new mandate
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore explains what his party needs to do in the wake of their midterm victories.
Voters pushed Republicans out — and kept Democrats like Moore in power — in part because of their concerns over a handful of critical issues, including the rising cost of living, the Iran war, and the growing dominance of AI and data centers. The question now is how Democrats can best wield their new power to act on the currents that carried them into office.
For Moore, the stakes may be particularly high: He’s often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down.
America, Actually host Astead Herndon spoke with Moore about his vision for how the Democrats should proceed. As Moore put it, this is a moment in which the party will have to move quickly on the problems that motivate voters most.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Lowering cost is the top priority for voters, and, frankly, it was where they penalized Trump the most. What’s the single biggest thing Democrats could do to address folks’ cost of living concerns?
Actually move fast to fix the things. No more studies. No more 10-year research reports. Move fast. For example, in Maryland, we’ve done permitting reform to be able to speed up affordable housing, right? And I did not need a 10-year research paper to tell me that we have an issue with affordable housing.
Get more housing around transit. Do more transit-oriented development. If it’s state-owned land, don’t tell me why we can’t do something. It is state owned land. Do something on it.
The reason we made the largest investments in childcare in our state’s history is because it is insane when you’re watching the fact that people are spending thirty and forty percent of their paychecks on child care and knowing how much that’s actually going to impact [them]. So there are things that we can do right now to be able to address it.
But I also think that there are things that we need Washington to be able to do. For example, gas prices: There’s no governor that can impact gas prices. We just need to stop fighting stupid wars. There’s no governor that is impacting national energy policy or national grocery prices. What we need to do is stop allowing illegal tariff policy to happen. So I do think that there are things that Washington Democrats have got to do, and that they need to move fast on. But I also think that we don’t need to wait for them to be able to put things in place that we know that actually work.
I wonder what universal healthcare means to you. Is that the government providing insurance?
If you look at what we’ve done here in Maryland, we’ve been able to actually come up with platforms through our Total Cost of Care [Model]. We’re actually working with our hospitals. Our hospitals have a universal budget, and are then able to make sure that people are getting the care that they need.
That has done a tremendous job of being able to help to break the cost curve. Maryland is one of the only states in the country where you’re watching the cost of healthcare actually go down, [while] also being able to increase coverage.
A lot of the Democrats’ affordability message came out of Mamdani’s win. I remember him telling me the one thing he would never budge on is the belief that billionaires shouldn’t exist. I wanted to pose that question to you. Do you think billionaires should exist?
I lose no sleep over the amount of billionaires in our society. I do lose sleep over the amount of children that are growing up in poverty. And I think those who [do] have, have a responsibility to support and uplift and create pathways for those who do not.
Here in our state, we actually cut taxes for the middle class. We cut taxes for military veterans. And I said [to wealthy Marylanders], you need to invest more to make sure that we’re doing things like we’re doing: having the fastest public safety turnaround story in the United States of America, having math and reading scores in our public schools now at five-year highs. And I did ask wealthy Marylanders to invest a little bit more to make sure we can get those kinds of results.
I wanted to move on to Iran. You served in Afghanistan and are a veteran. When we think about this incoming Democratic Congress, should they continue funding a war that Americans have mostly found is not in their interest?
No, and they shouldn’t have funded in the first place.
I’ve heard the argument that that leaves soldiers behind.
No, because we’re talking about a president who unilaterally went to war without even asking Congress for authority. The president does not have the authority to just wage war by himself. That is something that the Constitution lays out. Congress is the only one that has the authority for that. And truthfully, this Congress has been so caught up in the aura of the president of the United States that they have not been leaders; they have been cheerleaders.
Part of the issue is that this Congress needs to be held to account, and that’s exactly what I think happened on Tuesday. But I think about my experiences, right? I served in Afghanistan. I led soldiers with the 82nd Airborne Division, and we went over there with what we believed was an understanding of what was at stake and what needed to happen. That this was about the Taliban, and the Taliban could not be in charge of Afghanistan after 9/11. Twenty years later, trillions of dollars spent, thousands of American service members dead, and do you know who’s in charge of Afghanistan right now? The Taliban.
And so we are dragging ourselves again into another forever war. And the problem is that we have a Congress that is not actually asserting its authority to be able to check this administration. I think that Congress needs to get this done not in the first hundred days, [but] in the first hundred hours. Congress needs to assert its authority and say to the president of the United States: This needs to end.
Data centers also had a horrible night on Tuesday. But I still hear a lot of Democrats say that AI has a place in the economy of tomorrow. Is there a place for pro-AI Democrats in this big tent?
I am very concerned about what we’ve seen from AI, and I know a lot of Americans are. I’m hopeful for what I think the promise of what AI can bring to things like health care and what I think AI can bring to things like education. But I also know that there need to be guardrails.
What we have seen from Donald Trump and these folks is that there are no guardrails. They just let it do what it does. I don’t think that’s the right answer. I think that’s remarkably dangerous.
I don’t think that the answer is telling them, “Police yourself, guys, because that’s going to get us to the right answer.” And that’s why in Maryland, we’ve actually put together guidelines as to how we’re going to be protected from AI. That includes things like protecting our workforce. That includes things like protecting our pocketbooks. That includes things like protecting our children.
We put together some of the most stringent guidelines in the country that said things like, they have to pay for all their own energy and all their own upgrades. That our taxpayers do not pay a single penny for that. That they cannot pollute our air or pollute our water. They need to follow all environmental guidelines. That they need to hire local union workers. And also really importantly, that we need to make sure that the people of Maryland have control, not the data center companies, not the Trump administration. That control belongs to us.
About half of the local jurisdictions in Maryland have either a ban or a pause on [data centers]. And I’ve said the state will never override you, ever. If you have a ban or a pause, that is done, because control goes to the locals.

With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.
The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
What started as a test to understand how sun exposure was aging my skin took a turn that I wasn’t expecting.
Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.
This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.
I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.
The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.
The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.
There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.
The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.
The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.
My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.
The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.
That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.
I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.
At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.

I’m calling it: time of death, November 6th, 1:30 AM, by tweet.
Good riddance, Cybertruck!
We’ll always have our comically oversized windshield wiper.
Elon Musk’s declaration Friday that Tesla would be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck next year to make room for the Cybercab was fascinating for a number of reasons. First, it was a humiliating way to kill a vehicle that was once hailed as the pinnacle of Tesla’s engineering — faster than a Porsche 911, more powerful than an F-150, able to leap over the Model Y as a singular representation of Musk’s Blade Runner-inspired designs for the future. “I think the Tesla Cybertruck is our best product ever,” he declared during a 2019 earnings call. (He prefaced the statement by saying, “This could be totally wrong. I could be totally out to lunch here.” It would appear so!)
The fact that Musk would just quietly put an end to the Cybertruck without any fanfare was a sign of how far it had fallen, not just in the eyes of the public, but in the eyes of its creator, the man most responsible for brute-forcing this low-emission, low-poly technological nightmare into the world.
Tesla actually thought the Cybertruck would be a huge hit, targeting production and demand of 250,000 units per year. To date, the company has only sold 70,000 units — total. Musk’s other company, SpaceX, ended up being one of the largest single purchasers of Cybertrucks to absorb unsold inventory. Musk had to become his own customer to make the Cybertruck look better on paper.
But the death of the Cybertruck is even more noteworthy given the timing of Musk’s tweet, coming just three days after his epic flop at the ballot box. Musk poured over $445 million into Republican races, with most of his money targeting his home turf of Texas — headquarters to both Tesla and SpaceX. Between funnels of $168 million to super PACs backing Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton and nearly $35 million redirected from his own America PAC, Musk dropped more than $200 million on the Lone Star State alone.
All that money, and zero return. Democrat James Talarico crushed Paxton by 12 points to break a 38-year Democratic Senate drought, while Gina Hinojosa ousted Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion. Texas turned blue, despite the best efforts of the world’s richest man — or perhaps because of them?
Americans are fed up: they don’t want Musk meddling in their government, and they especially don’t want his stainless-steel monument to his own vanity and utter refusal to accept human feedback.
The Cybertruck was one of the most epic failures in modern automotive history. While it succeeded as a viral PR spectacle and initially became a top-selling premium electric pickup in early 2024, it ultimately collapsed under the weight of Musk’s own hubris.
The reasons for the Cybertruck’s failures are almost too many to enumerate: too expensive, not as much range or towing power as promised, too many recalls, and, well, it looked the way it did. But when Musk outed himself as a Trump supporter, forever tying himself to Trump’s MAGA brand, the Cybertruck went with him. Electric vehicles are typically associated with a style of coastal progressivism, but the Cybertruck crossed the aisle to become a physical avatar of Trump’s ugly brand of politics.
And more so than any other car in modern history, the Cybertruck was inseparable from its creator. By the time Musk threw hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump’s campaign, launched the America PAC, and took a prominent position in Trump’s administration as the head of the disastrous DOGE project, owning a Cybertruck had become a rolling liability. People who owned a Model 3 or Model Y could credibly claim they bought it before “Elon went crazy,” as the bumper stickers would later declare — a Cybertruck owner could make no such claim.
To be sure, most people who bought Cybertrucks were not interested in distancing themselves from Musk’s brand of trollish politics. A big part of MAGA culture is owning the libs. And because liberals, car purists, and environmentalists couldn’t stand the Cybertruck — mocking everything from its sharp edges to its build quality — buying one became a way to get under their skin. Before long, people were slapping Trump wraps on them, flying flags from the truck beds, and turning them into props for conservative rallies.
But vibes shift, as they always do. Edgelords lose their edge, and voters become weary and wary of efforts to divide them. The blue tsunami was a historic rejection of Trump and Musk’s brand of right-wing grievance politics. When the spectacle wore off, the bluster stopped feeling like rebellion and started looking like a shit way to run a government. In a single election, the country said it was done.
The results on Tuesday also rendered the Cybertruck an instant relic. The election stripped away the sheen of inevitability that once insulated both the billionaire and his pet project. It’s a relief, but a peculiar one at that. Has there ever been a vehicle so desperate to look like the future, only to become an immediate symbol of the past?

For two decades, researchers debated whether adeno-associated viruses, the small viruses used to deliver new genes into thousands of patients, could in certain cases drive tumors. That debate is over.
A series of cases this year has presented powerful evidence that adeno-associated viruses, or AAVs, can cause cancer, forcing researchers and families to weigh the newly confirmed risk against the technology’s lifesaving potential — and hopefully determine how to design better therapies in the future.
“It will change the calculus for some patients,” said Sam Mackenzie, a neurologist at University of Rochester, speaking specifically about spinal muscular atrophy patients.

High fares, longer journeys, delays make special trains less attractive to passengers: Officials
New Delhi, Despite the Railway Ministry's claim of operating 18,000 special train trips across the country to clear the festive rush, regular trains continue to be in much greater demand, with waiting lists often exceeding the permissible limit and ticket-booking websites displaying the 'Regret' status.
Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said on Saturday during a media interaction that all trains were being monitored closely through a special War Room set up at Rail Bhawan to ensure their safe and timely arrival at destinations.
However, railway officials admit that passengers don't prefer special trains due to their higher fares, longer journey times and poor punctuality.
The IRCTC website shows that regular trains on almost all routes have either long waiting lists or a 'Regret' status, indicating that the number of passengers on the waiting list has exceeded the permissible limit.
"If you look at the New Delhi-Patna route, Train No. 04096, a festival special, charges ₹1,745 for an AC 3-tier ticket, whereas the regular Sampoorna Kranti Express charges ₹1,390," an official said.
He added that the special train also takes considerably longer to cover the same distance.
While it takes 22 hours and 55 minutes, the Sampoorna Kranti Express completes the journey in 13 hours and 8 minutes.
"Despite the longer scheduled journey time, special trains hardly reach their destinations on time, often resulting in a tiring journey of 25 to 30 hours," he said.
He argued that this was one of the reasons why the Sampoorna Kranti Express has a much higher waiting list than the special train.
Similarly, special train No. 01143 from Mumbai to Danapur charges ₹2,235 for an AC 3-tier ticket and takes 35 hours and 20 minutes to complete the journey.
In comparison, the regular LTT-Rajgir Express covers almost the same distance in 32 hours and 35 minutes, with an AC 3-tier fare of ₹1,865.
Another official said that while regular trains generally run on schedule, special trains are often delayed by several hours, causing uncertainty and inconvenience to passengers.
They stated that regular trains get overcrowded during the festive season because passengers are willing to travel even with waiting-list tickets, as these trains generally operate according to their scheduled timings.
"Normally, fares on special trains are up to 30 per cent higher than those on regular trains. Moreover, we have to create separate paths for these trains, keeping in mind the capacity constraints on particular routes," a senior railway official said.
"That is why, despite our best efforts, we cannot assure the timely arrival and departure of special trains on high-density routes," he added.
Senior railway officials have suggested that the Railway Ministry should consider keeping fares on special trains lower than those on regular trains, given their longer journey times and uncertain arrival schedules.
"Why would I pay more for a longer and uncertain journey when I can travel on a shorter, more reliable and cheaper train?" an official asked.

AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues) reported a 6% growth in its net profit to ₹71.7 Cr in the quarter ended September (Q2 FY27) from ₹67.7 Cr a year earlier. On a sequential basis, net profit declined 15.4% from ₹84.8 Cr. Meanwhile, its operating revenue grew 46.5% YoY and 7.4% QoQ to ₹287.9 Cr during the quarter under review. Including other income of ₹2.8 Cr, total income during the quarter stood at ₹290.7 Cr. The fintech company’s operating EBITDA, excluding other income, grew just 3% YoY to ₹9.9 Cr. This came as its total expenses rose 49.4% YoY and 7.7% QoQ to ₹282.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, outpacing the growth in operating revenue. At the same time, its consolidated net revenue, after accounting for payment processing and other costs, declined 1% YoY to ₹151.3 Cr in Q2 FY27. AvenuesAI attributed the decline to its ‘competitive pricing strategy’ amid efforts to deepen merchant relationships and increase transaction volumes. As a result, its net take rate moderated 4% to 5.06 bps despite a 19% sequential increase in its total payments volume to ₹1.77 Lakh Cr. The company generated ₹282.2 Cr in revenue from its payment business, which includes its CCAvenue payment gateway, payment infrastructure services to banks (CPGS), and credit and lending-related services, accounting for nearly 98% of its operating revenue during the quarter. The remaining ₹5.7 Cr was derived from its ecommerce platform business, Rediff. AvenuesAI Looks To Unlock Value Across Subsidiaries Alongside its financial performance, AvenuesAI outlined its plans to expand its AI capabilities, with advanced technology development and AI software-related work remaining among the key objectives of its rights issue. In June last year, the company had raised ₹700 Cr via a rights issue, primarily for the repayment of outstanding loans, expansion of its IPO-bound digital content and ecommerce marketplace Rediff and further investments in its AI arm, Nueromind, for which it had earmarked ₹294 Cr. Almost 42.7%, or ₹297.2 Cr, of the net proceeds remained unutilised at the end of the September quarter. AvenuesAI has now announced that it will directly utilise the funds for AI development and software-related activities instead of routing the investment through Nueromind. It clarified that the change was limited to the mode of implementation, with no alteration to the end use of the proceeds. In the June quarter, AvenuesAI announced plans to amalgamate Nueromind with itself, subject to NCLT approval. It is also developing its Transaction Intelligence Score (TISco), an AI-led initiative that will use permitted transaction and merchant-behaviour signals for risk assessment, fraud prevention, merchant intelligence and financial services workflows. The company aims to use its transaction infrastructure to build an intelligence layer that can support merchant and enterprise services. On the investment front, AvenuesAI said it made investments in two financial services companies during the September quarter. It acquired a stake of up to 7% in Online PSB Loans Limited for a consideration of up to ₹65 Cr. It also invested up to ₹34.5 Cr to acquire a stake of up to 1.38% in Ratnaafin Capital Private Limited. The company also reiterated its plans to expand CCAvenue's international payments business, particularly in the US, by leveraging its payment technology, enterprise relationships and regulated infrastructure. Meanwhile, its ecommerce arm, Rediff, is on its way to the bourses for a separate listing. After filing for an IPO confidentially earlier this year, the markets regulator SEBI approved the draft papers in August. However, the Q2 disclosure did not provide an update on Rediff's proposed IPO. As per sources, Rediff would look to raise in between ₹600-800 Cr via the IPO AvenuesAI outlined that unlocking value from Rediff is one of its three strategic priorities for FY27. It plans to integrate Rediff's consumer and enterprise digital ecosystem with its payments and AI capabilities. This includes RediffOne, which offers digital commerce and communication services, and RediffPay, which is intended to expand consumer payment engagement. AvenuesAI has maintained its FY27 consolidated revenue guidance of ₹1,100-1,300 Cr. The company said its focus for the remainder of FY27 will remain on expanding merchant relationships, improving operating discipline and creating additional monetisation opportunities through Rediff, enterprise technology and applied AI. It is also monitoring potential changes to the merchant discount rate (MDR) policy for eligible UPI transactions, with any introduction, timing or scope remaining subject to government and regulatory decisions. Shares of AvenueAI ended today’s trading session 3.72% lower at ₹129.25.

The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) morning, while many parts of the city reeled under “severe” level of air pollution, according to official data.
Many parts of the city, including ITO, Dwarka, Rohini, Punjabi Bagh, Alipur, Bawana, and Jahangirpuri witnessed “severe” level air pollution.
Other cities and towns in north India, including Noida, Gurugram, and Panipat also witnessed “very poor” air quality, on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) morning.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi was 379 (very poor) at 9 a.m. on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), as per Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
“Severe” level air pollution affects healthy people and seriously impacts those with existing diseases, as per the CPCB.
The overall air quality of Delhi is likely to be in the “very poor” category for three days, as per the Central government’s ‘Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi’.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 350 (very poor) at 4 p.m. on Tuesday, up from 324 (very poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI.
A higher AQI means worsening of air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
- Published
European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
Read more
- Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash 
  - Published2 days ago
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds, external allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close Sánchez ally Óscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that Sánchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

The Jillaroos have qualified for the Rugby League World Cup final, but only after surviving an almighty scare against tournament debutant Fiji at Sydney Football Stadium.
The world champions conceded first and were level at half-time, but surged clear after the break to triumph 30-14 and avoid one of the sport's all-time upsets.
Winger Abbi Church scored four tries as the Jillaroos booked a date with New Zealand in next Sunday's final in Brisbane.
After cruising through the group stage with an aggregate scoreline of 242-6, the Australians were challenged for the first time in the competition, caught off guard by a disciplined, aggressive Bulikula outfit.
A penalty goal from five-eighth Luisa Yaranamua earned Fiji a shock 11th minute lead, before the same player dummied and then slid over to provide one of the most sensational scorelines in international rugby league history.
8-0 down after 16 minutes, the Jillaroos were far from their best and clearly rattled, with their hopes of a fifth-straight World Cup final seemingly under threat.
Two unconverted tries, courtesy of Church and Tamika Upton, ensured scores were level at half-time, but the hosts reached the break having completed just 12 of their 19 sets.
An improved second-half showing saw the Jillaroos hit the front and then find some breathing space, Church striking three times after the break.
A cause for concern was the absence of star winger Jaime Chapman, who crossed early in the second period but spent much of the half off the field, struggling with what was reported as cramp.
Fiji was able to conjure a second try late on, but Maria Paseka's late four-pointer, scored after a neat short-side play, was quickly cancelled out by Church's fourth effort of the day.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has arrested a government official and a private individual in an alleged bribery case involving the clearance of imported containers in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, according to news reports. The agency has alleged that the official sought ₹1 lakh from a private firm to facilitate the clearance process and was caught accepting the money through an intermediary. The CBI has arrested an Assistant Director of the Plant Quarantine Station (PQS) in Visakhapatnam and a private individual in an alleged bribery case involving the clearance of imported containers. The arrested individuals have been identified as Sudhakara TM, Assistant Director and in-charge of the Plant Quarantine Station in Visakhapatnam, and Sunkavalli Satyanarayana, a private individual who allegedly acted as an intermediary in the transaction. Sudhakara TM was serving as the Assistant Director and in-charge of the Plant Quarantine Station in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh. The second accused, Sunkavalli Satyanarayana, is a private individual whom the CBI has alleged acted as an intermediary between the government official and the private firm. The CBI registered a case on November 6 against two officials of the Plant Quarantine Station, including Sudhakara, three private individuals and other unidentified persons over the alleged demand and acceptance of an undue advantage. According to the CBI, Sudhakara allegedly demanded ₹1 lakh from a private firm for clearing containers that were awaiting approval from the Plant Quarantine Station. Following a complaint, the agency conducted a verification exercise and laid a trap on November 6. During the operation, the Assistant Director was allegedly caught accepting the ₹1 lakh bribe through Satyanarayana. The CBI said the entire bribe amount was recovered during the trap proceedings. Both individuals were subsequently arrested. Following the arrests, the agency conducted searches at premises linked to the accused in Visakhapatnam, Faridabad in Haryana and Thimanapalli village in Karnataka's Kolar district. The investigators are examining documents and other material recovered during the searches as part of the ongoing probe. The two arrested accused were produced before the competent court in Visakhapatnam on November 7. The CBI is continuing its investigation to establish the role of other individuals named in the case. West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday (November 8, 2026) announced that his government would institute the 'Seema Mitra' award from 2027 to recognise exceptional contributions by BSF, SSB, and state police personnel in securing the country's borders.
A selection committee would be constituted to decide the awardees, he said, while addressing BSF personnel at a border outpost in Hingalganj in North 24 Parganas district, which shares a boundary with Bangladesh.
"We will give the 'Seema Mitra' award from next year for BSF, SSB and West Bengal police personnel," Mr. Adhikari said.
The Chief Minister visited the border outpost to greet security personnel on the occasion of Diwali and Kali Puja.
The BSF guards the India-Bangladesh border, while the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) is deployed along the country's frontiers with Nepal and Bhutan.
Mr. Adhikari apologised to the BSF and CRPF personnel for what he described as derogatory remarks and behaviour by the previous State government.
"I, as the Chief Minister of the State, apologise to you for the derogatory remarks and behaviour of the previous regime towards BSF and CRPF," he said, targeting the erstwhile Trinamool Congress government.
He alleged that the previous Mamata Banerjee government had failed to provide the required land to the BSF for fencing nearly 600 km of the India-Bangladesh border in West Bengal.
Mr. Adhikari said the BJP government had handed over the required land to the BSF soon after assuming office and would provide any additional land needed for border fencing.
He said that his government will provide any additional requirement of land by the BSF in the border areas.
He claimed that the people gave their "appropriate retort" through the democratic process.
The Trinamool Congress lost to the BJP in the 2026 assembly elections in the State.
"We have to move ahead and ensure the security of the country," he said.
The Chief Minister said the State administration, BSF, and SSB were working in close coordination and that his government would work with the Centre to strengthen security infrastructure in the border districts.
West Bengal shares a border of over 2,200 km with Bangladesh, he said, adding that the government would facilitate the setting up of more police stations in frontier areas and provide the necessary infrastructure, logistics and manpower.
Mr. Adhikari asserted that every infiltrator should be identified and sent back.
"This country is for Indian citizens, and we are committed to them and the people of West Bengal," he said.
Referring to Union Home Minister Amit Shah's three-day visit to north Bengal in August, Mr. Adhikari said meetings had been held to strengthen border security and coordination between central and state agencies.
He said coordination meetings between border guarding forces and local police should be held not only at the district level but also at the police station level to address logistical and manpower requirements.
The Chief Minister, who also holds the Home portfolio, said the State had 105 police personnel per one lakh population, against the national average of 155.
His government would focus on creating employment opportunities for youths in border areas and had adopted the Centre's 'Vibrant Village' programme for their comprehensive development, he said.
The government would also ensure optimum utilisation of existing welfare schemes and development projects in the frontier districts, he added.
Mr. Adhikari said the State had started police recruitment and handed over appointment letters to more than 11,600 recruits.
The State cabinet had so far approved 29,000 police recruitments since May, he added.
He also announced that two India Reserve Battalions (IRBs) would be raised in the State with assistance from the Centre.
"Verbal discussion for this has been held, and official papers will be prepared soon," he said.
"It is my duty to come and greet you. When the whole country is celebrating Diwali, you are guarding the frontiers of the country," Mr. Adhikari said, addressing the BSF personnel.
He said he was inspired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has been visiting border outposts on Diwali to meet security personnel since his tenure as Gujarat Chief Minister.
Mr. Modi celebrated Diwali this year with security personnel at a CRPF camp in Chhattisgarh's Bastar district.
Mr. Adhikari said there was close coordination between the BSF and State police, but some issues, including border fencing along the Icchamati river in North 24 Parganas, remained pending.
The State's Irrigation and Waterways Department would work on the issue, he said.
"After completing this portion, the borders here will be 100% secure," the Chief Minister said.
Mr. Adhikari said he had travelled on the last floating jetty towards the Bangladesh border and alleged that people on the other side were waiting to cross over whenever BSF personnel moved away from the area.
Claiming that several lakh infiltrators had been pushed back, he said combing operations were being conducted up to 15 km inside Indian territory to identify and deport illegal immigrants.
"The rest of the infiltrators will also be sent back," he said.
He also asserted that infiltrators would not be entitled to social welfare benefits, including the Annapurna Yojana, under which eligible women receive ₹3,000 per month.
Mr. Adhikari also wished former Deputy Prime Minister L. K. Advani on his birthday, crediting him with contributing to the country's development and the Ram temple movement.
"In his leadership and with the intervention of the Supreme Court, we got the Ram Mandir," he said.
Recalling his association with Mr. Advani, the Chief Minister said the BJP veteran had visited Nandigram two days after the March 14, 2007, firing incident in which 14 people were killed.
"He was then the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha; I am ever indebted to him," Mr. Adhikari, who was a Trinamool Congress leader then and was a pivotal figure in the anti-land acquisition agitation in Nandigram, said.
Mr. Adhikari said that after he became a Lok Sabha MP in 2009, Mr. Advani would ask him about Nandigram whenever he met the BJP leader in Parliament.

Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year
After years of increasing to record-high levels, the homeless population in the U.S. dropped more than 6% in 2025. That amounts to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It's the second year in a row that homelessness has declined, with a smaller drop in 2024.
"President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release announcing the results of an annual count in communities around the country. The agency had not yet posted a detailed report.
A second independent analysis based on the same count, but commissioned by the advocacy group National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline but credited different reasons for it.
"It's good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working," said CEO Ann Oliva.
Both analyses find there's still nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. living in shelters or on the streets, significantly more than before the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Trump administration cited its changes in immigration policy as a key factor in the decline. During the Biden administration, New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw a surge in asylum seekers who turned up at homeless shelters. "That's also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently," said Devon Kurtz, Public Safety Policy Director at the Cicero Institute, an administration ally on homelessness policy.
Kurtz also pointed to declines in cities like San Francisco, which is moving to support more sober-living options, housing that bans drugs and alcohol. But critics say that can send more people back to the street if they relapse, which is common.
The Trump administration argues that the requirement to be drug-free would help more people achieve recovery, and wants to expand such programs. In fact, the administration wants to overhaul several billion dollars in homelessness spending and shift it toward short-term housing with mandated addiction and mental health treatment. So far that's been blocked by courts.
The administration says longstanding federal policy of getting people into permanent housing first, then offering voluntary treatment, has failed, and is to blame for the pandemic spike in homelessness. But Oliva, with the homelessness alliance, said programs that get people off the street without preconditions were a big part of the latest declines, especially among veterans.
"Investments in programs like that are much closer to the scale of need for veterans than for any other population experiencing homelessness," she said. Homelessness among U.S. veterans was down more than 7% last year, and has declined nearly 60% since 2010.
By contrast, Oliva said more permanent housing is needed for people who are chronically homeless, and more likely to suffer from mental health problems and addiction. Unlike other groups that saw a decline last year, there was a small uptick in people who've been homeless for a long time.
HUD also credited a crackdown on homeless encampments after the Supreme Court in 2024 said cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. Oliva said the analysis her group commissioned showed that cities with such bans "actually did worse than the national average."
Oliva noted last year's decline in homelessness was broad and likely due to a number of factors, including softening rental markets in some places. Even though rents are still high they're down from record peaks during the pandemic, and that could stem the flow of newly unhoused people.
There were also declines in places that saw major weather disasters, like western North Carolina and Hawaii. When HUD and other groups move in to help those displaced, unhoused people also get assistance they did not have before.

SA government plans to ban councils from issuing ticketless parking fines
In short:
The government will introduce legislation to parliament to make it mandatory for council inspectors to physically issue parking fines.
The changes will prevent councils from posting fines to drivers after a camera car has driven past.
What's next?
The Local Government Association of SA says it was not consulted on the planned changes and that a ticketless system allows for better efficiency.
The South Australian government plans to ban councils from issuing ticketless parking fines.
Under the planned reforms, councils would be banned from posting fines to drivers after a camera car has driven past, and it would be mandatory for inspectors to leave a physical ticket on the car or hand it to the driver.
The South Australian premier highlighted the City of Adelaide's Park Safe program — which uses a car with cameras on top to scan for illegally parked cars and take high-quality photos — as an example.
The council has previously said the images are reviewed by trained officers to verify whether an offence has occurred.
A recent council report showed that on average, 25 per cent of contested fines were withdrawn following requests for reviews by parking information officers so far this year.
Tour bus operator Dallas Coull, who spoke at the government's press conference about the reforms, said he had never received fines before the Park Safe program but had received "dozens and dozens" since its implementation.
"There's actually a hotel in the CBD that don't pick up [at] anymore because we get kept getting fines," he said.
In nearby Rundle Mall, shopper Fiona Garwood welcomed the planned changes, saying she would "rather have things done by a person".
Fellow shopper Levi Adams said he had seen the council's Park Safe car in the CBD before and agreed with the government's proposed reforms.
"I'm concerned about AI in every aspect of life, so I really don't need it to be in parking fines as well. The less, the better, in my opinion," the 23-year-old said.
Mr Malinauskas said AI technology could still be used, but any ticket would need to be physically issued by a council inspector at the time of the alleged offence.
"If they've got someone in the car and someone gets out of the car, looks at the circumstances … that's OK," he said.
"It's the practice of the car and the AI machine only forming the judgement that we are regulating out."
Local Government Association of SA president Heather Holmes-Ross said it was "unusual" that the state government had not consulted them on the planned reforms, and questioned whether it would extend to other ticketless fine systems.
"The technology we're talking about is the same technology that's used by red light cameras, phone detection — it's all the same software — so we're a little confused about why it would be that just parking data is being attacked here and not all data that's collected by AI," she said.
But the state government said there was an "important distinction" between enforcing parking restrictions and road safety laws.
"Parking fines are mostly issued to stationary cars whereas that is clearly not the case for a speeding car," a spokesperson said.
The spokesperson said the state government would consult stakeholders, including the LGA.
Ms Holmes-Ross, who is also the mayor of Mitcham in Adelaide's inner-south, said there were several councils trialling the technology around the state in a bid to improve efficiency, with human oversight.
"If you drive past 10 or 20 cars, then that video can be viewed, and those fines can be mailed out," she said.
"If you're stopping and you're giving out those 20 individually, it just takes more time.
"So if there's a way of doing it accurately and more efficiently, it's better for everyone."

Some Roku OS users have been sad to learn that their favorite screensaver will no longer be available as of December 1.
This week, affected users reported receiving an alert on their device that they will not be able to use the “Aquatic Life” screensaver after this month, as first reported by Cord Cutters News.
The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium, from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing.
Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen. He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku, a deal that closed today, Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn’t be renewing Roku’s license.
“I can’t be part of the Fox world,” he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News’ controversial style of news and entertainment.
Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements, according to the user notice.
The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS .
“When my head is in overdrive (very often with my ADHD), this screensaver grounds me and lets me exhale and become focused with myself again. It may sound over the top, but it’s true. It takes a lot for me to chill and relax, but this Aquatic Life [screensaver] is my go to. Totally gutted 😢,” a Reddit user wrote this week.

US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
- Published
The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.
The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.
President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated" following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.
Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.
Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.
The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.
As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.
Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.
A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".
It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".
Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.
There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.
In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.
The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.
However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.
On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.
"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

A strong 5.7-magnitude earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, injuring dozens of people, shattering windows and disrupting train services, officials and local media said.
The quake struck at 1:04 am in Shizuoka Prefecture, the Japan Meteorological Agency said. No tsunami warning was issued.
Authorities reported no deaths, but the quake shattered storefront windows and knocked items off shelves and caused transport disruption in parts of the country.
An emergency official in Aichi said authorities had received 16 reports of mostly minor injuries.
Authorities in neighboring Shizuoka said at least three women sought emergency medical care, including a woman in her nineties who injured her shoulder after falling from her bed during the shaking.
The local Chunichi Shimbun newspaper and Tokai Television separately reported at least 24 were hurt across the two regions.
In Toyohashi city in the Aichi region, windows of a car dealership were found shattered after the quake.
A large book store in Toyota city, also in Aichi, reported that its merchandise dropping from shelves.
The quake also forced temporary delays and suspensions of regional train services Sunday morning, including the Shinkansen bullet trains.
The quake was felt as far west as Osaka, where a foreign resident was taken to hospital after falling from a second-floor apartment when the shaking startled them, local media reported.
Officials in Osaka couldn’t be reached for immediate comment.
Separately, a 4.3-magnitude quake struck the Kumamoto region at 10:53 am (0153 GMT) Sunday, the Meteorogolical Agency said.
There were no immediate reports of serious damage or injuries from the second quake.
The southwestern region is still trying to recover from a 7.1-magnitude tremor that killed 38 people, flattened homes and left tens of thousands without power in July.
Japan sits on the Pacific “Ring of Fire” and experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year.
The country is haunted by the massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.

Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
- Published
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".
In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

Anjali Sardana and Pronto entered India’s domestic services market in 2025 to solve a familiar urban problem: finding reliable house help on demand. The result was a quick commerce-style home services platform, combining technology-led recruitment, standardised training and a hyperlocal network of professionals. Pronto, which competes with Snabbit and Urban Company, says it has served more than half a million households across 11 cities. But the real story of Pronto is being developed far away from the homes and houses that its professionals visit. This is being built in Silicon Valley. Footage recorded by professionals working in thousands of homes every day is helping shape the next generation of robots. The first signs of this ambition emerged in May 2026, when Pronto was reported to be exploring ways to generate physical AI training data using footage captured during household chores. And since then Sardana and Pronto’s ambitions have solidified. In July, Pronto formalised the experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which housekeepers and cleaners wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. In October 2026, Sardana set up Provision Labs, a physical AI venture based in San Francisco, which will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. It will work with developers building physical AI models. A few days later, Provision Labs announced that it is acquiring Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a 2023-founded company focused on perception technologies, which help machines interpret their surroundings. Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models. Watwani and his team are said to have developed a 3D hand-tracking model and built the first version of a lightweight tactile glove to capture touch-related data. Given this timeline, the fact that Pronto doubled-down on its experiment after the May 2026 introduction does not seem surprising at all. The relationship between Pronto’s household data collection and Provision Labs’ operations, however, remains unclear. Inc42 asked Pronto how the two businesses work together, if at all, but the company declined to comment. The unanswered question is significant: could a network originally built to deliver household services become an acquisition channel for the data needed to train global robotics systems? Why Record Workers? The first reports around Pronto’s collection of worker data triggered a backlash over surveillance and privacy of house help professionals. To assuage some of the critics, Pronto said that customers are informed about the terms several times before recording begins, while personally identifiable information is automatically blurred or removed on the device. “The raw footage is deleted immediately after the work is done, and no one ever accesses it. For 48 hours, an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording is available only to the customer, who can watch it in the app to check the work. After that, we use the anonymised footage for AI training, as our terms set out,” the company told Inc42. Pronto said more than half of the professionals participating in Verified already earn over ₹40,000 a month. The company claims workers feel safer knowing there is a record of their work, but no independent studies have been conducted to validate these claims. What’s the point of all this? Unlike chatbots, which can learn from the enormous repositories of text and images available online, physical AI systems need to understand how the real world works. A robot must learn how to pick up objects, fold clothes, navigate a room, and respond when something does not go as expected. This requires large volumes of real-world, multimodal data capturing movement, spatial information and interactions with objects. Such data is considerably harder and more expensive to collect than internet-sourced text and images. ANI quoted a Goldman Sachs report estimating that general-purpose robots could require around 10 Mn hours of high-quality physical interaction data to reach production-level capabilities. The Missing Data Layer One can see the physical AI stack through four layers. The data layer captures real-world interactions, while the model layer uses this information to train vision-language-action models that translate what a robot sees into actions. The simulation layer through platforms such as NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim allow these models to be tested in virtual environments before deployment. Finally, the edge layer runs them on physical robots, with real-world feedback informing and enhancing the training process. Global technology companies such as NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are building capabilities across the model and simulation layers of physical AI. India has some representation at the robotics and deployment end, with companies such as Addverb, CynLr and Perceptyne developing robotic systems and automation technologies. But it is the data layer that is seeing a growing crop of Indian startups, alongside global data companies building collection operations that rely heavily on India’s workforce and physical environments. Humyn Labs, EgoData, Egolab.ai, Neocambrian AI, Human Archive, and Objectways have deployed people on the ground to collect footage across household chores, but several are also working with manufacturing units and other industrial environments. Head-mounted or body-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves or even full body suits have become commonplace as the next phase of robotics takes shape. For India, the opportunity has echoes of its earlier role in the AI supply chain. Over the past decade, India has become a hub for data annotation, with workers labelling images, text and audio used to train AI models. Physical AI takes that outsourcing model a step further. Indian workers’ movements, workplaces and interactions with objects are becoming the training material. Abhinav Kukreja, founder of Neocambrian AI, sees India’s large and diverse physical environments as an advantage over markets such as the US, where access to comparable real-world data is more limited. He believes the next phase of robotics will see an explosion of different embodiments and form factors. For India to participate meaningfully in this transition, it needs to control an important part of the underlying ecosystem. “I strongly felt that this layer would not be compute, architecture or algorithms, but the data layer,” he said. Y Combinator-backed Human Archive is pursuing a similar opportunity, with a model that involves home service workers, cooks, cleaners and domestic help wearing cameras inside homes and private properties. Cofounder Rushil Agarwal told Inc42 earlier that the Indian market’s appeal lies in the diversity of industries accessible within the geographical boundary and the large labour pool. This is difficult to replicate in the US. Notably, Human Archive was evaluated by Snabbit too as it looked to launch a Pronto-like data collection pilot. However, the home services company eventually dropped the proposal. Human Archive raised $8.2 Mn in a seed round led by Wing Venture Capital and NVP Capital. Pronto’s $45 Mn Series B also saw participation from Lachy Groom, cofounder of robotics model startup Physical Intelligence; Groom has also backed Provision Labs. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs, led by former Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal, has committed $20 Mn towards expanding its data collection network. The supply side, meanwhile, is becoming more competitive. Data collection rates fell 30% between January and June this year, an industry executive told Inc42 earlier. More suppliers have since entered the market and synthetic data generation has improved rapidly. But in the long run, the demand for human-captured footage could shrink as physical AI models mature. The larger question is who captures the value and what happens to the workers. We’ll come to the latter soon, but the current situation does not give us any clarity on what this segment might look like in a few months. While Pronto says more than half of its Verified professionals earn over ₹40,000 a month, Human Archive has cited compensation in the range of $1-10 per hour for its data collection work. These disparate compensation structures highlight the lack of clarity on the economic model. One cannot draw parallels between the kind of data captured either till the industry further matures. At this point, companies are throwing a lot more money than they are willing to to attract workers who will readily collect data that can in a few years replace them. Indian manufacturers and industrial units may recruit workers, deploy cameras and collect footage, while the resulting models and intellectual property are developed and owned elsewhere. This value drain could have serious consequences on the Indian economy and the jobs landscape. For data suppliers, the challenge will be moving beyond one-off collection contracts to building differentiated datasets that command lasting value. As more and more companies come into the picture, the collection of egocentric data and first-person footage is about to become highly commodified and consumerised. The Elephant In The Room: What About The Workers? Like we mentioned, the business opportunity comes with a difficult labour question. The blunt reading of the matter is that Indian workers are training the robots that could eventually replace them. Videos circulating on social media have raised concerns about whether workers even understand why they are wearing cameras. Some workers have reported discomfort from prolonged use, which may stretch to 5-10 hours a workday, while others believe the devices are intended to monitor their productivity. Every company maintains that workers are informed about what is being captured and why. However, when collection happens through partner businesses, the responsibility for communicating this information shifts to those partners. An openDemocracy investigation, meanwhile, found that workers at two Delhi factories were asked to wear cameras supplied by Egolab.ai without being told their purpose. Such incidents raise questions about informed consent, compensation, the privacy of other people captured in recordings and ownership of the resulting data. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose implementation is scheduled for May 2027, adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty. Speculation is that the government may regulate these services, but to what extent can it stop individuals from participating is unclear. For Sardana and Pronto, the opportunity is significantly larger than just a quick home services platform. The data from the broad range of everyday human activity by Pronto workers can fuel Provision Labs and Basilisk’s next big plays and turn them into even bigger companies than Pronto. Whether Pronto and Provision Labs will eventually work together has not been answered. But the value of Pronto’s network may very soon be the footage of what its professionals do, rather than the quality of the service itself.

For the first time in a dozen years, a leading OB-GYN group has updated its guidance on managing hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and other disruptive symptoms that often come with menopause.
Doctors stressed the importance of hormone therapies, which many women are considering again after the removal of federal safety warnings. On Friday, federal officials said the Food and Drug Administration has been taking steps to ensure there's an adequate supply.
Doctors also described various nonhormonal options in the new advice released this month by the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, or ACOG.
“We would love our patients to go to their OB-GYNs regarding questions about menopause and really advocate for getting the treatment that they need,” said Camille Clare, the group’s president.
Menopause occurs when a woman has gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. In the U.S., it usually happens around age 50. The time leading up to it is called perimenopause, during which the body’s production of the hormones estrogen and progesterone declines sharply.
Problems commonly arise. More than half of women in menopause report having “vasomotor” issues such as hot flashes and night sweats, said ACOG. As many as two-thirds report menopause-related sleep disruption. And more than a third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women worldwide report depressive symptoms.
In the past, doctors said, many women quietly suffered.
There's growing consensus that "these symptoms should be treated,” said JoAnn Manson, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. “This should help to empower women to discuss their symptoms with their healthcare provider.”
Manson said ACOG’s new guidelines are similar to those put out by other medical organizations.
"Moderate to severe or bothersome menopausal symptoms should be treated with hormone therapy as the first line of treatment,” she said. While it's not appropriate for all women, she added, it’s a good option for many.
But some have been wary.
In 2002, a landmark study in women taking a pill-based combination of estrogen and progestin was stopped early because of links to breast cancer, blood clots and other serious issues. Concerns lingered even though later studies showed the benefits of today’s hormone therapies outweigh the risks for many women. For more than 22 years, all hormone-based menopause treatments carried a government warning, which Manson said discouraged patients and doctors from using them.
But last year, the FDA announced it would remove the boxed warning from more than 20 pills, patches and creams containing the hormones estrogen and progestin. On Friday, the FDA approved updated labeling for three additional estrogen-based patches.
Removing the boxed warning has helped revive interest in and demand for the treatments.
Since the FDA labeling change, some women have reported difficulty obtaining estrogen patches in certain doses and formulations.
FDA officials said Friday that despite such reports, they are unaware of “an imminent risk of a nationwide shortage.” Officials also noted that drug manufacturers have doubled their output of the products over the last year by adding extra manufacturing shifts and production capacity.
Stephanie Faubion, medical director at The Menopause Society, said she’s glad to see ACOG’s guidelines stress the importance of these treatments. “It’s undisputed that hormone therapy is the first line and most effective therapy for hot flashes,” she said.
ACOG reviews the latest evidence on hormone therapy and includes detailed information about the various types. Whole-body therapies, which come in pills, patches, sprays, gels and a vaginal ring, deliver doses of hormones into the bloodstream at levels high enough to have significant effects on symptoms like hot flashes. Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy is applied directly with very little circulating in the blood. It’s often prescribed to women whose biggest complaint is vaginal dryness.
ACOG recommends that decisions about hormone therapy should be made jointly by doctors and patients, and take into account the benefits and risks given a patient's age and medical history. If it’s appropriate, the group advises starting it before age 60, or within 10 years of menopause.
Some patients choose not to take full-body hormonal medications or are advised by their doctors to avoid them because of their medical histories or conditions.
For them, doctors pointed to different medicines. One is fezolinetant, which works in the area of the brain that controls body temperature and blocks a source of hot flashes and night sweats. Another is elinzanetant, which works similarly.
Doctors also said certain antidepressants can help manage symptoms like hot flashes and depression in patients with either or both of these problems.
There’s also evidence supporting some non-drug treatments for hot flashes, night sweats and sleep or mood problems, ACOG said. These include cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, exercise, clinical hypnosis and acupuncture. Such approaches can be used alone or alongside medications.
Clare said women may see misinformation and disinformation about menopause treatments online, and urged patients to come to their doctors with any questions. ACOG offers advice on sorting out truth from false claims as well as overall information on menopause.
“Women have options. They have lots of options, hormonal and nonhormonal,” Faubion said. “They shouldn’t be told that nothing can be done about their symptoms. Because again, we have evidence for many different things that can help.”
