At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
- Published
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.
A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.
But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.
Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.
The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.
"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.
Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.
"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.
He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.
He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.
Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.
President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.
Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.
- Tundu Lissu - the great survivor of Tanzanian politics 
  - Published24 April 2025
The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".
Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.
They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.
But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.
He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.
Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:
- Electoral commissioners should be independently appointed (not by the president)
- Police should allow all parties to campaign free of intimidation
- Government-appointed district chiefs should no longer act as returning officers
- Party agents should be able to observe counting without harassment
- It should be possible to challenge presidential election results in court.
During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.
These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.
His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.
Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.
Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.
The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.
He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.
In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.
He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.
The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years outside Tanzania.
He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.
Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.
His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.
But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.
Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.
His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.
Last week, rights group Amnesty International accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.
Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

Paraguay's former president charged after bank collapse
- Published
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.
He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles as Aramco building in Riyadh is damaged, and other Mideast news
Saudi Arabia has intercepted missiles targeting its capital and other regions
Saudi Arabia said it intercepted incoming missiles targeting the kingdom's capital and other regions on Sunday, with falling debris damaging a building belonging to the state-owned oil giant Aramco in Riyadh’s financial district.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates said it rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out aboard a cargo ship in the Sea of Oman, as risks to commercial shipping in the region remain high.

Witnesses in Riyadh said they heard a loud explosion Sunday morning and described damage across multiple floors of an Aramco building in the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh. Some floors appeared to be heavily damaged.
The witnesses spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns.
The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions early Sunday, accusing the Houthis of launching the weapons.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the attempted attack resulted in “falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building.” It added that there were no casualties.
The Saudi Center for International Communication and Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment by The Associated Press.
Also, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile overnight targeting Saudi Arabia’s southern region, which borders Yemen and has repeatedly come under Houthi attacks.
The latest developments follow Saudi airstrikes on Saturday near Sanaa, Yemen's capital that is held by the Houthis. Houthi officials said the strikes killed at least 27 people.

The UAE National Guard said the crew members — all of Arab nationalities — were in stable condition after receiving first aid following a rescue when their cargo ship caught fire in the Sea of Oman.
The National Guard did not identify the vessel or specify the cause of the fire.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a British military organization that monitors maritime security incidents, said Sunday that a tanker caught fire on Saturday about 8 nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, prompting the evacuation of its crew.
The British organization did not identify the vessel or say who targeted it. It was unclear whether it was the same ship whose crew the UAE had helped evacuate.

On Saturday, U.S. forces disabled a St. Kitts-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman, saying it had attempted to breach the U.S. naval blockade of Iran. The blockade has been enforced in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global oil shipments.
Separately, the Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had struck mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire. It did not identify the vessels’ flags or destinations.
After days of consultations with parties elected to the Israeli parliament on Oct. 27, President Isaac Herzog said late Saturday that he had decided to designate Eisenkot to form the next government.
Herzog’s decision is another blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority in the election, which produced no winner with a clear majority.
The president's decision does not guarantee that Eisenkot will be the next prime minister. After an official ceremony on Sunday, Eisenkot will launch complicated negotiations with potential coalition partners.
Residents in Israel, the Palestinian territories and across the Mideast expressed mixed reactions to Gadi Eisenkot’s efforts to form Israel’s next government, with some hoping for political change and others expecting little shift in Israeli policies.
In Jerusalem, some hoped for a government that would prioritize Israeli security and bring together deeply divided parties. Some say they wanted a new government to reverse Netanyahu's judicial overhaul and include an Arab party for only the second time in the country's history. “The majority of the country is against this dictatorial regime of Bibi Netanyahu and need a new start,” resident Anny Soronow said.
Palestinians in the battered Gaza Strip and in the West Bank say they felt less optimistic. In neighboring Lebanon, Rima al-Ghazal said he does not expect an Eisenkot-led government to end the ongoing strikes in southern Lebanon.
In Tehran, Iran, resident Ali Soroush said that Israel and the Islamic Republic's “enmity will more or less continue.”

Komatsu, Ishikawa Pref. – Usually, nicknames like “the god of sake” are platitudes. But for brewer Naohiko Noguchi, it’s now as close to a literal description as can be.
On Oct. 16, Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs made an announcement without precedent: ginjō-zukuri — the exacting techniques used to brew aromatic ginjō sake from highly polished rice at low temperatures — be designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property, with 93-year-old master brewer Noguchi recognized as its holder.
Once formally approved at a ceremony scheduled for Nov. 16 in Kyoto, Noguchi will become the first-ever tōji (chief brewer) to be named a ningen kokuhō (living national treasure) — a recognition with significance far beyond the world of sake.

Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.
The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It’s unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.
We regret to inform you…
Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It’s not clear why the company considered such information “non-sensitive.”
In a Wednesday update, the company said that part of the “ongoing multifront cyberattack” involved an “on-path attack” that exposed a subset of customer passwords, and that the attack vector had been identified and fixed. Also known as an adversary-in-the-middle attack, on-path attacks happen when a hacker gains access to a piece of infrastructure sending traffic back and forth between two parties. Chainalysis has yet to say where the infrastructure compromise occurred and if the data obtained from it was TLS encrypted.

After the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, a rumor spread that Time magazine had published a cover with a black-and-white photograph of Republican U.S. President Donald Trump with a sticker on his mouth that read "I Voted" and included the illustration of a U.S. flag.
The supposed magazine cover spread across social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. One X post read "TIME Magazine unveils new cover" (archived):
Several Snopes readers searched the website and emailed us seeking to confirm the claim was true.
The image is real; Time published it as the cover of its Nov. 23 issue.
The magazine's Instagram account shared the cover on Nov. 4, the day of the midterm elections (archived):
The caption read, in part (emphasis ours):
If Democrats had spent much of President Donald Trump's second term searching for a way to break his grip on Washington, voters had now handed them one. The midterms generated a blue wave that swept Republicans out of power in the House and the Senate, reversing the party's fortunes just two years after Trump's return to the White House. The results amounted to a decisive rebuke of a President whose handling of the economy, rising prices, and the war with Iran had fueled widespread discontent, and who spent the closing days of the campaign musing about candidates' anatomy and dismissing Americans' concerns over their bottom line.
Time also shared the image on its X account (archived) and its website, in a cover story analyzing the outcome of the elections (archived) and outlining the path ahead for Democrats.
The image appeared to suggest that voters in the U.S. had handed a definitive loss to Trump and his camp after two years of brash rhetoric and policies that resulted in the opposite of what his supporters believed he and his allies had promised, including an end to wars and more affordable cost of living.
According to Time, Trump has appeared on the cover of the magazine more times than anyone else.
For further reading, Snopes has verified other covers of Time, including a cover it titled "The Transgender Tipping Point" in 2014.

I've tried almost every digital wall calendar available (as is my job as WIRED's resident calendar tester), and the model that I've found increasingly impressive as time goes on is the Greenlight Hub.
Greenlight has a different premise than other digital wall calendars. The brand started as a debit card for kids before branching into more app-based categories: chores to attach to allowance distribution, family location tracking, and more. Greenlight launched its own Family Hub device to bring these features together and add a few more, like the digital calendar function, seen in popular tools like Skylight.
Now, Greenlight's Family Hub is at its best price, already on sale ahead of Black Friday. The 15.6-inch version I tested has a $100 discount, totaling $199 right now (significantly less than every other digital wall calendar I recommend, all of which usually retail for at least $300). There's also a smaller 10.1-inch model available for $30 off, currently selling for $169, if you want something a bit cheaper.
Meet Greenlight’s Hub
The Greenlight Hub leads with its family calendar tool that lets you see everyone's schedules in one place, but it also has tabs for chores, family locations, and even doubles as a digital photo frame at no extra cost. You'll have to subscribe to Greenlight's Family Hub+ plan to get family location sharing. That subscription also grants access to Greenlight's voice assistant, which allows you to ask the hub questions.
The Greenlight Family Hub is overall a great device, particularly for parents who want to track how well their kids complete chores. (Conveniently, you also have the option to attach an allowance, if you'd like.) I've been enjoying it just fine with a 4-year-old whose only chore is to brush his teeth at night.
But no matter whether you have kids, the Hub is a worthy addition to any home. I like the modern, stylish icons that feel cooler and more gender-neutral than the bubbly, pastel interface featured on the Skylight and similar tools. The Greenlight also doesn't share the decidedly Android feel of some cheaper models, despite being less expensive than those other options right now.
Ultimately, I'm impressed with how well the Hub performs as a digital photo frame, calendar, and even voice assistant. The sale is a big one—the perfect opportunity to get a handy, stylish digital wall calendar for your family ahead of the holidays, or perhaps a gift for your mom or another family you know would love it.

Psoriasis is an autoimmune condition that causes thick, scaly patches on the skin. However, it often remains unidentified and undiagnosed because it does not look the same on all parts of the body: it could be mistaken, for instance, for dandruff on the scalp, persistent eczema on the palms, or a fungal infection. You can’t always judge psoriasis by looking only at visible parts of the skin.
Why does this happen? Our skin isn’t the same everywhere. The thickness of the skin can vary considerably depending on the diversity of the environmental conditions that it is exposed to and the kind of treatment given to it. These factors can contribute to how psoriasis appears and feels.

Many forms of ear infections strike children and adults alike, but among the most common is acute otitis externa, also known as swimmer’s ear.
About 10% of Americans will experience swimmer’s ear during their lifetimes. Adults are affected more commonly, and children only rarely, generally ages 5 to 12.
But you don’t have to be swimming to get swimmer’s ear. Go out jogging or walking, or do yardwork on a hot day, and moisture from perspiration can drip in your ear. However, the occurrence increases fivefold in swimmers – thus the reason the condition came to be called “swimmer’s ear.” It also occurs more frequently in tropical climates because of humidity and higher temperatures.
As doctors who specialise in ear problems, we are actively involved in research and clinical treatment for children and adults struggling with ear, nose and throat problems. Practicing in the state of Florida, we’ve certainly seen our share of patients with swimmer’s ear.
Causes and symptoms of swimmer’s ear
Swimmer’s ear is an infection in the external ear canal, the tube leading from the ear opening to the eardrum. Typically, swimmer’s ear occurs only in one ear, and sometimes the eardrum itself is affected. Moisture trapped in the canal leads to a break in the skin barrier and creates an opening for certain bacteria types to enter or existing ones to overgrow.
One of these culprits is the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is present in soil and water throughout the world. These bacteria favor moist areas, such as sinks, toilets, inadequately chlorinated swimming pools and hot tubs, as well as outdated or inactivated antiseptic solutions.
If you have the infection, you’ll know it. Symptoms generally appear a few days after infection. The main symptom of swimmer’s ear is severe pain and discomfort. It’s particularly noticeable when the outer ear is tugged, or by touching the tragus – that’s the small bump at the front of your ear. Other symptoms include itchiness inside the ear, redness, swelling and drainage. A feeling of fullness, or the perception of a plugged ear, may also occur, along with disturbed balance and temporary hearing loss.
Predisposition to swimmer’s ear
Numerous factors can predispose someone to swimmer’s ear. They include a narrow ear canal, and skin diseases such as eczema or psoriasis. In addition, individuals wearing ear plugs, ear buds or hearing aids may be at an increased risk. Diabetics may also be more prone to the infection.
Swimmer’s ear can also come from something getting stuck inside the ear, excessive ear cleaning or contact with chemicals in hair dye or hairspray.
Diagnosis and treatment
Swimmer’s ear is diagnosed after a health care provider has gathered a thorough history and examined the inside of the ear. The ear canal will typically look red, swollen and moist. There is also a possibility of fluid drainage or the appearance of scaly, shedding skin. Depending on the degree of swelling, the eardrum may be hard to see. A sample of fluid may be removed from the ear and sent to a lab to look for bacteria or fungus.
Eardrops are commonly used to treat swimmer’s ear. These drops often contain antibiotics to kill the infection and steroids to stop the swelling.
One such eardrop is Ciprodex. It contains ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic, and dexamethasone, a powerful steroid. Patients will need to place about four to five drops in the infected ear canal twice a day for seven to 10 days.
Another commonly prescribed drop is Floxin, which contains an antibiotic but not a steroid. It is commonly prescribed in less swollen but still infected ears.
Other drop preparations include Cortisporin, which contains a commonly used combination of neomycin and polymyxin B, as well as hydrocortisone. However, neomycin is also damaging to the inner ear, so doctors nowadays often turn to Ciprodex or Floxin.
In some cases, the ear canal is too swollen for drops to reach the infected area, so the physician may place a wick or stent in the ear canal to keep it open. This will usually be left in place for three to five days until removed by the doctor, although occasionally the wick falls out once the swelling subsides. Usually, after 10 days the infection is resolved and the ear canal skin returns to normal.
Managing a persistent infection
Sometimes swimmer’s ear may not resolve after seven to 10 days of treatment with eardrops. Oral antibiotics are typically recommended if the infection has spread beyond the ear canal or in patients with poorly controlled diabetes. Hospitalization for swimmer’s ear is rarely necessary; however, complications that can occasionally lead to hospitalization include fever, worsening discharge, extensive narrowing of the ear canal or failure of previous treatments.
Among the precautions you can take to prevent swimmer’s ear: Keep the ear canal dry. Tip your head to one side to help the water drain. Use a soft towel or cloth, or gently use a hair dryer near it. If the self-cleansing mechanism of the ear canal is impaired, then the ear canal should be cleansed by a physician.
Since most bacteria prefer a pH-neutral environment, reducing the pH in the ear canal can prevent bacterial overgrowth. A homemade liquid tincture can be mixed from a solution of half rubbing alcohol and half distilled white vinegar. The alcohol combines with the water in the ear and then evaporates. This removes the water while the acidity of the vinegar keeps bacteria from growing.
Two to three drops are usually sufficient and can be applied as a preventive measure soon after the ear has been exposed to moisture. This liquid solution is not a replacement for medical treatment of an actual ear infection and is meant to be used only in people who are prone to such infections because of prolonged or frequent exposure to moisture.
Also, it is important to differentiate swimmer’s ear from a middle ear infection, the most frequent reason for the use of antibiotics in children under age 5. Middle ear infections are usually associated with a viral upper respiratory infection, and they are more often seen during fall and winter, when influenza and cold viruses are more prevalent.
(Thomas Schrepfer, Assistant Professor of Pediatric Otolaryngology, University of Florida; Rex Haberman Associate Clinical Professor of Otology and Neurotology, University of Florida)

If a good night’s sleep has become your holy grail, who are the knights in shining armour you will employ to reach that chalice? Most people seem to be deploying melatonin and magnesium supplements, over the counter, but the question that remains is: are they effective, and if so, at what combinations or levels?
The consensus among most sleep specialists, is that both melatonin and magnesium (glycinate) can have an ameliorative impact – in the short term. Both these supplements, however, work differently – while melatonin is a key body clock signal, magnesium helps relax the body. When and how you take both supplements makes a great deal of difference to your hours of sleep and sleep quality as well.

Nasdaq-listed traveltech major MakeMyTrip has expanded into the carpooling segment via the acquisition of a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick Ride for an undisclosed amount. In a statement, MakeMyTrip said that the acquisition will allow it “to establish a presence in the ride pooling segment, which is complementary to the group’s existing ground transportation portfolio.” As part of the transaction, Quick Ride’s brand and ride-pooling business have been transferred to a newly formed entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited, in which MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake. Quick Ride’s promoters will continue to lead the business. However, Quick Ride’s erstwhile electric vehicle (EV) taxi business will remain with its predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Pvt Ltd. Founded in 2014 by KNM Rao, Quick Ride offers a ride-sharing application that connects passengers to riders. It connects the commuters travelling in the same direction. It also offers an enterprise solution for shared mobility and counts IT companies such as Wipro, TCS, Infosys, IBM and Cognizant, among others as its clients. Its services are available in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Kochi, Delhi NCR, Mumbai, and Kolkata. The startup has raised over $14 Mn from investors like Sequoia, Prosus and Venture Highway. Sequoia exited the startup in 2021. MakeMyTrip's Acquisition-Led Expansion The Quick Ride acquisition is part of MakeMyTrip's broader strategy to expand its presence across adjacent travel and mobility segments through strategic investments and acquisitions. Commenting on the acquisition, MakeMyTrip group CEO Rajesh Magow said that the investment would help the company establish a presence in daily intra-city commutes while strengthening its intercity travel offerings. “As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel,” he added. The company plans to leverage its experience in building redBus across India and overseas markets to scale Quick Ride's ride-pooling business. In the past few years, MakeMyTrip has acquired Savaari to strengthen its car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, and Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages. It has also made a strategic minority investment in visa processing platform Atlys. The development comes as MakeMyTrip looks to deepen its presence across the travel value chain, moving beyond conventional travel bookings towards a broader set of transportation and ancillary services. On the financial front, the travel tech major’s consolidated net profit for the three months ended June 30, 2026 (Q1 FY27) plunged 65% to $9.1 Mn from $25.8 Mn in the year-ago period. MakeMyTrip’s revenue grew 6% YoY to $285.6 Mn.

Trump doubles down on everything that lost him the midterms
Stephen Miller will be the new White House chief of staff, Trump said on Friday.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is doubling down after a midterm annihilation.
What happened? On Friday afternoon, Trump announced that longtime aide Stephen Miller would take over as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. In a post to Truth Social, Trump said that Miller would start on Monday, but the change appears to be effective more or less immediately — Wiles has already resigned.
Why the change? Trump was reportedly angry with Wiles over the GOP’s collapse in the midterm elections, which saw Democrats winning up and down the ballot even in traditionally deep-red parts of the country.
Trump, for his part, told reporters on Friday that Wiles had “done a very good job.” But, he added, “we gotta make moves. Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”
What should I know about Miller? Miller is currently the White House deputy chief of staff for policy, as well as homeland security adviser. More importantly, he’s the architect and engine of some of Trump’s most vicious immigration policies, including family separation (during the first Trump term) and ICE’s current campaign of indiscriminate, militarized immigration enforcement.
He’s also an ally of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has to be feeling a little bit better about his imperiled job (though it won’t keep Hegseth from facing impeachment in the near future).
What does this mean for the Trump presidency? More of the same, cranked up to 11. Miller is as hardline as they come, and he’s certain to push Trump to be even more aggressive on immigration and attempts to use the machinery of government to attack their shared political enemies.
It’s all going to be extraordinarily unpopular, if Tuesday’s midterm results are anything to go by — but with just over two years left in the White House, there’s little reason to believe that Miller and Trump won’t try to push the power of the presidency to its breaking point.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

After protests in Arunachal Pradesh against the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent on October 23, the state has unleashed a massive crackdown on the movement. The response has included the use of force by armed forces and law enforcement agencies, internet shutdowns, a paid PR campaign, censorship of social media content, and action against journalists and lawyers.
A 12-hour Arunachal bandh was called by local bodies and youth groups, including the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF), Adi Baane Kebang United and the Adi Galo Welfare Society, on October 23. The bandh was followed by large-scale arson in Pasighat, East Siang district, targeting an office of the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC), a police station, and the homes of two MLAs and the BJP’s state president.
The proposed SUMP, with an estimated capacity of 11,200 megawatts, is planned on the Siang River across the Upper Siang and Siang districts. First proposed in 2008-09 by the UPA government, it was initially conceived as two smaller projects, with memorandums of understanding signed in 2013. On September 26, 2017, following a meeting between chief minister Pema Khandu, state delegates and NITI Aayog, the plan was changed to a single 250-metre-high dam, which would be the country’s largest in terms of installed capacity. However, stiff local resistance forced survey teams to withdraw, bringing the project to a temporary standstill.
The BJP-led governments at the Centre and in Arunachal Pradesh revived the project in 2020, following reports of China’s plan to build a dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo River, known as the Siang in India. In April 2022, the Centre directed the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) to conduct a pre-feasibility survey to assess the project’s technical, economic, social and environmental viability. The exercise involves geological investigations, including drilling, and identifying villages that may require relocation.
Chief minister Pema Khandu and other state representatives have maintained that the survey does not amount to a decision to build the dam. NHPC has said that preliminary topographical, geological and geophysical work is complete, but core drilling to assess rock characteristics remains on hold because of local opposition.
However, the manner in which the survey was pursued has fuelled distrust. In May 2025, Central Armed Police Forces were deployed at several locations. Police maintained that the deployment was necessary to maintain law and order and that the required clearance had been obtained months earlier.
In September 2026, the state Cabinet approved an empowered committee to oversee the survey, alongside a significant deployment of central forces. Villagers, however, fear that the survey is a precursor to the dam’s construction and have accused the government of using security forces to suppress their opposition.
Questions over consent have further deepened the mistrust. Activist and politician Tadak Nalo alleged that many consent forms cited by the government were false, with endorsements largely coming from villagers whose lives would not be directly affected by the project.
Several indigenous communities, including the Adi, Galo, Nyishi, Apatani and Idu Mishmi, inhabit the Siang valley and depend heavily on the river, not only for their agricultural practices but also for their cultural identities and religious beliefs. They call the river Ane Siang, or Mother Siang. According to independent fact-finding reports, the SUMP would completely submerge nearly 27 villages across the Upper Siang and Siang districts and displace an estimated 1.5 lakh people, almost 11% of Arunachal Pradesh’s population.
With their homes, livelihoods and cultural heritage at stake, people in the Siang valley have only intensified their resistance over the past two weeks. The BJP government’s response, however, has been one of force and intimidation rather than dialogue. It bears resemblance to the way dissent has been dealt with elsewhere under BJP rule — in Delhi, for example, against ongoing protests demanding accountability from chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Use of Force, Detentions and Internet Shutdown
One of the issues against which the October 23 bandh was called was the detention of anti-SUMP protesters since October 9. According to reports, The state government invoked the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (APUAPA) and detained at least 10 protesters. Four of them — Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, picked up from Pasighat — were reportedly held under APUAPA. Among those detained was the president of the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF) Youth Wing, a vocal opponent of the mega project.
The crackdown intensified after the October 23 violence. A further 69 people were arrested and four detained in connection with the violence. A total of 55 cases were reportedly filed: 26 criminal cases in Upper Siang, 21 in Siang and six in East Siang district. Arrests and detentions were also carried out under the APUAPA. Those arrested reportedly face charges relating to rioting, the torching of vehicles and the vandalism of office buildings and residential houses.
The state has also significantly increased its security deployment in the region. At least 30 companies of Central Armed Police Forces and three companies of Assam Police have been deployed, in addition to Arunachal Pradesh Police personnel. The Centre also flew in two additional companies of the Rapid Action Force (RAF).
There were also reports of police using tear gas and batons against protesters on October 23. Five women were reportedly taken to hospital after experiencing breathing difficulties. The police, meanwhile, maintained that some protesters had allegedly attempted to breach barricades and attack security personnel.
The crackdown has not been confined to Arunachal Pradesh. On October 31, a solidarity protest against the SUMP outside Arunachal Bhavan in New Delhi, organised by Youth for Change (YFC) Arunachal and Himkhand, also ended in the detention and alleged manhandling of protesters by the Delhi Police.

🙏 We are United in This https://t.co/nkLHBL3u6X
— CJP Gems | (@GameonNewbie) October 31, 2026
The protesters alleged that the Delhi Police used brute force and even subjected some of them to sexual assault during the detention. A member of Himkhand alleged that they were pinched in their private parts and their shirts were lifted. Around 40 protesters were detained during the protest in Delhi, including female protesters who reportedly were detained after 9 pm.
All of the detainees were later released after the intervention of senior Congress leaders.
As of November 2, internet services were suspended in Upper Siang as the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF) and the SUMP Affected Area Youth Association (SAAYA), with the support of various student unions and community-based organisations, enforced a 36-hour bandh in parts of the Siang and all Upper Siang districts from 5 am. Protesters demanded the release of the detainees under APUAPA.
Censorship of Social Media Content
The crackdown on the anti-SUMP movement has also extended to the online space, with social media accounts of activists, journalists and news outlets being restricted or taken down. The censorship is part of a wider pattern in India, where government orders and platform restrictions have increasingly curtailed the circulation of content critical of those in power.
Tadak Nalo, founder and president of the political party Arunachal Frontier Tribal Front (AFTF), released a video statement after his Facebook account was restricted. Describing the situation in Arunachal Pradesh as “emergency-like”, he said fundamental rights, including the right to freedom of speech and expression, were being suppressed.
“My Facebook page, ‘Tadak Nalo for Revolution’, has been misused under the Information Technology Act and restricted completely within India today. If you want to view my page, you will have to go outside India. That is how they have set it up,” he said in the video.
Nalo alleged that his commentary on the SUMP was among the reasons behind the restriction. “A project this big is being built in our Arunachal, and it will cause displacement and render the indigenous inhabitants here landless. I had made some commentary on this and written some posts,” he said.
Several journalists and news pages have also reported having their Facebook pages disabled. Shaan Jijong, managing director of Upper Siang News 24*7, released a video statement saying that the outlet’s official Facebook page had been disabled. He also named two others, Ebo Mili and Katon Moyong, whose Facebook pages had allegedly been taken down.
“We are journalists, and we have been covering the SUMP from the ground also. But our news channel was disabled. Is this okay? We are journalists; we are the fourth pillar of democracy,” Jijong said.
The #Facebookpage of Upper Siang 24X7, a social media-based news channel, has been #blocked by the Government of India. The channel extensively reports on people’s resistance to the government’s proposal for the #SiangUpperMultipurposeProject, a 10,000 MW-plus #hydropower project on the #SiangRiver. Shan Jijong, the reporter behind the popular news platform, says he will continue to report on the issue. Several other Facebook accounts critical of the government’s action have also been withheld.
— The Arunachal Times (@arunachaltimes_) October 5, 2026
Katon Moyong, popularly known as Aborman Anbo, also found his Facebook page had “disappeared”, Northeast Today reported. He created a new account and published a post declaring that the censorship would not silence his opposition to the SUMP and that he had not lost his voice. However, we could not locate the new account on Facebook either, suggesting that it may have been taken down as well.
Two news reports published by Arunbhoomi News were also made unavailable for viewing in India. The outlet’s editor-in-chief, Takam Sonia, released a video statement condemning the move.
Human rights lawyer and activist Ebo Mili, whose Facebook account was also restricted, reportedly described the action as “deliberate and linked to his use of social media to raise public awareness about the project”.
The Facebook page Save Aborland and the general secretary and spokesperson of Adi Baane Kebang United, Datik Ratan, have also faced restrictions.
The Arunachal Press Club (APC) and the Arunachal Pradesh Union of Working Journalists (APUWJ) have condemned the restrictions on news reports and videos relating to the SUMP on social media platforms in India, and demanded transparency and their immediate restoration.
Targeting Arunachal Times Deputy Editor and Lawyer Defending Activists
Arunachal Pradesh Police have also moved against a journalist covering the anti-SUMP movement, seeking a search warrant against Tongam Rina, deputy editor of The Arunachal Times, in connection with the violence in Pasighat on October 23.
Police have also sought a search warrant against her lawyer, Sunny Tayeng, along with youth leader Otul Jerang, who has been arrested, and activist Tajong Talom, who was previously detained and allegedly harassed.
Rina took to X to assert that the police action would not deter her from her journalism or activism. “…I have seen enough intimidation in my life, so this isn’t something that will stop me from writing or my activism. More power to the people of Siang Valley and Arunachal. We owe it to Siang and her people…” she wrote.
She also criticised the move against Tayeng, pointing out that the lawyer was representing several activists, including Ebo Mili, Tajong Talom and Otul Jerang. Rina said she wanted Tayeng to be able to “focus on her practice rather than be burdened by extra work”.
The application for the search warrant, as reported by The Wire, describes Rina and the three other individuals as “accused persons”. It states that searches were “necessary to establish the individual roles of the accused, ascertain their alleged involvement in the offences and collect relevant material evidence”. However, the application does not specify how Rina or the other three individuals were linked to the violence.
The application states: “It is reasonably suspected on the basis of the facts and material collected during the investigation that certain articles and material connected with the commission of the alleged offences including clothing worn during the incident, mobile phones and digital devices containing relevant photographs or video recordings and other case-related articles may be found at the residences or premises…”
The Press Club of India also issued a statement expressing solidarity with Rina and condemning the Arunachal Pradesh Police’s move.
Paid PR Campaign
Actress Taba Reema, who has been vocal against SUMP, has posted a video alleging that PR firms were reaching out to content creators to speak about the construction of the dam in a positive light. “A few months ago, I also got an email from PR teams and agencies… they said they would pay this much for one reel and a list of pointers of advantages of building a dam. And now every reel or content like this I see… same to same…”
According to Reema, they tried to reach out to a lot of content creators from Arunachal, but they all declined. “And not that Arunachali creators have refused; they are using outsiders for this kind of content….”
View this post on Instagram
According to an Indian Express report, Mumbai-based Concept Public Relations was awarded a one-year contract in July 2025, which was subsequently extended until November 2026, to build opinion in favour of the project, at a total cost of Rs 10.91 crore.
Asked about the agency’s appointment, an NHPC official told the newspaper that it had been hired to put forward “their side” and help supporters within the community speak out, despite “the pressure from violent elements”.
Alt News located several X posts which appear to be part of a concerted effort to delegitimise the protests by portraying protesters as Chinese stooges and calling for them to be “dealt with an iron fist”. While these posts do not, by themselves, establish any link with the PR campaign, they illustrate how opposition to the project was being framed in online discourse.

Saudi Aramco tower damaged after Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh
A building belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco was damaged in Riyadh on Sunday as Saudi Arabia reported a series of missile attacks launched by Yemen’s Houthi movement.
An official at Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said Aramco's administrative building sustained minor damage after falling shrapnel struck it.
No injuries or deaths were reported, the official said, adding that the relevant authorities had responded and taken the necessary measures.
A Reuters witness reported seeing windows blown out across several floors of the Aramco Tower in the King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD), one of the Saudi capital’s main business districts.
The damage followed reports of loud explosions in Riyadh and an early-warning alert issued by Saudi Civil Defence. Authorities later said the danger had passed.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched towards Riyadh on Sunday.

Amid rising concerns over the spread of Ebola to neighbouring countries, the Department of Health, Medical and Family Welfare, A.P., has stepped up surveillance at three airports — Bhogapuram (Visakhapatnam), Vijayawada, and Tirupati — as a precautionary measure.
According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an official U.S. government website, the outbreak is spreading “substantially faster” than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.
In this connection, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare held a video conference on November 5, Thursday, with State governments regarding the precautionary measures to be taken. The Union government officials also reviewed the implementation of the Ebola guidelines.
A.P. Health Secretary G. Veerapandian, who took part in the conference, explained the arrangements being made in the State as part of the preparedness.
Arrangements at 5 govt. hospitals
According to a release from the department on Thursday, isolation beds at five government hospitals, medical personnel, emergency equipment have been readied. Mr. Veerapandian informed the Union government that medical teams had been deputed at three airports to screen passengers arriving from Ebola-affected countries for any symptoms. Similar arrangements are also in place at Visakhapatnam, Kakinada and Nellore ports.
A total of 46 beds, 3,288 personal protective equipment (PPE) kits, 104 sample collection kits and five ambulances had been kept ready to deal with any eventuality, he said.
Mock drill
A mock drill will be conducted on November 12 to assess preparedness at the State and district levels, he said, adding that the departments concerned would be alerted to ensure that the guidelines are followed.
The Central officials have advised that passengers arriving from Ebola-affected countries be screened for symptoms, and those who had direct contact with infected persons be placed under observation. The medical teams should verify travel history of even those who do not exhibit any symptoms, the officials said.
If any person exhibits any symptoms, they should be taken to the hospital where isolation beds have been set up, the officials told the States.
As of October 31, Democratic Republic of the Congo reported 10,467 cases and 5,103 deaths, Kenya nine cases and two deaths, Uganda 20 cases and two deaths, Nigeria one case and France one case. Overall, 10,498 confirmed cases and 5,107 deaths were reported across five countries.

Imagine the bright tones of coral under the sea. What do you see? What colors come to mind?
One of the ways that climate change will alter — or has already altered — our world is by shifting the familiar colors of nature. When warming ocean waters bleach the vibrant colors of coral to white, that’s one example.
“Many young scientists who are working on coral reefs don’t realize that what they’re seeing is vastly degraded,” says Anya Salih, a scientist who has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. “It’s often hard to perceive how it was to what it is now.”
This change of color isn’t just aesthetic. For coral, bleaching leaves them vulnerable to disease and other stressors that can lead to death. In other situations, these color changes have more complex impacts, ones that scientists are still trying to understand.
How climate change transforms the colors of our world
An illustrated journey
Published Nov. 8, 2026
A shifting landscape in the Arctic
Every summer, massive climate-driven wildfires spread soot across huge swaths of the Arctic, covering the ice in a blanket of black particles. Soot pollution from oil and gas operations, as well as commercial shipping and increased tourism, contributes to the problem at both poles.
The dark particles coat white snow and soak up heat from the sun, exacerbating melting that was already happening more quickly because of climate change. Increased melting in the Arctic leads to sea level rise, which threatens communities across the world. And the soot itself pollutes the air and water it seeps into. 
“We know that the high northern latitudes are warming faster than the rest of the planet,” says Douglas Morton, an Earth scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. These changes are shifting the colors of the Arctic landscape.
The Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the planet
Annual surface air temperature, departure from the 1991-2020 mean
Beyond the Arctic ice at the pole, farther south, lie vast regions of permafrost: soil that has remained frozen for years.
But the warming climate is causing permafrost to thaw.
And in some places, crack and collapse.
As permafrost thaws deeper into the soil, nutrients become more available and plants can grow deeper roots. These conditions can stimulate plant growth and enable larger vegetation like trees to gain a foothold, turning the landscape greener.
These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.

These conditions can stimulate plant growth and enable larger vegetation like trees to gain a foothold, turning the landscape greener.
These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.
A 2020 study in Nature Communications used satellite data to estimate Arctic vegetation over time, sampling thousands of sites across Alaska, Canada and western Eurasia. The researchers found that between 1985 and 2016, about 38% of the sites showed greening.
“Not everywhere in the Arctic is green,” says Logan Berner, a terrestrial ecologist with the University of Alaska Southeast, who led the study. “But there’s enough greening that if you look at the average greenness of the Arctic over time, it’s going up.”
According to Berner, who grew up in southern Alaska, this consistent increase in average greenness tracks strongly with an increase in summer temperatures.
The Arctic is becoming greener
Scientists measuring annual peak greenness have found that the Arctic has overall become greener since 2000. Greener locations are areas where plants increased over time, becoming taller, denser or healthier. Some locations have become less green due to extreme weather and wildfires.

Though the Arctic might seem far away from us, Berner notes that it’s a “bellwether for the kinds of impacts that climate change can have.” And increased greening can negatively impact the people who live in the Arctic and rely on its natural resources. For example, as shrubs expand across northern lands, they can shade out berry patches that people rely on for food; changing weather patterns can also affect the timing of fruit and its quality.
Changes in our water
“People have coined the term that lakes are sentinels in the landscape,” says David Butman, a professor at the University of Washington who focuses on biogeochemistry and satellite remote sensing. Lakes react quickly to changes in the environment, so measuring lake color through satellite monitoring can help quantify those changes.
Butman worked on a 2021 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS) that measured green wavelengths in more than 400,000 lakes in the boreal Arctic zone in North America. Researchers found that green values declined by 15% between 1984 and 2019, meaning that, to the naked eye, these lakes got significantly darker.
Thawing permafrost is a possible reason. As it thaws, soil can mix with lake water, making it darker. The researchers found that the greatest declines happened in warmer and wetter regions.
The darker a lake gets, the more heat it can store, according to Butman. “You can imagine, you know, a black car and a hot day,” he says. The darker a lake is, the longer it stays warm after the summer, disrupting the natural timings of processes like fish life cycles and algae production. When soil or other outside material sinks to the bottom of a lake, microbes consume oxygen to break it down, leading to the production of methane, a potent planet-heating gas.
On a global scale, many lakes fall within the green-blue color spectrum. Bright blue lakes, often depicted in illustrations, are rarer than green lakes.
In 2022, scientists Xiao Yang and Catherine O’Reilly led a study in Geophysical Research Letters that analyzed the color of more than 85,000 lakes. They found that blue lakes are generally found in northern places with cooler summers and are covered in ice in the winter, such as Moraine Lake in Canada or Lake Baikal in Russia.
Globally, approximately 31% of the Earth’s lakes are blue.
Yang and O’Reilly predict that fewer blue lakes will exist as summers get warmer and winter ice cover decreases due to climate change.
The birds and the bees
Many animals have appearances that blend in with their surroundings for survival. When those surroundings start to shift, animals such as the snowshoe hare begin to stand out. The snowshoe hare’s white winter fur sticks out with less snow on the ground, leaving it more vulnerable to predators.
Researchers haven’t found evidence that hares are adapting the timing of their molts to align with their changing winter. But some insects have already changed coloring. North American male dragonflies, for instance, have adapted to warmer climates by losing color on their wings, according to a study in PNAS.
Losing some of the heat-absorbing color can help the dragonflies stay cooler, but the males also lose color that helps attract females. And researchers predict this will continue to be the case in the future as the climate continues to warm. An even tinier example is a specific kind of bee.
Sevan Suni is an associate professor at the University of San Francisco who studies interactions between plants and pollinators. She has been going to Costa Rica for the last 15 years to study a group of bees commonly known as orchid bees.
These bees are the sole pollinators for about 200 species of orchids in Central and South America. Their bodies look almost jewel-like, with shiny iridescent shells.
Year after year, Suni noticed that one species of bee, the champion’s orchid bee, seemed to shift color from blue-green to orange-red. She and others discovered that, in hotter areas, the number of orange-red bees has increased over time while the number of blue-green bees has decreased.
The areas that increased in temperature faster over time also had more of the red-orange bees. It’s unclear what’s driving this change. The darker blue-green color could be hotter, absorbing more heat. Or the blue-green bees may be more vulnerable since the color of their environment is changing. Due to deforestation in Costa Rica, they may be less camouflaged in a less green environment. Either way, Suni has concerns about potential impacts.
“As a biologist, I’m always interested in biological variation,” she says. “It worries me a little bit if the blue-green morph has an important ecological function and they’re getting less prevalent over time.”
A last gasp of hidden color
Warming ocean waters bleach colorful corals, turning them white. The corals expel symbiotic algae, losing a food source and becoming more vulnerable to disease. Corals can recover after bleaching, but the longer and more frequent the bleaching, the more difficult recovery is. In some cases, corals turn stunningly fluorescent and colorful at the start of bleaching and after — a last bright gasp of life.
These neon colors, usually visible only under ultraviolet light, are always present to some degree, says Anya Salih. Salih, a fellow at the University of Technology Sydney, has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. She dives at night to scan reefs with blue lights.
“Sometimes when I dive with people who are not used to seeing this, I would have to hold their tank so that they don’t turn upside down,” she says, “because in that very colorful, psychedelic world, you lose the perspective of up and down in the water.”
Algae in healthy coral absorb sunlight for energy. When the algae leave due to stress, turning the coral white, more light travels through the remaining skeleton.

A 2020 study in Current Biology found that this excess light encourages coral to produce the shockingly colorful pigments. This tends to occur when heat stress is mild and coral cells can still function. These colorful pigments act as a kind of sunscreen barrier protecting the coral from light damage, which encourages algae to return. Researchers believe corals that bleach colorfully have a higher chance of recovery. 
Salih has seen reefs glow, bleach and recover, even multiple times. Still, climate change is causing ocean temperatures to rise, creating more bleaching. “So the scope for recovery is low,” she says.

Coral bleaching has ripple effects on the larger ecosystem of the reef. A 2022 study in Global Change Biology found, for instance, that fewer fish with colorful bodies were found in the Great Barrier Reef following a specific bleaching event. In the future, reef ecosystems might be less diverse, bright and colorful. 
“The neon glows of the reefs are a stress response. It’s a cry for help,” says Salih. “They’re fighting for their survival. They’re using their colors to protect themselves. But in many ways they’re failing in many parts of the world. And the reefs are collapsing.”
Now imagine a glacial lake. A pristine ice sheet at the North Pole. Or the vibrant shades of coral.
What do you see now?
Color can be a fleeting, subjective thing, simply how one perceives light reflecting off a surface. But it’s also how we see and know our world, and our world is slowly changing around us, even if we don’t notice.
Salih remembers when she accompanied a group of scientists to an Australian reef. “I was also recently on that reef, which was dying, pretty much,” she says. “And they’d never been on the reef and they thought it was beautiful.”

Srinagar, Nov 7: Real Kashmir Football Club (RKFC) and Sreenidi Deccan FC shared points after playing out a 1-1 draw in an Indian Football League (IFL) match at TRC Ground in Srinagar on Saturday.
The match, as per a statement, played under floodlights, witnessed a large turnout of spectators who gathered at the venue to support the home side amid cold weather. 
RKFC made an aggressive start to the encounter and put Sreenidi Deccan under pressure from the opening minutes. The home side's attacking approach paid off early as they found the back of the net to take a 1-0 lead.
The Snow Leopards maintained their advantage throughout the first half, heading into the break with a one-goal cushion.
However, Sreenidi Deccan FC staged a comeback in the second half, managing to find the equaliser and bring the contest back on level terms.
Following the equaliser, RKFC pushed forward in search of a winner and created several opportunities. The home side dominated large parts of the game and looked determined to secure all three points, but failed to convert their chances into goals.
Despite sustained efforts from both teams in the closing stages, neither side could find the decisive breakthrough.
The match eventually ended in a 1-1 draw, with both teams settling for a point each.
The result denied RKFC a home victory despite a promising performance in front of their supporters.

Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund remained level on points at the top of the Bundesliga standings after registering narrow 2-1 victories over Mainz and Elversberg, respectively on Saturday.
The two sides, which played out a 2-2 draw last weekend, have 21 points each from nine matches, with defending champion Bayern retaining the top spot on goal difference.
Harry Kane provided assists for both Bayern goals as Joshua Kimmich opened the scoring in the 14th minute before Lennart Karl doubled the advantage after the interval.
Mainz pulled one back through Phillip Tietz in stoppage time, but the late goal was not enough to prevent Bayern from securing all three points.
Kane, who has not scored in three matches since winning the Ballon d’Or in October, continued to contribute creatively, taking his tally to 10 assists alongside 10 goals across all competitions this season.

Bayern midfielder Kimmich, who recently returned from bereavement leave following his father’s death, was visibly emotional after scoring.
The victory came despite Bayern’s injury concerns, with Jamal Musiala, Luis Diaz and Serge Gnabry among those unavailable. Coach Vincent Kompany was also absent through illness.
Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer became Bayern’s oldest-ever player at 40 years and 225 days but was forced off before half-time with a foot injury.
Nmecha double keeps Dortmund level
Borussia Dortmund maintained its unbeaten start to the Bundesliga campaign after Felix Nmecha scored twice in the second half to secure a 2-1 home victory against Elversberg.
Nmecha broke the deadlock in the 55th minute before doubling the lead in the 71st, with both goals coming from outside the penalty area.
Noel Futkeu reduced the deficit for Elversberg nine minutes from time, but Dortmund held on for its sixth league victory of the season.
The host was without injured striker Serhou Guirassy, while Carney Chukwuemeka was also forced off during the opening half.
Elsewhere, RB Leipzig recovered from conceding in the opening minute to defeat Augsburg 5-2 and remain three points behind the leading pair.
Ezechiel Banzuzi, Christopher Nkunku, David Raum, Romulo and Christoph Baumgartner scored for Leipzig, which maintained its perfect home record in the Bundesliga this season.
Eintracht Frankfurt, meanwhile, drew 2-2 against promoted Paderborn, with Jonathan Burkardt scoring both goals for the visitors.

The Best Automatic Litter Boxes Tested by Our Spoiled Cats

I can confidently say that having an automatic litter box has been the biggest game changer for me when it comes to cat ownership. I can't recommend them enough. They can be pricey, but never having to scoop poop again is priceless.

Throughout testing, I was generally happy with the product—it cleaned consistently after my cats used it, the app was responsive, and both of my cats adapted easily to the familiar open-top design. However, many people online have complained about litter and urine getting trapped under the globe, as well as litter tracking onto the top of the globe, which adds more frustrating disassembly and cleaning. PetPivot AutoScooper 12 for $140: If your budget is $200, this is so much better than a traditional box. However, I still think the picks above are the cream of the crop. This is the new-and-improved version of the 11 model below. It doesn’t have a connected app, which I don't love because I like to track my cat’s weight and usage, and I like being able to adjust settings from afar. But if you’re looking for a more hands-off model without much maintenance, a simpler, budget box like this may be a good option.. My main gripe is that my cats kicked out so much litter during use due to the low, open-top design. If you go with this model, be sure to use litter tracking mats or have a vacuum cleaner on standby.
PetPivot Autoscooper 11 for $160: Though it doesn’t have all the bells and whistles of some others on this list, I still liked this PetPivot model. The litter box is the smallest and lightest I’ve tested, and the only assembly required was popping on the legs and inserting the drawer (and putting a waste bag liner in). When you want to completely empty the litter, you attach a plastic cover that pops on to scoot all of the litter into the drawer below. Since this has no app, you won’t be able to closely monitor your cats’ usage or get alerted when the drawer is full, so this requires more check-ins than other WIRED-tested automatic boxes on this list.
Homerunpet Self-Cleaning Litter Box CS106 for $773: This model is huge, with a 106-liter capacity (and holds 8 liters of litter, plus a 4.5-liter reservoir), making it ideal for big, chonky cats weighing up to 20 pounds (or multiple-cat households). I like that it dumps and refills its own litter, and that it has anti-pinch sensors and two escape routes that are always open. There’s a drawer for storing the waste bags that line the poop drawer, as well as underneath the box, so you can dump all the litter at once. It cleaned itself efficiently and quietly. One thing to note is that the box is absolutely massive upon arrival—I couldn’t fit it in the back seat of my Mazda 3—and the litter box itself is huge, with a frustratingly short cord that might make placement inconvenient.
