Australia
Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. The country’s media has been much quieter on Cop than previous host countries, and although Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is unlikely to stay long.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, will be in daily charge of the negotiations. As aspects of Australia’s energy supply also fall under his portfolio, he has been in the sometimes uncomfortable position of having to boost fossil fuels while insisting on the need for a clean energy transition.
Yet Australia has a positive story to tell on decarbonisation: while remaining one of the world’s major fossil fuel exporters, the country has also invested heavily in renewables, and solar power has now expanded so much that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity.
Turkey
Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Turkey’s autocratic president, showed little interest in climate and environmental concerns before bidding to host this year’s Cop summit.
In the last five years, Cop has also been held in Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Azerbaijan, all in the same broad region. This has given an outsize role to the Arab group of countries, who are neighbours in the region and have a strong interest in ensuring that fossil fuel interests – including their lobbyists – are well represented.
Australia runs the overall direction of the negotiations, and Turkey’s government, with the environment minister, Murat Kurum, has control of the action agenda, a programme of voluntary initiatives. Erdoğan has used this to push forward a key interest of his wife, Emine Erdoğan, in cutting waste and promoting the circular economy. She has called for an end to “throwaway culture” and for recycling instead of landfill – though Turkey still has sites that leak vast quantities of methane.
Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency and one of the world’s leading energy economists, is understood to be one of the advisers behind this year’s emphasis on electrification, displacing fossil fuels with electricity for heating, transport and industrial uses. This could halve the amount of energy we need, and is the next biggest step, after boosting renewable energy generation, needed for a low-carbon world.
Brazil
The recently re-elected President Lula da Silva will come to Cop31 for his first trip abroad after winning his historic fourth term, and will bring two roadmaps, one a global plan for the transition away from fossil fuels, the other for halting and reversing deforestation. These are non-binding, and contain no deadlines or firm requirements from governments, but show a series of steps that governments can take to achieve these goals.
China
Xi Jinping, the president of China, will not come to this year’s Cop, but his country’s rapid energy and industrial transformation will determine the course of the planet’s future. China is the world’s second biggest economy and the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, making up nearly a third of global annual carbon output, owing mainly to the use of fossil fuels to power its explosive economic growth for the last 25 years. But it has also invested in renewable energy, which is reshaping the global energy business.
Xi may not be present in Antalya, but the top officials he sends will know that petrostates – including Russia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are his important allies. However, countries pushing for a low-carbon future may be more important still – as China’s customers.
India
For several months this year, India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, mulled an intriguing proposition: to host the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028. In the end, India withdrew its bid in April without specifying why, leaving the field open. India is torn between its burgeoning clean energy sector – it now has the world’s third biggest installed capacity of renewable energy, after China and the US – and its coal sector, which still supplies about 70% of electricity, and has close links to Modi.
Bhupender Yadav, India’s environment minister, who leads its Cop delegations, enjoys a mutually supportive relationship with the UK’s Ed Miliband, and a reputation as a forward thinker.
US
The attention of Donald Trump has been fixed on the crucial midterm elections, a verdict on his second term as president that has shown Republicans the electoral dangers of an unpredictable White House. No US delegation is expected at Cop31, and soon Trump’s withdrawal of the country from the UN framework convention on climate change will mean none can take part.
Trump’s shadow was felt at Cop30 in Belem last year, as he started to dismantle the US’s renewable energy sector and boost fossil fuels, setting the US on course to start increasing greenhouse gas emissions again, after decades in which they fell. But his administration’s unpopularity with the US electorate, and a drought and fire-filled summer, has bolstered the pro-climate stance of scores of Democratic congresspeople and state governors, despite a campaign of “climate hushing” before the midterms. Some of them, and a scattering of business leaders, may attend Cop31.
UK
Andy Burnham will attend Cop for the first time this year, after a mixed record on the climate since taking office. During the record-breaking heatwaves and droughts of this summer, the British prime minister was criticised for failing to speak out on the climate crisis. He subsequently made strong interventions affirming his support for the UK’s target of reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, but then backed the Jackdaw gasfield. No decision has been announced on the Rosebank oilfield yet.
From December, Burnham will have a much bigger opportunity to craft climate policy on the international stage: the UK will take over the revolving presidency of the influential G20 group, which comprises the world’s biggest developed and developing economies. The Guardian understands that the UK will emphasise building resilience against the impacts of the climate crisis as a key focus of the G20 for its year-long presidency.
Miliband, now foreign secretary, and a veteran of many Cops in government and opposition, is expected to accompany the prime minister to the leaders’ summit segment of Cop31. Miliband was hailed, in public and private, by many participants last year for his patient bridge-building that helped Brazil to rescue a deal from the fractious final hours of Cop30.
At this year’s UN general assembly, he also briefed other governments on the findings of the UK’s joint intelligence committee, which warned that the impact of collapsing ecosystems around the world posed a national security risk, threatening food shortages, mass migration and potential nuclear war.
The energy and net zero secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, will head the UK’s Cop31 delegation for the final negotiations in the last days of this fortnight of talks, after the leaders have departed.
Europe
The EU has faced a quandary over its climate convictions in recent years. Far-right populists are on the rise, pushing climate denialism, and the bloc has backed down from some key regulations, watering down its green deal package, loosening the strings on corporate climate liabilities, delaying rules on trade in goods from deforested areas, and extending the phase-in of new car rules. The failure of Europe’s car industry to move decisively to electric vehicles – preferring lobbying against emissions standards, which has turned out to be a poor strategy as consumers turn in droves to cheap-to-run EVs – has led to threats to slap tariffs on China.
The EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen called this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves and drought a “summer of truth” that must be answered: she is now confirmed for the summit. Wopke Hoekstra, the Dutch climate commissioner, will oversee the final stages of the talks for the EU, and is expected to make competition with China a key focus.
UN
Cop31 will mark the final outing at a UN climate summit for António Guterres, the UN secretary general, who has regularly intervened powerfully on this subject. A successor to Guterres has still not yet been chosen – the US has tried to get Viktor Orbán, the far-right former president of Hungary, into the role, or a former minister from the United Arab Emirates, Lana Nusseibeh.
Simon Stiell, the determined executive secretary of the UNFCCC, will oversee the talks, with an added twist to his job this year, having to liaise between the two co-hosts as well as the fractious parties.
Saudi Arabia
Saudi failed to confirm with the Guardian before Cop who would lead its delegation, but the country’s recent behaviour at international climate meetings tells its own story. The country has a long history of obstructing the UN climate negotiations, though its behaviour was sometimes muted when the US intervened. With Trump in the White House, Saudi has felt emboldened to interfere further, with allies including Russia, Venezuela, members of the Arab group, and the Like-Minded Developing Countries grouping.
At Cop30, the Saudi delegation refused to allow even an oblique mention of the pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, made at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, in the final text until the final moments.
At recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Saudi led a small group of countries – including China, India, Russia and Kenya – that fought to delay publication of the next comprehensive assessment of climate science. Publication of the landmark report, which is expected to warn of catastrophic impacts from further temperature rises, was expected in 2028, in time for Cop33 at which countries will assess their progress on meeting emissions-cutting goals under the Paris agreement, a process known as the “global stocktake”. Delaying it by a year or more, as Saudi wants, would mean a loss of urgency for the global stocktake, and could help countries to get away with inadequate measures on decarbonisation.

British writer Tom Rob Smith led an enlightening Q&A session on the difference between writing prose fiction and writing for the screen this afternoon at the Thessaloniki Film Festival, where he is one of the headline speakers.
During the session, the Emmy winner, best known for the novel Child 44 and the series The Assassination of Gianni Versace: American Crime Story, also shared his next project: A fiction book based on the West Memphis Three murder case.
“I can tell you because I’m coming right to the end of it,” Smith said when Deadline asked about his next project in Thessaloniki.
“It’s based on an American crime. A case called the West Memphis Three. It was a killing that took place in 1993. No one was interested in it when it happened. Then HBO made a documentary about it called Paradise Lost. Everyone got involved, including Peter Jackson and Johnny Depp. I’m doing a fictionalized version of that account.”
Watch on Deadline
Smith added: “It’s not like Versace, which was a kind of mirror of the case. This is more like Child 44, where you’re taking a real case and telling a story about its ideas rather than the real people.”
Damien Echols, Jessie Misskelley Jr., and Jason Baldwin, known as the West Memphis Three, were convicted as teenagers of the 1993 murders of three 8-year-old boys in West Memphis, Arkansas. The prosecutors at the time said the murders were committed as part of a satanic ritual. Echols was sentenced to death, while Misskelley Jr. and Baldwin were given life sentences. The trio was freed in 2011 after serving 18 years. New DNA evidence excluded the three men from all of the crime scene evidence found at the scene.
Echols, Misskelley Jr., and Baldwin’s received public support from several high-profile figures, including Johnny Depp and Peter Jackson, who funded their legal defence. The men were also the subject of three Paradise Lost HBO documentaries by Joe Berlinger and Bruce Sinofsky.
Deadline covered the documentaries and the trio’s release extensively at the time. The story was also captured in Devil’s Knot, a 2013 fiction feature directed by Atom Egoyan and starring Colin Firth and Reese Witherspoon. The Arkansas Supreme Court reopened the murder case and ordered fresh testing of the DNA found at the crime scene in 2024. The case is still ongoing.
Thessaloniki runs until November 15.

The measure, which may face legal challenges, requires girls who want to play in girls' sports to produce documentation from a healthcare provider who has verified "the student's biological sex" relying on the student's reproductive anatomy — in other words, a genital exam — genetic makeup or their natural testosterone levels. Due to how expensive genetic and testosterone testing can be, the genital exams are the most accessible option.
In the aftermath of Election Day, social media users circulated a rumor that Washington voters passed an anti-trans measure that would allegedly subject girls who want to play school sports in the state to genital inspections. 
The rumor spread on X, Threads and Bluesky. Some posts shared additional alleged context, claiming that the ballot measure would subject children who want to play in girls' sports to genital inspections. Others dismissed these claims as a "fantasy."
Washington voters did, in fact, pass a measure called Initiative 26-638 aimed at banning trans girls from playing in girls' sports. The act requires medical providers to "verify" a student's biological sex using reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels.
In theory, the law does not explicitly require genital exams for anyone because it provides three options for sex verification. In practice, due to how expensive genetic and testosterone testing can be, the genital exams are the most accessible option, according to child advocacy groups and medical providers who oppose the provision.
It is worth noting these tests cannot necessarily definitively determine a person's biological sex, which scientists say is a complex category.
The measure subjects every girl who wishes to play in girls' school sports to sex verification, but does not subject students who wish to participate in boys' sports to the same scrutiny. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association reportedly said earlier this year that it was aware of 10 trans student athletes total in the state; it's unclear how many of these athletes are trans boys, as opposed to trans girls. 
While the Washington secretary of state website indicates that there are still ballots left to count, as of this writing, support for the measure has a 13-point lead over opposition. Furthermore, The Associated Press called the race, stating that the "Yes" vote won.
Snopes, like many credible media publications, relies on AP calls for elections. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
(Some posts stated that the measure was "winning" or had won before AP called the race; ultimately, those posts turned out to be true, even if they called the race early.)
It's worth noting that the act may face legal challenges.
"Many have said that I-638 is likely unconstitutional and we understand there are legal groups and organizations considering litigation," said No Hate in WA State, the main coalition opposing the measure. The American Civil Liberties Union-Washington said in its own statement that it was "exploring all potential next steps to uphold the rights of transgender girls and their access to school sports."
I-638's text, examined
The complete text for I-638 is available on the Washington secretary of state's website. Here's the relevant section (emphasis ours):
NEW SECTION. Sec. 3. A new section is added to chapter 28A.600 RCW to read as follows:
(1) Policies, procedures, rules, and other requirements adopted in accordance with RCW 28A.600.200 by a school district board of directors or a voluntary nonprofit entity must prohibit biologically male students from competing with and against female students in athletic activities with separate classifications for male and female students if the athletic activity is:
(a) Intended for female students only; and
(b) An individual or team competition activity.
(2) A student who elects to participate in individual or team competition activities intended for female students only governed under subsection (1) of this section shall provide, as part of the required routine sports physical examination, a health examination and consent form or other statement signed by the student's personal health care provider that verifies the student's biological sex, relying only on one or more of the following: The student's reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.
As opponents to I-638 have noted, a birth certificate would not be an acceptable form of sex verification under I-638. About 28% of K-12 school-age girls in Washington do not have a personal doctor or nurse, meaning that it's likely many families would not be able to rely on an established medical history with a health care provider.
The nonpartisan Washington State Parent Teacher Association, the largest volunteer and child advocacy organization in the state, opposed I-638 on the grounds that it would likely require many girls to either undergo an intimate, embarrassing and medically unnecessary genital examination or forgo playing in girls' sports. Here's what the organization said (emphasis ours):
Two of the three permitted methods, genetic testing and testosterone measurement, are expensive and unlikely to be covered by insurance for this purpose, since neither is clinically indicated. That makes an examination of reproductive anatomy the most accessible pathway for most families.
The burden falls hardest on rural, uninsured, and lower-income families, and on families without an established relationship with a healthcare provider — who face the added problem that the measure never says what qualifies someone as a student's "personal health care provider."
Doctors and medical professionals opposing the initiative shared similar warnings and noted that major medical organizations advise against pelvic exams for adolescent girls, with some citing psychological harms and potential future avoidance of medical care. The Washington Academy of Family Physicians and the Washington State Nurses Association opposed the measure.
The Seattle Times reported that doctors may interpret the measure differently, given that it's vague and, in some views, "poorly written."

Toll in Old Delhi's Chawri Bazar building collapse rises to 3 as another body pulled out
The deceased was identified as Pankaj Sharma, a resident of Hanuman Nagar village in Bihar’s Khagaria district.
The body of a 40-year-old man was recovered from the debris of the collapsed building in Old Delhi’s Hauz Qazi in the early hours of Saturday, taking the death toll in the incident to three, police said.
The deceased was identified as Pankaj Sharma, a resident of Hanuman Nagar village in Bihar’s Khagaria district, deputy commissioner of police (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh said.
With the latest recovery, five people have now been pulled out of the debris, including three who died and two who sustained injuries. Both injured workers have received medical treatment and are stable, officials said. Rescue operations were continuing at the site at the time of filing this report.
The Hauz Qazi collapse
The recovery comes two days after a three-storey building under construction collapsed in the narrow lanes of Chawri Bazar on Thursday morning, trapping construction workers under the debris.
The building, located in Gali Sitara near Chawri Bazar Metro station, reportedly collapsed in two stages around 9.30am while construction work was underway.
The collapse has also raised questions about alleged negligence during construction, with the police arresting three contractors in the early hours of Friday. The contractors allegedly ignored repeated warnings from workers about the poor quality of the construction materials and the structure's inability to support another concrete slab, according to the first information report (FIR) registered in the case.
DCP Singh identified the accused as Siraj, Tajuddin and Furkan, all residents of the Ajmeri Gate area. They were arrested from Sirohi village in Faridabad's Dauj tehsil.
Workers raised concerns
In his complaint to the police, Firoz, a 37-year-old construction worker from Bihar who lives in Mandawali and survived the collapse, alleged that the contractors repeatedly disregarded workers' concerns about the building's structural stability.
According to his statement, he and other workers had been engaged by the contractors to carry out construction on a plot measuring around 70 square yards. Three concrete slabs, locally referred to as lanterns, had already been laid at the property.
The workers allegedly warned that the existing slab was not strong enough to support another slab and that it required additional cement and wooden support.
“We had informed the contractors that the lintel had not dried up and we cannot put another one... to support the lintel, more cement and wood is required... but they asked us to continue, saying that the cost would increase,” Firoz said in the FIR, a copy of which was accessed by HT.
Firoz also told the police that they had attempted to raise their concerns with the property owners. However, the owners allegedly told them that the contractors were handling the construction and that they should approach the contractors instead.
Around 9.30am on Thursday, Firoz and the other workers were carrying out construction when the building suddenly gave way. Two of his fellow workers were trapped under the debris, while he was working in the rear portion of the structure and managed to survive.
The FIR
The FIR names Tajuddin and Furkan as accused and invokes sections 105 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder), 290 (negligent conduct with respect to pulling down, repairing or constructing buildings), 125(a) (negligent act with respect to buildings) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
The collapse has also brought renewed scrutiny on the civic authorities, particularly after it emerged that Delhi Police had alerted the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) about construction activity at the property nearly five months before the incident.
Police flagged construction
In a letter dated June 15, the station house officer of Hauz Qazi police station had alerted the deputy commissioner of MCD's City SP Zone about new residential construction spread over around 70 square yards at property number 4547-48 in Wali Sheesh Mahal, Ajmeri Gate, and sought action.
The MCD acknowledged receipt of the communication but said a subsequent inspection found that the owner was undertaking repair work that its maintenance department had advised in April.
However, an inquiry by the civic body alleged that the owner used the repair advisory as a cover to clandestinely undertake fresh construction on the second and third floors without the requisite permissions.
The MCD inquiry report also flagged discrepancies in the property's tax declarations, alleging that excess floor coverage had been declared to mislead authorities and to claim protection under laws applicable to older structures.
The building reportedly lacked a sanctioned building plan, raising questions about how construction was allowed to continue despite earlier police communication to the civic body.
Issues facing rescue
The rescue operation on Thursday was severely hampered by the extremely narrow lanes of the walled city, which prevented heavy machinery, including JCB excavators, from reaching the site of the collapse. Fire personnel and other rescue teams had to rely largely on manually removing debris to reach those trapped beneath.
Residents of neighbouring buildings were also evacuated after police warned that one of the adjoining structures was in a precarious condition.
Meanwhile, chief minister Rekha Gupta ordered the immediate suspension of the junior engineer and assistant engineer concerned, a detailed inquiry into the collapse and registration of an FIR against the contractor. She also directed officials to ensure the best possible medical treatment for the injured and provide ex gratia assistance to the families of the deceased.
Police are continuing their investigation into the circumstances leading to the collapse, including the alleged violations during construction and the role of the contractors and property owners.

Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs, most likely.
Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019, back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup’s unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all.
The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.

The year 2026 has been a breakthrough for action RPGs. We have already had the likes of Onimusha: Way of the Sword and Control Resonant performing beyond expectations. However, gamers had been waiting for one action RPG, and it was Phantom Blade Zero. The game had captured everyone’s imagination with incredibly fluid and impactful combat during its multiple showcases.
So, did Phantom Blade Zero meet its promised hype? After playing almost 40 hours of Phantom Blade Zero, I can most definitely say that it has the best combat I have seen in any recent action RPG releases, but sadly that’s not the entire picture. Here is our Phantom Blade Zero review to help you know whether the game is worth playing or not.
Combat Straight Out of a Fever Dream
Phantom Blade Zero doesn’t take long to send you right into action. From the very beginning, you get to experience what the absolute peak of the game’s combat can do when Soul fights his brother in the prologue, one of the earliest Phantom Blade Zero bosses. The game gives a fully powered Soul to players and allows them to fight Zuo Shang, the Shadow Sovereign.
Although Soul constantly regenerates HP to avoid losing during this fight, it lets us see the full potential of the combat at a very early stage, also acting as the perfect hook for the game. The combat is very energetic and is unlike anything I have played before. It feels straight out of a Shaolin or Kung Fu movie, and Donnie Yen’s touch is clearly noticeable in every movement.
The closest combat to Phantom Blade Zero I have seen is in Black Desert Online, but that’s only in terms of visuals. In terms of responsiveness for high-speed combat, Phantom Blade Zero is in a class of its own, untouched by any other game.
Parry, Parry, and Parry
From a distance, the combat can seem spammy, but when you actually play the game, every movement, parry, dodge, and block requires precision. Even though enemy attacks feel too fast at a glance, the combination of sound makes it feel trackable, allowing you to parry without feeling unfair.
And parrying in Phantom Blade Zero is absolutely spot on. The constant ringing sound of parrying and blocking in every boss fight will make any action RPG fun and ecstatic. The last time I had this much fun was while playing Sekiro, but even then, parrying in Phantom Blade Zero feels like a whole other level of enjoyment.
Combos Straight Out of a Fighting Game
But the game is not all about parrying. It also features combo attacks, different for every weapon. The combos in Phantom Blade Zero are very similar to fighting games, but a tad bit less complicated. Although you can win the game without using any combos, once you have mastered it, the combat reaches an entirely different level.
Pulling off powerful combos can literally destroy an enemy’s health bar or allow you to apply specific stat effects much quicker. One combo I loved using throughout the second half of the game was Fiend Saw’s, which applies Fiend Aura erosion.
However, it’s not just the statistical aspect when it comes to combos; I largely did it in fights because it looked extremely cool. Combos on every weapon have unique animations, some of which look so extraordinary that I was even willing to ignore the damage drop, if any, to perform them.
A Weapon Arsenal That Makes Every Other Game Ashamed
Ever since I finished Elden Ring, I had never expected to see another game introduce that many weapons with unique abilities. Weapons in Phantom Blade Zero have gone beyond that, not only having unique abilities, but also having unique animations for each. The best part about the weapons is that you directly obtain most of them by defeating bosses. So, you are basically taking their weapon after defeating them.
There are over 55 weapons in Phantom Blade Zero, and each weapon having its own identity is truly unbelievable. Players can carry two weapons at the same time, while also having a third Phantom Edge. Letting players freely swap between these is another expert addition to the combat that feels incredibly satisfying to perform.
Another thing to note is that every weapon has specific effects and abilities. These abilities get stronger the more you upgrade the weapons. Some abilities completely change how you fight with the weapon. For example, the Fanatic’s Broken Blade can get you drunk for 20 seconds, literally, completely changing your combat style until you sober up. And there are countless other examples.
An Interesting Story Plagued by Subpar Voice Acting
Phantom Blade Zero tells a story inspired by Chinese mythology. After playing Black Myth Wukong, I was extremely excited to have a similar level of immersion from this game. The story starts with a fight between Soul and his brother, who end up piercing each other’s hearts.
Soul has been falsely accused of assassinating the leader of the Order, which is why he is fighting his brother and rival, who now acts as the Shadow Sovereign. After dying, the Flesh Sculptor offers a new heart to Soul, which only allows him to live for 66 days. Within this time, Soul has to find the mastermind behind the assassination, while fighting his former allies.
Sounds interesting, right? Sadly, that entire notion fell flat just 20 minutes into the game. The reason was the subpar English voice acting in the game.
Most of the English voice acting in Phantom Blade Zero literally felt emotionless. Only very few characters actually did a good job. Compared to Black Myth Wukong, which had incredible voice acting for every character, Phantom Blade Zero was a big letdown.
And sadly, the voice acting also ruined my experience of the game’s story. Although the essence of Phantom Blade Zero’s story feels great, especially the connecting lore in the game, I couldn’t be bothered to pay too much attention to it.
And that’s coming from a person who loves getting into the lore of any game he likes. However, for anyone who understands Chinese, you may have a better experience than I did because the Chinese dub sounded much better.
Exploration is Expansive but Comes with Too Much Handholding
Phantom Blade Zero is a linear game, but most of its levels are very open-ended. The map has multiple regions, each being an open level. However, even though the levels are open, the pathways are fairly linear, so not a lot of parkour is possible. Even then, the game does have some hidden nooks and quests.
The best part about it is that the game forces you to return to older maps, as new keys or quests are obtained later down the line that open specific segments of older areas. Even story missions change regions. Reaching a specific point in the story can turn all the NPCs you have met in previous maps into enemies when you return.
Some guards who blocked you from certain sections would then become defeatable to unlock the area.
However, Phantom Blade Zero does too much handholding in exploration that I personally dislike. Almost every detail that you even cross over without noticing would appear on the map. This often kills the ‘exploration through eyes.’ If everything appears on the map, what’s the need to actually look for it yourself?
Enemies and Bosses Are All Teeth and No Bite
Phantom Blade Zero has an incredible cast of enemies and bosses. Although the normal enemies don’t have that much variety overall, they have some unique personalities that make them stand out. Like the puppets in Village of Lu, who throw their heads at you as attacks.
The bosses, on the other hand, are pure spectacles. Every boss fight is a well-animated action movie sequence, with Soul and the enemy going at each other no holds barred. Unfortunately, even though the fight looks and feels good, it never ends up becoming too challenging.
This can be a good thing for traditional action RPG players who are never into too much difficulty, but for soulslike players like me, the game can feel very easy at times. Excluding a couple of bosses, most of the fights only take one or two tries to finish.
Even at the Hellwalker Phantom Blade Zero difficulty, the game never felt too challenging. Normally, I wouldn’t have paid too much attention to this. However, S-Game had marketed their Hellwalker mode as a challenging alternative for hardcore players, with more boss movesets and better AI. That, I personally think, did not live up to my expectations.
Another reason for the boss fights to feel too easy is that bosses actually retain their second or third phases after your death. So, instead of redoing the fight from scratch, if you have finished the first phase, you can directly start fighting in the second phase with full heals after dying. Also, any enemies killed in the overworld remain dead.
I don’t think either of these things are bad. They provide a different experience from games of this genre. The enemy not respawning factor also helps greatly in exploration, as you truly get a feeling of 100% clearing an area.
Performance: Phantom Blade Zero Runs Smoothly, but Clips A Lot
The impactful and fluid combat of Phantom Blade Zero would have ended up being a complete disaster if the game didn’t run as smoothly as it does. Even at ultra graphics with DLSS turned off, I was comfortably getting above 50 FPS in combat. With DLSS set to quality, the FPS went up to 120+.
With Frame Generation set to 4x, I was getting above 180 FPS with no latency. However, when changing Frame Generation to 6x, the latency becomes very noticeable, so you’d better avoid it.
My Setup:
CPU: AMD Ryzen 9 7900x
CPU Cooler: CORSAIR H150 RGB
Motherboard: GIGABYTE B650M Gaming X AX
GPU: MSI Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB
RAM: 32GB (32GB x 1) ADATA XPG DDR5 5600FSB LANCER
SSD: 1TB AORUS Gen 4 5000E NVMe storage
Monitor: 1080p @165hz
Although the game runs extremely well, it does have a fair bit of clunk and glitches. The terrain can often be a big issue, as you will find yourself constantly getting stuck on even a slightly protruding stone. For a game that has such good combat movement, it can feel very odd to have such basic issues.
Also, sometimes a level’s or cutscene assets can take time to load. But it was rare enough that I didn’t end up having a bad feeling. In terms of graphics, the game looks gorgeous. Some of the locations in the game are extremely scenic and can make you want to wait there for eternity.
Verdict: Phantom Blade Zero is a New Standard for the Action RPG Genre
Phantom Blade Zero is unparalleled in action combat, leaving behind all its competitors, whether in the past, present, or even in the coming future. Featuring over 55 unique weapons, each providing a unique playstyle, paired with an incredible number of cinematic boss fights, the game has completely left me mind-boggled and impressed.
However, it also suffers from terrible English voice acting, making players detached from the main story and the incredible visuals it offers. Alongside that, the game can feel very easy for soulslike players, but it also allows the game to be more accessible for others who simply prefer playing normal action RPGs.
Phantom Blade Zero overall is a masterfully crafted game that will grab you from the first parry, and won’t leave you until you have performed over a thousand different combos to get every possible achievement in the game. It is a true testament to how incredible and impactful combat can feel in the coming age of gaming.
So, that’s our Phantom Blade Zero review. What’s your opinion so far of the game? Let us know in the comments section below.

In late October and early November, a photo circulated on social media supposedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump, late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and singer Beyoncé aboard a private jet. The image shows Trump and Epstein sitting shirtless next to each other, with Beyoncé standing behind them.
"The Epstein files have leaked again !! As Jeffrey Epstein, Trump and Beyonce are all seen chilling on board," one X post (archived) captioned the image.
(X user @TomthunkitsMind)
The image spread primarily on X and Facebook.
In short, the photograph wasn't real. We didn't find it in any reputable news outlets and AI-detection tools indicated it was artificially generated. Google Gemini detected a watermark showing that the image was created or edited using Google AI. As such, we have rated the image fake.
How we know the image is fake
First, we didn't find the image in news outlets or any other credible sources — it spread solely on social media. If it were real, it would likely have been widely reported by news organizations. Another sign that the image was fake was Trump's physical appearance, as he looked much older than he did when Epstein was still alive.
Moreover, an analysis using Hive Moderation, an AI-detection tool, determined with 99.8% confidence that the image was "likely to be AI-generated."
(X user @TomthunkitsMind, Hive Moderation)
We also ran the image through Google Gemini's SynthID check, a tool that scans for watermarks embedded by artificial intelligence software. That scan detected a SynthID watermark and concluded, "this image contains a SynthID watermark, which indicates that it was generated or edited with Google AI."
(Google Gemini)
Readers who want to check whether an image contains a SynthID watermark can do so by uploading the photo to Google Gemini and asking, "Does this image have a SynthID watermark?" However, the absence of a SynthID watermark does't automatically mean an image is authentic, as it could have been created using other AI tools.
It's unclear who created the image, but it has circulated online at least since Oct. 26.
Some social media users sharing the image suggested Beyoncé was involved in Epstein's crimes. While the singer's name does appear in the Epstein Library, the references we found don't accuse her of any wrongdoing and, for example, concern such matters as tickets to her concerts:
(www.justice.gov/epstein)
(www.justice.gov)
All in all, while genuine photographs of Trump and Epstein together exist, the image above isn't real. It's one of many fabricated images of the two that have circulated on social media.

A 27-year-old man, a member of a village anti-drug committee, was allegedly shot at by a group of people at his home in Kaleke village here, police said on Sunday (November 8, 2026).
The injured Amandeep Singh was admitted to hospital and his condition was stable, they said, adding that four people have been identified in connection with the incident that took place on Saturday (November 8, 2026) .
He sustained a bullet injury to his thigh after some people opened fire at him at his residence, Deputy Superintendent of Police Rajinder Pal said.
Mr. Amandeep is out of danger and his condition is stable, he said.
Dhanaula SHO Baljinder Singh said the matter is under investigation. "We are investigating the motive behind the incident," he said, while adding that four people, who are locals, have been identified.
When pointed out that some media reports said Mr. Amandeep had earlier informed the police about the activity of some suspected drug peddlers in the area and whether they could have held a grudge against him, Mr. Singh said, "Amandeep was part of a group or the anti-drug committee. In the past, an FIR was registered against some people based on the information given by him to the police."
In Saturday's firing incident, however, investigations are ongoing to find out the motive behind, he said, adding that "We are verifying whether the incident was related to personal enmity or whether any other angle is involved."
Notably, last month, anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota was shot dead in broad daylight at a medical store in a busy marketplace in Mansa town on October 13. The store owner, who had fired at Jhota after the activist confronted him over the sale of addictive drugs to an elderly man, was subsequently arrested.

Fast, fearsome, and fragile were words often associated with former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond, whose promising cricket career was drastically curtailed by injury.
He debuted as a 26-year-old against Australia in Hobart in 2001, but it was in his next series, against Bangladesh, where he truly announced himself.
He took 11 wickets in two Tests at an average of 13, and it looked like the beginning of a long and lucrative career.
But Bond's back had other ideas. A stress fracture kept him out the game for almost two years from 2003.
A meeting with back surgeon Grahame Inglis offered him hope he could overcome his injury by undergoing a little-known surgery that is now commonplace in the fast bowling fraternity.
"If I can't fix this, then the career is potentially over," Bond said of his decision to undergo pars stabilisation surgery in 2004.
"He [Inglis] talked about a procedure that he had done, one on a New Zealand high jumper and one other athlete.
"He thought that the chances I came back and bowled fast were slim, but ... I was prepared to give it a go."
While other injuries limited Bond to just 14 more Tests before he retired in 2009, his back didn't trouble him again.
Last surgeon standing
Renowned New Zealand spinal surgeon Rowan Schouten was working with Dr Inglis at the time and said Bond was "patient zero in this whole story."
The success of that surgery laid the groundwork for a procedure that Schouten and his team have now performed on around 30 professional cricketers.
When surgeons in the UK stopped performing the procedure and Dr Inglis retired, Dr Schouten became the world's leading authority on repairing spinal stress fractures in fast bowlers.
"We were kind of left as the last man standing with experience on international fast bowlers and since then it's taken off essentially," he said.
"We're dealing with calls and connections from all around the world, from the UK, India, South Africa, Europe, Bangladesh, everywhere."
Bond still helps fast bowlers who have struggled with back issues and is often approached for advice.
He's coached Jofra Archer, Jason Behrendorff and James Pattinson, who all had the surgery and returned to play at the top level.
What is pars stabilisation surgery?
When a fast bowler is considering spinal surgery, like Australia's Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris did in 2025, it sounds like a drastic step.
Loading Instagram content
But Dr Schouten said the surgery was straightforward and "not that extreme".
It involves grafting the spine to stimulate repair, before putting screws and wires around the injured portion to provide stability.
"We've got a few little added components to it that we believe are important ... but it's a pretty standard technique," he said.
The injury, often referred to as a stress fracture, is common across sport and very prevalent in cricket.
Dr Schouten stressed the surgery is not a fusion, and most stress fractures do not need it.
"You need to preserve all that spinal motion that these guys need to be able to bowl full pace," he said.
If a player did opt to go under the knife, the recovery involves a six-to-nine month rehab program.
"Some stress fractures in some players become a recurring theme," Dr Schouten said.
"And then if you do that, if you have that two or three times in a row over multiple seasons, it can really disrupt a career."

Just after 3.48 a.m. on May 3, 2026, fire ripped through a four-storey building in Vivek Vihar, East Delhi, killing nine. The suspected origin was an AC blast or short circuit.
Ten newborns died in an overcrowded Jhansi NICU in November 2024, a unit meant for 18 babies packed with 55. Three newborns in Amravati this August, dead not from flame but from smoke inhalation, even though the fire itself was out within 30 minutes. One newborn in Chhindwara two days before that. Ten patients at Cuttack’s SCB Medical College this March, when a short circuit in a trauma-ICU air-conditioner ignited an oxygen-rich ward at 3 a.m.
Fire accidents in India used to happen in industrial units, firecracker factories and mass gatherings. No more. The more devastating ones happen right in our neighbourhoods, in hospitals and high-rises. They are almost always triggered by electrical fires.
Delhi Fire Service attributes over 80% of the capital’s fires to electrical faults. Mumbai Fire Brigade, analysing 26,855 incidents over five years, attributes nearly three in four to the same cause. New Delhi alone saw a 37% rise in residential fires this year over last, with roughly 70% traced to short-circuiting, faulty wiring, overheating, and overloaded circuits. The National Crime Records Bureau recorded 7,566 fire accidents and 7,435 deaths in 2022, with short circuit consistently among the largest single causes.
Indian electricity demand hit 256.11 GW on April 25 this year, against air temperatures of 47 degrees, roughly double the early-2010s peak. A/Cs draw about 50 GW at peak. And projections place the A/C load at 180 GW in another 10 years. Indians bought more than 15 million air-conditioners in 2025 alone, and the International Energy Agency expects the installed base to climb from 93 million units in 2024 to 240 million by 2030.
Air-conditioners draw heavy current that electrical systems in older buildings are unable to withstand, resulting in the wiring burning up. What’s called an A/C blast is the overworked compressor in the refrigeration exploding due to sheer heat caused by overworking. Investigation into these fires has been hampered by shortage of certified fire forensic investigators. Too often, the causes are dismissed as blasts or short circuits. Root cause analysis and systemic remedies are rarely formulated.
How electrical fires happen?
An electrical circuit has three parts. The load is whatever draws current. It could be just a light or an air-conditioner. The wiring carries that current, insulated to keep two conductors from touching. The protection device, typically a miniature circuit breaker, is meant to cut the current flow the instant something goes wrong. The circuit breaker switches off the current within about a tenth of a second for a short circuit, or within a longer window, from a minute to an hour, for a sustained overload. A fire needs two failures at once: something in the load or wiring goes wrong, and the protection device fails to trip in time.
A peer-reviewed 2025 review in the journal Fire identifies six recurring failure modes behind that first failure: short circuits, overloads, loose or oxidised connections, series and parallel arc faults, ground faults, and equipment ageing. Of these, a loose connection is often the quietest killer. Research on wiring practice, cited in Indian engineering literature reviewing fire risk in electrical installations, shows that loose terminal connections, whether from bad workmanship, thermal expansion and contraction, or simple ageing, create a phenomenon called glowing contact: a slow-building hot spot that can smoulder in a wall or panel for months before anything is visible from outside.
There is a second, slower mechanism that gets far less attention and could explain a great deal about how India’s fires happen: harmonics. Every inverter-driven air-conditioner, along with every UPS, LED driver, ventilator and EV charger, draws current in short, jagged pulses rather than a smooth wave. This injects distortion into the electrical supply at multiples of the base 50 Hz frequency. In three-phase buildings, certain harmonic orders, called triplen harmonics, do not cancel out in the neutral conductor the way normal, balanced current does. Instead they add up. The neutral wire, which was never designed to be load-bearing and carries no circuit breaker of its own, quietly overheats. A loose joint nearby could make an overheated neutral become an ignition source ripping up ordinary insulation.
Fire investigators suspect that many chemicals and solvents are used in ICUs and the vapours they generate don’t get evacuated well-known enough because of poor maintenance of ventilation systems. They point out that ICUs have dedicated ventilation systems and need much care. While these vapours provide the fuel, a source of heat is required for ignition. And that is where harmonics-generated heating could come into play, says a fire forensic engineer who didn’t wish to be named. “Electrical fires are a gray area and require a lot of precautions. Sadly, in India, compliance with regulations is considered a financial burden,” he adds.
Among the first cases of a spectacular failure due to harmonics happened in September 2010, when a capacitor inside a harmonic filter aboard the cruise liner Queen Mary 2 failed while the ship approached Barcelona with 3,823 people aboard. The explosion blacked out the vessel.
Investigators from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigation Branch found that the ship’s only warning system, a current-imbalance detector meant to flag a degrading capacitor, had been silently broken for years, and nobody knew. The capacitor had likely been failing since 2006. Regular inspections had “passed” the unit on paper using tests that were, on the ship’s own sealed equipment, physically impossible to perform properly. The UK’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency issued a formal notice afterward warning the shipping industry that harmonic distortion, if left unchecked, can shorten equipment life and “potentially result in fire”.
The shipping industry has since then been probing harmonics angle in several accidents including the Dali case where an Indian-managed and crewed container ship rammed a bridge in Baltimore, U.S., leading to the highest-ever marine accident insurance payout in history.
Where does India fall short?
A 2023 peer-reviewed analysis in the Journal of Failure Analysis and Prevention, examining Indian hospital fires since 2010, found that electrical short circuits accounted for 89% of all hospital fire outbreaks, with at least half the hospitals studied in documented non-compliance with fire-safety norms.
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare revised its National Guidelines on Fire and Life Safety in Healthcare Facilities in 2026 which say plainly that electrical faults, specifically short circuits and malfunctioning air-conditioners or medical equipment, are the predominant cause of hospital fires in India. It adopts the international Group 0/1/2 classification of medical locations by electrical risk, requires Medical IT systems with insulation monitoring and fault-location devices in ICUs and operating theatres, and lays out a genuinely detailed testing regime, insulation resistance, earth-leakage tripping, protective-device coordination, at defined intervals of 12 and 36 months. It even specifies fire-extinguisher classes by hazard type, which would have caught the wrong-extinguisher problem reported at Jhansi.
The report prescribes fire safety certificates, audits and mock drills with real specificity in the new guidelines, but they remain, as before, dependent on State rules and largely self-reported compliance, with no penalty structure of the kind that would make a hospital treat an electrical audit as more than paperwork.
Moreover, hospitals, especially ICUs, are loaded with state-of-the-art electronic devices. Ventilators, infant warmers and phototherapy units (relevant to the Chhindwara accident), oxygen concentrators (relevant to Jhansi/Vivek Vihar), anaesthesia machines and ventilator-integrated ICU beds, CT scanners, MRI machines, inverter A/Cs and dialysis machines are heavy harmonics generators.
But the report does not mention harmonics, total harmonic distortion, or power quality. India’s most current hospital fire-safety document treats “electrical safety” as a matter of insulation, earthing and load capacity alone.
The Bureau of Indian Standards’ newly revised National Building Construction Standards 2026, the country’s overarching building code, is the first version to define harmonics explicitly, require load calculations that account for them, and mandate that buildings with heavy non-linear load plan for active filtering at the design stage. It closes a specific, long-standing loophole: Indian practice had allowed a half-size neutral conductor in three-and-half-core cabling, adequate for the balanced loads of an older era but not for a neutral now carrying triplen harmonics on top of ordinary current. The 2026 code mandates full four-core cable for internal wiring instead, precisely to stop the neutral from quietly overheating. It also lists, for the first time, an Indian standard for arc-fault detection devices, IS 17121, adopting the same IEC standard behind America’s AFCI mandate.
The arc-fault detection is listed among the code’s accepted reference standards but is not actually mandated anywhere in the operative text, unlike residual current devices, which the code requires repeatedly. A standard existing on paper is not the same as a clause requiring its use. Further, the code’s rigorous regime, power-quality monitoring, arc-flash hazard analysis, thermography-based inspection, tiered maintenance schedules, are all written specifically for data centres, not for hospitals, homes or the ordinary commercial buildings where, as this year’s numbers from Delhi and Mumbai show, most of India’s electrical fires actually occur. The text specifies that periodic inspection and testing for installations below the “notified voltage,” which covers the overwhelming majority of Indian homes, hospitals and small commercial buildings, is self-certified by the owner rather than independently verified by an Electrical Inspector. More fundamentally, the NBCS, like the national codes before it, is written for buildings still to come. Its requirements apply as new buildings are constructed or as existing ones are formally altered; the code’s own text exempts existing buildings from its new requirements entirely unless they are altered, or a local authority separately judges them hazardous.
There is no mechanism that reaches back into the country’s existing building stock and brings it up to the 2026 standard on any fixed timeline. That means the older wiring installed under weaker rules, in Amravati, Jhansi and Vivek Vihar, or even in the Kolkata fires, will keep operating exactly as it is. In any case, renovation and repurposing often happens on the sly, is unregulated and therefore under the safety audit radar.
Field data from Delhi and West Bengal, gathered by The Energy and Resources Institute for two of the country’s largest electricity distribution utilities, shows harmonics is not an abstract worry. As rooftop solar and other non-linear loads rise on real low-tension feeders, on-site harmonic measurements already show distortion levels climbing toward, and in places past, the very IEEE 519 thresholds India has chosen not to enforce inside buildings.
India lacks the fire-forensic engineering capacity to distinguish, after the fact, between a generic short circuit and a harmonic-driven neutral failure. Most post-fire accounts stop at “electrical fault” or “technical fault”, language broad enough to close the file without ever identifying the actual failure mode, and in doing so, without ever generating the kind of evidence that would justify updating a standard.
West Bengal: the retrofit problem
West Bengal serves as an egregious case of what is everywhere in India. Densely populated urban neighbourhoods featuring buildings built for another era of low electrical loads being repurposed for a much more electrically heavy application. Since 2025, the State has recorded six major building fires, three of them in hotels and two in godowns, killing roughly 65 people, a disproportionate number of them migrant workers and pilgrims.
The pattern in each case traces directly back to the mechanism at the centre of this piece: old buildings, never engineered for the load now running through them, repurposed without anyone reassessing what the wiring could actually carry. The Shikha Inn, gutted by fire on Mirza Ghalib Street in central Kolkata, occupied a century-old building that was not built to be a hotel at all; five separate hotels operated across its five floors. As with much of India’s old commercial building stock, its electrical systems were sized for a different era, then loaded, piecemeal and without engineering review, with air-conditioners and other equipment. The August 17 fire at a hotel in Tarapith followed a similar trajectory: an electrical origin, and a death toll driven less by flame than by smoke, worsened by the use of flammable material in the hotel’s interior. Rituraj Hotel, which burned in April 2025, had also been repurposed from its original use, and had only one stairway; when fire broke out on the first floor, it cut off the sole escape route, trapping guests on the upper floors in smoke exactly as at Mirza Ghalib Street.
What makes West Bengal’s cluster an especially sharp illustration of the national problem, rather than a separate one, is how closely it mirrors the failure already documented in hospitals. Undocumented load growth on old wiring, safety measures that exist on paper without being verified in practice, and an accountability structure that responds to disaster with promises, in this case a statewide fire safety audit, rather than with sustained correction of the underlying infrastructure.
What needs to be done
It is worth being precise about what “addressing harmonics” would actually require, since good equipment already exists. Many quality inverter ACs and medical devices include some internal filtering or power-factor correction, tuned to that single device. But this filtering is a manufacturer’s design choice calibrated to the appliance alone, not to the building it sits in, and cheaper appliances often skip it entirely. Even where every individual device filters its own output well, none of that filtering is designed to work in concert with the others.
A ward or a home may have a dozen separately filtered, well-behaved appliances whose combined harmonic signature still overwhelms a shared neutral conductor sized for an earlier, simpler load, because nothing at the building level coordinates or caps what they collectively put onto that wire. The new code’s data-centre-grade rules, mandatory total-harmonic-distortion limits referencing IEEE 519, periodic THD measurement at distribution boards, panel-level filters above a defined load threshold, and neutral-conductor thermal monitoring may well need to be expended to hospitals and heavy-load commercial buildings.
There have been cases of root cause analysis by Indian agencies. But these are sporadic. A published, root-cause forensic chain after every major electrical fire will name the precise mechanism of failure rather than settling for “short circuit”.
Fire-NOC renewal should be tied to licence, not just self-certification. Sprinklers, even if they activate, are inadequate for heavy duty fires especially electrical. CO2 or clean-agent extinguishers specifically for ICUs and electrical panel rooms, not the ABC-type units reportedly used at Jhansi, would add to firefighting capabilities of hospitals. The new Health Ministry guidelines now specify this. For repurposed buildings of the kind seen in Kolkata’s hotel fires, a mandatory second stairway and an engineering reassessment of electrical load should be non-negotiable conditions of the change-of-use approval itself, not left to a subsequent, and largely theoretical, audit. For individual building owners, a power-quality audit and periodic thermography scan of the main panel, not just a load check, alongside ISI-marked wiring and modern combined circuit-breaker and earth-leakage devices replacing decade-old MCBs needs to be mandatory.

India’s anaemia burden is not in doubt. The fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) found that more than half of women and about two-thirds of young children are anaemic. In this context, double-fortified salt (DFS) — fortified with iodine and iron — is often proposed as a potentially transformative solution. However, the case for DFS rests on convenience: everyone consumes salt, so why not add iron to it? But convenience is not efficacy, and a policy that asks the country to continue consuming salt to deliver iron deserves closer scrutiny.
Iron fortification of salt is a vehicle that cuts against public health. Indians consume, by most estimates, roughly twice the five grams of salt a day recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). About one in three adults has hypertension, and India’s own non-communicable disease (NCD) action plan commits to a 30% relative reduction in salt intake.

Insurtech Go Digit reported a 31.1% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) to ₹142.4 Cr from ₹206.8 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. The insurtech major's profit also declined 62.4% sequentially from ₹378.61 Cr in the June quarter. The decline in profitability came despite a marginal increase in insurance revenue, which rose 1.7% to ₹2,720.5 Cr during the quarter from ₹2,674.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. Sequentially, insurance revenue increased 2.1% from ₹2,665.6 Cr. Segment-wise, Motor Third Party (TP) insurance remained Go Digit's largest business, contributing ₹1,066.1 Cr to insurance revenue in Q2 FY27, up 8.3% YoY. Motor Own Damage (OD) insurance revenue grew at a faster pace of 11.4% YoY to ₹640.64 Cr. The company's gross written premium for the quarter dipped by 3.6% YoY to ₹2,571 Cr while gross direct premium, dipped 1.2% to ₹2,351 Cr. However, the company's insurance service result, which reflects the profitability of its insurance operations before investment and other financial income, sunk 73.4% YoY to ₹43 Cr from ₹161.98 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The figure also fell 62.3% sequentially from ₹114 Cr. The deterioration in the insurance service result came as insurance service expenses increased 22.4% YoY to ₹2,607.73 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹2,130.85 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Incurred claims rose 9.2% to ₹1,968.03 Cr from ₹1,802.96 Cr, while employee benefit expenses increased 4.3% to ₹95.48 Cr. Commission expenses, on the other hand, declined 2.6% YoY to ₹781.88 Cr from ₹803.10 Cr. Other insurance service expenses increased 1.7% to ₹94.52 Cr. On the investment front, Go Digit reported a 20.6% YoY increase in investment income to ₹368.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹305.5 Cr in the year-ago period. However, investment income declined 39.2% sequentially from ₹606.47 Cr. The company's net finance result, which includes investment income and insurance finance income or expenses, increased 28.6% YoY to ₹196.94 Cr. Consequently, Go Digit's profit before tax (PBT) declined 31.2% YoY to ₹190.18 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹276.30 Cr in Q2 FY26. The figure was also down 62.4% sequentially from ₹505.96 Cr in Q1 FY27. Total tax expense stood at ₹47.79 Cr during the quarter, comprising current tax of ₹3.93 Cr and deferred tax of ₹43.86 Cr. This compared with a total tax expense of ₹69.51 Cr in Q2 FY26. For the first half of FY27 (H1 FY27), Go Digit reported a 3.2% YoY decline in net profit to ₹521 Cr from ₹538.23 Cr in H1 FY26. Insurance revenue increased 4.5% YoY to ₹5,386.09 Cr during the six-month period. Shares of Go Digit ended today’s trading session 1.05% higher at ₹260.30.

The Supreme Court has refused to lift the ban on the preparation, sale and storage of non-vegetarian food near Gujarat's Somnath Temple. The court said a balance needed to be maintained and declined to interfere with an interim order of the Gujarat High Court that keeps the restrictions in place. A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale heard a petition filed by restaurant owners challenging the restrictions imposed by the Gir Somnath district administration. During the November 6 hearing, the owners argued that the ban was affecting their businesses and livelihoods. The Supreme Court, however, refused to grant immediate relief and asked the Gujarat High Court to decide the pending appeals preferably within two months. "We need to maintain a balance. We don't say anything," the bench observed. The dispute began with a notification issued by the Gir Somnath District Magistrate on 10 August, 2026. It prohibits the preparation, sale and storage of non-vegetarian food, including meat, fish and eggs, at restaurants, hotels, shops and roadside stalls in specified areas around the Somnath Temple. The restrictions cover designated routes in Prabhas Patan and areas within 500 metres of the temple. Six restaurant owners challenged the notification in the Gujarat High Court. They argued that it affected their right to carry on a lawful business and threatened the livelihoods of people working at their establishments. Some of the restaurants had reportedly been operating in the area for 35 to 40 years. On October 30, a single-judge bench of the Gujarat High Court set aside the notification, holding that the restrictions went beyond the powers available under the Gujarat Police Act, 1951, and affected the owners' fundamental right to carry on a trade under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. However, the Gujarat government challenged the decision, following which a division bench stayed the single judge's order. This brought the restrictions back into force. During the hearing, senior advocate Huzefa Ahmadi, representing the restaurant owners, argued that the restrictions would affect businesses, particularly during the festive season. He also questioned the need to regulate people's food choices. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Gujarat government, defended the restrictions by referring to the religious significance of the Somnath Temple. He argued that restaurants could continue selling non-vegetarian food outside the restricted areas. The Supreme Court chose not to interfere with the High Court's interim arrangement. It did not deliver a final ruling on whether the ban was legally valid. The Supreme Court has asked the Gujarat High Court to decide the pending appeals preferably within two months. The matter is scheduled to come up before the High Court on 25 November, 2026. Until then, the restrictions will remain in force. Restaurant owners will have to wait for the High Court's decision before they can resume preparing and selling non-vegetarian food in the notified areas. The Supreme Court's refusal to lift the ban does not mean it has finally upheld the restrictions. Their legality is still being examined by the Gujarat High Court. ‘Apologise to Ram Bhakts first’: Yogi Adityanath ahead of Akhilesh Yadav's visit to Ayodhya
UP chief minister Yogi Adityanath said the same forces that had opposed the Ram temple movement were now trying to take political mileage from it.
Ahead of Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav's proposed visit to Ram temple in Ayodhya, chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday sought an apology from those who opened fire at karsevaks in 1990. Without addressing Yadav directly, Adityanath demanded that an apology be tendered to 'Ram Bhakts' before visiting Ayodhya.
The chief minister was referring to the firing that took place on October 30 and November 2 in 1990, during the government of Samajwadi Party patriarch Mulayam Singh Yadav. The SP has maintained that the then government had to act to maintain law and order.
ALSO READ: Akhilesh Yadav to visit Ayodhya Ram Temple with family for first time since consecration
Akhilesh Yadav is set to visit the Ram Temple in Ayodhya with his family on December 12. This will be his first visit to the temple since its consecration in January 2024.
Taking aim at Yadav, Adityanath said, "Tender an apology to Ram Bhakts first for firing on karsevaks before coming to Ayodhya." The chief minister was addressing seers at Ram Katha Park in Ayodhya at the 10th edition of Deepotsav.
"Those who got bullets fired on karsevaks, who shed the blood of Ram Bhakts on the streets of Ayodhya, are coming here to seek blessings. First, they should apologise to the karsevaks, to the seers, and to the people of Ayodhya," the chief minister said.
Adityanath also said Ayodhya does not belong to any one party or family. "Ayodhya is the land of Maryada Purushottam Shri Ram. Those who insulted the sentiments of crores of Ram Bhakts cannot wash away their sins merely by visiting the temple," he said.
The chief minister said the same forces that had opposed the Ram temple movement were now trying to take political mileage from the Ram temple. “Earlier, they used to say Ram did not exist. Today they are coming to Ayodhya. This is the victory of the faith of the people," he said.
The chief minister further claimed that Ayodhya has transformed from a neglected town into a global spiritual destination under the double-engine government. Adityanath credited 10 years of Deepotsav, the construction of the Ram temple and infrastructure development for restoring Ayodhya's ancient glory.
"For decades, Ayodhya was kept in darkness. Today, 30 lakh diyas (earthen lamps) are being lit here. This is not just Deepotsav, this is the celebration of the return of Ram Rajya," he said.
He also warned that those who play with the sentiments of Sanatan Dharma will not be forgiven by the people. "The people of Uttar Pradesh have seen who stood with Ram and who stood against Ram," he added.
The seers present on the occasion welcomed the chief minister's remarks with chants of 'Jai Shri Ram'.
Vice-President CP Radhakrishnan was the chief guest at the Deepotsav where governor Anandiben Patel was also present
Earlier in the day, Samajwadi Party leader Tej Narayan Pandey alias Pawan Pandey had said SP national president, along with his family, would visit the Hanuman Garhi temple and Ram temple in Ayodhya on December 12.
“Akhilesh ji is coming with his family for darshan of Hanuman ji and Ram Lalla. This is a matter of faith. The BJP should not do politics on faith," said Pandey, former SP MLA from Ayodhya Sadar assembly seat.

Injured Wainwright soldiers benefit from cutting-edge Canadian burn research
Dozens of Canadian soldiers remain hospitalized weeks after deadly fire
When news broke about the deadly training exercise at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent dozens more to hospital with severe burns, Véronique Moulin knew she had to help.
Her research group is nearing the end of clinical trials on a ground-breaking process to reconstruct and manufacture a permanent, human-like skin substitute by taking a toonie-sized biopsy of the patient's healthy skin and extracting the cells.
"If everybody can survive and [I] can help to treat some, I will be happy," said Moulin, head of the regenerative medicine division at the CHU de Québec-Université Laval research centre.
Unlike other lab-grown skin technologies, Moulin's method coaxes the patient's own cells to create a completely natural skin tissue containing both the dermis and epidermis layers.
Véronique Moulin, head of the regenerative medicine division at the CHU de Québec-Université Laval research centre, is seen placing cells into liquid nitrogen for long-term preservation. (CBC)
While it's not completely identical to the patient's skin because it doesn't have pigment and sweat glands, Moulin said it's useful in cases where the burns cover too much of the body to harvest skin for grafts.
Clinical data on 50 Canadian burn patients treated since 2005 shows that, unlike grafts from cadavers, their body doesn't reject the skin substitutes. The tissue grows, fuses and stays flexible, which means less scarring and reduces the need for repetitive surgeries as the patient heals, she said.
Lab now growing skin from wounded soldiers
As of Nov. 4, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) said 25 soldiers remain in hospital. Four have been moved to health-care facilities in British Columbia and Ontario to continue treatment closer to their home communities and families.
Skin biopsies from several of the hospitalized soldiers have been taken, and cells are now growing in Moulin's lab.
But it takes up to eight weeks to grow the first batch of skin substitute grafts from the initial biopsy — which is only enough to cover part of a torso — and her lab is already running at capacity.
"Usually we have three, sometimes four, but it's very rare that we have so many patients at the same time," Moulin said.
"But at least we can start, and after the first one, we can continue and send them every two weeks, we can send the same surface area."
Burn research advancing across the country
Moulin is just one of the Canadians on the front lines of research meant to help burn patients heal faster, with less pain and fewer scars.
Halfway across the country, in a University of Manitoba lab, an interdisciplinary team of researchers is also developing skin substitutes that mimic the features of human skin, including its layers, blood vessels, nerves and different skin colors.
A close-up of the skin substitute that an interdisciplinary team of researchers is developing in a University of Manitoba lab. It mimics the features of human skin, including its layers, blood vessels, nerves and different skin colors. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)
"Currently, we are working on one type of skin substitute that we are planning to test on animals. So that is the first step. You test on animals, then if it works, we will go to clinical trials," said Hamed Alizadeh Sardroud, a postdoctoral fellow and researcher in biomedical engineering and tissue engineering.
The lab is also exploring ways to engineer donor cells to be compatible with the recipient’s immune system and avoid rejection. They're using a 3D printer to create patches that would be used for burn wounds.
"Those cells are live and they can grow. And when you implant it, transplant [it] on the skin, they will just regenerate," Alizadeh Sardroud said.
Just a few doors down, one of his colleagues is testing a biosensor that can detect bacteria causing infection in a wound.

"You can see it's yellow and then as soon as it's in contact with bacteria and their enzymes, it becomes green," said Farinaz Jonidi Shariatzadeh, a post-doctoral researcher, as she did a demonstration.
"It's like an early warning system that shows you that the bacteria are present in the wound and … infection is going to start soon."
The postage stamp-sized nanofibre membrane can be placed in the top layer of a dressing so it doesn't have to be removed to keep an eye on the wound. A patient can monitor it at home, and contact their doctor when they see the colour change.
It has already been licensed by an American medical technology company that has begun clinical trials, Jonidi Shariatzadeh said.
"Compared to what's commercially available, it is groundbreaking because none of the available biosensors can actually show the colour change in real time that can be observed with the naked eye."
The University of Manitoba team is also developing a smart dressing that will release an antibiotic as soon as an infection is detected, said Dr. Sarvesh Logsetty, a burn surgeon and director of the Manitoba Firefighters Burn Unit at Winnipeg's Health Sciences Centre.
"The science fiction of yesterday is the treatment of today," he said.
"The goal is to decrease the pain and suffering and improve the quality of life and the quantity of life of individuals that have burns and also injuries of any kind."
Dr. Sarvesh Logsetty, a burn surgeon and director of the Manitoba Firefighters Burn Unit at Winnipeg's Health Sciences Centre, leads a multi-disciplinary team of researchers that's become a hub for clinical innovation. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)
'The journey is a long and painful one'
It's welcome news for Tyler Pelke, who survived third-degree burns over 25 per cent of his body more than 35 years ago.
"The journey is a long and painful one," said Pelke, a former firefighter who is now a CAF reservist and head of Alberta's Emergency Health Services. He spoke as a burn survivor, not on behalf of those organizations.
"So yeah, some pretty amazing advancements, but it's a pretty impactful and horrific injury, especially when a large burn."
Pelke said he was lucky because doctors were able to take skin grafts from his own legs, but he dreaded the bandage removals and dressing changes.
Anything that can help ease the physical and mental suffering for burn patients is welcome, he said.
