A major California strawberry grower is cutting ties with six farms and laying off more than 500 workers as soaring water and labor costs squeeze the industry.
SoCal Berry Growers, a supplier for strawberry giant Driscoll’s, plans to permanently close its operations at six locations in Ventura County, according to a letter sent to Oxnard city officials Saturday. The closures, which will affect farms along California's Central Coast, and the resulting job cuts, are expected to take place between January 11 and January 25, 2027.
“As a result and based on currently available information, all the Company’s operations will cease and approximately 572 employees may suffer a permanent employment loss,” the letter states.
Driscoll’s, the world’s largest berry producer, sources its strawberries from independent family farms in growing regions including Florida, Mexico and Virginia, as well as other locations around the world, according to its website.
“We are deeply saddened by the news that SoCal Berry Growers plans to close its farms in Ventura County this January,” a Driscoll’s spokesperson told The Independent Saturday. “It’s a difficult day for California agriculture when a family farming business that has spent decades supporting livelihoods and contributing to the agricultural heritage of the Central Coast decides to close its farms.”
“These closures will affect far more than the farms themselves. Our thoughts are with the farmworkers whose livelihoods will be affected, their families, and the broader communities that have depended on these operations and taken pride in their contributions for generations,” the Driscoll’s spokesperson added.
The news comes as California farmers grapple with soaring production costs, including water, fuel, fertilizer and labor.
“Water quadrupled. Labor nearly doubled,” a recent study by the Farm Bureau of Ventura County titled "The $2.4 Billion Crisis,” states, pointing to how much more expensive it has become to keep farms running.
Strawberries were the county's top cash crop in 2025, generating approximately $807.8 million in revenue. But it cost farmers more than $815 million to produce them, according to Louise Lampara, CEO of the Farm Bureau of Ventura County.
“They didn’t make a penny and paid $8.1 million out of pocket,” Lampara told SFGATE.
Irrigation water prices jumped from $22.10 per acre-inch in 2007 to $88.83 in 2025, the report found. Meanwhile, hourly labor costs increased from $13 in 2020 to $25.16 in 2025. “It's an industry in crisis,” Lampara said.
The rising expenses are making it increasingly difficult for American growers to compete with imported produce, Lampara added. Farmers have little control over what grocery stores and other buyers pay for their crops, even as the cost of producing them continues to climb.
"We have such pressure right now from importers," she said, pointing to record volumes of imported strawberries, avocados and lemons.
Lampara said that overseas growers may operate under different regulatory requirements, making it harder for California farms to compete on price.
SoCal Berry Growers ceasing operations with the six farms comes months after the company’s employees voted to unionize with the United Farm Workers of America in July. The company challenged the unionization effort, alleging misconduct, but the California Agricultural Labor Relations Board upheld the election in August, ruling that it had not been conducted improperly.
"SoCal management is now saying it will shut down, in what we believe is a clear violation of the law to avoid their legal and moral obligations to the workers who pick the strawberries," United Farm Workers Vice President Roman Pinal said in a statement to the Ventura County Star this week.
The union said it plans to pursue legal options to protect its members.
The Independent has contacted SoCal Berry Growers and the United Farm Workers of America for comment.

Erstwhile real money gaming (RMG) giant Dream11’s cofounder and CEO Harsh Jain has hinted at plans to launch a revamped version of the platform by 2026-end. In a post on social media platform X, Jain said that the “brand new Dream11” would be built by sports fans and for sports fans. He did not disclose the upcoming platform’s features, commercial model or a specific launch date. “A brand new Dream11 is launching (at the) end of Dec - by sports fans, for sports fans. Stay tuned…,” said Jain in his post. The move signals Dream11’s next phase of evolution after the ban on online real-money gaming last year disrupted the platform’s paid fantasy sports business. While the teaser points to a product overhaul, it remains unclear how substantially the new offering will differ from its existing services. This comes more than a year after the Parliament passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Bill, 2025, which prohibited online real money games and restricted their promotion and advertising. Following the legislation, Dream11 discontinued paid contests and pivoted to a watch-along platform where users can follow gameplays of prominent content creators. It has also been exploring alternative ways to engage sports fans. Last year, parent Dream Sports forayed into the wealth tech space under Dream Money and began offering mutual funds, digital gold, fixed deposits, and loans. It later also forayed into stockbroking with DreamStreet and forayed into the SaaS space with Dream Horizon. However, it has been rethinking many of its newer bets. The startup shut down Dream Money in June this year. Dream Sports also quietly shut FanCode’s sports merchandise business earlier this year amid persistent issues with commercial viability. It also shut down its AI-powered sports performance analytics app Dream Play in June this year. Nevertheless, the startup’s portfolio still remains substantial. FanCode continues to operate as a sports streaming platform, while DreamCricket represents its push into AAA gaming. It also has its investment platform DreamStreet. Beyond the business challenges, Dream Sports is also facing GST dues of more than ₹20,000 Cr. In a blow to the company, the Supreme Court (SC), earlier this year, also upheld the tax authorities’ move to impose a 28% retrospective GST on real money online gaming companies over the full face value of bets placed through their platforms.

The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
- Published
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.
This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.
But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia.
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago.
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says.
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience.
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting.
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.
The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.
Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.
But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.
Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline.
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness.
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas.
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia.
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.
For Sucdi, that potential is personal.
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu.
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.

Social media platform X has told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices purportedly issued by the Delhi Police against digital rights organisations Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC.in) were fake. According to a post by IFF today, X said an internal investigation found the purported police communications to be fake and that it had filed a complaint with law enforcement authorities. X’s counsel told the court that an imposter had submitted the requests in the Delhi Police’s name. “X stated that it is not likely to take any action at this stage,” IFF’s post added. The court recorded X’s statement and disposed of the organisations’ petitions, granting them liberty to approach it again if the platform takes action against their accounts. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, representing both organisations, placed X’s transparency reports and a legal notice purportedly sent on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) on record. IFF said it had written to the RSS seeking confirmation of the legal notice’s authenticity but received no response. Separately, SFLC.in said an email seeking verification of the takedown requests had bounced back from the Delhi Police address mentioned in the communication. How The Dispute Began IFF said X forwarded two ‘Illegal Content Reports’ to it on Tuesday (November 3), submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police. The first, dated October 31, sought the removal of a post IFF published on October 30 and another by SFLC.in. The second, dated Monday (November 2), sought the removal of 37 posts and the withholding of the accounts of IFF, SFLC.in, and GeoBlockedIndia. The reports alleged that the posts defamed the RSS under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The posts reproduced and commented on a legal notice the organisations said they had received in the RSS’s name. IFF contested the requests, arguing that its posts were protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. It also questioned their legal basis, saying the reports cited no complaint, FIR, Magistrate’s order, or court order. Through its counsel, IFF subsequently served a legal notice to the Delhi Police, with a copy to X, seeking withdrawal of the reports and details of the authority under which they had been submitted. It also asked X not to act on the requests pending their withdrawal or adjudication. IFF approached the Delhi High Court after receiving no official withdrawal or clarification from the Delhi Police. Platform Accountability Under Scrutiny The dispute comes amid a wider debate over content takedowns, transparency, and platforms’ responsibilities when responding to government requests. In July, former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey claimed that the Indian government had directed GitHub to remove three URLs linked to bitchat, an open-source messaging app that enables peer-to-peer communication without internet connectivity or centralised servers. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre’s (I4C) reported directive gave GitHub three hours to remove or disable access to the URLs. These covered the project’s main source code repository, Android repository, and Android releases page. The agency cited concerns over anonymous communication and difficulties in lawful interception and investigations. Meanwhile, MeitY is reportedly exploring withdrawing safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000, from social media platforms. The provision limits intermediaries’ liability for third-party content, subject to prescribed conditions.

European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, with the FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, down 1.5%, or 166 points, at the start of trading to 10,615.
The pharmaceuticals company AstraZeneca opened down 2.8%, the biggest faller on the FTSE 100. Other big fallers included IAG, the owner of British Airways and Iberia, which fell 1.5%, after it missed profit forecasts in a trading update, and the miners Antofagasta and Anglo American.
Germany’s Dax index opened down 1.5%, France’s Cac 40 has dropped by 1.2% and Spain’s Ibex is down 1.1%.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.
“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.
Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8% in early trading.
Despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.
The Nasdaq Composite index, for example, is still up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

One child dead, 269 people treated for firecracker-related burn injuries across Tamil Nadu during Diwali
As per the official bulletin, the state 108 emergency ambulance network received 16,079 calls between 7 am on November 7 and 7 am on November 8.
One child succumbed to burn injuries, and 269 people were treated for firecracker-related burns across Tamil Nadu during the Deepavali festivities, according to official data tracking emergencies over a 24-hour window.
As per the official bulletin, the state 108 emergency ambulance network received 16,079 calls between 7 am on November 7 and 7 am on November 8.
Of the total distress calls, 2,475 were related to accidents, 396 for minor injuries, and 98 specifically for burn injuries.
Deep Dive
To manage the festive emergency load, 1,283 ambulances were deployed on active duty across the state.
Statewide government hospitals recorded a total of 1,387 inpatient admissions during this period. The admissions included 956 for accidents, 321 for minor injuries or assaults, and 110 for burn injuries. One burn-related fatality was recorded, involving a child under the age of 15.
No adult deaths due to burns were reported during this timeframe.
Demographic data for burn injuries shows that men formed the largest group of victims, with 92 treated as outpatients and 76 admitted as inpatients.
Children under 15 were the second most affected demographic, with 48 outpatients and 17 inpatient admissions. Adult women accounted for 19 outpatients and 17 inpatients. In total, hospitals saw 159 outpatients and 110 inpatients for burn cases.
The Thanjavur Government Medical College Hospital recorded the highest patient volume for burns, accidents, and minor injuries, treating 36 outpatients and admitting 87 inpatients.
Other major medical centres handling the bulk of the emergency caseload included the Madurai Government Medical College Hospital with six outpatients and 84 inpatients, and the Chengalpattu Government Medical College Hospital with 85 inpatients.
The Periyar Nagar Government Hospital recorded one outpatient and 64 inpatients, while the Thoothukudi Government Medical College Hospital treated 46 outpatients and 13 inpatients.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh visited members of the armed forces at multiple locations in West Bengal on Saturday (November 7, 2026) and highlighted a changing nature of warfare while describing the northeast as India’s “first edge” rather than its “last edge”.
The security landscape around the country has become increasingly complex and the armed forces must maintain the highest level of operational readiness to effectively counter any threats to national security, he told personnel at the Bagdogra Air Force station. Delivering his message on the eve of Deepavali from the key airbase near the frontier with China in the Eastern sector, Mr. Singh, without naming any country, said the adversary now avoids direct confrontation but seeks to exploit certain "vulnerabilities".
He called upon the armed forces to keep special focus on strengthening domain awareness, cyber resilience, and information integrity to effectively counter emerging security threats, according to the Defence Ministry. Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, Air Officer Commanding, Air Force Station, Bagdogra Air Commodore Manish Sharma, and other senior officials of the IAF were present on the occasion.
Describing Bagdogra as a strategically important region and a crucial link in India's security framework, Mr. Singh commended the courage and dedication of the defence personnel towards safeguarding national interests. He stated that the Air Force personnel deployed in the region serve as a robust shield for the security of the eastern sector, and their preparedness is fundamental to maintaining stability in the region.
The Defence Minister later reviewed the operational preparedness of the Army’s Trishakti Corps at Sukna, with a focus on infrastructure development along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), deployment of advanced military equipment, and adoption of emerging technologies to enhance combat effectiveness.
Mr. Singh expressed satisfaction with the operational preparedness of the corps and appreciated its contribution to infrastructure development and community welfare initiatives in border areas aimed at strengthening ties with local communities.
Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth, Eastern Army Commander Lt. Gen. VMB Krishnan and Trishakti Corps Commander Lt. Gen. Man Raj Singh Mann were present during the review.
Addressing personnel during a ‘barakhana’ on the eve of Deepawali, Mr. Singh commended their courage, professionalism, and dedication in safeguarding the country’s frontiers under challenging operational conditions.
Highlighting the changing nature of warfare, he said security challenges were no longer confined to conventional exchanges of gunfire and artillery but increasingly involved hybrid warfare, proxy wars, cyberattacks, drone incursions, and information warfare.
He cautioned that adversaries were using social media to spread rumours, deploying drones to monitor sensitive locations, and attempting to compromise military systems through cyberattacks. He exhorted personnel to remain vigilant and prepared to tackle emerging threats across all domains.
Describing Sukna as a critical logistics hub for eastern India, Mr. Singh said its geographical sensitivity necessitated round-the-clock operational readiness. He highlighted its importance in the movement of supplies, weapons, food, medical provisions, and personnel to forward locations.
The Defence Minister said budgetary allocations for roads, tunnels, border infrastructure, and modern equipment had been increased as the country progressed towards self-reliance in defence production.
He noted that Indian start-ups and industries were manufacturing drones and anti-drone systems, while the armed forces were increasingly embracing emerging technologies and training in drone operations and cybersecurity.
Mr. Singh also stressed the importance of soldiers’ mental health and emotional well-being, urging them to communicate openly with their colleagues and seek support to deal with stress arising from demanding duties and separation from families.
Mr. Singh expressed gratitude to the families of the personnel for their sacrifices and contributions, and emphasised that while the soldiers remain committed to safeguarding the borders, the nation will always stand by their families and ensure their well-being.

Manchester City defender Marc Guehi will undergo a scan on a hip complaint on Sunday to determine whether he can report for England duty this week.
The 26-year-old was substituted at half-time of City's loss at Nottingham Forest on Saturday and manager Enzo Maresca revealed afterwards the centre-back had requested to come off because of the injury.

Guehi started in all but one of England's games at the World Cup and all four of the team's Nations League fixtures in September and October.
England face Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November, before travelling to Madrid to face World Cup winners Spain on Saturday, 15 November.

The Japan Coast Guard said that the “Godzilla Megamullion,” a massive seafloor formation discovered during its 2001 continental shelf survey, has been selected for the International Union of Geological Sciences’ list of 100 Geological Heritage Sites.
The JCG announced the designation of the megamullion, located southeast of the remote Tokyo-administered Pacific island of Okinotorishima, on Friday.
A megamullion is a dome-shaped seafloor structure formed when mantle rocks are exposed on the ocean floor through fault activity associated with seafloor spreading.
Located on the Philippine Sea plate, the Godzilla Megamullion measures about 125 kilometers in length and 55 kilometers in width, making it roughly 10 times larger than a typical megamullion. It is believed to be the largest such formation ever discovered.
The megamullion was named after the giant monster Godzilla because of its enormous size and was registered internationally under that name in 2021.
Studies of the Godzilla Megamullion conducted by an international team led by Japanese scientists have produced important findings on mantle structure and the processes involved in plate formation. The site was recognized as a globally significant geological reference point for scientific research, according to the JCG.
This marks the third round of selections for the IUGS geological heritage list. Other Japanese sites previously chosen include the Nojima Fault in Hyogo Prefecture, which triggered the 1995 Great Hanshin Earthquake.

TMC Chief Mamata Banerjee addresses a press conference, in New Delhi on Thursday. TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee also present.
NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee joined Trinamool Congress (TMC) national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee in a protest in Kolkata’s Kalighat. She accused the BJP of hooliganism and alleged a breakdown of law and order in the state.She said she had written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla over the incident.The protest followed an overnight confrontation outside Abhishek’s residence, where clashes reportedly broke out between TMC workers and BJP supporters around 2am. Abhishek alleged that BJP workers attacked his residence after conducting reconnaissance of the premises for two days.He later claimed that the confrontation continued until 7am, accused police personnel of failing to stop the attackers and alleged that some officers were assaulted while trying to intervene. Several people were reportedly injured, while police imposed prohibitory restrictions around the residence and detained some people.BJP rejected the allegations, blaming the confrontation on a birthday gathering organised on a public road.
The incident has since triggered a political war of words, with leaders from both sides trading accusations over the violence and the state’s law-and-order situation.
Mamata joins protest, writes to Lok Sabha Speaker
Mamata reached Abhishek’s Kalighat residence later on Saturday and joined the protest. She accused the BJP of creating disturbances in the area and alleged that a group of people had attacked a Kali Puja celebration.She also raised concerns over the arrangements for traditional pujas ahead of Kali Puja and Diwali. Mamata claimed that permissions for some long-standing puja celebrations had been revoked while a new puja was allowed to be organised on the main road.“Tomorrow is Kali Puja and Diwali. Last night, at 2:00 AM, an attack was carried out at Abhishek Banerjee’s house. This is our locality, a route through which many processions of Goddess Kali pass. Why are you causing such a disturbance? You have revoked permissions for our traditional, long-standing pujas while allowing new ones to be held instead,” she said.She alleged that the new puja arrangement had blocked access to their own celebration and accused the authorities of high-handedness. She also said she had written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla over what she described as a breakdown of law and order.
What happened outside Abhishek’s residence
The confrontation reportedly began around 2am on Saturday, when BJP supporters allegedly raised slogans calling Abhishek a “chor” (thief) outside his Kalighat residence. TMC workers had gathered in the area. According to reports, the slogans were followed by counter-sloganeering, arguments and a clash between the two groups.The confrontation involved allegations of assault, stone-pelting and vandalism. Abhishek, who came out of his residence during the night to meet injured party workers, alleged that the attackers used wooden rods fitted with nails and vandalised a local TMC office.Police and party accounts put the duration of the initial clashes between 2am and 3.30am. Abhishek, however, later claimed that the confrontation continued until 7am.He alleged that four to five of his supporters sustained serious injuries. One of them, he said, required plastic surgery, while another suffered a fracture. Police sources said several people from both sides were injured. A separate report put the number of injured at eight, including three who were seriously hurt.
The incident came hours after Abhishek raised allegations of surveillance outside his office and residence. On Friday, he claimed that unidentified individuals had been conducting reconnaissance of the premises for two consecutive days.He said the individuals claimed to be police personnel when confronted. Abhishek questioned why the state police were allegedly keeping watch on an elected MP’s residence and demanded an inquiry into who had authorised the surveillance and for what purpose.He tagged Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, Kolkata Police, West Bengal Police and the Union Home Ministry in his post, seeking an investigation to establish the identities of those involved.Hours later, he alleged that his residence had been attacked by BJP workers. Sharing a video purportedly showing the incident, he wrote on X: “After two days of continuous recce, this is how BJP hooligans attacked my house at 2 am today. Watch the footage and see for yourself. If this is what can happen to an elected Member of Parliament, imagine the plight of the common man in WB.”PTI said it could not independently verify the authenticity of the video.Abhishek described the incident as the seventh attempt on his life in six months. He also accused the police and the judiciary of failing to act against those allegedly targeting him.
Abhishek accuses police of inaction
Escalating his criticism after the confrontation, Abhishek alleged that police personnel present at the spot failed to prevent the violence. He claimed that some officers remained silent spectators, while others who tried to intervene were assaulted.“The attack continued till 7 am. Although the police were there, some of them acted as silent spectators, and others who tried to stop the BJP goons were beaten up by them,” he said.“The police who can’t protect themselves cannot protect the common people anyway,” he added.Abhishek also shared a video that he claimed showed a BJP worker slapping a plainclothes police officer. The TMC accused the BJP workers of assaulting police personnel and questioned why those involved had not been arrested.He said the incident showed how vulnerable ordinary people could be if police personnel themselves were unable to protect themselves. He also cited figures on alleged crimes in the state between May and October, claiming that around 2,500 rapes, 600 murders and more than 32,000 crimes had taken place during the period. These figures were claims made by Abhishek.
What police said
The Kolkata Police said a commotion had broken out between supporters of the two parties and that a police team intervened. An investigation was underway, a police officer said, without providing further details.Prohibitory orders were imposed around Abhishek’s residence, barring gatherings of more than five people. A large police contingent was deployed in the area and several people were detained in connection with the incident.Police sources said people from both sides had been injured and the situation remained tense through the night.
BJP rejects charges, blames birthday gathering
The BJP rejected Abhishek’s allegations and accused TMC supporters of provoking the confrontation by holding a birthday celebration on a public road.West Bengal minister Dilip Ghosh dismissed the claims as an attempt to mislead people. He questioned why anyone would want to kill Abhishek and said a disturbance was bound to follow if a public space was occupied for a celebration.Union minister Sukanta Majumdar also criticised the decision to hold the gathering on a footpath. He said there was no objection to celebrating a birthday but argued that it should have been organised inside a residence or at a venue rather than on a public road.“If you block public roads in front of your house and hold a birthday celebration on the footpath, naturally people will get angry. The public is already upset with you; on top of that, if you behave like this, confrontations are bound to happen,” he said.Majumdar rejected allegations of BJP involvement and said the party did not want to “dirty its hands with small fry”.BJP leader Ritabrata Bandopadhyay also disputed the TMC’s account. He claimed local residents were angry because the gathering had obstructed roads used for transporting idols ahead of Kali Puja. He said the birthday celebration should have been held inside Abhishek’s residence.
TMC leaders allege planned attack; opposition voices concern
TMC MP Sougata Roy accused BJP workers of conducting a prior reconnaissance of the area before attacking Abhishek’s residence. He alleged that police personnel were present but failed to control the situation, and that some officers were also assaulted.Roy described the incident as an attempt to intimidate people and suppress the opposition.TMC MP Kirti Azad alleged that men armed with stones and sticks attacked the premises for 30 to 45 minutes. He claimed CCTV footage was available and accused the police of escorting those involved instead of arresting them.TMC MLA Kunal Ghosh also alleged that party workers were being targeted and questioned the police action following the incident. Party spokesperson and advocate Arka Nag described the episode as an alleged attempt to murder Abhishek and his supporters. He said the party had lodged a police complaint and questioned the imposition of prohibitory restrictions, arguing that they could affect the movement of Kali idols during the festival.The incident also drew reactions from leaders outside the two parties. Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury said nobody should be denied the right to celebrate a birthday. Congress leader Udit Raj described the incident as an unconstitutional act and an attack on democracy.
Rashtriya Janata Dal MP Sudhakar Singh demanded President’s Rule in West Bengal, alleging that the state government had failed to maintain law and order.
Political tensions in Bengal
The confrontation comes against the backdrop of the BJP’s victory in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections, which ended the TMC’s 15-year rule. The BJP is now in government, while the TMC, led by former chief minister Mamata Banerjee, is in opposition.The two parties have since traded allegations of violence and intimidation. The latest clash in Kalighat has added to the political tension in the state, with both sides blaming the other for the confrontation.With Kali Puja and Diwali approaching, the incident has also brought the arrangements for celebrations in Kalighat into the political dispute. Further details of the investigation and action against those detained are awaited.

How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats
Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.
It's a stunning shift from 2024, when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.
But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.
How young voters powered Democrats to victory
Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.
However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference, is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.
The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points, however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.
Loading...
Explaining the massive shift from 2024
When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.
But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.
Loading...
Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18-29 year olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.
The young voters Trump lost
Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.
Democrats made gains with some young voters that backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees.
Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.
How the election results broke down by age
Loading...
The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.
"The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."
Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll, notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.
"I also think we shouldn't over read what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."
By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate, a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.
"Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.
"They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

As various factions try to make the case about what won the midterms — moderation or progressivism, populism or the establishment — perhaps the easiest and most universal way to describe 2026 was as a contest between decency and cruelty.
Maybe Americans don’t like cruelty after all
For years, the MAGA movement embraced cruelty, with not much of a downside among voters. This week, judgment came.
For nearly a decade, bullying, scape-goating, and just plain meanness have been the dominant tone of Republican politics. From Donald Trump relentlessly picking on minority groups in the 2016 campaign, through family separations in 2018 — all while demeaning political rivals and journalists and anyone who criticized him — a generation of Republican politicians have seen the president reach new levels of nastiness in politics and be rewarded for it. Other candidates picked up on it, often attempting their own imitations: Vice President JD Vance mocked “childless cat ladies” in 2021, while other Republicans joked about political violence against Democrats or critics, their physical appearances, or their ethnicities.
And yet somehow, in the 2026 midterm campaigns, the MAGA right went even harder on cruelty up and down the ballot. Pivotal campaign moments, particularly in the closing weeks of the cycle, weren’t just about bare-knuckle politics and nasty campaigning, but actually punching down at the weak and vulnerable. Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy trotted out his opponent’s estranged mother to suggest the candidate was lying about childhood abuse. Trump and GOP Sen. Tim Scott used a transphobic slur to to mock a candidate while campaigning for Darline Graham. Michigan GOP senatorial candidate Mike Rogers fanned the flames of Islamophobia, accusing his opponent of “pledging” his support to Islamist extremism, something other Republicans echoed. And in Texas, a statewide candidate doubled down on racist anti-Indian-American tweets.
In 2018, the writer Adam Serwer coined the phrase, and concept, that “the cruelty is the point” — that the easiest way to understand the MAGA movement was as a desire to inflict pain and suffering on marginalized people, specific minorities, and political opponents through political power. Cruelty wasn’t incidental; it was intentional.
For Republican candidates and campaigners this cycle, cruelty became almost a central campaign tactic. Many of them struggled to mount a serious policy case, and found themselves stuck with a historically unpopular president as party leader, so they fell back on the tried-and-true maneuver of beating up on the weak, hoping it would work as well as it seemed to throughout the Trump era.
Yet on Tuesday night, voters delivered a verdict: They were fed up with that cruelty in both the administration and Republican campaigns. Instead, decency — or, at least, voters’ impression of it — won.
Even some conservatives, as they try to sort through the wreckage and blame game post-Election Day, made that case. The Christian broadcaster Erick Erickson noted that in addition to the Iran war and affordability crisis, Republicans lost because of “the impression of cruelty. The overly aggressive deportations. The accidental arrests of American citizens who were Hispanic. The arrogance.”
And, of course, many Democrats agreed, too.
“The American people were loud and clear [Tuesday] night that they want to like their neighbor, that their neighbor is not the enemy from within, and even if they disagree politically with their neighbor, they want them to do well and they want their kids to do very well,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who led the party’s efforts to elect Democratic governors around the country, told me. “People [Tuesday] night showed us that they want decency in the White House and they want decency in Congress.”
All the Republicans above lost their races. The set of people who won — and especially those who flipped seats from red to blue – noticeably embraced a more compassionate tone of politics.
Republicans centered cruelty; Democratic candidates chose decency and won
It’s hard to summarize just how nasty the 2026 GOP campaign strategy was. Hate, racism, and xenophobia were the go-to tools used on the right this cycle — on top of a year of hardline immigration policies and spending cuts pushed by the Trump administration. And it all came up short, Joe Walsh, the former GOP member of Congress and current anti-Trump activist, told me.
“Republicans tried to win again this year by being as cruel and fearful and divisive as they could. That’s generally worked in the past, but there were extenuating circumstances this year,” Walsh said. “People [on the trail] would tell me, ‘This is not the kind of country we are. This is not who we are.’” They were referring, he said, to masked ICE agents, the targeting of Black and brown people, and talk of white Christian nationalism.
“There was something more profound at stake here,” Walsh continued. “And I think it was the American people recoiling against the cruelty they’ve seen.”
It was all a sharp contrast to the way Democrats talked and the policies they supported on the trail. Take Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico’s words in his Tuesday night victory speech:
We didn’t win by alienating our neighbors, or by shaming our neighbors, or by ridiculing our neighbors. We embodied a new kind of politics. A politics rooted in a deep love — for our state, for our country, and for all of our neighbors. My faith teaches me that love is the strongest force in the universe…love requires that we stand between the bullies and the bullied. Love requires that we look evil in the eye and not blink.
Beshear told me that beyond concerns about gas prices, the Iran war, and tariffs, voters’ frustrations reflected a rejection of the fear and divisiveness that Trump embodies. He said he saw this rejection of cruelty while stumping for candidates in red states, and he saw the opposite coming from the Democratic candidates who won.
“Everywhere I traveled, our gubernatorial candidates were talking about being a good neighbor,” he said. “[Iowa Gov.-elect] Rob Sand talked about it at every one of his town halls, and you could see people nodding about it. [Ohio Gov.-elect] Amy Acton talked about it in each of her speeches. People are craving decency, especially given the cruelty that this president governs with.”
This contrast was apparent in some data and focus group research, too. In polling conducted by The Argument before the election, Democrats had a 20-point advantage when voters were asked which party they thought was more “compassionate,” a 12-point lead when they were asked which party “cared” for voters, and a 10-point lead when they were asked which party was more moderate.
“The party of compassion won,” the writer Jerusalem Demsas wrote for The Argument. Republicans just couldn’t shake the association, their polling showed, with “words like ‘bold,’ “strong,’ and ‘extreme.’”
And in Ohio, perhaps the most obvious example of cruelty becoming the closing message of a Republican campaign, focus groups conducted by the political strategist Sarah Longwell for The Bulwark before the election showed how quickly the infamous ad became associated with the Republican brand. Longwell wrote about the session:
The first thing to note is that everyone in the group had heard about Ramaswamy’s ad already. The second thing to note is that several of the Ramaswamy-curious voters in the group said it was pushing them toward either supporting a third-party candidate or sitting out the election altogether. The fact that everyone had heard of or seen the ad and the universal revulsion to it suggest that this could be an all-time backfire for Ramaswamy — and it raises the possibility that Trump and Vance will also suffer politically for rushing to defend it.
In follow-up focus group conversations on Wednesday, the day after the election, voters told Longwell they wanted a hard break from this era of politics.
This rejection of cruelty was also most evident in backlash to the Trump administration’s immigration policies — in places that saw ICE raids or which saw stricter enforcement in heavily Hispanic areas of Florida, Kansas, and Texas, voters swung hard against the GOP.
“These are voters who were very supportive of securing the border, very supportive of Border Patrol, which is a huge employer down there,” the Democratic strategist Lis Smith told me. “But the cruelty of what ICE was doing, tearing apart families and communities was just a bridge too far. That’s in part why you saw a big backlash in the Hispanic community because there’s a huge element of racial profiling with it.”
In contrast, the most successful candidates this week were not the ones that tried to match Republicans by being more combative or extreme. They were those who embraced themes of decency and compassion. They seemed to offer an antidote, Smith said.
“There’s sometimes this idea, a theory in the Democratic Party, that to beat Trump, you need to be Trump,” Smith said. “And so you see Democrats going out on Twitter and calling Republicans cucks and engaging in the same sort of race to the bottom of name-calling that Trump and the Republicans do. But if you look at the top Democratic over-performers, people like [Sen.-elect] Adam Hamilton in Kansas, like Rob Sand in Iowa, like James Talarico in Texas, these were people who were going out and preaching love.” Smith pointed to a Talarico interview where he called his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a “child of God.”
“Yes, Americans were fed up with corruption, et cetera, but you can’t watch those candidates and say the defining feature of these campaigns was anger.”
— Michael Wear, Center for Christianity and Public Life who once advised the Obama administration on faith outreach
A kind of broad-based compassion was specifically a hallmark of some more explicitly religious campaigns, said Michael Wear, the head of the Center for Christianity and Public Life who once advised the Obama administration on faith outreach. He pointed to Talarico in Texas, and Hamilton, a megachurch pastor poised to become Kansas’s first Democratic senator in nearly a century.
To Wear, that should offer some lessons for other Democrats as they think about preserving and expanding the new national coalition they built as they move into the 2028 election cycle.
“Yes, Americans were fed up with corruption, et cetera, but you can’t watch those candidates and say the defining feature of these campaigns was anger,” Wear said.
And that’s also how they talked about voters themselves, Smith said: trying to expand the tent by welcoming Republicans or even former Trump supporters who were fed up with this style of politics.
“They explicitly asked for their vote and said that, ‘We don’t judge you. I’m not going to judge you for how you voted in the past. And you’re welcome in my tent, you’re welcome in my coalition,’” Smith said. “That’s a different tone than you hear from a lot of Democrats.”
Smith said it was a risk — the most liberal of the Democratic base might enjoy “the sick warfare,” she said, “but most other people are really exhausted by it. … They’re really exhausted by just seeing neighbors turn against neighbors and find this approach of turning the temperature down refreshing.”

In early November, an image circulated online purportedly showing Pope Leo XIV meeting with American folk singer Bob Dylan, 85, who was dressed in a black hoodie.
"What's the deal with the hoodie? Why is he wearing it all the time?" one Reddit user commented on a post. Other people wanted to know if the image was created using generative AI.
The image was authentic. The Vatican's official social media pages posted the image (archived) of the two men, who both hail from the American Midwest.
"Pope Leo XIV met with American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in a private audience on Wednesday, November 4," the photo's caption read.
Writer Salvatore Cernuzio contributed a story (archived) to the Vatican News about the meeting that read, in part:
The meeting between Pope Leo and Dylan—who wore a black hooded sweatshirt—was brief, consisting of greetings and a few lighthearted exchanges. The Holy Father presented the singer with a rosary, while Dylan reciprocated with a book: Chronicles: Volume One, his autobiography, which has been published in the United States and other countries around the world.
It wasn't the first time Dylan made a public appearance in a black hoodie, nor was it his first time meeting a pope (he also met Pope John Paul II in 1997). Though the singer was born and raised Jewish, he converted to Christianity in the 1970s.
Antonio Spadaro, an Italian priest who arranges meetings with public figures for the pope, formerly known as Robert Prevost, wrote in an Instagram post: "Born in Chicago in 1955, Prevost grew up with the American music of the era" (translation via a native speaker).
For further reading about Leo, we've previously verified an image showing him wearing Nike sneakers with his vestments.

Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.
The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.
The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.
The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.
"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.
"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.
On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.
In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".
He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.
He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.
Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.
On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.
The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

Samsung One UI 9.5 beta may be coming soon: Here's how to sign up for the program
Beta firmware for the Galaxy S26 Ultra is already on Samsung's servers.
If you've been aggressively refreshing the Samsung Members app on your Galaxy S26 in the hope of seeing the One UI 9.5 beta, you're wasting your time — although you won't have to wait much longer. A One UI 9.5 beta build for the Galaxy S26 Ultra has appeared on Samsung's Korean and US update servers, which is typically the last step before the company opens registrations.
Samsung hasn't announced the beta or a launch date, but its last point-five update, One UI 8.5, opened to testers on December 8 2025. One UI 9.5 is expected to launch with the Galaxy S27 early in 2027, so a beta release is definitely imminent. If you're interested, signing up will work the same way as last time: register in Samsung Members, then download the beta from your phone's settings once it's available. That is, provided you live in one of six countries — Germany, India, Poland, South Korea, the UK or the US — and own the right phone.
The build that's been spotted is firmware version S948BXXU6ZZK3, and it's for the S26 Ultra only, though other S26 phones and servers will almost certainly get the beta. Enthusiast site SammyGuru also expects the S25 series, Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 to get the beta as well. Even if you have an S26, though, you may miss out if you bought it through a carrier. The One UI 8.5 beta was only available for unlocked phones in the US, and users with a carrier-locked S26 will probably have to wait for the stable release.
When the beta is likely to open
Samsung opened the One UI 8.5 beta on December 8, 2025, for the Galaxy S25, S25+ and S25 Ultra, but not everyone got it on day one: Owners in Poland and India had to wait until the second beta build on December 22. Samsung launched One UI 8.5 on the Galaxy S26 at its February 2026 Unpacked event, and released a beta for the Galaxy S24 series, Z Fold 6, Z Flip 6, S25 FE, S24 FE and Galaxy Tab S11 in late March.
The One UI 9.0 beta rolled out on May 13, and the stable version released with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 on July 22, in step with Google's Android 17 release. One UI 9.5 is still based on Android 17, putting it in the same mid-cycle slot 8.5 filled last year and timed for the next Galaxy S phones. As of writing, Samsung hasn't announced a date for the S27's Unpacked event, though it'll probably mirror recent years and fall somewhere in January or February.
Enthusiast site SammyFans has pencilled in early December for the beta, while SamMobile thinks registrations could open in November. Both sites are working from a single previous point-five release, though; the S26's Ultra build sitting on Samsung's servers is a far better indication that a beta is imminent.
How to sign up
To sign up for the beta, you'll need a Samsung account and the Samsung Members app, which you can download from the Galaxy Store or Google Play. Once the beta itself goes live, you'll simply need to open Samsung Members, tap the One UI 9.5 banner or beta card on the home screen and select Registration for One UI Beta Program. If your phone and country qualify, Samsung will enrol you. From there, head to Settings > Software update > Download and install to get the beta. Samsung rolls builds out gradually, so don't panic if it doesn't show up immediately.
Before installing the beta, you should update all your apps and back up your phone to a computer with Smart Switch, since beta software can corrupt your data. If you come across any bugs, you can report them through Samsung Members > Participated Beta test > Beta feedback > Send feedback.
Exiting the beta is the more awkward part. You can withdraw by navigating via Samsung Members > Settings > Beta program settings > Withdraw from beta program, but that doesn't remove the beta build itself. Instead, you'll need to plug your phone into a computer and use Smart Switch to run a Downgrade, which will wipe everything you've done during testing. If you choose to stay on the beta, you'll get the finished One UI 9.5 as a normal update, whenever that is. So, if your S26 is your only phone and you don't keep regular backups, it's worth sitting this one out and waiting for the stable release.

Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.
President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday.
Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages. Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.
Eisenkot leads the centrist Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.
That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give another lawmaker a chance to form a government. If those efforts also fail, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the meantime.

Kolkata witnessed an unusual procession on Saturday, October 31, as thousands of book lovers took to the streets carrying books instead of political flags. Called “Let’s Walk for Books”, the march was organised in protest against the alleged vandalism of Left-affiliated bookstalls by BJP workers and police during Durga Puja festivities across West Bengal.
The procession began at College Square, the hub of Kolkata’s literary and academic life as well as the publishing industry, following an appeal circulated on social media over several days. Among those who urged people to join were prominent academics, writers and public figures, including Pabitra Sarkar, Shamik Bandyopadhyay, Jawhar Sircar, Kumar Rana, Malini Bhattacharya, Ziad Ali, Paranjoy Guha Thakurta and Shobhanlal Dasgupta.
The appeal, which urged participants to carry a book each, said books were facing a ‘barbaric’ attack across the state.
Bookstalls have long been part of Durga Puja festivities in Bengal, along side fairs, music, theatre and poetry events.
This year, however, several bookstalls were allegedly vandalised, their organisers assaulted, and books thrown onto the streets and trampled underfoot, the appeal noted. In Jadavpur, an attempt was allegedly made to demolish bookstalls with the help of central forces. A Kolkata Municipal Corporation garbage truck was also brought in to remove newly printed books.
The appeal described the incidents as an assault on Bengal’s cultural traditions and warned that continued attacks on books could damage the state’s reputation and values. It called on writers, artists, students, teachers, publishers, booksellers and others to assemble in front of the Vidyasagar statue at College Square, carrying a book of their choice as a symbol of resistance.
The Rally
Responding to the appeal, people began gathering around College Street from 3 pm. Students from colleges and universities joined participants across generations, from middle-aged people to the elderly. Almost everyone carried a book.
The collection reflected a wide range of political, literary and religious traditions. Participants carried works by Rabindranath Tagore, Karl Marx, Bhagat Singh, Sukanta Bhattacharya and Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, alongside books by contemporary writers such as Arundhati Roy. Some carried works by Syama Prasad Mookerjee, while others held copies of the Bhagavad Gita, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and books on Swami Vivekananda.
Scheduled to begin at 3.30 pm, the march started around 3.45 pm, with several thousand people taking part. In a city accustomed to processions marked by political flags, banners and party slogans, this one stood out. Participants carried books and sang songs.
They sang the Bengali translation of Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet’s song “They Don’t Let Us Sing”, as well as Rabindranath Tagore’s “Bnadh Bhenga Dao”. International protest songs, including “We Shall Overcome” and its Bengali version, “Amra Korbo Joy”, also featured in the procession.
Large banners, or tifos, carried messages such as “Don’t Burn Books, Read Them” and “Books versus Bulldozer”.
The procession also offered glimpses of solidarity among participants. An elderly newspaper vendor distributed candies to those taking part. In a video shared on social media, he said he had joined the march because of his love for books. Although financial difficulties had prevented him from completing his education, he said, he had always loved reading and ensured that his daughter completed her education.
Starting in front of College Square and Calcutta University, the march passed the National Book Agency and the iconic sweet shops, Putiram and Mouchaak, on Surya Sen Street, before entering Bankim Chatterjee Street. It then proceeded past the College Street Coffee House and Presidency University before returning to College Square.
Several videos shared on social media showed people standing on balconies and outside shops, recording the procession on their smartphones. Marchers waved at onlookers along the route.
Left leaders Mohammed Salim, Sujan Chakraborty and Biman Basu also joined the procession, walking at the back.
After the march, the Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA) organised a brief cultural programme in front of the College Square gate. Activists performed songs including “Tu Zinda Hai”, Paul Robeson’s “Ol’ Man River” and Bhupen Hazarika’s Bengali adaptation, “O Ganga Boichho Keno”.
Addressing the gathering, senior Left leader Biman Basu said people who believed in reading books had come together for the march. He added that efforts to promote reading must continue whenever books come under attack.
Participants said the protest was not about defending any particular political ideology. A book, they said, was neither Left-wing nor Right-wing; it was simply a book. Some described the attacks during Durga Puja as an assault on education, free thought and rationalism, and said they had joined the march to collectively resist such incidents in the future.
SFI central executive committee member Shuvajit Sarkar (in blue shirt in photo below), who participated in the march, said, “Fascists and communal forces oppose books because books promote rationality and reject blind subordination. We will defend books and continue the struggle against the divisive politics of the RSS and BJP until we defeat it.”
