Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

The Cat in the Hat was no match for the mighty Godzilla. “Godzilla Minus Zero” climbed to the top of box office charts with $31.6 million from 3,254 theaters, a roaring start for a foreign language epic in North America. Meanwhile, “The Cat in the Hat” stumbled with $20 million from 4,003 locations, a weak debut for an animated movie that’s based on one of the most well-known children’s books of all time.
Ticket sales for “Godzilla Minus Zero” register as the largest opening for a foreign language live-action film in North America. The R-rated monster movie benefitted from sterling reviews and strong audience scores (a 90% on Rotten Tomatoes and “A” grade on CinemaScore exit polls), as well as outsized interest from premium large formats. It’s the first Japanese production ever filmed for Imax, and the company’s bigger and brighter screens have contributed a huge $12.7 million, or, 40% of domestic grosses. It wasn’t just Imax that resonated with audiences. PLFs, including Dolby, accounted for a staggering 74% of ticket sales. By comparison, “The Odyssey” collected 53% of opening weekend returns from PLFs.
“We’re so happy to see audiences embrace ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ at an unprecedented scale for an international film,” says Chance Huskey, VP of distribution for Gkids, which distributed the movie in the U.S. “This landmark release is the result of a thoughtful campaign by Gkids and Toho that emphasized the ‘must see’ intensity of the theatrical experience.”
“Godzilla Minus Zero” built on the success of the prior kaiju adventure, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One.” That sci-fi epic secured a better-than-expected $11.4 million start and powered to $57 million in North America and $113 million globally, in addition to winning a visual effects Oscar. Produced by Japan’s Toho and directed by Takashi Yamazaki, the movie takes place two years after the previous installment as Godzilla regenerates and resurfaces to combat a new monster that’s tormenting postwar Japan.
“‘Godzilla’ is a hit,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Critics’ reviews and audience scores are once again outstanding. This weekend’s opening takes the Japanese production to a new level.”
“The Cat in the Hat” was well-received by audiences, earning an “A” grade on CinemaScore, which could help in terms of box office longevity. Critics weren’t as kind, saddling the movie with a 45% on Rotten Tomatoes. Bill Hader voices the titular character in the cartooned version, which revolves around the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous cat (wearing a hat) arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a new town. Overseas, “The Cat in the Hat” collected just $10 million from 60 international markets for a global start of $30.5 million. Unless “The Cat in the Hat” rebounds in the coming weeks, the $92 million-budgeted movie will rank as another dud for Warner Bros. (Theater owners keep roughly 50% of ticket sales.) The studio, which recently merged with Paramount Skydance, has endured a brutal year at the box office with flops, including “Digger,” “The Bride!” and “Supergirl,” which have resulted in hundreds of millions in theatrical losses.
“This is a soft opening,” Gross says. “However, family animation does extremely well in ancillary windows, earning more in digital sales and rental, streaming and TV licensing than in theatrical. That is where the film should recover its costs.”
This is the second adaptation of the Dr. Seuss classic following 2003’s live-action comedy, starring Mike Myers as the Cat. That film opened to $38 million, not adjusted for inflation, and ran out of steam with $134 million, a disappointing result given the budget was above $100 million. More recently, Dr. Seuss adaptations like 2018’s “The Grinch” (which opened to $67 million) and 2012’s “The Lorax” (which opened to $70 million) were big hits for Universal and Illumination. Yes, the theatrical landscape has changed a lot since those films were released. But “The Cat in the Hat” is based on popular IP, and it didn’t have any competition. (Families with young kids haven’t had much to see since since Universal’s “Forgotten Island” in September.) Even this spring’s “Hoppers,” an original offering from Disney and Pixar, managed to debut to $45 million.
Overall, this weekend reached $114 million across all films, up 86% from the same frame a year ago when “Predator: Badlands” was No. 1 at the box office. Exhibitors are hoping the momentum continues through November, which sees the release of Paramount’s Christmas fantasy “Ebenezer,” starring Johnny Depp, Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” Universal’s comedy “Focker in Law,” with Ariana Grande joining Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, and Disney’s animated “Hexed.”
“It’s another encouraging sign as we head toward the all-important holiday movie season,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian.
Also this weekend, Searchlight’s dark comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and directed by Martin McDonagh, opened at No. 8 with $6 million from 1,100 theaters. It’s a promising debut for the Oscar hopeful, which has a much larger initial footprint than McDonagh’s prior film, 2022’s “The Banshees of Inisherin.” After starting in limited release, “Banshees of Inisherin” became a slow and steady box office hit with $10.5 million domestically and $50 million globally. “Wild Horse Nine” follows Malkovich and Rockwell as CIA officers who are dispatched from Santiago to Easter Island shortly before a Chilean military coup.
Another newcomer, the Indian epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” earned $8.6 million over the traditional weekend and $12.1 million during its first four days in theaters. Sony is distributing “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” in 1,300 theaters, marking the widest North American release for an Indian film. Nitesh Tiwari‘s two-part adaptation of the ancient Hindu epic are the most expensive Indian films ever made, costing a combined $500 million to bring to screens.
“Indian epics do some business in English-speaking countries, but they can make a fortune in India,” says Gross. “It’s going to need to make a fortune there.”
“Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” opened in fifth place behind of A24’s electric Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything.” The zeitgeist-capturing movie has earned $8.8 million from 2,473 theaters in its fourth weekend of release, boosting its domestic tally to a staggering $79.8 million. “You Can See Everything” will leave theaters as one of the biggest documentaries in decades. And it will be very profitable for A24, which produced the nearly three-hour movie for $7 million.
“Drummer Boy,” a Christian musical from Angel Studios, landed at No. 3 with $9.3 million from 2,850 theaters. “Jimmy,” a faith-based biopic starring KJ Apa as the actor and military vet Jimmy Stewart, finished the weekend in 12th place with just $2.2 million from 1,470 theaters.
Elsewhere, A24’s heartwarming comedy “Club Kid” and Amazon MGM’s drama “I Play Rocky” scored in limited release. “Club Kid” earned $390,583 from six screens in New York and Los Angeles, translating to $65,097 per location. Jordan Firstman wrote, directed and stars in the film, which revolves around a hard-partying club promoter who finds out he has a 10-year-old son. “I Play Rocky” captured $345,000 from seven theaters, averaging $49,200 per location. Directed by Peter Farrelly, the movie depicts the real life story of Sylvester Stallone bringing the 1976 classic “Rocky” to the big screen. Both films will expand nationwide around Thanksgiving.
“We’re incredibly encouraged by the response to ‘I Play Rocky,” so far,” says Amazon MGM Studios head of domestic distribution Kevin Wilson. “The enthusiasm from audiences reinforces our belief that we have a film with both awards potential and commercial appeal.”

Under its influence, the Met Dept noted that “isolated heavy rainfall/snowfall likely over Kashmir valley on 12 November.”

The IMD has outlined potential hazards resulting from the severe weather, including localised landslides, waterlogging in low-lying areas, and minor damage to kutcha houses and vulnerable structures.
The weather agency also warned of tree branches breaking and potential damage to plantations, horticulture, and standing crops.
Urging caution, the IMD issued a strict advisory for residents in affected areas: “People are advised to keep a watch on the weather for worsening conditions and be ready to move to safer places accordingly.”
It also stressed, “take safe shelters; do not take shelter under trees, as there could be lightning. In case of expected lightning, unplug electrical/ electronic appliances, immediately.”

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said that while armed Naxalites had been eliminated from the forests, the threat of Naxalism was not over, claiming that "Dimagi Naxals" had taken control of several organisations including political parties.Addressing security personnel while celebrating Diwali at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) camp in Karanpur in Chhattisgarh's Bastar district, PM Modi said the country needed to identify and defeat such elements to ensure national security."We must remember one thing. Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of 52.
He was best known for the Oscar-winning trans drama A Fantastic Woman and his English-language films included Gloria Bell and The Wonder.
His partner Amalia Kassai announced his death on Instagram without specifying the cause of death but telling followers, in Spanish, that it was a painful time for his family. Chilean media reports that he died at his home in Las Condes, Santiago.
Lelio was born in Argentina but moved to Chile at the age of two. He studied journalism for one year before graduating from film school and then released 9/11 documentary Cero in 2003. His first narrative film The Sacred Family premiered at the San Sebastián film festival in 2005.
His follow-up, 2009’s Christmas, premiered at Cannes but it was 2013’s Gloria that provided him with a major international breakthrough. The drama, about a woman in her late 50s who starts dating again, premiered at Berlin and won its lead star Paulina García an acting award at the festival.
Lelio followed it up with A Fantastic Woman, a drama about the life of a trans woman, another breakout that became the first Chilean film to win the Oscar for best international feature. In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a sublime study in the exalted ordeal of grief”.
“When we released it in 2017, a gender identity bill had been dormant in congress for seven years,” he said in a Guardian interview in 2018. “Somehow, the film’s release, and the year in which it became globally known, helped to reactivate the discussion in Chile.”
He made his English language debut with London-set drama Disobedience which told a queer love story between women played by Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams. It was nominated for five British independent film awards.
Lelio then remade Gloria as Gloria Bell, then set in America and starring Julianne Moore in the lead role. He followed it with a critically acclaimed adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel The Wonder starring Florence Pugh.
“I love working with actors, and need to know they trust me and can explore, get lost, be foolish or brave, and I’ll take care of them,” he said to the Guardian. “I love working on set – it is where the sparkle is.”
His final film was 2025’s The Wave, a musical protest drama that premiered at Cannes.
“Making a film is like a gift you leave somewhere – you then hide and see what happens,” he said.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum. The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage. Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation. The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services. What Changes For Operators? The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships. For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation. In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage. However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation. The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years. Connecting Phones To Satellites TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators. For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India. For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity. However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use. TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them. TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee. Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator. Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz. For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue. The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market.

Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
- Published
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.
"The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.
The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.
Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.
Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.
However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration.
"Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987.
Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.
They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.
Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.
Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.
Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

An Indian film that nobody would release is finally a hit - 18 awards later
- Published
A film about the tender love and quiet loneliness of an elderly couple, which took two years to reach cinemas after it was completed, is wowing critics and audiences across India.
The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration which has left hundreds of picturesque Himalayan hamlets abandoned and turned them into ghost villages. It further reflects on the impact of climate change, which has made the region's weather increasingly harsh.
On social media, many Indians have shared videos showing audiences leaving theatres with tears in their eyes. Others have posted that they have not been so moved by a film in a long time.
The film's lead actors, ordinary villagers who had never faced a camera before, have also won praise from some of Bollywood's most respected figures, including Naseeruddin Shah and Anupam Kher.
Pyre's protagonists - Padam Singh (played by Kapri's uncle, Padam Singh) and Tulsi (played by Heera Devi) - are Bubu and Aama, local terms for grandfather and grandmother. The couple live in a small home in the mountains of the northern state of Uttarakhand .
It's a place where age is measured against momentous events. Singh was born two years before the outbreak of World War II. Tulsi was born in the year atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.
There are no roads and no electricity. Whenever the couple need help – which is often as Tulsi frequently has to be carried to hospital – Padam Singh uses a traditional long-horn instrument to summon neighbours. In return for their kindness, he pays them with goats.
"There's nothing here – just mountains," as one character puts it. So the young leave in search of greener pastures, and those who depart this beautiful, but blighted, land rarely return.
Kapri says his film remains focused on the "soulful love story of the ageing couple in their last days".
"They have shared a life together for 65 years and, for the last 28 years, they've been waiting for their son, Hariya, who's gone to Mumbai in search of work, to come back," Kapri tells the BBC. "It's a story of companionship, of loneliness and of waiting."
Their wait takes on a new urgency when suddenly, after all these years, a letter arrives from Hariya setting a date for his visit.
As Padam Singh and Tulsi count down the days, the handful of villagers around them leave one by one, until the couple find themselves alone in the vast mountain landscape.
"You and Tulsi should also leave as soon as possible. Otherwise, you won't even have four people to carry your body down the mountain to the funeral pyre when you or Tulsi die," one departing villager advises Padam Singh. "Or die before we leave," he adds in jest.
With no one left to call for help, Padam Singh builds two funeral pyres side by side right outside his door – one for his wife and one for himself.
"How will I carry you down the mountain if you die?" he tells Tulsi when she questions the decision.
Despite the bleak setting and the weight of the topics covered, Pyre is suffused with humour. The central couple are delightful. Like many long-married spouses, they seem to treat bickering as a love language.
Kapri, who is from Uttarakhand, got the idea for the film in 2018 after meeting an 84-year-old man in Munsiyari, a scenic hill town in the state.
"I visited him after seeing his photo in a Facebook post. The wrinkles on his face really fascinated me. His face was unique."
Kapri said he asked him and his wife what their biggest worry was.
"He said, 'My biggest worry is, if I die first, who is going to take care of her?' And she said, 'He doesn't know how to cook. So if I die first, I don't know who is going to cook food for him.' That was so heartwarming for me."
Kapri says he initially tried to make his film with "the real couple", but abandoned the idea after a week of shooting, when it became clear it was not working. He then approached actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak - a couple themselves - for the lead roles.
Shah loved the script, Kapri says, but felt that he and Pathak did not belong to the region and would struggle to do justice to the characters.
Kapri finally found his Padam Singh within his own family – his father's younger brother, a retired army soldier who expressed an interest in acting. He found his Tulsi in another village. Heera Devi, an elderly widow, had raised her children through years of farming, cutting grass and tending to her buffalo.
Over the years, Padam Singh and Heera Devi tell the BBC, they have watched stories of ghost villages, of children migrating for work, abandoning the elderly, play out all around them. They say today they are overwhelmed by the attention Pyre has got.
Since 2024, the film has been screened at some of the world's biggest festivals. It has won 18 awards, Kapri says, including three for best feature and 12 audience-choice best film prizes.
Despite its success at festivals, Kapri says, Pyre spent two years without a distributor. Even OTT platforms passed on the film and it finally reached cinemas only when a producer friend of his stepped in to fund a theatrical release.
But, he says, the modest 70-screen release on 30 October sparked favourable word-of-mouth reviews and with the demand for tickets going up, there was an increase in overall screenings too.
Meanwhile, the misgivings that both Padam Singh and Heera Devi say they initially had about stepping in front of the camera and forgetting their lines are gone now.
Heera Devi says she was even concerned about what her children would think - and what would society say?
Today she and Padam Singh are basking in the positive reviews of film critics and the affection of their audiences.
They have met teary-eyed people at multiple screenings - many wanting to touch their feet and hug them, many who said the film reminded them of their own parents and grandparents who are waiting in villages, towns and cities that they had come from.
"We felt immense joy and happiness. We've received so much love and inspiration - something we had never imagined," says Padam Singh.
But the best moment for him came when he met Naseeruddin Shah in Mumbai. "He watched the entire movie and had tears in his eyes. He hugged me. He said, 'Bubu, the role you have performed, I wouldn't be able to pull off even in seven lifetimes.'"
The film's appeal, Heera Devi says, is because "in reality, our village is just like this".
"Across villages in India, the elderly are left alone. No one's children stay at home anymore and it's the same situation for all parents. They keep waiting for their son and daughter-in-law, hoping that their grandchildren would visit and spend a few days with them. The loneliness is simply unbearable."
Padam Singh says he has a message for the younger generation in Uttarakhand and the rest of India.
"I want to tell them they must not abandon their motherland, the land where they were born," he says. "I also appeal to the government to bring education and employment to where people are - so that they don't have to wander away. When that happens, the parents who are being left behind will also be cared for."

US President Donald Trump on Saturday (local time) said that he has offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States to Dana White, the President and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. Trump, while describing White as a ‘violent Fighter and warrior ’, also requested the 57-year-old to “please take the job”.
The White House has been without a Press Secretary after Katie Zacharia was fired on October 16, after serving just five days in the role.
In a Truth Social post, Trump also said he has asked White to bring along some UFC fighters, including Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris.
Quick answers to key questions
Dana White has not said whether he is seriously considering the position. He confirmed the offer and said he would meet Trump on Monday.
Trump described White as a “violent Fighter and warrior” and said the country needed people to defend it against what he called the “Lunatic Left.”
Trump named Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes and Kayla Harris.
The position was vacant after Katie Zacharia was fired on October 16, following five days in the role.
White confirmed that he would meet Trump on Monday. He did not say what they would discuss.
“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” Trump said.
White, who has a decades-long association with Trump, confirmed the development and said that he will meet the US President on Monday.
The head of the largest mixed martial arts (MMA) organization didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States.
White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, declined to say what conversations he had with Trump but said, “I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that.
The development comes as Trump is making some key changes in the administration, following the massive defeat of the Republican Party in the US midterm elections.
Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.
Harmeet Dhillon, the Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division at the US Justice Department, was the first to announce her resignation. There are also growing speculations that more resignations or firings could follow in the coming days.
This includes Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, who has been on the receiving end of criticism from Democrats and Republicans alike for the war in Iran. There are also reports that the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, another Trump confidant, could announce his resignation in the coming days to announce his 2028 US presidential election bid.

Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is “not cool anymore” and so much of the internet has been compromised.
“I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC,” Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair.
Ohanian has a complicated relationship with the internet. He resigned from Reddit in 2020, following the killing of George Floyd, to make room for a Black board member and to pressure the company to reform its content moderation policies. The social site had been notorious for hosting violent and harmful rhetoric. Ohanian reflects on recently learning someone with a Reddit tattoo—once a sign of the site’s success to Ohanian—had since covered it up: “I don’t blame him.”
He now runs venture capital firm Seven Seven Six, which has over $1.3 billion in assets under management. He focuses on sports, where he finds real-life communities “in the age of AI slop” and a “manipulated” internet.
Ohanian is a proponent of the “Dead Internet Theory”—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. “The internet that I grew up on … that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away,” said Ohanian, “because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people.”
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. “Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs,” Ohanian said.
But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google’s AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialisation of these conversations means they are full of “bullshit.” “The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so,” he said.
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, “there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy.”
An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. “There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure,” he said. “I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better.”

Windows 11 is testing eight upgrades in Insider builds to reduce daily friction. Key updates include flexible taskbar positioning, faster Windows Search with inline actions, a Battery Status widget, phone-to-PC integration, per-app privacy controls, smarter Windows Hello, anti-glare tools, and enhanced File Explorer previews.
I can’t count how many times I’ve had to drag the window to full size, squint at a bright screen, or open Settings just to turn on dark mode. Each one takes a few seconds, but you repeat them all day. Thankfully, Windows 11 is about to trim a lot of that. Microsoft seems to have noticed, and over the past few months, it has been stacking up small but genuinely useful changes for Windows 11. The best part is that all these features are coming with future updates.
With new optimized features, Windows now feels up to 20% more responsive, with the gains showing up in Start, File Explorer, Search, and more. With the latest Windows Insider release notes, you are in for a eight-feature treat you should know about. One heads-up before we start: not everything is available to everyone yet. Many of these are still being tested in the Windows Insider Experimental channel, so I’ll tell you where each one stands.
Table of Contents
Taskbar customization
For years, the Windows 11 taskbar has been stuck to the bottom of the screen. There was no way to change its position. That is finally changing. Microsoft’s Windows Insider blog confirms that, with the current insider update, users can now park the taskbar on the top, bottom, left, or right edge. Here’s what you can do:
- You can choose icon alignment for every position. On the sides, icons can be top-aligned or centered. On the top or bottom, they can be left-aligned or centered.
- Start, Search, and other flyouts follow the taskbar. Meaning, if you put the taskbar at the top, Start opens from the top.
- On a vertical taskbar, when you choose “Never combine” and turn on labels, every app window gets its own labeled button, so you can see all your windows at a glance.
Moving the taskbar to the side can give you vertical space, handy for developers who want to see more code. To tweak the taskbar, you need to navigate to Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors. You can also choose to make the taskbar smaller, optimal for small screens. Simply choose the “Show smaller taskbar” option to Always, and you get smaller icons and a shorter bar. No restart or sign-out needed.
Things may not work perfectly, though. Auto-hide and the tablet-optimized taskbar don’t work in the new positions, touch gestures are still in progress, and the search box shows up as a plain search icon for now. Aside from this, the Recommended section is getting renamed to Recent, and you can hide your name and profile picture. There are also separate toggles to show or hide Pinned, Recent, and All.
Smarter Windows Search
This one might be the biggest everyday upgrade. Microsoft has confirmed that a new search built on WinUI 3 is incoming and says it makes it faster and lighter on resources. Windows Search also understands you better. Typos and synonyms are matched more intelligently, so a sloppy query is more likely to give you the right result.
The main highlight is inline actions. So, instead of finding a setting and then opening Settings to change it, you can enable/disable a setting from search. This means you’ll be able to:
- Switch to dark mode, turn on night light, or turn on Bluetooth
- Dim your screen or mute your PC
- Minimize all your windows or arrange windows on screen
Phone actions are coming soon too, allowing you to quickly do things like sending a text through a Phone Link-connected device. Search is soon expected to get inline previews of files, richer file details, web answers (think weather or “how tall is the Eiffel Tower”) and filters. This new experience is also expected to arrive for the Start menu, but only next year. Other features are expected for broader availability later this year.
Battery status widget
This is not a big update, per se, but if you want to know what the battery level is on your wireless mouse? Your headphones? Your laptop? Or any other connected device, usually you’d have to hunt through different menus for each answer.
With the Windows 11 26340.9616 release, Microsoft introduced a Battery Status widget that shows the battery levels of your PC and your peripheral devices in one view. To get it, you need to open the Widgets board > Add widgets > Battery Status. It is rolling out to Insiders on newer builds. Widgets are also getting lighter. Microsoft says on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets now load only when you open them. This helps free up more than 200 MB for your apps.
Phone to PC continuity
Microsoft seems to be making sure that your phone and PC act like one setup. With the upcoming updates, Windows 11 could allow users to reply to messages, answer calls, and open phone apps without picking up their phone. Here are all the features, reportedly available in the insider build:
- Messages and notifications: You will be able to preview them from your Android phone or iPhone right in Start. When you want to reply, you can open a window focused on that chat.
- Quick Settings: Put your phone in silent mode or ring a misplaced phone right from your PC.
- Phone apps on your desktop: Supported Android phones can open phone apps in separate, resizable windows.
- Files: You will be able to browse your phone’s files in File Explorer.
- Photos: You can snap a picture on your phone, and your PC shows a notification that you can open with one click.
- Resume: Pick up supported activities where you left off when you switch devices.
One thing to note is that this requires a compatible Android phone or iPhone, and features vary by platform. The rollout date, similar to other features, isn’t confirmed, but it may arrive by next year.
Better privacy controls
Until now, regular desktop apps were controlled by a single device-wide switch for things like your camera, microphone, and location. That was not something one would want, especially when you want to have granular controls. According to the 28120.3302 release notes, Insiders can now allow or deny access for each desktop app individually. For that, you need to head to Settings > Privacy & security, then open Camera, Microphone, or Location.
The rollout is gentle on your existing setup. All the apps that were granted access will continue to keep it, and apps that were denied stay denied. Nothing will reset. Apps that haven’t asked yet will prompt you the first time they request access.
Smarter Windows Hello
According to Microsoft, with the latest insider builds, it has introduced faster Windows Hello sign-ins, made them easier, and more reliable, with improvements to both face and fingerprint recognition. There’s also a very practical new trick for face sign-in. If you’ve ever tried to unlock your laptop in a dim room, you know the struggle. You have to turn on the light so that your face is detected correctly.
The 26340.9750 release notes say Windows Hello facial recognition can temporarily brighten your screen to help you sign in when the lighting is poor. To use it, go to Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Facial recognition (Windows Hello) and turn on Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition. This one is currently in the Experimental channel.
Anti-glare mode
Although Microsoft doesn’t use the name “anti-glare mode,” that’s exactly what the newly added option does. Notably, it’s a contrast theme toggle inside Magnifier, as mentioned in the 28120.3302 release notes. While many people use Night light or color inversion to calm a bright screen, but the downside of using is that it flips everything, including photos, charts, and videos.
With the new toggle, it will recolor the interface only. This way, your images keep their real colors. The dark theme is the default, and you can pick a different contrast theme under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. You still get the “Color inversion” option, and it isn’t going anywhere if you prefer it.
Magnifier also learned some multi-monitor tricks:
- Zoom per display: With your monitors set to Extend, each screen can have its own zoom level. So, one screen where you are writing can sit at 300% while your reference screen stays at 150%.
- View locking: Press Ctrl + Windows + K while pointing at a screen to hold its view in place, then press Windows + Esc to release all locks.
If you just want a softer tint, Windows 11 is also testing a “Screen Tint,” which lets you pick a color overlay and adjust its strength.
File Explorer previews
You might already be using third-party software for file previews inside File Explorer, but wait. Microsoft is also cooking the same feature, and it may arrive very soon for Windows 11. A couple of preview-related changes are incoming:
- Thumbnails in the Recommended section on File Explorer’s Home page are sharper, so they’re crisper and easier to read without needing you to open them.
- You can now preview and install fonts from File Explorer and desktop right-click menus.
If you work with fonts, that second one saves a few steps. For everyone else, it’s a polish update, and it’s good to see File Explorer getting some attention.
Can everyone try these features?
Unfortunately, these features aren’t available for everyone, for now. Most of the features above live in Windows Insider builds. If you’re comfortable with a few bugs, you can join through Settings > Windows Update > Windows Insider Program. You will see most features in builds 26340.9616, 26340.9750 and 28120.3302 in the Experimental channels.
These builds can be unstable, and features in them might change, be removed, or never ship. Many are also rolled out gradually to a subset of Insiders first, so you may not see everything right away. For those who are using Windows 11 on their primary device, you should probably wait.

For a woman who has been a witness to some of the most significant political moments in modern Indian history, Sonia Gandhi likes to insist her life has been far from remarkable. “Oh, I don’t know that I would say it’s an extraordinary story,” she says, shifting uncomfortably.
It’s hard to reconcile this modest characterisation with the course her life has taken over the last 79 years. Born to a working-class family in a small town in northern Italy, today she sits at the heart of Indian political power, having weathered assassinations and personal tragedy to become one of the country’s most influential figures. She held Indira Gandhi’s bloodied body after the then-prime minster, her mother-in-law, was gunned down at their home in Delhi in 1984. She then became India’s first lady when her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, took his mother’s place as prime minister. And when Rajiv, too, was killed, she threw aside her distaste for politics to step up and lead his fragmenting party. In 2004, having taken Congress to electoral victory, she famously turned down the prime minister post. She can still boast of being the longest-serving president of Congress, both when India’s oldest political party was in power and later, when it became the flailing opposition. When Gandhi stepped down in 2017, her son Rahul was appointed her successor.
Gandhi’s entrance into Indian politics began in Cambridge in the 1960s when, at 18, while she was studying at a language school, she fell in love with a bright-eyed boy at a Greek restaurant. At the time, she had no idea that Rajiv was heir to India’s most consequential political dynasty. “It was a coup de foudre,” she says. “After that, nothing else really mattered. He was, first of all, a handsome man. But I think his eyes told of the way he was – of his inner self. He was loving, he was comforting, he was caring. Everything I could have possibly dreamed of.”
Only later would she learn that Rajiv’s grandfather was Jawaharlal Nehru, Indian freedom fighter and the country’s first prime minister, and his mother was Indira Gandhi, who in 1966 became India’s first female prime minister.
Does she still recognise herself in that innocent Italian girl who was swept off her feet and transplanted to an alien land and culture? “Not really,” she says quietly. “Too much has happened, too much has changed.”
We meet at the grand white Delhi bungalow she has lived in for 36 years – a relic of British colonial rule, where peacocks roam the grounds. It was in this house in 1991 that Gandhi heard her husband had been assassinated by Sri Lankan Tamil separatist terrorists. Over the years, as she took on the mantle of Congress leader, her home became the centre of party operations.
The ghosts of Congress leaders past loom large in her study. A painting of Nehru, photographs of Rajiv, a carved stone bust and portraits of Indira line the walls, while a painting of Mahatma Gandhi, the freedom fighter who shaped the ideology of Congress, also hangs prominently. Heavy gilded tomes fill the floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, and a long meeting table dominates the space, but the vibrant rugs, patterned blinds and scattered antiques suggest Gandhi’s own light touch.
In a dark blue sari and maroon blouse, her signature neat grey hair pushed back with a black headband, Gandhi looks every inch the composed Indian political matriarch as she sits on the sofa. The only hint of her heritage is softly accented English and recognisably Italian gesticulation.
She has, she confesses, been very nervous and tense about our meeting. Gandhi has not done an interview in a decade, and throughout her life in the public eye, has tried fiercely to maintain her privacy. She has only agreed to this rare meeting to discuss her forthcoming memoir, a strikingly personal account of her life, and has asked her daughter Priyanka, also a senior Congress leader, to sit in for moral support.
India’s media has often cast her as cold and aloof, yet today she seems warm, open and often a little unsure of herself. She’s anxious about how personal the book is, worried it will be eviscerated by the Indian media, but suggests that after years of “horrible and crazy things written about me”, it will be comforting for people to know “the truth”.
Gandhi has good reason to be nervous of the press. In today’s India, the mainstream media landscape has been crushed into submission by the hardline, rightwing Modi government and is largely devoted to promoting the prime minister’s agenda, while mercilessly attacking the Congress party, in particular the Gandhi family. She does not hold back on criticism of Narendra Modi – accusing him of being an “authoritarian force bent upon changing the very nature of our country” – and of his party, BJP, which she says has “systematically dismantled our democratic institutions”.
The Hindu nationalist vision of India that Modi has enacted over his 12 years in power is directly opposed to the pluralistic, secular India that was championed by successive Congress leaders and which remains enshrined in India’s constitution. It has led to well-documented oppression of the country’s minority groups, in particular its 200 million Muslims.
“More than disappointing, it’s very painful, having known a different India,” Gandhi says. “In parliament, we are not allowed to debate. In the past, there were discussions, there were meetings between the opposition and the government, there was consultation. Now the opposition counts for nothing.”
Since Modi came to power, she has had barely any interaction with him; he tends to avoid eye contact when they’re in a room together – a stark contrast to the past, when opposition leaders would often meet the government and “treat each other with cordiality”.
A “Congress-free India” is one of the openly declared goals of Modi’s BJP, resulting in highly personal attacks on Gandhi and her children, who have found themselves with numerous police cases filed against them. As we talk, Gandhi’s phone lights up with a call from her son Rahul – later, we learn a judge has just cleared him of defamation in one of these many cases, this time for criticising Modi’s home minister back in 2018. “They are very vindictive and vicious. There doesn’t seem to be a heart there,” Gandhi says.
So effective is the BJP’s crackdown on any form of dissent or criticism – what Gandhi describes as an “atmosphere of fear” – that her memoir almost didn’t see the light of day in India. Penguin Random House India were originally meant to release the book domestically, but after she sent them the manuscript she was met with a deafening silence. Gandhi says simply that Penguin were “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and that after she refused to make certain suggested edits, the publisher dropped the book, just a week before it was due to be announced. It will now be published by another imprint. In a statement, the publisher denied dropping the book, adding, “Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish Belonging because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances.”
Gandhi admits she was disappointed, though not altogether surprised, at what she sees as an attempt to censor her book. It is far from an isolated incident. In the days before we meet, Gandhi’s 26-year-old grandson, who is an artist and curator, is forced to take down dozens of his photographs depicting political protests that had been due to go on show in Delhi.
Gandhi had an early insight into the difficulties and loneliness of being a female leader in India’s deeply patriarchal society. When she arrived in India in 1968, she and Rajiv moved in with his mother, who at that time was two years into her first term as prime minister. Her husband, also a politician, had died years before.
They lived all together in another crumbling colonial Delhi bungalow, in relatively close and modest quarters. To outsiders, Indira was often seen as severe, an “iron lady”, and Gandhi admits that, to begin with, she was deeply intimidated by her formidable mother-in-law. Yet while Indira was imposing in public, she could be vulnerable in private, once confiding to Gandhi how terrified she was when she first bcame prime minister.
“In the newspapers she was portrayed as tough or harsh, but at home she was just like any other mother,” Gandhi says – although Indira’s notoriously explosive temper, frequently directed at political colleagues, would erupt through the house on occasion. Gandhi’s memoir recounts one incident where Indira lost her temper during a family dinner and threw her thali plate across the table.
Gandhi’s book documents the hostility Indira grappled with, both from political opponents and rightwing groups, but also from the old guard of her own party. “I saw her work day and night, constantly under pressure, constantly attacked,” Gandhi says. “It did affect her, like it would anyone. And of course, in that position, there is a loneliness. She had many interests and many friends, but it is a lonely kind of life.”
For several years, Gandhi says, her own life was “carefree”. She and Rajiv were madly in love, often embarrassing their children with public displays of affection that were highly unusual in Indian households at the time. “For this man, I was ready to do everything, to lose even my Italian identity,” she says. Rajiv was working as a commercial airline pilot, and as relations warmed with her mother-in-law, Gandhi set about redecorating the austere Delhi bungalow with some Italian flair, and learning how to cook Kashmiri food. After a traumatic miscarriage, she gave birth to two children, who were doted on by Indira. Even her pangs for fresh Italian ingredients, impossible to find in India in those days, eventually ebbed.
But in 1975 Indira would make the most controversial decision of her political life. Amid mounting political unrest, economic hardship and a concerted effort by the opposition to bring down the Congress government, Indira decided to impose a state of emergency on the country, in a bid to instil order. The repercussions were profound: the constitution was suspended, civil liberties and democratic freedoms abandoned, the media silenced and opponents detained en masse without trial. It lasted for almost two years, and is still seen as the darkest period of India’s democracy; it is regularly used to tarnish the Congress party today.
According to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision. Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her hotheaded younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, “They must be stopped.” Sanjay’s forceful influence over his mother was a great source of public controversy at the time. Gandhi recalls that it inflamed tensions within the family, too; Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen. “Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” Gandhi writes in her book.
Today, she says it was a mistake for Indira to call the emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same. “I always feel that Mrs Gandhi was a democrat at heart,” she says. “I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her.”
In the following years, Indira would lose one election and be returned to power in another. Rajiv would also be persuaded to enter politics after the premature death of Sanjay. But by 1984, darkness came to their door again.
Months of escalating violence had stricken the north Indian state of Punjab. As separatist militants prepared to declare an independent Sikh state, Indira authorised a military operation at one of the holiest sites in Sikhism, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where the group were hiding out. The operation caused cataclysmic damage, killing Sikh pilgrims as well as militants, and led to desecration of the temple by tanks and heavy weaponry. Gandhi says that when her mother-in-law was shown images of the devastation, tears rolled down her face.
For Sikhs in India, it was a profound and painful attack on their religion, and Indira was inundated with threats. “She told us what to do in case she died – so she knew,” Gandhi says. “She was making preparations for her death. She told Rahul he must be brave and not to cry.” That summer Indira took her grandchildren on a trip to her ancestral home of Kashmir; Gandhi believes this was to “say goodbye”. Indira also defied advice to remove her Sikh bodyguards – something that turned out to be a fateful decision.
Gandhi was at home on 31 October when she heard what sounded like fireworks going off. Sprinting over to Indira’s office next door, she was confronted by her mother-in-law’s bloodied body, riddled with bullets, lying on the ground. Indira’s own Sikh bodyguards had opened fire on her in retribution for the attack on the Golden Temple.
What came next remains seared on Gandhi’s memory. After Indira was put into a car, she held her bleeding body and tried to revive her mother-in-law as they raced to the hospital. “There was blood everywhere and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she says.
Even after so many years, the story is clearly painful to recount and she speaks hesitantly, her soft voice growing even quieter. “I remember the drive from the house to the hospital was excruciating. There wasn’t much traffic, but it felt so slow. I also knew that because she wasn’t speaking, it must be over.”
Gandhi admits there are still parts of that experience she can’t bring herself to discuss. “I never talk about it. Only if I’m asked, then I struggle to.” Indira would be declared dead at the hospital. Her body was still lying there, cold, when Rajiv broke the news that he had been asked to step in as prime minister. Gandhi had begged him to stay out of politics and describes that conversation as a “knife going into my heart”.
In the aftermath of Indira’s death, she was traumatised and depressed, living “like a ghost”. Rajiv, too, had no time to grieve. Newly announced as prime minister, he immediately had to deal with deadly anti-Sikh riots that erupted after Indira’s death. He would later be accused of not doing enough to stop the bloodbath. “Rajiv never really showed his pain,” Gandhi says. “I remember seeing him in his mother’s study, on one of the chairs where she sat, with tears. But in public he felt he had to hide it.”
Fear took over their lives. The house became a fortress, with uniformed commandos stationed in the children’s bedrooms. Rahul and Priyanka were pulled out of school and no longer allowed to roam freely. She would worry if Rajiv didn’t come back from an engagement on time. He, meanwhile, would always want her by his side. “Fear was a very real thing,” she says. “My thought was always: he will be killed next.” By 1991, her premonition had come true.
A silence settles over the room as Gandhi struggles to recall how she went on living after Rajiv’s death. A Sri Lankan separatist militant had set off a suicide bomb while he was on the election trail, killing him instantly. Throughout our conversation, she still refers to Rajiv as “Papa”, as he is known to their children.
Priyanka, who sits on the sofa with us, interjects gently. She tells me how her mother would sit in the dark all day, listening to Mozart’s Requiem, engulfed by grief. “You were angry at him,” she says, speaking to her mother. “When you used to cry, you used to shout: how has he left me, why did he leave?”
Gandhi sits quietly for a moment. “After my mother-in-law was killed, we thought that, as we were always together, if something happens to one, it will happen to the other one,” she says. They had even written notes on how they wanted their funerals.
Yet when Gandhi’s sister pleaded for her to return to Italy, the thought was unfathomable. “India was my home, my children’s home,” she says. Gandhi last went back to Italy four years ago, when her mother died.
She found out later that, prior to the attack, Indian intelligence had intercepted death threats against Rajiv by the Sri Lankan separatist Tamil Tigers, angered over India’s intervention in the country’s civil war. However, these had been ignored by the newly elected government, who instead took away his top-level security. She still believes the truth of a wider conspiracy behind his death has yet to come out. The most recent commission to investigate it was shut down by the Modi government. “I don’t think we will get the truth now,” she says with a sigh.
Crucially, just as the foundation of her world was shattered, a wind of change was blowing across north India. A claim that a mosque in the city of Ayodhya was built on the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple had been gaining traction among hardline, rightwing Hindu nationalist organisations and political groups. In December 1992, supporters of the movement – including BJP figures – violently tore down the mosque.
Gandhi recalls crying as she witnessed the demolition on television. She says she knew then that they faced “a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build”. She accepts that failures of her own party in part contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics. “I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude,” she says. In 2024, Modi delivered on the BJP’s longstanding promise and inaugurated a vast Hindu temple in the place where the mosque had once stood.
Throughout her memoir, Gandhi is open about her distrust of politics, describing it as “menacing”, driven by “ambition, greed and hypocrisy”. But with Congress facing an existential threat and looking likely to fracture, Gandhi succumbed to mounting pressure and agreed to become its president in 1998. It was a decision, she says, driven by a sense of duty to her lost husband. Not only did she have to fight against her own ingrained shyness, she also had to take on political opponents in Hindi, her third language.
She insists she never had political ambition. Despite helping the party to win the most votes in the 2004 election, she shocked everyone by refusing to become prime minister. “It was clear in my mind I would never do it,” she says. “It was just not me.” Nonetheless, until she stepped back from the day-to-day of Congress leadership a few years ago, she had little time for herself. She would carry books to political events, history and autobiographies, to read on the way home. Music, both Indian classical and European operas, also became her solace. Having previously studied art restoration, “once in a while, I would slip away to an art exhibition”.
Today she stays out of the messy day-to-day of politics, though is still kept in the loop by her daughter and attends the occasional meeting. She finds joy in her small vegetable patch, but more than anything in spending time with her children and two grandchildren. Theirs has always been a dog-loving family (Priyanka once had seven golden retrievers) and Gandhi is devoted to her two jack russells, Noorie and Lapo, who were gifts from her son.
Nonetheless, the fortress of security that surrounds her home is a stark reminder of the restrictions still imposed on her freedom. Armed police man the barricades on the road outside, and my car is thoroughly inspected by security before I am allowed to drive through a towering metal gate and into her driveway.
While she was once credited with reviving the fortunes of Congress, over the past decade the Gandhi family have overseen its calamitous decline. Their previous government, in power till 2014, was marred by allegations of rampant corruption. (“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” is Gandhi’s defence.) After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Modi, and Congress remains in power in only a few states. Meanwhile, the BJP’s Hindutva has become the country’s dominant political ideology. As the family has maintained its control, Congress has been unable to shake off allegations that it is nepotistic and run by political elites.
Why can’t Congress free itself from the Gandhi family’s leadership, I ask? She is dismissive, perhaps a nerve touched. “You would have to ask the party,” she says. Gandhi also skates over the question of nepotism, simply saying, “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have.” But after so many losses, can a Gandhi-led Congress still be a credible alternative to the BJP? While she is adamant they can, many in the country remain unconvinced.
It is true that we are meeting at an interesting moment, for both Modi and the bruised opposition. As gen Z youth erupted on to the streets in protest against the government over the summer – satirically calling themselves the “Cockroaches” after an online joke transformed into a serious political movement – the long-crushed space for dissent has opened up.
In recent weeks, young Indians have once again been taking to the streets against the government, despite being met with draconian state force. The question of whether they can shake the BJP’s grip on power remains to be seen; so far, the Cockroach movement has kept its distance from the opposition alliance. But “what encourages me is young people are coming out and demonstrating,” Gandhi says. “With determination, they’re calling out the government on things that are not right. I feel like this is a real shift.”
Congress, too, has become more energised than it has been for many years. Images of Rahul and Priyanka being manhandled by police as they tried to protest against the government have gone viral in recent weeks. After once pleading with her children to stay out of politics, Gandhi now says, “It’s good that they’re there. Now more than ever before.” The Gandhi family, it seems, are not done just yet.

Philippines rebukes officials over public comments about China
MANILA: The Philippines' foreign ministry issued a rare rebuke to government officials and agencies on Sunday (Nov 5) over public comments about China, stressing the need for a unified voice as the country heads into a key regional summit.
The uniformed services of the Philippines have been engaged in a long-running war of words with the Chinese government over the South China Sea, a busy waterway that Beijing claims almost entirely despite an international ruling that its position has no legal basis.
Multiple senators also called last month for Beijing's ambassador to be declared persona non grata after he suggested China could "easily win" any confrontation with the Philippines.
Beijing subsequently accused Manila of "erecting multiple obstacles" to its attendance at an ASEAN defence ministers' meeting, pointedly sending only an embassy defence attache.
"Public statements that undermine the government's diplomatic approach do more than complicate the work of our diplomats," the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said, without specifying particular incidents.
"They risk eroding the country's credibility in international affairs and project an image of internal division that external parties can exploit. Such actions can ultimately weaken the Philippines' negotiating position."
The statement specifically addressed the country's national security establishment and uniformed services, which have engaged in months of heated exchanges with the Chinese Embassy on social media.
US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China at sea over disputed areas of the strategic waterway, with repeated incidents occurring in recent months.
Sunday's statement said that while the armed services were indispensable in documenting incidents, "civilian authority directs the country's international relations".
It noted that the 2016 international court verdict that broadly dismissed China's claims to the South China Sea came via "rigorous legal proceedings under international law, not through public messaging or social media".
Defence Minister Gilberto Teodoro was banned from visiting China this year, with Beijing citing "irresponsible remarks".
Chester Cabalza, a Manila-based security analyst, said the foreign ministry had gone public with its message to "assure its counterparts, particularly China, that they are in control of the Philippines' foreign policy".
"(The defence department and coast guard) are obliged to carve out the security policy of the country but not its foreign policy. DFA's statement is an assertion of their role in the bureaucracy."
China's top diplomat, Wang Yi, urged the Philippines in a phone call with counterpart Theresa Lazaro last week to rein in politicians who had "smeared" Beijing and crossed its "red lines".
Lazaro called the conversation "frank and constructive", adding that "both sides emphasised the need for continued diplomatic dialogue and the proper management of differences anchored on mutual respect".
Manila is set to host a major Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit next week, with attendees to include US President Donald Trump and recently re-elected Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Beijing has yet to announce publicly who it will send.

‘We heard about 20 shots’: Witnesses describe terror of Krakow shooting as Briton among six killed
One British national was among the six killed when the gunman opened fire in Krakow’s main market square on Saturday

Terrified witnesses have described the moment a gunman opened fire in Krakow’s main market square, killing six people, including a British national.
Police said the man drove a car into the tourist spot on Saturday just before 3pm, and then began firing randomly at people as panic broke out.
Armed officers rushed to the scene and engaged in a shootout, with two officers injured, including one in a critical condition after suffering three gunshot wounds.
Among the four women and two men killed, one was a British national, Poland’s police chief Marek Boron told reporters on Saturday evening. Three others were Polish while the remaining two are yet to be identified.
The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen who was shot and taken to hospital, had been “influenced by far-right ideology”, said Polish interior minister Marcin Kierwinski.
Polish prime minsiter Donald Tusk later said that two women and one man were found dead during searches of the suspect’s home. They are believed to be his close family, Mr Tusk said.
Witnesses of the shooting have recalled the moment they heard gunshots and ran for cover. One person reported hearing “about 20 shots”.
The main market square is typically busy with traditional horse-drawn carriages and is popular with tourists.
“We were walking to the store and heard gunshots. Suddenly we turned around, people started running, tourists from other countries didn’t know what was happening. We heard about 20 shots,” Aleksander told Poland’s Faktowi.
He said that he “ran into the store, the lady closed the door, and we waited a moment”.
“I’ve never witnessed such panic. People were running into stores to hide,” he said.
Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle flew to the city on Saturday and said that she had heard the shots ringing from her hotel.
“We heard shots from hotel room but didn’t realise what it was until we received a call from the hotel confirming there had been a shooting,” she told the BBC.
She said that police were outside the hotel “barricading” the street.
Witnesses told TV Republika that they saw black Subaru drive up to the location.
“I saw the guy, he started loading his machine gun,” one witness told the news station.
“I don’t think he was firing blindly, these were deliberate shots. He had a sort of police mask on and goggles on. Then he shot at the church and fled towards Grodzka Street. Everyone was running away from there, people in horse-drawn carriages.”
One man described how several people cowered for safety in a police station after the shots rang out.
“I saw shots being fired from the driver’s side window, and smoke was coming out,” the man, who said his name was Konrad, told Interia.
“I ran to the police station in the main market square; when I burst inside, it was full of people hiding on the floor.”
A 67-year-old man called Julek told Reuters that he had narrowly missed being shot himself.
Julek saw a dark car appear suddenly before the driver started shooting at a group of people and drove off.
“If we had been two minutes earlier, we might have been shot,” he said.
The victims of the shooting have yet to be identified.
Mr Kierwinski told journalists on Saturday evening that the suspect was interested in far-right ideology.
“Everything points to the fact that the shooter was influenced by far-right ideology, a matter that will also be subject to investigation,” he said. “Police officers are on-site, as are agents from the Internal Security Agency, both here at the scene and at the individual’s family home.”
Police spokesperson Andrzej Fijolek told private broadcaster TVN 24 that the assailant used an AR-15 rifle and that he had a firearms licence.
A period of national mourning will take place on Sunday and Monday.

Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has achieved another significant milestone at the worldwide box office. The much-awaited mythological epic has entered the Top 5 highest-grossing Bollywood films of 2026 worldwide, accumulating an impressive Rs. 412.77 crores gross globally. The film, which released on Thursday, November 5, has achieved the feat within just four days, establishing itself among the year's biggest commercial performers.
According to the latest worldwide box office rankings, Ramayana occupies the fifth position, behind Dhurandhar The Revenge, Drishyam The Conclusion, Border 2 and Hanuman Ansh.
The Ranbir Kapoor–Yash starrer has collected Rs. 211.53 crores nett in India, translating into domestic gross collections of Rs. 254.86 crores. Overseas markets have contributed another Rs. 157.91 crores gross, taking the worldwide total to Rs. 412.77 crores.
Ranveer Singh's Dhurandhar The Revenge continues to occupy the top position among Bollywood's worldwide grossers of 2026. The blockbuster has amassed a staggering Rs. 1,852.44 crores globally, including Rs. 1,376.51 crores gross from India and Rs. 475.93 crores from overseas markets.
Drishyam The Conclusion occupies the second position with worldwide collections of Rs. 575.75 crores. The film accumulated Rs. 371.39 crores nett in India, with domestic gross collections of Rs. 442.13 crores. Overseas territories contributed Rs. 133.62 crores. Border 2 ranks third with Rs. 464.50 crores worldwide, comprising Rs. 406.79 crores gross from India and Rs. 57.71 crores overseas. Meanwhile, Hanuman Ansh occupies the fourth position with a worldwide gross of Rs. 442.50 crores. Its India nett collections stand at Rs. 325.98 crores, while international markets contributed Rs. 54.43 crores.
One of the most interesting aspects of the ranking is Ramayana's substantial overseas contribution. Of its Rs. 412.77 crore worldwide gross, approximately 38.26% has come from international markets. This is considerably higher than the overseas contribution of several films ranked above it. For comparison, overseas markets account for approximately 12.42% of Border 2's worldwide collections and 12.30% of Hanuman Ansh's total. Even Drishyam The Conclusion, which ranks second globally, has generated approximately 23.21% of its worldwide business from overseas territories. This makes Ramayana's international performance a particularly important component of its early box office success.

On November 3, Soumya Pathak, 23, a final-year medical student studying at a medical college in Ambala, Haryana, is exploring exhibits showcasing relics from prehistoric times at the Bihar Museum in Patna. Pathak belongs to Muzaffarpur in Bihar, and is looking at some coins from the Mauryan (321–185 B.C.E) and Gupta ages (early 4th to mid-6th Century C.E.).
She passes through interactive galleries which highlight Bihar’s pivotal role in shaping two major world religions: Jainism and Buddhism. “I have been thinking of coming here for a long time, but after reading on social media that the museum is ranked the best in Asia, I decided to spend a day here,” she says. Pathak is enroute to Muzaffarpur for the Deepavali holidays and came to the museum directly from Patna’s Jay Prakash Narayan airport, about four kilometres away. Pathak is proud of her State that is often in the news for poverty and violence.
