More than eight months into the war between the United States and Iran, several countries have stepped forward to broker a deal and take part in regional efforts to end the conflict and prevent further escalation. While Pakistan took a prominent role in the diplomatic push, with leaders from both sides meeting in Islamabad in April, another country that had largely worked behind the scenes is now positioning itself as a key mediator in talks between Washington and Tehran: Qatar. The Gulf nation had previously distanced itself from direct mediation efforts after coming under attack from Iran, saying that it would support Pakistan-led efforts. However, it has since re-engaged in the diplomatic process and is continuing its efforts to prevent further escalation. On Friday (local time), Qatari Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani said during a public interview at Oxford University that mediation efforts remain active to prevent a major escalation in the region. He warned that the crisis “cannot be left unresolved”, Al Jazeera reported. Thani said, "For the past couple of weeks, we have worked with colleagues in the US administration who have very genuine intentions to find a way to contain the situation and de-escalate it”. He further said that mediation efforts continue "to prevent the situation from spiralling out of control," and added, "thanks also to some wise voices in Tehran, we have prevented that from getting out of control”. The Qatari PM's remarks came a day after Reuters reported that Iran had sent the US a nuclear proposal via Qatar. The proposal is to be discussed only after Washington agrees to meet Tehran's seven demands, which Iran included in a seven-day ceasefire proposal in September that US President Donald Trump rejected. The latest proposal highlights Qatar's growing involvement in efforts to bring Washington and Tehran closer to an agreement. However, Doha's role in the diplomatic process has not always been as prominent, with the Gulf nation initially reluctant to take on direct mediation after coming under Iranian attack. Earlier in March this year, nearly a month after the US and Israel launched a joint operation against Iran, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson told Reuters that there was no direct Qatari mediation between the two countries, but added that Doha supported all formal and informal diplomatic channels to end the war. However, two months later, a Qatari negotiating team visited Iran in May, in coordination with the US, to try to help secure a deal to end the war and resolve outstanding issues, Reuters reported. Doha, which has worked as a mediator in the Gaza war and other areas of international tension, had distanced itself from playing a mediation role after coming under attack from Iranian missiles and drones. According to a report by The National News dated June 16, Doha, which hosts the largest US base in the region and has a long history of acting as a diplomatic bridge between adversaries, changed its stance in May. It reportedly refused to enter negotiations under Iranian fire but hosted an Iranian delegation after a ceasefire was in place to discuss the release of frozen funds. Qatar's re-engagement came despite Iran having launched hundreds of missiles and drones at the country, targeting civilian infrastructure and its vital liquefied natural gas (LNG) production facility at Ras Laffan. The attack wiped out roughly 17% of the country's LNG export capacity. Qatar had already halted LNG production on March 2 following Iranian strikes. A report by The New Arab dated June 16, citing analysts and diplomats, said Qatar's role was less about formal mediation this time and focused more on facilitating communication. Tehran received several high-level Qatari delegations, with one visit taking place just hours before the agreement was announced. Discussions during earlier trips centred on key issues that had stalled negotiations, including Iran's nuclear programme, frozen assets, regional security and arrangements for navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani also visited Washington twice, first in late March and then again in mid-May. During the visits, he held discussions with US Vice President JD Vance on the regional conflict and the conditions needed to reach an agreement. In another diplomatic engagement in late May, Doha welcomed a senior Iranian delegation comprising Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati. The talks reportedly addressed the release of frozen Iranian assets, maritime security, confidence-building measures, and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Doha's renewed diplomatic involvement comes at a crucial time as Washington and Tehran continue to explore a way out of the conflict despite disagreements over the Islamic Republic's nuclear programme and other regional issues. While Pakistan has played a prominent public role in the peace efforts, Doha's ability to maintain communication with both sides has made it an important part of the diplomatic process. Whether its latest efforts can help bridge the remaining differences and bring the two countries closer to an agreement remains to be seen. The new sports debuting at Africa's first Olympics
- Published
After a spectacular opening ceremony which celebrated Senegalese national identity and wider African culture on Saturday, the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics are in full swing.
The continent's first ever Olympic event is showcasing new sports which have never appeared at any version of the Games before and has offered athletes predominantly aged 15 to 17 a place in the history books.
First-time Olympic medallists have been crowned in baseball5 and wushu taolu, while some of the rowers who secured places on the podium in coastal beach sprint events may well be eyeing up potential glory at the senior Los Angeles 2028 Games.
BBC Sport Africa examines what has attracted the most attention during the first week of competition.
Wushu taolu
Arguably the most eye-catching sport on show in Senegal has been this modern Chinese martial art, better known around the world as kung fu and practiced competitively in two forms via choreographed sequences or sparring.
Promoted by the government of the People's Republic of China to encourage friendly international exchange, the International Wushu Federation was established in 1990 to formalise centuries-old disciplines popularised by the likes of movie stars Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Michelle Yeoh.
Wushu has featured as an exhibition event or part of the cultural programme at past Games, but medals in changquan and tajiquan were up for grabs on its official debut as an Olympic sport.
Changquan combines speed, kicks, jumps and acrobatics while taijiquan is akin to tai chi and involves controlled movements which flow together in a precise performance set to music.
National team uniforms were dispensed with to allow competitors to wear their own flowing robes, which were often brightly coloured and enhanced with detailed designs.
"Everybody has a different kind of flavour to their moves," the United States' Marshall Brayton said.
"I think that uniqueness in every person's routine is the essence of wushu."
As jumps, flips and flourishes with weaponry caught the eye in changquan, setting moves to music came with its own challenges in tajiquan.
"I was advised to sleep to the song (used in performance)," eventual champion Zhe Nin Ng of Singapore said after day two of competition.
"I had to understand it more and have it in my muscle memory. I keep playing it again and again until I fall asleep."
- All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics 
  - Published26 October
Rowing coastal beach sprints
While rowing has been an Olympic staple since 1900, a new twist has been added with the arrival of this discipline on Senegal's Atlantic coast.
The competition begins on dry land with an athlete running down the beach, boarding their boat and rowing out 250m to a marker buoy before turning sharply and racing back.
Once they return to shore, they then jump out of the boat and sprint back up the beach to touch a buzzer on the finish line. The fastest time wins.
"It's super fun. It's a lot more exciting than traditional rowing," 17-year-old USA's Isaac Moos told Olympics.com.
"Things can change in an instant."
Beachfront spectators have the benefit of being able to witness a whole race and the unpredictability of sea conditions adds an extra element to competition.
"The waves are constantly changing and one small mistake can cost you," said Su Juntao, who won gold for China in the mixed double sculls.
"You have to push for more speed while keeping your mistakes to a minimum. That's what makes it so challenging and exciting."
And this is just the start for coastal rowing at the Olympics, because it is set to replace the lightweight double sculls category at LA 2028.
Baseball5
Baseball will also be included on the schedule in California in four years' time, but an urban, simplified version of the sport kicked off the action in Dakar last Friday.
Introduced to increase accessibility and taking inspiration from street games, the five-a-side version does not require equipment and featured mixed-gender teams on its Olympic debut.
With no pitcher, players for the 'batting' side using their hand to hit the rubber ball from a standing position on an 18m x 18m court featuring four bases.
There are no strikes, meaning each 'batter' gets just one chance to hit the ball legally as they attempt to score as many runs as possible before their team suffers three outs.
Played over five innings, it is faster-paced than its bigger brother and skills are rewarded over strength.
Cuba, the nation at the top of the all-time Olympic baseball medal table with three golds, fittingly opened the competition with a victory over Turkey.
"We have baseball running through our veins and in our hearts, and we will always, always, always put Cuba at the top," player Jean Carlos Machado Casado told Olympics.com.
Other firsts
While Olympics fans are used to seeing beach volleyball, two more traditional sports have been given a twist in Senegal.
Handball and wresting events have also been relocated to Saly's beach, known for its fine sand and turquoise waters.
Featured in continental and world championships, and promotional events organised by governing body United World Wrestling, beach wrestling fittingly makes its Youth Olympics debut in Senegal, where traditional forms of wrestling remain incredibly popular.
Two athletes contest bouts inside a circular area on sand, scoring points through throws, takedowns, or forcing the opponent out of bounds.
Matches, to be contested this weekend, are expected to be short and fast-paced.
Eight-a-side handball, which also featured at the Buenos Aires Youth Games in 2018, will be among the final events contested at Dakar 2026.
Skateboarding, first included in the senior Olympic schedule at Tokyo 2020, also made its Youth Games debut in Dakar.

A video featuring Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is being circulated on social media. In the video, Lavrov allegedly describes India as merely a trading partner, stating that India is neither a Russian ally nor a superpower and has no right to interfere in or advise Russia on its foreign policy decisions concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States, or other countries (here, here, here). Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated that India is neither a Russian ally nor a superpower and has no right to interfere in or advise Russia on its foreign policy decisions concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States, or other countries.
Fact: The viral clip has been digitally manipulated by altering the original footage and adding fabricated statements about India’s relations with Russia. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A keyword search related to the viral claim led to no credible reports confirming that Sergey Lavrov made such statements.
Further, we conducted a search using the ‘M World’ logo visible at the top of the viral clip. This led us to the M World News Instagram page, where we found the original video featuring Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. The video was posted with the caption, “Lavrov Fires Back Over Claims Putin Refuses to Meet Zelensky.”
Based on this clue, we found in the original footage that Lavrov dismisses claims that Russian President Vladimir Putin is refusing to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He emphasises that any potential negotiations must address the underlying issues. During the briefing, he discussed US-Russia relations, possible peace talks on Ukraine, and international diplomatic responses (here, here).
Upon closer examination of the video, we noticed certain inconsistencies, particularly that Lavrov’s lip movements do not appear to be properly synchronised with the audio.
To further verify the video’s authenticity, we analysed it using multiple AI detection tools. Hive Moderation’s AI-generated content detector gave an aggregate score of 99.4%, indicating that the media likely contained AI-generated or deepfake content. Similarly, NVIDIA’s Synthetic Video Detector classified the footage as synthetic media.
To sum up, this Video of Sergey Lavrov making derogatory remarks about India is digitally manipulated.

Winter’s knocking? Cold front to slash Hong Kong temperatures to 16 degrees
New Territories are expected to be cooler, with temperatures in Ta Kwu Ling dropping to as low as 13 degrees
Temperatures in Hong Kong are forecast to plunge to as low as 16 degrees Celsius (61 Fahrenheit) on Tuesday, a further drop from an earlier prediction, as a cold front is expected to hit the city early this week.
The Hong Kong Observatory on Sunday revised its forecast for the coming week, saying it expected an intense northeast monsoon to bring cool, very dry weather to the city. An earlier forecast had put this week’s lowest temperature at 18 degrees.
“A cold front will move across the coast of Guangdong at first tomorrow. Under the influence of the associated intense northeast monsoon, winds will strengthen from the north and temperatures will fall appreciably over the region,” the forecaster said.

New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.
On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.
But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.
Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.
With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind.
Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.
Labour, led by Chris Hipkins, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.
Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.
“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour.
The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.
Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition.
Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance.
That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee, will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.
On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.
With all the extra seats, there could be 130 in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.
The country faces a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Luxon said caretaker government conventions would apply in the meantime.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well-established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
- Published
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.
"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."
In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhihia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

A new British startup believes that artificial intelligence is the key to speedrunning the slow and temperamental process of drug design.
Potential Sciences plans to build large-scale chemical datasets by using basic principles of physics to simulate interactions between atoms, then small molecules, then complex amino acids and proteins. With that data, it’s betting it can train AI models and prediction systems capable of identifying highly targeted drugs for specific diseases, bypassing costly and time-consuming lab experimentation.
“We want molecules that are never going to work in the clinic to fail fast,” Hatem Helal, Potential Sciences founder and CEO, tells WIRED. “That means having better predictors of how they will behave as they interact with human biology.”
The startup, which launched on November 5, says it has seed funding in the tens of millions of dollars from SovAI—the UK government’s AI venture capital fund—and Twin Path Ventures, among other investors. The founders declined to disclose the precise figure or valuation.
If things pan out as Potential Sciences hopes, it could pave the way for the accelerated development of new treatments for all sorts of diseases. By reducing the cost of experimentation, Helal says, the company’s approach could also make it economical for pharmaceutical companies to pursue drugs for rare conditions that have previously gone untreated.
“We want to make it possible to have more bespoke treatments for diseases—this idea that medicines can be one-off molecular combinations that are tailored to your unique human biology,” he says.
The question is whether Potential Sciences will be able to predict how well drug candidates will bind to disease-related proteins as accurately as it hopes, which would require a marked leap forward.
“I’m sure it will be an improvement,” says Peter Wolynes, a professor of chemistry at Rice University. But currently, “the engineering is at the level of the Romans, not of the Renaissance, in terms of how protein engineering is done,” he says.
Industry luminaries like Demis Hassabis, who won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for his work at Google DeepMind, have long said that advances in AI will eventually lead to momentous scientific breakthroughs, in the same way the technology has recently carved up mathematics. The hope among startups like Potential Sciences is that drug discovery will be one of the first scientific frontiers to be transformed by the technology.
At the moment, a large proportion of AI drug discovery labs are developing models on top of a single public database of 3D atomic structures—the Protein Data Bank—which researchers have expanded over decades with the results of new experiments. The problem, according to Helal, is that the dataset remains too small to train AI models advanced enough to reliably accelerate the search for viable drug candidates.
“Of all the atoms in the universe, there’s around 1060 ways that you could assemble them into molecules that you could potentially give to a human,” says Helal. “Think of drug discovery as a search problem; it’s about how fast you can navigate and prune that space into promising molecules for a particular disease.”
To address that issue, Potential Sciences is trying to construct far larger datasets made up of synthetic data, produced by simulating interactions between different chemical compounds. From far larger pools of data, the theory goes, the startup will be able to train far more advanced AI models and prediction systems.
Academics see the potential in the simulation-based approach that Potential Sciences has adopted. “If we could calculate accurately the interactions between all molecules in the cell and the fluctuations in their structure we could predict where molecules would bind and that would indeed revolutionize drug development,” says Alan Fersht, an emeritus professor of chemistry at the University of Cambridge who specializes in protein engineering. “I am optimistic that this will eventually happen.”
In receiving investment from SovAI, Potential Sciences joins fellow AI drug discovery companies Basecamp Research and Isomorphic Labs, and materials discovery startup CuspAI.
The UK government established SovAI earlier this year with a mandate to invest in British startups capable of becoming indispensable components of the global AI supply chain, affording the country vital geopolitical leverage. The fund has at its disposal roughly $800 million and the ability to offer its portfolio companies access to the UK’s national AI supercomputer.
“Coming at drug discovery from a physics angle—the physics of chemistry—sets [Potential Sciences] apart from other companies,” says Joséphine Kant, head of ventures at SovAI, who has joined the startup’s board as part of the investment. “Giving them access to computing resources, they can do this work at a scale that would be very difficult otherwise for a small startup.”
However, AI drug discovery is a crowded market. Even with a leg up from the UK government, Potential Sciences will face steep competition from a multitude of entrepreneurs and academics racing to solve the same bottlenecks from varying angles of approach.
Nor does the ability to more quickly identify promising drug candidates eliminate the cost and time required to test their safety and efficacy, meaning new treatments will continue to take a long time to come to market, regardless of advances in AI. “The cost of designing a drug is nothing compared to figuring out what it will do to mice; to really sick patients; to normal people,” says Wolynes. “In some sense, it’s not the rate-limiting phenomenon.”
As the field progresses, startups like Potential Sciences will also have to contend with the prospect that technologies able to identify effective treatments could be abused to develop highly dangerous chemicals, too. “If we can design tools that perfectly minimize toxicity, it’s a bit flip to maximize it as well,” Helal says.
Potential Sciences doesn’t yet have all the answers. The startup hasn’t settled on a way to generate revenue from the various technologies it’s developing nor decided whether to make its models freely available, given the potential for misuse. But Helal is convinced that there are few more worthwhile problems to try to remedy with AI.
“There have been many waves of promising breakthroughs that don’t quite have an impact in drug discovery,” says Helal. “It’s a fundamental, high-impact problem for us to try and solve.”

Growing up, I dabbled in gymnastics and ice skating but never joined a team or had formal training. When I had children, I wasn't opposed to any of the four of them playing sports if they wanted to, but it wasn't a priority.
My oldest three showed a fleeting interest in athletics, but nothing ever stuck. We tried soccer for tots, tennis in early elementary school, a rec basketball team that anyone could walk on to, and Girls on the Run, a non-competitive program for young girls. However, none of my younger kids showed much interest in playing at a higher level in a club.
I briefly looked into club sports, but lost all interest once I discovered they cost thousands of dollars and require an extensive time commitment from the entire family on weeknights and weekends. That's particularly true for travel teams, which involve more serious coaching and play than rec teams.
I never regretted not signing my kids up for tryouts until my youngest son developed a passion for soccer and dove headlong into the sport. Now I see what my older kids were missing, and I regret not encouraging them to try club sports, too.
I reluctantly signed my son up for a club team
My son started playing soccer during recess at school. Before long, he was taking a skills class and playing soccer after school, too. Then came a rec team. He had fun, but I didn't feel like the parent leading the team had enough coaching experience to help him improve. My son trained hard in our backyard and at school, and his skills soon surpassed his teammates. In fourth grade, he asked to try out for a club with an advanced travel team. He already had a passion for the sport and showed talent, but I still hesitated before saying yes.
The cost and grueling schedule gave me pause, and I wasn't sure I wanted him to focus heavily on one activity while he was still so young. Nevertheless, I begrudgingly filled out the necessary paperwork and drove him to multiple rounds of tryouts. Part of me hoped he wouldn't get a spot, but I wanted to give him the chance to shine.
When the email offering my son a place on the team arrived, I surprised myself by being thrilled. After getting over my sticker shock and confusion about how club sports actually work, I handed over my credit card and, just like that, we were all in. I bought my son multiple uniforms and worked out a complex schedule with my husband to get our son to practices and games near and far.
I learned that club sports offer benefits that go far beyond better training
Since joining a club team over a year ago, my son has improved tremendously in soccer, as expected. While he may never achieve his goal of playing in the World Cup, he now passes with precision and defends the ball admirably.
In a short time, I've also noticed how the benefits of a club sport go far beyond better coaching. At least three times a week, I watch from the sidelines as my son takes direction and correction with grace. Being open to suggestions for improvement is a new skill I see spilling over into other parts of life, whether it's ideas about keeping his homework organized or a better approach to keeping his room clean.
Additionally, although I love seeing my son's joy when his team wins, he is slowly but surely learning to handle losses better, too. Instead of getting upset immediately as he used to, he now talks through what he could have done differently. Sometimes, he accepts that his team simply had bad luck or that an unfair referee made a win more difficult than it should have been. I see these skills spilling over into other parts of his life when things don't go his way.
More on youth sports
He has also dealt with adversity, playing in the cold and rain, dealing with aches and pains, and sometimes playing with teammates he doesn't like very much. This has taught him the importance of pushing through unpleasant circumstances and finding a way to get along with everyone. I've also seen my son shift from wanting to be the team's star player to wanting to be a part of something bigger than himself through cooperation and teamwork. Plus, being part of a team has given a whole new group of friends outside of school.
Club sports are a sacrifice, but it's one I wish I had made for my older kids, too
More than a year into our club sports journey, my only regrets are not starting sooner and not giving my older children the same opportunities my youngest has now. I recognize what a privilege it is to offer my son this experience, something many families can't afford because of the cost and time commitment.
Sometimes I lament having to plan my family's entire weekend around soccer matches and feeling rushed on so many weeknights, but I have no plans to stop and would do it again in a heartbeat. I've surprised myself by feeling disappointment when a weekend goes by and I can't watch my son play. I'm excited to see where my son's club sports journey takes him next, and what other lessons he will learn along the way.

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing side effects of cancer treatment in children. Preventing them is essential not only to improve quality of life, but also to help patients complete treatment. Yet the medicines used to prevent vomiting can themselves cause adverse effects, making the search for safe alternatives an important challenge in paediatric oncology.
An Indian multicentre clinical trial suggests that olanzapine may offer an alternative to dexamethasone, a corticosteroid routinely used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy — treatment with a high risk of inducing vomiting. The current regimen using dexamethasone is a guideline that is used regularly, but dexamethasone is a corticosteroid. The study was aimed at finding a comparable, non-corticosteroid option.

During the final stretch of his campaign to protect Republican fortunes in the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance adjusted his approach, speaking less about President Donald Trump and focusing more on the issues defining his own political identity.
Vance framed his argument for Republicans, who ultimately lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote, almost entirely through his own policy portfolio, according to a review of six speeches delivered since the Republican convention in September.
He bypassed signature White House policies, including deportations and the war in Iran, as public polling indicated that the president's declining popularity was dragging down Republican candidates.
Two sources familiar with the strategy described the pivot as intentional. Vance and his advisers viewed his primary themes—economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint, and public safety—as potent topics he could address with authority. While Trump integrated those concepts into his MAGA platform, Vance had positioned himself as their chief proponent, the sources noted.
This tactical change offers an early look at how the 42-year-old vice president could chart an independent course as Republicans begin to look beyond Trump.
Vance has not stated whether he intends to run for president in 2028, and Trump has offered no endorsements. Nevertheless, Vance is considered a premier potential contender who party officials say must inherit much of Trump’s coalition while distancing himself from his superior's political liabilities.
Vance moved more publicly on Wednesday to reinforce his personal political brand with a strikingly candid election postmortem. Writing on social media, he attributed the Republican defeat to the Iran war and laid out a strategy for a party recovery.
He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to concentrate on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations, and reform the US relationship with Israel.
Trump, by contrast, has previously described voter concerns over affordability as a Democratic "hoax." He launched the military intervention in Iran following prolonged lobbying by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom Trump later endorsed in the Israeli election.
The online post marked the first time Vance openly advocated for concluding the war.
Three individuals familiar with White House and vice-presidential communications said the vice president was not breaking with Trump, adding that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles had advance knowledge of Vance’s message.
On Friday, however, Trump restructured his senior White House team, replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller—a movement suggesting the administration intends to double down on several hardline positions.
While Trump acknowledged that high gas prices resulting from the Iran war contributed to the Republican defeat, he defended the conflict. "I would have done nothing different," he told reporters on Wednesday.
It could not be confirmed whether Trump was informed of Vance's statement beforehand.
Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, publicly backed Vance's commentary on social media, alongside several conservative allies.
The exchange has further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, according to Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan.
Ricci noted that Vance’s intervention pushed conservatives to debate the merits of the conflict and consider which core principles Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028.
"It’s simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump," Ricci said. "This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate."
Spokespeople for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred inquiries to Trump's Wednesday remarks, in which he expressed an understanding of Vance's view on the election results.
Democrats are preparing to link Vance—or any eventual Republican nominee—directly to Trump in 2028, particularly if the president remains central to vetting potential contenders.
"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring," said Democratic strategist Igor Volsky.
Vance’s personal brand did not come through the midterms completely unblemished. Republicans suffered losses in states where he stumped, and some tactics he supported—including an ad from Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy casting doubt on sexual abuse reported by victorious Democratic candidate Amy Acton—may have turned voters away from Republicans.
Other prospective 2028 contenders have shared their own diagnoses of the defeat. US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said Republicans had failed to do enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis argued that defeated candidates spent too much time on transgender issues while overlooking voter concerns regarding data centers and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has remained silent.
Vance's push to frame the conversation was evident throughout the campaign's final days.
In stump speeches, he told voters to back Republicans to ensure investigations into fraud within federal healthcare and antipoverty programs, connecting those topics to cost of living and the White House's immigration agenda. He largely ignored gas prices and the Iran war, and rarely mentioned Trump by name.
"I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the simple things," Vance told one of his final rallies in North Carolina. "And because I want that for me, I want it for you too."

What needs to happen for Canada to join Europe's flagship student exchange program?
EU wants Canada to fully join Erasmus+, but there are details Canada must iron out
Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe.
At last month's Canada-EU summit and in his 2026 budget, Prime Minister Mark Carney reaffirmed the government's interest in expanding Canada's participation in Erasmus+, Europe's internationally recognized student and skills exchange.
"Through this program, a Canadian student can pursue their studies in Barcelona just as easily as they could at McGill," Carney said at the summit in Montreal.
An expert in European integration says the prospect is complex and likely to be expensive — but that it would come with major benefits for Canada's youth and deepening ties with the EU.
Through Erasmus+, students in the EU and select other countries have direct access to funding, institutions and grants that help cover travel and living costs when participating in exchange programs between institutions.
Students are also exempted from the fees for tuition, registration and exams that a Canadian exchange student might typically pay to study in Europe.
But Erasmus+ isn't just an opportunity for students. Its benefits extend to people starting their careers across a wide range of fields, including trainees, apprentices, youth workers and academic staff.
"An apprentice welder in Manitoba could bring or complete their placement with an employer in Italy, bringing new skills home," Carney said.
Many Canadian universities are already partnered with Erasmus+ through independent agreements, but they're limited mostly to exchange opportunities for master's students and faculty members.
Further participation in Erasmus+ could expand funding opportunities for undergraduates as well as youth, training and sport exchanges — all of which are available to EU members and the program's current six associate countries.
How would this work?
Oliver Schmidtke, a University of Victoria professor specializing in European integration, called Canada's proposed involvement in Erasmus+ "a lot of ambition."
"Education is largely a provincial thing in Canada, so how this would land and how the federal government would interact with provincial governments in trying to regulate this … that's a whole range of questions that are open," Schmidtke said.
And buying into an international exchange program isn't exactly cheap. The United Kingdom is rejoining in January and will pay over $1 billion for its first year.
Canadian universities would have to "pay substantial amounts to be eligible for the full array of services" and provide housing supports and staff to accommodate the Erasmus+ students coming to Canada, Schmidtke said.
The provinces and European Union would also have to iron out credit transfers for participating students — no simple feat.
All current Erasmus+ members and associated third countries follow the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS), simplifying the academic credit transfer process.
When the United Kingdom rejoins, it will be using its own system, but has set up a national framework for how credits will be transferred.
In Canada, even credit transfers between institutions within the same province aren't consistent.

This work would come at time of "a lot of financial stress at Canadian universities," Schmidtke said.
He said some of that comes from a reduced number of international students in Canada in recent years — who generally pay higher tuition rates directly to the institutions.
Carney has indicated that the expected costs of joining Erasmus+ won't stop Canada from pursuing that goal. Joining was one of the most concrete examples Carney gave when he announced in September that Canada was pursuing an "alliance for the future" with the EU.
"We don't view this as paying for something," Carney said in Montreal about the overall costs of closer EU integration. "We view this as coming together."
Despite these potential complications, Schmidtke believes integration with Erasmus+ will be an "invaluable opportunity" for Canadian students.
"Canada is a bit behind the curve when it comes to internationalizing student experiences, mobility and so forth," Schmidtke said. "So the Erasmus+ program could be a great incentive to expand the international experience of many Canadian students."
Some Canadian universities already involved
The University of Victoria, University of Waterloo, McMaster University, Simon Fraser University, University of Toronto, University of British Columbia and the University of Calgary told CBC News they would be open to exploring participation — or further participation, as some already partner with Erasmus+ — as more details become available.
Western University president Alan Shepard said international engagement is a key part of the student experience at Western, and the university was excited about the opportunities Erasmus+ could create.
"We encourage our students to see themselves as global citizens through opportunities to study, conduct research and gain hands-on experience around the world," Shepard said.
In late October, Université Laval rector Sophie D'Amours and Sorbonne University president Nathalie Drach-Temam penned an open letter in La Presse encouraging the government to integrate Canadian universities into the program.
"The Sorbonne is the oldest French-language university in Europe. Université Laval is the oldest French-language university in the Americas. Our traditions are strong, as is our capacity to help address the challenges of tomorrow," the letter said.
By joining forces, we will be even better placed to promote the common good that universities represent for society."

New Zealanders won't know for weeks who won the election as neither side secures clear victory
New Zealanders face weeks of uncertainty after Saturday's election, with no clear winner emerging
WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday’s election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.
The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon's center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday's numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.
The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand's economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.
Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday's results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.
Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, “who won the election 2026” was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won’t begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they’ve won.
With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon's National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn't claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.
Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand's trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters' rancor over living costs.
Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn't appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.
Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.
Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can't be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.
“I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks,” Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.
Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party.
Several of National's most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party's traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.
Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.
New Zealanders don't vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.
The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand's direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.
National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separateconfidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.
However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.
Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.
The total number of seats in New Zealand's Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.
Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.
Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc's seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.
Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

On Nov. 1, two days before the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the conservative political commentator Tucker Carlson posted (archived) on X that "the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran."
In a more than 700-word post, Carlson claimed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was seeking to pressure U.S. President Donald Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and U.S. Central Command head Brad Cooper to take out Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected key location in Iran's nuclear program, using a nuclear bomb.
According to Carlson's "informed observer," Trump could make a decision on whether to carry out a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain as soon as Nov. 7.
Carlson's post also circulated on Facebook and Bluesky (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about Carlson's claim.
At the time of this writing, neither the Trump administration nor the Pentagon had confirmed that the president was considering using nuclear force against Iran.
The U.S. has not used nuclear power in warfare since dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, a move that forced a Japanese surrender and led to the end of World War II. Over the past month, Trump has given mixed signals in media interviews about his plans for ending the war in Iran, but has not suggested he was considering using nuclear force.
Experts warned that using nuclear force against Iran would have a devastating impact on the entire Middle East region, could inspire existing nuclear powers like Russia or China to use their arsenal in conflicts in Ukraine and elsewhere and would lead to a nuclear arms race.
A White House spokesperson said in an email to Snopes on Nov. 5:
President Trump has a wide range of options available regarding Iran, and he will do what is right to keep the American people safe. Tucker Carlson lost his way long ago due to a debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome, and he has no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief's thinking.
We contacted the Department of Defense to ask whether Carlson's post was true. We also contacted Carlson to ask about the credibility of his anonymous source and any updates he had gotten on the situation since publishing his initial post on Nov. 1. We await replies to our queries.
Why is Pickaxe Mountain important?
Though there was no proof that the Trump administration would use nuclear power to do so, Trump has been considering striking Pickaxe Mountain — the target Carlson claimed would require nuclear force — since at least July. For example, on July 21, Trump told reporters at the White House (time code 26:34), "We'll be hitting that area pretty soon and very heavily."
In September, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan think tank, wrote that Israeli intelligence reportedly indicated that Iranian authorities moved "uranium centrifuges and centrifuge parts," which are necessary to enrich uranium for commercial or combat use, to Pickaxe Mountain, which is near the Natanz nuclear facility.
At the time, the think tank wrote that Pickaxe Mountain would be "difficult" to destroy "even with the heaviest non-nuclear U.S. munitions." The facility is reportedly buried deep in a granite mountain and the U.S. does not have access to blueprints that would give away its size and shape, or whether it has weak points like the ventilation shafts the U.S. targeted at the Fordo nuclear facility during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025.
Trump has repeatedly said since the start of the war in Iran that his and Netanyahu's primary goal is that Iran does not get access to enough enriched uranium to obtain a nuclear weapon. To achieve this aim, the U.S. and Israel would need to curtail Iran's nuclear material and capabilities like the site at Pickaxe Mountain through either force or diplomacy.
Carlson's post suggested without proof that the Trump administration was weighing up using its ultimate military power to achieve its aims in Iran.
Mixed signals about Trump's next steps in Iran
Trump has given mixed signals about how he wants to approach his and Netanyahu's goals in Iran. By October, Trump was still saying that he wanted to strike Pickaxe Mountain, though no reports suggested such a strike had taken place.
For example, Trump told Newsmax on Oct. 15, "We're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there. We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast."
Starting after Oct. 20, several U.S. news outlets reported that the Trump administration was drawing up plans for strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. These reports did not say that Trump was considering using nuclear force.
In fact, Trump said on Oct. 15, in response to a question about whether he would use tactical nuclear weapons in Iran, "No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to."
This remark could suggest that the U.S. had non-nuclear ways of destroying Pickaxe Mountain or that Trump wanted to allow time for diplomatic negotiations to take place.
However, by the start of November, PBS reported that negotiations between Washington and Tehran on a deal to end the war were "tense." According to the report, Washington wanted early assurances that Iran would not develop a nuclear weapon, while Tehran wanted to defer the issue for later talks.
On Nov. 2, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi appeared to signal that the ball was in the U.S.'s court. He reportedly said:
We have put forward our conditions and proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political judgement. If it opts for sincere diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if it intends to resort to deception or military action, it will face a response more bitter and more severe than before.
Carlson published his post alleging that the U.S. was considering a nuclear resolution to the war in Iran that same day.
By Nov. 3, despite the October reports that the U.S. was planning strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, Trump reportedly told the Financial Times that the U.S. seemed to be "getting everything we want" in diplomatic negotiations and had no plans for immediate strikes.
However, that same day, Trump also told Fox News (time code 13:57) the U.S. had to "do something large" in the war with Iran. He did not specify whether "something large" was in reference to diplomacy or military attacks, but did add, "A lot of people would like to do the heavy hitting."
Trump must balance input from Tel Aviv and Washington
It was unclear from Trump's Election Day interview with Fox News who "a lot of people" were, or who exactly the president was taking advice from on the war in Iran.
On Oct. 28, news broke that U.S. Vice President JD Vance reportedly sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's top security body, in a bid to restart peace talks. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance sent the letter at Trump's request, though Trump himself appeared to suggest it was Vance's idea. Either way, the letter suggested the U.S. had not given up on the idea of a diplomatic solution to the war in Iran.
On Nov. 1, Carlson claimed that Netanyahu had pressured both Trump and other officials, including Hegseth, to use nuclear power in Iran. PBS reported that there had been "growing fears" that Netanyahu could be pushing Trump to escalate the conflict in Iran.
Netanyahu, whose coalition failed to secure a majority in Israel's October elections, will lose his position as prime minister if he cannot form a 61-seat majority in the Knesset. PBS reported that Netanyahu could be, "pushing for new strikes against Iran in an effort to stay in power in an emergency government during renewed war." Snopes has not independently verified this claim.
Trump reportedly spoke to Netanyahu on Oct. 31, the day before Carlson's post, though the details of that call were unclear. However, the Telegraph newspaper reported it was unlikely Netanyahu would have pushed for a nuclear strike on Iran, writing that if Israel "were seen to be involved in any way in breaking the taboo on the use of nuclear weapons, it could rebound horribly. It would take only one strike on Israel to make it unliveable, given that it is such a tiny country."
Therefore, while Netanyahu might have reason to encourage refreshed strikes on Iran, it's unlikely he would push for those strikes to use nuclear weapons.
Ultimately, the mixed reporting throughout October and November and Araghchi's statement on Nov. 2 suggested the U.S. and Iran were preparing for both a diplomatic and a military resolution to the war, potentially developing at the same time. The available evidence did not suggest that the Trump administration, regardless of input from Netanyahu or anyone else, was planning a U.S. nuclear strike on Iran, something that could set off further strikes in the Middle East and Europe and lead to a nuclear arms race.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the war in Iran.

You can attach your Fitbit Air to almost any old-school watch
There are some ways to combine analog watches with Google's lightweight fitness tracker.
There's no need to sacrifice your beloved mechanical watch for fitness tracking. If you own a Fitbit Air, there's a way to attach a traditional watch to the tracker's band, keeping the dial on top of the wrist and the Fitbit sensor tucked underneath. It's a clever solution for those who want fitness tracking without awkwardly wearing a separate device on each wrist.
One user connected the tracker to a Seiko wristwatch, and others have tried various watch designs. The $99.99 Fitbit Air monitors heart rate, exercise and sleep, but doesn't have a screen, and the data is accessible via the Google Health app. Paired with a standard watch, it offers the best of both worlds: a watch face you're used to and the latest in health tracking, without an extra screen to distract you.
How to combine a Fitbit Air with a regular watch
The easiest way is to replace your watch's original strap with the Fitbit Air's 18mm Performance Loop. Remove the current watch band, leave the spring bars on, then slide the Fitbit band under both spring bars, like a NATO-style strap. The watch sits on top of your wrist, with the Fitbit underneath.
Not all watches will play ball, of course. The ideal lug width is 18mm, while watches with 19mm or 20mm between the lugs (where the strap attaches) can work with small gaps on either side of the band. Anything narrower than 18mm won't accommodate the stock strap, while particularly wide watches could look a little ridiculous. You'll also need enough space between the spring bars and the watch case to thread the band through.
If you'd rather keep your existing strap, some users have designed 3D-printed adapters that attach the Fitbit Air's removable sensor underneath regular watch straps. One influencer demonstrated the setup with a Hamilton Khaki Field King while keeping its original strap. The adapter must fit the strap width and hold the tracker securely, especially if you plan to exercise while wearing it.
The compromises worth knowing about
While the concept is great, there are some practical questions about putting the Fitbit Air under the wrist. Google recommends wearing the tracker on top of the wrist for the most accurate readings, but hasn't said whether wearing it underneath is just as accurate. It's also likely to be uncomfortable when you lean on your wrist on a desk or type for extended periods.
Plus, consider swimming. While the Fitbit Air is water-resistant up to 50 meters, your normal watch may not be. Older watch cases and leather straps can have trouble with moisture or perspiration. If you go with the custom approach, a 3D-printed attachment could also come loose during a heavy workout, so it may be better to use the original Fitbit band for exercise.
The tweak doesn't change the Fitbit Air's app requirements, though. You'll still need to have a Google Account and the Google Health app to access your fitness data. Basic activity and sleep tracking don't require a subscription, while Google Health Premium adds personalized coaching for $9.99 a month or $99 a year.

(Bloomberg) -- The gunman who killed six people in the historic Old Town district of Poland’s second largest city on Saturday is likely a domestic far-right extremist, according to Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski.
The alleged perpetrator, a 24-year-old Polish national whose name hasn’t been made public, was injured during an exchange of gunfire with police near the Main Market Square in Krakow and taken to the hospital, where he’s undergoing an operation, Kierwinski said.
The suspect drove onto the main Krakow square in a car and opened fire with an automatic rifle at what appeared to be random targets, according to government officials. Those killed included four women and two men, while a further 16 people were injured, the regional police said. 
Three police officers were injured in the shooting, including one with several wounds in critical condition in a Krakow hospital, Kierwinski said.
“Everything indicates he was fascinated by far-right ideology,” Kierwinski told reporters in Krakow. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Poland was dealing with an act of terrorism.
Video taken by a witness and showed by broadcaster TVN24 showed the suspected shooter apparently injured, laying on a sidewalk, dressed in military gear, a bullet proof vest and with a rifle. The defense minister said the suspect had no links to the Polish military.
Kierwinski said the suspect had a license for a firearm and that his car was full of ammunition and other guns that probably belong to his family. 
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said police are looking into “all the circumstances of the attack,” while President President Karol Nawrocki said he’s in contact with the relevant authorities and expects a full explanation of the circumstances. 
The district in Krakow, a city of some 800,000 located about 250 km (150 miles) south of Warsaw, is a Unesco World Heritage Site known for its medieval architecture. It’s a popular destination for tourists.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.
On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.
“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.
“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”
Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.
“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.
He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.
Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.
Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”
Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.
Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.
Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.
“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.
Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.
Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.
It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.
In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.
Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”
