Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.
On Thursday the one-time MTV host turned Christian and spiritual influencer was found guilty on three counts of sexual assault and one of rape, after a four-week trial that garnered massive media attention.
Brand had denied all charges and said he never had sex without consent.
After the jury handed down the verdict, Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand, 51, that he faced a "significant custodial term."
Danny Shaw, a crime commentator and former BBC correspondent, posted on X that while the maximum sentence for rape in the UK is life, 10 years is the average sentence, and Brand was likely to receive between four to 13 years of prison time.
The trial examined seven historic charges against Brand, brought forward by six different women. He was found guilty on four of the charges: for raping a woman who'd been to one of his comedy shows in 2009, and sexually assaulting three others between 2004 and 2009. The locations of the sexual assaults were a bar, radio station and TV studio. Brand was also found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand's lawyer asked the judge on Thursday to grant his client bail so that he could spend the weekend with his three children, which the judge denied. Instead the one-time celebrity darling spent his first weekend in a prison cell in London.
He showed little emotion when the verdict was handed down, though his wife Laura — who has supported him throughout — quickly left the courtroom.
Many have called the verdict a significant milestone in the #MeToo movement, which has seen influential men held to account for using their power to abuse women.
Brand has also faced allegations of crimes in the United States. In 2023, a woman, named only as "Jane Doe," accused Brand of sexually assaulting her while she was working as a film extra during the making of the 2010 comedy movie "Arthur." That year, Brand married pop star Katy Perry, though the union lasted for just over a year before they divorced.
Addressing the media last week, London police detective Andy Furphy said that Brand had "used his influence, status and fame to prey on women — as his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."
Camilla Long, a journalist for The Sunday Times — one of the first newspapers that investigated allegations of abuse against Brand — wrote in a column this weekend that "To sit in court 3 at Southwark crown court, hearing how Brand grabbed, pushed, groped and degraded his victims, was one of the most disgusting experiences of my life."
Long questioned how Brand got away with his behavior for so long, saying: "Never has a predator so loudly declared himself, yet been so roundly ignored."

Hamirpur (HP), Nov 8: Diwali was celebrated with great enthusiasm across India on Sunday, as homes and streets lit up with lamps, candles and colourful lights. But in Himachal's Sammoo village, the festive excitement was missing. For over 100 years, residents have refrained from celebrating the festival of lights, a tradition they attribute to a longstanding curse that, according to local belief, hangs over the village.
A village elder who has seen more than 72 Diwalis pass without celebration said the villagers have little reason to prepare for the festival. He said that whenever someone tries to celebrate Diwali, misfortune or loss strikes the village. Over generations, this belief has taken deep root, leaving villagers convinced that celebrating Diwali could invite calamities ranging from fires and disasters to untimely deaths.
Savitri Devi, an elderly resident of the village, said, "This tradition is very old. Generations have come and gone, but no one has celebrated Diwali here. A woman from our village committed sati and cursed that Diwali would never be celebrated here. Even today, the fear is so deeply rooted that people refrain from celebrating the festival."
Sati was a historical practice in which a widow immolated herself on her deceased husband's funeral pyre. The practice was subsequently outlawed.
Sachin, a resident, said, "No one cooks special food on Diwali here. If someone tries, something bad happens. There was a time when someone died unexpectedly. Only then do we light lamps in our homes." Sammoo is about 25 kilometres from the Hamirpur district headquarters.
While residents may light lamps, they set off no fireworks and prepare no festive dishes in the village on Diwali. Locals claim that despite attempts to "lift the curse" through rituals, the tradition persists. Many residents remain indoors on Diwali.
Ram Singh, a resident, said, "No one makes preparations for Diwali because celebrating it is taboo here. Attempts to break the tradition have often ended in mishaps, including fires and deaths. As a result, no one dares to celebrate Diwali."
Children grow up knowing Diwali is not celebrated because of the woman's curse.
Anita, a villager, said, "We haven't celebrated Diwali for years. Elders insist it brings disaster if anyone celebrates."
An older person, Raghuveer Singh Rangra, expressed sorrow at the lost tradition. "We feel the joy of Diwali, but cannot celebrate. No decorations, no lights. It has been over 100 years, but the curse holds strong." Vidya Devi, another villager, said, "Every year, when Diwali comes, my heart fills with joy because there are celebrations everywhere. But in our village, no one lights a lamp on this day."
She said that villagers sometimes had to travel to nearby villages to witness how others celebrated Diwali.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

East Bengal and Chennaiyin’s season could not have been more different ahead of their Indian Super League clash. The reigning champion had a 100 per cent record with nine goals scored, while the host was winless in four games, finding the back of the net just once.
But at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium here on Saturday, anyone ignorant of these numbers would have struggled to tell which team was languishing in the bottom half of the table. The Diwali fireworks came early on a humid night in the city as Chennaiyin shocked East Bengal 5-3, powered by braces from Brison Fernandes and Irfan Yadwad.
The visitor, who was coming off a continental defeat in midweek, was given no time to gather their bearings by Chennaiyin, which opened the scoring in the fourth minute.
Loanee Ramon Tanque, who has faced criticism for his lack of output in front of goal so far in the tournament, somewhat redeemed himself after his deft one-touch pass released Yadwad into the right side of the box.
The rest was all too simple for the Indian forward, whose squared pass was astutely left in front of goal by Madil Talal, allowing Brison to come in behind and grab his first goal of the season.
Buoyed by the early advantage, Chennaiyin kept its foot on the pedal, with Talal often joining the forward line to stretch the East Bengal defence. The overload reaped rewards as Ramon and Yadwad sent warning shots, with Prabhsukhan Gill staying alert to deny them.
But the East Bengal custodian could only dive and watch helplessly for what came in the 18th minute.
Brimming with confidence, Brison took the ball from Talal on the left edge of the box and put his marker Lalchungnunga off balance before wrapping his foot around the ball, which struck the inside of the right post before going in.
ALSO READ | Project reset at Chennaiyin FC–Clifford Miranda looks to repay faith in ISL 2026-27
The action continued to be centred in East Bengal’s half, and the lead could have been extended if not for some sloppy finish from Yadwad. And when nothing seemed to be going right for the title holder, it was handed a way back on a platter.
A threat seemed to be neutralised when Ayush Dev Chhetri dispossessed Dani Ramirez near the Chennaiyin box in the 29th minute. But the 23-year-old took long to find a pass, allowing the Spaniard to wrestle back control and feed it through for Ake Loba. The Ivorian made full use of the chance and blasted the ball into the roof of the net to halve the deficit.
Matters deteriorated when Chennaiyin was forced to replace Talal with C. Lalhriatpuia (Hriata) after the Frenchman experienced some discomfort in his right leg. But despite the quick setbacks, Miranda’s men refused to let up and hand East Bengal a hold in the game.
With just five minutes of regulation time left, Brison once again found himself in the box, but this time was denied a shot by Jeakson Singh, who was found guilty of committing a late challenge by the referee.
Ramon stepped up to the spot and sent Gill the wrong way for his first goal in Chennaiyin’s blue, a moment wildly celebrated by Miranda, who ran all the way past the East Bengal dugout to get involved in the celebrations, while a few thousand Chennaiyin faithful in the stands brought out the Poznan.
East Bengal seemed to have been reminded that it is the champion by Antonio Lopez Habas during the break as it returned from the break with fresher intent and legs. Just 75 seconds after the restart, another avoidable opportunity fell into East Bengal’s lap after Muhammed Saheef handled the ball inside the area. Ramirez, who had a frustrating night until then, made no mistake in burying the ball into the top left corner.
But once again, Chennaiyin failed to taper off. The crosses were flowing; possession was controlled in midfield, and subsequently Chennaiyin’s lead grew.
And this time, it was Irfan’s moment to shine. His first of the game came on the stroke of the hour mark when Hriata’s attempt deflected off him to leave Gill wrong-footed. While that goal could be deemed lucky to an extent, nothing can be taken away from the 25-year-old’s second.
Hriata won the ball in the middle of the opposition’s half, played it to Ramon, who beautifully threaded it through for Irfan, who kept his head to beat an advancing Gill.
Both benches were utilised as the minutes ticked away, and East Bengal substitutes could muster only a consolation goal in the first minute of added time, with Hardik Bhatt’s long ball carefully brought down David Lalhlansanga before placing it past Mohammad Nawaz.
Now as the league heads into a break, East Bengal remains sixth in the standings, while Chennaiyin has climbed to eighth.

Spain’s former world number three David Ferrer will join Casper Ruud’s coaching team for the 2027 season, the Norwegian said after his semifinal defeat by Carlos Alcaraz at the Paris Masters.
Ferrer, who is set to step down from his role as Spain’s Davis Cup captain after this month’s Finals, will join Ruud’s father Christian and Pedro Clar in the 27-year-old’s team.
The Spaniard, a French Open finalist in 2013, coached Alexander Zverev in 2020 and 2021 shortly after his retirement as a player in 2019.
“Good news travels fast! David Ferrer will be joining the team next year, and needless to say, we’re all really excited about what’s ahead,” Ruud wrote in a post on Instagram after his 6-4 6-4 loss to Alcaraz on Saturday.
The appointment comes after a disappointing campaign for Ruud, a three-times Grand Slam finalist and former world number two.
He has not won a title in 2026, the first time that has happened since 2019, dropping to 23rd in the world rankings.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) held that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance due to the falling fertility rate in India.
“We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance. The foundation of such laws, that is, the fear of overpopulation, has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades,” a Bench headed by Justice P.S. Narasimha observed in a 37-page judgment.
The court said its 2003 judgment (in Javed versus State of Haryana) which upheld such penal laws, needed a revisit by a larger Bench. India’s Total Fertility Rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.02 to 1.9. A TFR of 2.1, known as the replacement rate, would allow one generation to completely replace itself.
“Even though India’s population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Therefore, laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost their significance,” Justice Narasimha observed.
The 2003 judgment in the Javed case had referred to the situation that existed in China as of 2000 and drew inspiration from the measures that it had undertaken to control the population.
Justice Narasimha said the decades-old view that population explosion was an impediment for progress was outdated.
Healthy growth
“The earlier perception that population harms development does not hold water anymore. Rather than society and the courts being concerned about the negative consequences of high population, it should instead focus on the need to encourage a healthy growth of population,” the judgment, by a Bench comprising Justice Alok Aradhe, said.
The judgment pointed out that the share of persons aged 60 and above had already risen from about 8.3% in 2014 to 9.7% in 2024, and government projections place that share at nearly 15% by 2036.
India’s falling fertility rate, the court said, would necessarily mean a smaller proportion of younger persons in the future, and, correspondingly, a larger ageing population. It said the issue had been of significant concern in recent years.
The court said the failure to take notice of demographic changes would lead to only serious consequences for India. Failure to adapt not only produced injustice, but was also an abuse of power.
The judgment was based on a petition filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat in Maharashtra was set aside on the ground that she had more than two children. The lower courts and State authorities found that she had given birth to a third child in 2014, but still contested and won the panchayat elections in 2022. They had held that she acted in violation of Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, which upheld the two-child norm.
Justice Narasimha found such laws linking motherhood to political representation a violation of Article 21 (right to life) under the Constitution.
“Allowing such laws to stand excludes an entire class of citizens from political representation on grounds bearing little rational connection to their capacity to hold public office. It compels an unconscionable choice between bearing children and democratic participation, impinging on the right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21,” Justice Narasimha observed.
Seeking an immediate re-visitation of the Javed judgment of 2003, the court permitted the appellant to continue in her elected position as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat while staying any proceedings against her.

Heavy rains awaken a hidden world beneath Chile’s Atacama DesertEl Niño rains have transformed Chile's Atacama Desert into a spectacular sea of color, awakening a fleeting ecosystem of flowers and wildlife in one of the driest places on Earth.
A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
Audio will be available later today.
A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert into a vibrant landscape during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom.
Tamara Merino for NPR

Tamara Merino for NPR
COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.
This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.
Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.
A field of wildflowers blooms across Chile's Atacama Desert during the rare flowering phenomenon known as Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom, triggered by unusually heavy rainfall that awakens dormant seeds. The brief blooms transform the world's driest nonpolar desert into a landscape of pink, purple, yellow and white. Huasco, Chile, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026.
Tamara Merino for NPR

Tamara Merino for NPR
But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.
The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.
A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert.
Tamara Merino for NPR
The blooms last only a few weeks before the flowers dry out and release their seeds, which remain in the soil until the next rainfall brings the desert back to life.
Tamara Merino for NPR
This extraordinary event occurs when unusually heavy rainfall awakens seeds that have remained dormant beneath the desert soil for years, sometimes decades.
Tamara Merino for NPR
Within weeks, thousands of flowers emerge, covering vast stretches of the desert in shades of pink, purple, yellow, and white.
Tamara Merino for NPR

More than 200 species are in flower. A month ago, the first plants to emerge created a pale-yellow haze. This was followed by a soft purple hue as other bulbs germinated. Now, almost every indentation and crevice in the desert is streaked with color.
Scientists studying the phenomenon say there are patches of desert in bloom where flowers have never previously been recorded, suggesting that bulbs have remained dormant there since before the phenomenon was first studied in detail in 1997.
Moisés Grimberg has served as the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park for the past three years and has worked in protected area management for 18 years. His work focuses on protecting the flora, fauna, and fragile ecosystems of the coastal desert near Huasco, Chile, while also managing the influx of tourists during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. "But it's a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months."
Llanos de Challe is a 113,000-acre national park along the arid coastline, where waves lap at pristine white sand beaches.

Grimberg says the park normally receives about 10,000 visitors a year. But with the desert in bloom, 15,000 tourists have visited over the last few weeks alone.
Across the desert, the roads are lined with tourists' cars. According to Chile's national tourism board, the region is expected to see around 300,000 overnight trips during the two months the desert is in bloom.
Among the star attractions are the nectar-filled, crimson flowers of the garra de león, with their long tails of flame-like green leaves. This endemic flower is coaxed out of dormancy by the rains and grows along just a few miles of this stretch of coastline in the Atacama Desert — nowhere else in the world.

Trump's global health strategy is emerging. What will the Democratic Congress say?
By all appearances, it was a classic government ceremony. Officials in suits. Big black chairs around a wooden table. A cluster of microphones. It happened on October 8 in Lusaka, Zambia. Amid applause, U.S. and Zambian officials signed a global health agreement, called a Memorandum of Understanding or MOU.
But Mich Coker — the Chargé d'Affaires at the U.S. Embassy in Zambia — said this agreement was anything but classic.
"This MOU represents a fundamental shift," he said, speaking at the signing ceremony. He explained that the relationship between the two countries was moving "from a traditional donor-recipient model to a true partnership, one grounded in Zambian leadership, in Zambian ownership and in shared accountability."
Global health experts on all sides of the political spectrum and all over the world agree with Coker that there's been a fundamental shift in the U.S. approach to global health.
"The shift that's currently unfolding is very large and it's very rapid," says Janeen Madan Keller, acting co-director of the Global Health Program at the Center for Global Development.
The story of this fundamental shift starts at the beginning of the second Trump Administration with months of global health turmoil — Madan Keller and other experts say — but has given way to a clearer strategy. One with big goals, a short timeline and a lot less transparency than what came before.
Here is a look at where things stand now and how a Congress controlled by the Democratic Party might impact the new landscape.
First, the "chaos"
President Trump's second term started dramatically. When he dismantled USAID (the U.S. Agency for International Development), citing alleged "fraud, waste and abuse," everything changed overnight.
"It is a period that is best described as chaos," says Madan Keller. The repercussions were massive and immediate, she says, "for people and communities in some of the poorest countries of the world."
Clinics shut down suddenly. Patients ran out of HIV medications. In Zambia, as well as a number of other countries, many patients who relied on U.S.-supported clinics and programs faced tons of uncertainty and, often, dire health consequences.
"For the first half of 2025, there was a complete upheaval," says Jennifer Kates, senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at KFF.
A strategy emerged
Next came a new stage in the history of U.S. foreign aid. "Starting over the summer of 2025 and going into September, there actually was a sort of step back to develop an actual strategy and a plan," says Kates.
What emerged from the State Department was the America First Global Health Strategy with the stated goal of making "America safer, stronger, and more prosperous." The main way this strategy is being implemented is through agreements with individual countries. In the past, the U.S. had done more work through large international organizations or local non-governmental organizations.
Experts say one defining feature of these agreements is that they are transactional. For example, in Zambia "there was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," says Asia Russell, executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP. Her organization helped expose this situation.
While the part of the agreement about minerals was separated from the global health agreement after the public outcry in Zambia, many of the global health agreements do require the recipient country to share data such as pathogen information.
Big (but not new) goals
Speaking at the signing ceremony in Zambia, Coker ticked off some of the top priorities in the new strategy, including that recipient countries increase their financial contributions to health in the years ahead and that they are transitioned off aid in the near future.
He said in the Zambian MOU, the U.S. would pay $1.5 billion over five years "with Zambia simultaneously committing to increase its own domestic health expenditures by $975 million. We are charting a path toward a stronger, more self-reliant health system."
Another priority has been building up a country's own health infrastructure — and not a parallel system run by non-profits and NGOs.
"We are looking to have up to about 40,000 healthcare workers recruited through this support," said Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi at the same ceremony.
The priorities in the MOUs — such as recipient countries contributing more and being weaned off aid money — are not new ideas. In the world of global health they have long received bipartisan support. But, up until now, they've been hard to implement. "This approach really does kickstart them in a new way that had not occurred before," says Kates.
But in her view the chaos before this kickstart makes implementing these goals more challenging — as does the fact that everyone's now operating within a greatly diminished U.S. global health system.
The speed of the transition also troubles some. Madan Keller says that the strategy aims to achieve major changes in just a handful of years. "It's happening on a compressed timeline with arguably limited capacity to manage it, and that's where some of the risks and concerns are coming from," she says.
And Russell, for her part, is worried that the main goal of the Trump Administration has been hammering out MOUs rather than setting ambitious health-related goals, such as reducing HIV transmission. The Trump administration is focused on "process indicators — not impact indicators — as its first measure of success, which is basically a loser's gambit when it comes to pandemics," she says. "Rubio crowed about signing documents. That doesn't save lives."
The State Department declined an interview request but said in a statement that most African countries with MOUs now have drawn up implementation plans and "U.S. embassies globally are now focused on operationalizing these implementation plans [and] recipient country governments are also executing on the commitments they have made in the MOUs."
"Very hard to get the information"
Another major challenge in assessing the new strategy has been a lack of information provided to the public, says global health experts.
This represents a big break from past U.S. global health initiatives. For example, the U.S.'s flagship program for HIV/AIDS — called PEPFAR – "was a gold standard for collecting data on a regular basis and sharing it transparently — and then using that data to really inform decision making," Ramona Godbole, the former deputy director of policy, planning and programs at the now-defunct U.S. Agency for International Development, told NPR earlier this year.
"Now it's much more opaque and very hard to get the information. The agreements themselves have not been publicly released by the U.S. government," Kates says. Although, the text for some of the agreements have become available through litigation or Freedom of Information Act requests filed by advocacy groups.
There is even less information on the implementation plans, she says, which are supposed to contain detailed goals and metrics for how the money will be spent and what programs will be supported.
Kates says this is true despite the fact that U.S. taxpayers are underwriting the aid, which totals $16 billion committed across the 36 agreements that have been signed. That money comes from U.S. taxpayer dollars that Congress allocated to foreign aid. KFF has calculated that this represents a 34% drop in U.S. global health aid and it has left some countries without an agreement. For instance, Zimbabwe lost U.S. global health aid since the two governments were not able to agree to MOU terms.
In its statement, the State Department said: "Claims of a lack of accountability and transparency are unfounded….We have and will share every signed MOU with Congress."
A new blue Congress
In the wake of this week's midterms, there are new questions about how this fundamental shift in global health will play out. With the Democratic Party returning to the majority in Congress, many expect that lawmakers will demand more transparency.
"I think 100% they are going to demand: give us the MOUs, show us the implementation plans, come in and tell us more detail about what you're doing," Kates says.
Another question is whether the new Congress might try to resurrect what was dismantled. Kate says there are still a lot of unknowns about what the new Congress will do after it convenes on January 3 and how the Trump Administration will respond, but she expects lawmakers will first push for the public to get more information on what global health work the U.S. is and isn't currently supporting.
Russell says many global health activists are calling for more oversight — and she is one of them. "Congress needs to slam its feet, both feet, on the brakes unless and until it gets this information, gets this accountability," she says.

Singapore-based executive shot dead at Faridabad home after disputes over parking, pet dog
Police say the suspect fired multiple rounds and was arrested the next day. Relatives say the families had argued over a dog and parking-related issues.
A 43-year-old software company executive who lived in Singapore was allegedly shot dead by a neighbour at his Faridabad family residence late on Friday, with the assailant firing 15-19 rounds that left the victim dead at the spot.
The victim was identified as Paramjith Dhankhar, 43, who was employed by Vietnam-based FPT Software Company Limited at its Singapore office and was visiting his family for Diwali. He was previously a senior executive at Indian tech firm Tech Mahindra.
The suspect was identified as 42-year-old Mohan Sharma, a contractor and scrap-processing businessman. He was arrested from Ballabgarh on Saturday and his licensed handgun, with 59 live cartridges kept inside the bag used for storing the weapon, and two magazines—one of which was partially loaded—were recovered, police said.
Deep Dive
The two men lived on different floors of four-storey building in Faridabad’s Sector 21C.
Relatives of the victim said that the two families had been embroiled in a dispute for the past three months over the Sharma’s German Shepherd pup defecating in the parking on the ground floor, following which Dhankhar’s family had filed a police complaint. “A week ago, Sharma had broken one of the three stilt entrance gates Dhankhar had constructed to avoid a dispute. He had filed a police complaint,” a relative, requesting anonymity, said.

Dhankhar is survived by his parents, wife and two children—a 14-year-old daughter and an 18-year-old son— who lived in the same building. The suspect’s family lived on the second floor, police said.
On Friday morning, police had summoned Sharma to the Ankhir police post on Dhankhar’s complaint. In the complaint, Dhankhar’s family had alleged verbal abuse and damage to the entrance gate for objecting to the pup defecating in the parking lot, including over the opening of the underground water tank.
“My cousin also reached there. I had got to know from my brother that Sharma had misbehaved with the police too inside the station. He issued there that he would teach him a lesson,” the relative said.
Around 8.30pm, Sharma asked Dhankhar to come to the parking lot and move his car, after saying that the issue was resolved and he didn’t want any more conflict, another relative said. As soon as he went downstairs, he was shot dead, the family said.

A senior police officer privy to the investigation, said that Dhankhar tried to save himself but Sharma opened fire at close range. “He emptied one magazine and then loaded another one and emptied it too. Overall, he had fired at least 19 rounds, with at least nine hitting Dhankhar. There were multiple bullet marks on Dhankhar’s Mahindra XUV 7XO, floor and walls of the stilt area,” the officer said.
An FIR was filed, naming Sharma, his wife and two children under sections 103 (1) (murder), 109(1) (attempt to murder), 351(2) (criminal intimidation), 3(5) (common intention) and 61 (criminal conspiracy) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita at Surajkund police station on Saturday.
Pinta Ram, an eyewitness, who lives on the first floor, said he heard multiple loud bangs in quick succession. “Within seconds, we all heard screams and rushed downstairs to find that Sharma had shot Dhankhar dead,” he said.
Ram said they rushed him to a private hospital, but doctors declared him dead on arrival.
Varun Kumar Dahiya, assistant commissioner of police (crime), said Sharma was arrested from Dealer Chowk in Ballabagarh. “He will be taken on police remand. His wife and children have also been made accused for criminal conspiracy but were yet to be arrested,” Dewan said.

Family members and police said that Sharma probably planned to murder Dhankhar, since he had gone downstairs with the handgun and two loaded magazines. “When we reached the spot, the handgun holster, pistol and two magazines were recovered from the stilt area by police,” Manuj Bajaj, Dhankhar’s close friend, told HT.
The family said that Dhankhar had also planned to attend a nephew’s wedding in Faridabad on November 24.

The mortal remains of slain anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota, whose murder last month triggered protests and a political row, were brought to his native place here on Sunday for last rites.
Following a post-mortem at PGIMER in Chandigarh on Saturday (November 7, 2026), Jhota's body was taken to his native place, where last rites would be conducted.
Jhota was shot dead in broad daylight at a medical store in a busy marketplace in Mansa town on October 13. The store owner, who had fired at Jhota after the activist confronted him over the sale of addictive drugs to an elderly man, was subsequently arrested.
A large number of people turned up at his home to pay their last respects before the cremation was held.
On Saturday (November 7, 2026), a member of the joint action committee had said Jhota's cremation would take place at his native place in Mansa on Sunday.
The joint action committee (JAC), also known as the Parminder Singh Jhota Insaaf Action Committee, is a coalition of various social organisations and activists formed in Punjab after Jhota's murder.
The cremation will be held at Jhota's fields on Chakerian Road in Mansa. Jhota's father, Bhim Singh, on Saturday (November 7, 2026) called upon the youth of Punjab to pledge against drug abuse.
"We will take the body to our residence first and thereafter, between 12 and 1 pm, Jhota will be cremated on Diwali Day," said Singh while speaking to reporters in Chandigarh on Saturday (November 7, 2026).
Jhota's body was brought to PGIMER Chandigarh from the mortuary of Civil Hospital in Mansa in the early hours of Friday, after his family ended their 22-day agitation and agreed to a post-mortem following a meeting with Punjab government representatives.
On Friday (November 6, 2026), Jhota's father said he would go on a fast demanding the immediate transfer of Mansa Senior Superintendent of Police Vaibhav Chaudhary.
Jhota's family, along with the JAC, had been sitting on a protest in Mansa seeking justice for the slain activist. On October 28, two JAC members, Lakhvir Singh and Mohanjit Singh Sheron, were arrested during the protest.
On the evening of November 5, the JAC members were released from Nabha district jail after a meeting between the protesters and government representatives, including Assembly Speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan and Agriculture Minister Gurmeet Singh Khudian, on November 4.
The murder incident, which took place while Jhota was hosting a Facebook Live session, triggered a political slugfest in Punjab, which goes to polls early next year.
Opposition parties in Punjab had stepped up their attack on the Mann government over the drug issue and law and order after Jhota's murder.
The JAC had been pressing for the resignations of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann and Director General of Police Gaurav Yadav.
The Punjab government had earlier handed over the probe into Jhota's death to the CBI following his family's demand. The state government had suspended a station house officer, a deputy superintendent of police and a drug inspector in connection with the case.
The family has been demanding setting up a trauma centre in Jhota's name and compensation for each of the four injured persons in the incident, which were agreed to by the government.
Other demands the government agreed to include installation of Jhota's statue at either a park or a stadium.

ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
- Published
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.
For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.
The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.
Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.
A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".
"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.
Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done
Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.
The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.
DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.
The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".
She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".
Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.
These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.
Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.
Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.
Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.
The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.
The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.
Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.
A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.
Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros.
"We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.
Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.
Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.
South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

Watch: Moment woman rescues young koala from large snake
Queensland woman Nell was taking her dog for a walk in Brisbane, Australia, when she saw a distressed koala trying to protect its joey - which was being strangled by a snake.
Nell rushed to disentangle the young koala from the python, and was able to successfully reunite mother and baby. Though Nell was not injured by the snake, she did sustain several scratches and bites from the distressed joey.
Queensland’s government has published strict guidelines on how to approach native wildlife, and reminds people to never attempt to handle wildlife without expert advice first.
Nell is passionate about wildlife conservation and told local media she hoped the video of her rescue inspired people to take up volunteering and put more pressure on government bodies to make the lives of koalas safer.

Malaysian palace says house arrest order for imprisoned ex-leader Najib must be respected
Malaysia's national palace says the royal decision allowing former Prime Minister Najib Razak to serve his prison sentence under house arrest is clear
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- Malaysia's national palace said Saturday that the royal decision allowing imprisoned former Prime Minister Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest was clear and must be respected, warning that attempts to challenge it amounted to defying the king.
The palace statement came a day after the attorney general temporarily blockedNajib's transfer from prison to house arrest, saying more legal clarification was needed.
Najib had left the prison Friday, after his political party paid a 50 million ringgit ($12.3 million) fine required under the terms of a royal pardon that would see him serve the remainder of his graft sentence at home. But he was brought back to prison hours later, following the attorney-general's intervention.
Najib has been imprisoned since August 2022, when Malaysia’s top court upheld his conviction in his first graft trial linked to the multibillion-dollar looting of state investment fund 1MDB. Malaysia’s king in September granted Najib clemency, allowing him to serve the rest of his sentence under house arrest once he pays a court-imposed fine.
The palace said all conditions attached to Najib's conditional pardon had been fulfilled and that the royal prerogative of pardon must be respected. It said there should be no confusion regarding the interpretation of the pardon and that there should be no prolonged uncertainty over its implementation.
“The conditional pardon order is clear, explicit and without any ambiguity, and is unrelated to any other cases against him,” the statement said.
“Given that all the conditions in the conditional pardon order have been fulfilled, any arguments challenging the order would amount to disobeying the command" of the king, it added.
There was no immediate response from the attorney-general's office.
The house arrest applies only to his reduced six-year sentence in the first trial. It doesn’t cover a separate 15-year prison sentence imposed in December 2025 for corruption and money laundering in a second major trial tied to the 1MDB scandal. He’s appealing that sentence.
The attorney general’s office cited legal ambiguities in the house arrest order and raised concerns over how it could affect Najib’s consecutive 15-year prison sentence. It said the delay was not meant to contest the royal pardon allowing house arrest, but to ensure it was implemented accurately and in line with the law.
Najib set up the 1MDB development fund shortly after he took office in 2009. Investigators say at least $4.5 billion was stolen from the fund and laundered by Najib’s associates through layers of bank accounts in the U.S. and other countries.
He was originally sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined 210 million ringgit ($51.5 million) in 2020 for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving 42 million ringgit ($10.3 million) channeled into his bank accounts from SRC International, a former unit of 1MDB.
In January 2024, the Pardons Board halved his sentence to six years and reduced his fine to 50 million ringgit.
King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar subsequently granted Najib a conditional pardon, paving the way for house arrest until Aug. 23, 2028, provided he paid the fine. If Najib fails to win his appeal in the second case, he could face a further 15 years in prison after the current sentence ends.
Public outrage over the 1MDB scandal led to a historic 2018 election defeat of the ruling coalition, which had governed Malaysia since independence from Britain in 1957. Despite his conviction, Najib still wields influence in his party, United Malays National Organisation, which is now part of a new government that took power in 2022.

The best smart ring does a lot without asking much of you, passively tracking your activity, health, and sleep. Some models go even further, with meal logging, AI coaching, and cycle tracking. No distracting screens. No bulky smartwatch banging you in the face while you're deep in REM sleep.
Once the preserve of wealthy wellness buffs, top-of-the-line smart rings are becoming increasingly affordable and available. Although our top pick is still Finnish pioneer Oura's Ring 5 (from $399), the company is no longer the only fish in the smart-ring sea, thanks to upstarts like Ultrahuman and RingConn, established fitness-tracking brands like Amazfit, and even tech giants like Samsung. I expect to see more entrants in the coming months, but for now, these are the best smart rings we’ve tried.
For more wearable recommendations, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Smartwatches, the Best Fitness Trackers, and the Best Fitbits.
Featured in This Guide
How I Test Smart Rings
WIRED has been testing smart rings since the NFC Ring and the first-ever Oura Ring. I wear each smart ring 24/7, for at least a month, to assess how it performs in everyday life. Every ring is worn during activities like commuting, exercising, and sleeping to see how comfortable it feels over extended use and whether the design causes irritation, scratches easily, or gets in the way of everyday tasks.
- Sleep tracking: Sleep tracking is one of the biggest reasons people buy smart rings, so I wear each device overnight for several weeks and compare data trends against other trackers I regularly use, including wearables and sleep-tracking mats. I also evaluate whether the personalized insights (readiness metrics, sleep apnea detection, and coaching recommendations) are useful.
- Fitness tracking: I wear each ring during a range of workouts—including walks, runs, and high-intensity training—to evaluate how accurately it tracks movement, heart rate variability (HRV), and other exertion metrics. I compare data trends against other fitness trackers I regularly use.
- Durability: I expose all smart rings to daily handwashing, temperature fluctuations, and bumps. I check for scratches, coating wear, and water resistance performance.
- Companion app: Since most smart rings lack screens, companion apps need to be user-friendly. I evaluate how easy the apps are to navigate, how clearly they present health data, and whether paywalled subscriptions lock away essential features.
- Battery life: Battery life claims are tested. I track how long each ring lasts with all available features, such as continuous heart-rate monitoring, workout recognition, and sleep tracking. I also look at how quickly each ring charges and whether its charging accessories are practical to use.
- Sizing: Because fit is critical for accurate readings and usability, I take note of sizing ranges and kits. I test multiple finger placements when possible and track performance to determine how dependable the readings are.
- Value: Some smart rings cost as much as a premium smartwatch, and many also require monthly subscriptions. To determine whether a ring is worth buying, I consider its build quality, the accuracy of its features, the app experience, and any ongoing fees.
What Am I Testing Next?
I am testing the new Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the RingConn Gen 3, and the Pulse Ring.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Smart Ring Overall
The original Oura Ring unilaterally created the health smart ring category. This stylish, unobtrusive ring, popularized by biohacking billionaires, soon brought miniaturized fitness tracking to the masses.
Why WIRED recommends: The latest Oura Ring 5 is 40 percent smaller than its predecessor, making it one of the comfiest wearables to keep on all day and night. The titanium exterior has a new coating applied with physical vapor deposition (PVD) to improve scratch resistance, and the ring itself features redesigned sensors, stronger signal detection, and consequently, better accuracy. It also has improved battery life, lasting up to nine days of use.
The biggest upgrade is Oura's push toward AI-powered health guidance. Similar to Google Health Coach, the Oura Advisor can answer wellness questions, provide personalized recommendations, and help identify patterns across your long-term data. New health features, including blood pressure signals and nighttime breathing insights, expand Oura's focus beyond basic fitness tracking.
The trade-offs: While it now supports live activity tracking through the app and can work with compatible heart rate monitors, the Ring 5 isn't the best choice for athletes who need live workout stats or a built-in GPS. If you already own a Ring 4, I'd probably wait another generation, considering that most software additions are coming to older hardware anyway. Finally, you'll need an Oura membership ($6 per month or $70 annually) to unlock most of its insights. (Without it, you can only view your Readiness, Activity, and Sleep Scores.)
Is There a Class-Action Lawsuit Against Oura?
Last August, San Francisco’s Clarkson Law Firm filed a class-action lawsuit alleging that Oura rings cannot measure one’s sleep stages and rely on the company’s AI models to do the guesswork. The complaint argues that sleep is “defined by brain electrical activity, eye movements, muscle tone, and other signals measured through electrodes placed on the scalp, leads on the eyes, and sensors on the chin. [Oura] doesn’t measure any of these parameters.”
In an email statement to WIRED responding to the lawsuit, an Oura spokesperson wrote, “Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature.”
According to Oura, its sleep-staging algorithm is informed by research based on more than 1,200 nights of collected data. “We published a peer-reviewed paper that describes how the sleep-staging algorithm was developed and how it uses the signals collected by the ring,” wrote the spokesperson. “Multiple third-party, independent studies support our claims of accuracy, and we have transparently reported on the mechanisms and measures that inform Oura’s sleep staging.”
As of November 2, the court has yet to rule on Oura’s response to the complaint. I’ll continue to monitor the lawsuit and report back on any significant developments. For now, though, nothing has surfaced that changes my judgment of Oura as my top pick.
TL;DR: Though still subscription-based, the Oura Ring 5 is the best sleep tracker, one of the best fitness trackers, and the best smart ring for most folks. Read my full review.

Best Subscription-Free Smart Ring
I'm currently testing the RingConn Gen 3, but the Gen 2 Air remains one of our budget picks thanks to its affordable price and subscription-free model.
Why WIRED recommends: The RingConn Gen 2 Air is slimmer, lighter, and much more comfortable than previous models. It tracks your steps, calories burned, heart rate, blood oxygen, and sleep. It can prompt you to get up when you’ve been sedentary for too long and nudge you to take a breather if your stress levels spike. It's also compatible with colored ring protectors to swap out with your outfits if you're someone who likes to color-coordinate.
RingConn added an AI assistant to the app that generates a plan for you, adjusting your targets weekly based on your activity and feedback. This feature is fine. You can ask questions and get tips, but it doesn't dramatically change the overall user experience or make me more motivated to use the ring.
The trade-offs: Compared to the Gen 2, it's made from cheaper steel, has a slightly shorter battery life (still up to 10 days), can’t detect sleep apnea, and comes with a basic charger instead of a nifty charging case. Workout tracking is limited and does not work well when your heart rate is elevated. It also consistently overestimated reviewer Simon Hill's sleep and underestimated his steps and activity compared to the Oura and Apple Watch.
TL;DR: The RingConn Gen 2 Air is worth considering given that it's comparatively affordable and subscription-free.

Best for Samsung Users
The Samsung Galaxy Ring works seamlessly with the Galaxy Watch8 series and Galaxy Watch Ultra, extending each device's battery life by trading tasks and keeping tabs on your activity while the other is charging.
Why WIRED recommends: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So found this ring's accuracy similar to the Apple Watch Ultra. It accurately auto-detected workouts—even pool workouts—and the heart rate tracking is also reliable. Its cycle-tracking feature, powered by the fertility-tracking app Natural Cycles, uses skin-temperature sensing to track when your period will come—and it works.
It comes in an attractive, clear charging case with an LED that shows you how much battery life you have left.
The trade-offs: While you can use the Galaxy Ring with most Android phones, it costs about as much as the Oura Ring 5 upfront and doesn’t require a subscription. The most useful features, like your daily Energy Score and wellness tips (what the company calls Booster Cards), also rely on Galaxy AI, which means you'll only be able to see them if you are using the ring with an Android phone and the Samsung Health app. Lastly, Adrienne found the Galaxy Ring to be a bit too generous with its sleep tracking, which makes sense since it lacks a gyroscope.
