More Smart Rings We’ve Tested
Over the years, the WIRED Reviews team has tested several other entrants in this category. Here are some more smart rings to consider.
Oura Ring 4 for $349: While the Ring 5 is the smallest smart ring on the market, the Ring 4 is still slimmer and lighter than its predecessor. There's also a ceramic version. Reviewer Simon Hill had issues with dwindling battery life and some scuffing with his silver Ring 4, but he hasn't encountered those issues with the ceramic version.
Leep Ring for $199: A British smart ring that's affordable and subscription-free, and offers simplified stats on your activity, sleep, and stress. Unfortunately, sleep is woefully inaccurate and tends to report that I’ve been asleep for my entire time in bed, even if I was watching TV or reading. One night, it suggested I slept 8 hours and 43 minutes (Oura said 6 hours and 52 minutes). The app could also use some polish. For example, it doesn’t take into account that it’s only a couple of hours into the day before telling me my movement for today is “Bad.” I also lost data on the first night it ran out of battery, and there was no warning notification to tell me to recharge. A fully charged ring is meant to last up to eight days, but I’ve been getting closer to five. —Simon Hill
RingConn Gen 2 for $299: Despite being $100 more than the Gen 2 Air, this is still a relatively affordable, subscription-free smart ring. The main differences here are that the Gen 2 offers sleep apnea monitoring and it's a titanium build; the Gen 2 Air is made of stainless steel.
Avoid These Smart Rings
Amazfit Helio Ring: Amazfit is a purveyor of affordable fitness trackers like the Active 2, so I expected its smart ring to be competitive, but the Helio falls short in several areas. I like the textured bronze finish, but it is the only color you get. Sizes are limited to 8, 10, or 12 for now (sizes 7 to 13 are coming). Also, the Helio was often inaccurate, with heart rate measurements wildly out of step with other wearable tech. It lacks automatic workout tracking, battery life averaged three days for me, and it frequently disconnected from the busy and confusing Zepp app. There's no monthly subscription fee, but there is Aura AI ($70/year) for sleep insights and content or Fitness ($30/year), which includes an AI coach. They are expensive and confusing. (Why have two separate subscriptions?) The Helio works much better in conjunction with a smartwatch (I tried it with the Amazfit Cheetah Pro), as it can merge the data, but as a stand-alone device, it is impossible to recommend. —Adrienne So
Movano Evie Ring: When the subscription-free Movano Evie Ring first came out, it was touted as the fitness tracker for women’s health. However, its menstrual health features are pretty underbaked compared to those offered by its competitors. Now that the Oura and the Galaxy Ring can track cycles accurately, this ring's time may have passed. It's also currently sold out.
FAQs
How Do I Choose the Right Smart Ring Size?
Some smart rings come in standard sizes, but there is variation, and half sizes are rare, so it's worth taking some time to ensure you get the best possible fit. Most manufacturers will send you a free sizing kit, enabling you to wear a dummy ring for at least 24 hours. Your smart ring should be snug to enable the sensors to measure accurately, but you don't want it so tight that it restricts blood flow. Bear in mind that your fingers swell and shrink throughout the day.
Note: You may have to buy the ring directly from the manufacturer to get the sizing kit for free.
Which Finger Should I Wear My Smart Ring On?
You can wear your smart ring on any finger, but most manufacturers recommend wearing these gadgets on your index finger for the best accuracy, though the middle or ring finger can also work. These three fingers all have large blood vessels for more accurate pulse monitoring. What’s really important is that the ring fits tightly and securely around the base of your chosen finger, so if you have a big knuckle and a narrower finger base (more common with the middle or ring finger), this can be tricky. I recommend wearing it on the index finger of your less dominant hand, because I found wearing it on my right index finger, as a right-handed person, led to more damage on the ring and scrapes.
How Do I Care for My Smart Ring?
Regular cleaning can help maintain accurate tracking and prevent skin irritation. Use mild soap and water to remove buildup and oils. Wipe the inner sensors with a soft cloth. Always dry the ring and your finger completely after handwashing.
Most smart rings are built to handle everyday wear, but if you want to avoid damage, it's best to remove them when working with tools, lifting heavy weights, or playing contact sports. I'd also remove mine during chores like washing dishes or cooking, especially when abrasive products are involved.
How Often Do I Need to Charge My Smart Ring?
Most models need to be charged every five to eight days. I tested the smart rings above with all the functionalities turned on, so my battery life estimates are typically lower than the manufacturer's claims.
Smart rings come with a charging cable (and sometimes a charging case), but you will generally have to provide your own wall adapter. From dead, they take anywhere from an hour and a half to three hours to fully charge, but you should avoid letting the battery run down completely, or you run the risk of losing health data. Oura recommends charging your ring in short bursts and during moments of low activity, such as cooking or showering. The company also suggests charging your smart ring to at least 30 percent before bed to ensure uninterrupted sleep monitoring.
What Smart Ring Features Should I Look For?
Choosing the best smart ring for you comes down to a few key considerations:
- Biometric tracking: At a minimum, it's worth looking for essentials like continuous heart rate monitoring, sleep tracking accuracy, and daily activity tracking, all of which are pretty common across most modern models. For users who want deeper wellness insights, some devices offer more advanced features. These can include readiness or recovery scores that help you decide when to rest or push harder, body temperature sensing that can detect changes linked to stress or illness, and blood oxygen (SpO2) monitoring that may help flag potential breathing disturbances during sleep. Some smart rings also offer cycle tracking, which can help women monitor menstrual cycles, predict fertility windows, and better understand patterns related to hormonal changes.
- Materials and build: Materials like titanium and ceramic are popular choices because they're durable, lightweight, and often better suited for sensitive skin, thanks to their hypoallergenic properties.
- Water resistance: A rating of at least 5 ATM (or 5 atmospheres) is ideal, as it offers protection for swimming and showering.
- Companion app: Since smart rings don't have screens, the companion app becomes the only way you view and interact with your health data. A well-designed app makes all the difference, so make sure to choose one that feels intuitive, easy to navigate, and engaging to use daily. Compatibility matters too. Depending on your device ecosystem, you may want a ring that syncs with platforms like Apple Health, Google Health Connect, or Samsung Health.
- Battery life: Most smart rings last around five to eight days on a single charge, depending on usage and the specific model. Choose one that fits your lifestyle, especially if you plan to wear it overnight for sleep tracking. Some newer models also include a portable charging case, which can be useful if you travel often or tend to forget to charge your devices.
- Price and subscription costs: The upfront cost of a smart ring is important, but some brands also lock advanced insights behind a monthly membership. Before buying, consider whether the total long-term cost fits your budget. Otherwise, you may end up paying for a device without access to the features that make it most useful.
Are Smart Rings Better Than Smartwatches?
Neither is better per se. Smartwatches are designed to do more than just track health data, offering broader functionality and interactive features that allow users to check notifications, reply to messages, and even make calls right from their wrist. They're built to combine fitness tracking with everyday convenience, making them a versatile option for people who want multiple functions in one device. Smart rings take a more understated approach. Designed to be low-maintenance and discreet, they specialize in tracking health and wellness metrics in the background without the need for a display screen or interaction.
That said, here are a few reasons why you might consider a smart ring over a traditional fitness tracker or smartwatch:
- Better battery life. Smart rings are smaller and less power-hungry, which often translates to longer battery life. Most current models can run for about five to eight days on a single charge, though this varies depending on usage and brand. Smartwatches tend to require more frequent charging. Battery life varies widely, but many last around one to three days before needing a recharge. Some fitness-focused trackers—like Whoop and Fitbit—tend to last longer, offering battery life of up to two weeks.
- Reliable sleep tracking. When it comes to tracking sleep and resting heart rate, smart rings often have the edge. Because they fit securely on the finger, they maintain skin contact throughout the night, which ensures more consistent readings. Because of their longer battery life, you're more likely to keep a ring on overnight without needing to recharge it, whereas many smartwatches require overnight charging. Plus, smart rings are generally more comfortable to wear to bed than bulkier wrist-based devices.
- Looks like jewelry. Smart rings are compact and often available in a range of finishes that give them the look of everyday jewelry. Their discreet design makes them suitable to wear in almost any setting, including formal occasions where a smartwatch might look out of place. For users who prefer something low-profile, smart rings offer a more discreet option for health and fitness tracking.

Multiple witnesses told AFP on Sunday (November 8, 2026) that Riyadh's financial district was targeted and the area's Aramco tower was damaged, after the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it had intercepted missiles launched by the group.
"Aramco tower in KAFD has been targeted, that's the sure thing," said one witness, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building.
A 2022 truce that had paused fighting in Yemen's long-running conflict fell apart in July and Saudi Arabia has since traded blows with the Houthis, who have struck Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military sites.
The Iran-backed Houthis seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014, with the Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.
The King Abdullah Financial District is one of the most visible manifestations of the kingdom's ongoing economic and social reforms drive, with towering glass skyscrapers, high-end retail outlets and green spaces dotting the area.
Targeting the district would mark a major escalation in the kingdom's fight with the Houthis.
The area is also home to residential housing and a large metro station with heavy commuter traffic during the morning rush hour.
Multiple floors of the Aramco tower appeared to have sustained damage, said another witness, with glass shattered and damage to part of the tower's facade visible.
Syrian troops

Thousands of Syrian troops are set to deploy to Saudi Arabia and Yemen, with some already on the ground, multiple Yemeni officials told AFP.

Six people have been killed and 15 injured after a shooting in a market square in Kraków, Poland.
A man who had driven into the square at about 3pm began “firing at random people from his car”, according to a statement by local police on X.
The gunman was a Polish citizen who acted alone and was shot and wounded during a gunfight with police nearby, authorities said.
He used a long military-type firearm, the police said.
Police officers are among the wounded.
The incident took place in the main market square, a popular tourist destination in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city.
A tram driver reported about 3pm that his vehicle was shot at from a man in a moving car while passing nearby the main square, the Krakow municipal transport company said. The window to the tram driver’s cabin was shattered.
The prime minister, Donald Tusk, confirmed the shooting after initial reports by local media, which cited police and the fire department.
“I am being kept informed by the minister of the interior about the situation in Kraków following the tragic shooting,” he wrote on X, adding that “the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack”.
Later in the evening, government spokesperson Adam Szlapka wrote on X: “Today’s event in Kraków has shaken all of Poland,” adding that “Prime minister Donald Tusk is on his way to Kraków”
The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, wrote on X that authorities would “ensure that the perpetrator of this crime is held fully accountable and severely punished”.
The Polish president, Karol Nawrocki, said he was “deeply concerned by reports of the tragic events” in Kraków, and that his thoughts are with victims, those injured and their families.
An interior minister is heading to the scene, according to reports.
Earlier this year, Euronews reported that the number of legally owned firearms in Poland surpassed 1 million for the first time.
Poland issued a record 50,700 gun permits in 2025, and the number of active permits registered in 2025 was almost double the number registered in 2015, according to the police statistics cited in the report.

The dry-stone wall ruins of Great Zimbabwe—an ancient African capital that once presided over a thriving kingdom across much of modern-day Zimbabwe—are one legacy of the Bantu-speaking people who migrated there from western Africa.
Credit:
evanfh/Getty
It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.
At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.
Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.
“The number and size of these furnaces, together with the use of natural-draft technology, indicate intensive and technologically sophisticated iron production,” says archaeometallurgist Ezekiel Mtetwa of Chicago’s Field Museum of Natural History, who has long studied the furnaces.
Scientists are extremely interested in the peoples who created this and other iron-powered societies across eastern and southern Africa. Research points to an adaptable and innovative group from western Africa as the masterminds. Known as Bantu speakers, these communities began gradually expanding across the continent’s southern half, starting from 6,000 to 4,000 years ago. In doing so, they introduced a fundamentally new, sedentary way of life—characterized by farming, raising livestock, pottery-making, and metalworking—to regions previously dominated by hunter-gatherer communities.
This migration transformed not only the region’s history and technology, but also its languages: Today, around 350 million Africans speak one of roughly 500 distinct Bantu tongues, from southern African Zulu to eastern African Swahili. And at least as many Africans—as well as many African Americans and Afro-Latinos—carry Bantu ancestry in their DNA.
Reconstructing this expansion has been a tough puzzle, especially given the region’s sparse written historical records and limited research funding. But a unique blend of scientists—linguists, archaeologists, and geneticists—have teamed up to unearth clues about the deep origins of the Bantu-speaking people, their path across Africa, and their relationships with other cultures. Although much debate and uncertainty remain, little by little the work is uncovering one of history’s largest and longest human migrations.
“It completely reshaped the demography in sub-Saharan Africa, and we are really interested in trying to understand it,” says population geneticist Sandra Beleza of the United Kingdom’s University of Leicester.
People on the move
The first evidence of the Bantu expansion came from observations of similarities among Bantu languages. They’re so alike, in fact, that when the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around the southern tip of Africa in 1497, a Portuguese crew member who had spent time in west-central Africa could reportedly communicate with locals in southeastern Africa.
Linguists working in the 19th century started referring to the language family as Bantu, the plural of muntu, meaning “human being” in many Bantu tongues. Later linguists reasoned that the languages stemmed from an ancestral people who migrated across the continent from western Africa, which harbors the greatest diversity of Bantu languages (as would be expected for where the languages originated).
Soon, archaeologists found supporting evidence: across eastern and southern Africa, pieces of pottery of similar yet diverse styles, alongside first-time traces of village life, metal-making, domesticated animals, and western African crops—all developed within the last 2,000 years. Northern sites usually dated back to earlier time periods than sites farther south. “You can clearly see a north-to-south progression,” says archaeological scientist Shadreck Chirikure of the University of Oxford.
By the 1990s, however, some scholars began to question the idea that Bantu languages and skills spread through a migration. Couldn’t these cultural habits have spread while people stayed in the same place, with hunter gatherer communities passing along new technologies, languages, and habits to each other?
Genetic techniques that could analyze people’s ancestry helped to resolve that debate. All of us share DNA with our relatives: 50 percent on average with siblings, 12.5 percent with cousins, 3.3 percent with second cousins, and so on. Though these proportions become minute the further back in time a shared common ancestor lived, statistical techniques can tease out patterns.
Sure enough, a 2009 genetic analysis of 2,432 Africans found that Bantu-speaking people from western, central, and southern Africa are much more closely related than one might expect given their geographic distance. And in 2024, a team of scientists analyzed the genomes of 1,763 Africans and found the greatest genetic diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa. As distance from the region increased, diversity declined. “This is a typical signature of a population expanding from one place to another,” explains coauthor Carina Schlebusch, a geneticist at Uppsala University in Sweden.

Mysterious roots
But while linguistic and genetic data point to western Africa—particularly the Grassfields region of Cameroon—as the Bantu homeland, conclusive archaeological proof is thin. At the best-studied archaeological site in the Grassfields, a rock shelter called Shum Laka, pottery fragments appear dating from 7,000 to 6,000 years ago and become abundant by 5,000 to 4,000 years ago. Bowls and jars at first decorated simply with incisions and stamps and later bearing the marks of carved or braided tools rolled over wet clay are a possible, yet inconclusive, trace of Bantu ancestors.
South of Cameroon, archaeologists have searched for artifacts in one of the Bantu-speaking people’s first destinations: the Congo rainforest. A handful of times between 2010 and 2023, archaeologist Alexandre Livingstone Smith of Belgium’s Royal Museum for Central Africa traveled via boat along the Congo River as part of a team led by linguist Birgit Ricquier. In a number of villages, Smith found pottery shards of a style consistent with that found farther west, dating back to 2,300 to 2,000 years ago. “That would be the potential first Bantu settlers of the forest,” Smith says.
Many experts interpret the trails of pottery as evidence that ceramics traditions were brought by Bantu-speaking people all the way from their original home. What’s unclear, however, is when and how Bantu-speaking peoples acquired their farming and metalworking skills—and, in particular, whether they invented iron smelting themselves or learned it from neighboring, iron-extracting cultures.
Scientists have been able to deduce the path that Bantu speakers took to eastern and southern Africa. Some scholars have argued that the path split into two before entering the Congo rainforest, with one group heading east while another went south through the forest. But evidence is now mounting that these groups crossed the rainforest together, and only upon reaching its southern fringes roughly 2,500 to 3,500 years ago did they split into east-moving and southward-moving groups.
Some of this evidence comes from linguistic studies. Not unlike the evolution of species, languages diverge and transform over time, creating “trees” that linguists can reconstruct from similarities in grammar and vocabulary. In 2015, a group of researchers did this computationally using data from about 400 Bantu languages. They observed a much larger diversity—and deeper splits—among the Bantu languages spoken in the Congo rainforest, suggesting that Bantu-speaking ancestors spent a long time there, allowing their languages to diversify. Languages spoken farther east and farther south appeared to stem from a less diverse subset of this larger group, explains coauthor Koen Bostoen, a linguist at Belgium’s Ghent University.
Later linguistic studies, as well as genetic analyses, have reached similar conclusions. In 2023, Beleza and her colleagues compared the genomes of Bantu speakers from Angola—south of the Congo rainforest—with those from the eastern African country of Mozambique and ones from Cameroon, the Bantu homeland.
Remarkably, the eastern African samples were more genetically similar to those from Angola, hundreds of miles to the south of Cameroon and south of the rainforest, than to any of the samples from Cameroon. That points to a recent common ancestor in the Angola region—suggesting that the Bantu split into eastern and southern streams only once they reached the rainforest’s southern edge, Beleza explains.
By the time the Bantu people commenced their movement east and south, they had already come into their own as a farming, iron-making, livestock-herding, and pottery-making people, Chirikure says: Many ancient Bantu settlements across eastern and southern Africa contain evidence of this Bantu “package.”
Mixing and mingling
Key to the Bantu’s success in southern and eastern Africa, experts suspect, was their sedentary lifestyle. This—and their iron tools—would have allowed them to produce more food and grow in number, propelling them to occupy new territories. Their lifestyle affected the landscape as forests turned into farmland, and it also affected the hunter-gatherer communities who were already living there. Some groups were likely crowded out and disappeared, experts suspect, while others were probably pushed to marginal regions, including Indigenous groups such as rainforest hunter-gatherers and Khoisan peoples, who continue to live in central and southern Africa, respectively, to this day.
Still, scientists are learning that Bantu peoples had deep relationships with these two groups. In the 2024 genetic analysis, Schlebusch and her colleagues found that some Bantu-speaking groups in central Africa share about an eighth of their DNA with rainforest hunter-gatherers, and some southern African Bantu speakers share a similar amount with Khoisan groups. Clearly, their ancestors once intermixed.
Curiously, in the case of the Khoisan, this mixing tended to arise from pairings of Bantu-speaking men with Khoisan women. One 2021 study of southern African Bantu speakers found that the DNA inside their mitochondria—which people inherit only from their mothers—had greater-than-expected proportions of Khoisan DNA. But the Y chromosomes, which come from fathers, had much higher proportions of DNA with Bantu ancestry. Some experts speculate that this pattern could be the result of Bantu men raiding Khoisan women or preferentially marrying Khoisan women for whom the traditional bride prices would have been cheaper. “Whenever there is a power difference… between two groups, it tends to melt down to this,” says coauthor Ananyo Choudhury, a geneticist at the University of Witwatersrand in South Africa.
This pattern also left marks on the language. The characteristic clicks of Khoisan languages also occur in southern African Bantu languages Zulu and Khosa. Bostoen suspects that the children of Khoisan-Bantu pairings were, at first, bilingual. Eventually, “they lost their mothers’ languages, but they left a substrate of the mothers’ languages in the Bantu language.”
Archaeologists are also studying the relationships between Bantu farmers and their neighbors. While there may have been conflicts over land, the groups also cooperated with and learned from one another, says Décio Muianga, an archaeologist at Eduardo Mondlane University and the research institute Kaleidoscopio in Maputo, Mozambique. He’s been excavating a rock shelter in Mozambique containing thousands of years’ worth of stone tools, wild animal bones, and wild plant remains—telltale signs of hunter-gatherers living at the site. But interestingly, Bantu-style pottery also appears. “My assumption is that the hunter-gatherers were getting these ceramics from the farmers,” Muianga says. “They were interacting, communicating, and exchanging resources.”
There is evidence, too, for cultural exchanges: European anthropologists have reported that some Bantu-speaking groups would solicit San hunter-gatherers to conduct traditional rainmaking ceremonies, for example.
Bantu social networks eventually extended well beyond Africa. By 1100 to 1600 AD, many of the complex state societies that Bantu speakers built developed trade networks across the Indian Ocean. Archaeological data shows they imported Chinese porcelain and glass beads; in return, they exported gold, ivory, and iron. In fact, a 12th century Muslim cartographer once wrote that iron from parts of southern Africa—likely referring to Great Zimbabwe’s iron-producing hinterlands, Mtetwa suspects—was deemed to be of much higher quality than that from other places like India.
Mtetwa has found evidence that iron smelters near Great Zimbabwe would add bone fragments to the furnaces, perhaps as part of a smelting-blessing ritual, but one with scientific merit: This material contains calcium, which can accelerate the separation of iron from the rest of the ore. That may be a testament to the Great Zimbabweans’ iron-smelting skills: “Some materials introduced within ritual or medicinal practices may simultaneously have had technically beneficial effects on the smelt,” says Mtetwa.
A future full of research
Though they’ve made great progress in reconstructing the Bantu world, scientists are aware of, and trying to address, the limitations of their research so far.
Linguistic studies, for instance, have been a popular tool to reconstruct Bantu history, but Bostoen cautions that very few Bantu languages have been documented thoroughly enough to definitively trace linguistic trees back in time. Linguists may never get a complete dataset, because some old branches of the Bantu language family may have died out.
Another limitation of computational Bantu language-family reconstructions is that they’ve usually assumed that languages have evolved in isolation after different Bantu groups separated. But there may have been extensive cross-pollination among languages as different groups met and interacted.
In fact, when linguists factored in the possibility of contact among Bantu languages in a 2026 study, they couldn’t reconstruct the diversification patterns described by previous linguists, says coauthor Igor Yanovich of the University of Vienna, who wrote about the challenges of Bantu linguistic studies in the 2025 Annual Review of Linguistics. In his view, linguists should first focus on thoroughly documenting Bantu languages before attempting to use them to understand Bantu history.
In hopes of adding new insights, Schlebusch is working to obtain DNA from ancient human remains. By revealing the identity of people who were living in particular places at particular times, this could help to elucidate when and where different Bantu communities moved into, overlapped with, or repopulated areas. “What we see more and more in genetic data is that the movement was probably complex—that it was these ‘spread over spread’ events,” Schlebusch says.
Archaeologists, for their part, hope to fill in the vast gaps in the archaeological record of sub-Saharan Africa—by both conducting new excavations and re-examining existing artifact collections for fresh insights. But all this work requires funding for research and laboratories, especially from African governments, says Chirikure; he, like many of his colleagues, has largely relied on funding from Europe, which is limited. Without more funding, “you are not generating fresh ideas, you are not formulating new hypotheses and testing them using some of the cutting-edge science,” he says.
Scientists from all three disciplines are hopeful that they will eventually tell the complete story of how an innovative people spread and diversified across sub-Saharan Africa, mixing traditions with those of earlier peoples and of others who still live there, to create myriad cultures, each one a unique blend of food, philosophy, language, music, and traditions. “If you travel from West Africa today all the way to East Africa, you have a unique cultural diversity that is very hard to find in many other parts of the world,” Muianga says. Combined with the legacy of other groups, he says, “this is the result of the Bantu migration.”

Or that Jean-Philippe Mateta had just got himself sent off 13 minutes into his second Premier League start since August - and will now miss the next three games.
Sage may be well advised to avoid walking under any ladders with the level to which his luck seems out. Though beyond that, there are also pertinent questions to ask regarding Palace's rationale that he was a good fit for their squad in the first place.
His first problem may have dropped into his in-tray long before he even took the job. Marc Guehi's sale to Manchester City in mid-January, without a replacement, saw Oliver Glasner's Palace ship 26 goals in their remaining 16 games at a rate even more porous than Palace's defence this season.
It was clear a rebuild was necessary - and possible, after banking solid sums for Guehi and Eberechi Eze across the previous 12 months. Even more so following the departures of Munoz and Lacroix.
That would prove director of football Matt Hobbs' first real test since succeeding Dougie Freedman. The results have been mixed at best.
Munoz's replacement Anan Khalaili is creating chances at barely half the rate of the Colombian while loanee centre-back Axel Disasi has been unable to match Lacroix's dominance in defence, winning only 54 per cent of his aerial duels. That has not helped with shipping five goals from set-pieces already, a record only beaten by his parent club Chelsea.
Replacing half a team's worth of talent in Eze, Guehi, Munoz, Lacroix and Michael Olise across the last two years was never going to be easy but while Palace look on enviously as old rivals Brighton thrive despite having their best players picked off, it is hard to argue any new arrival at Selhurst Park has come close to filling their precedessor's shoes bar Jeremy Pino.
Of those who still remain at Selhurst Park, Sage has been robbed of Palace's most profitable attacking outlet from last season with Sarr, who scored 21 goals from 45 games, struck down by a recurrence of a groin injury.
Palace's league goals dried up by almost half to just 0.71 a game when he was unavailable last season though even then, Mateta still managed to plunder 12 as their top league goalscorer. The pair have been on the pitch for a combined total of just 183 league minutes from a possible 1,170 under the new head coach.
Wharton should be Palace's best player regardless, but Sarr's availability and the absence of Munoz has had a knock-on effect on him too with few players waiting for early balls forward when he is in possession.
His lack of rhythm may have affected his out-of-possession game too. Over the previous two seasons Wharton won the ball back in the middle third more than three times a game on average. Now his tally sits barely above one.
The 22-year-old would likely have thrived in Sage's Lens system last season, built around throttling opponents, high turnovers and rapid transitions. His ability to pick a pass and spot a runner would have provided a dangerous weapon, just as it had done for Glasner's Palace.
But this is not that side. And that is a problem in itself, because Sage's beliefs have not changed. When asked about Palace's porous defence after defeat to Newcastle last week, he replied: "My idea is that the best way of defending is to have the ball, because then you cannot concede."
He inherited a team which had racked up 42 per cent possession or less in 19 games in 2025/26, also contributing seven of its 11 wins. Since he came in Palace have won the possession battle just twice and only two sides have seen less of the ball. Keeping it as he would like is not their forte and their goals against column is paying the price.
Sage is clearly a talented coach to the point he was briefly on Liverpool's radar this summer, but the 3-4-2-1 he deployed at Lens which may have lured Palace in was predicated on opposition-half pressure and high tempo rather than the counter-attacking unit Palace have become known for.
His Lens side produced the second-most high turnovers ending in a shot last season. No team has managed fewer across the Premier League this season than Sage's Palace.
Beyond the other issues, it presents a question of whether he might be the right fit at the wrong time. His demands sit far closer to that of Iraola who, ironically, Palace courted for so long this summer before he joined Liverpool and whose Bournemouth team were also far different stylistically to the Eagles.
Ultlimately, should the club's poor form continue and his position become untenable then perhaps it is not so much because he is the wrong man for Palace, but they are not the right club for him.

My husband and I are caregivers for our middle son, who has multiple disabilities and requires full-time support. We do our best to keep one another up to date on the activities that fill his daily life while also managing his numerous medical specialists, procedures, and therapies. We have to stay in constant communication while also working our jobs, caring for three teenagers, and managing a household. It’s tough.
We’re not alone in our struggles. According to AARP, in 2025, an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability. On average, these caregivers spend up to 27 hours per week providing care.
This caregiver crisis, where so many Americans provide ongoing, complex care and, as a result, endure poor health, financial strain, and isolation, is worsening as caregivers need more support and better systems.
Helpfully, to lighten the mental load, caregiver apps are aimed at families who are supporting seniors, children, or anyone with a diagnosis that needs regular management.
Apps for Different Types of Caregivers
Every caregiver’s situation is different, and the apps and programs in this space reflect a diversity of needs.
Medisafe, which was created in 2013, tracks medications and sends reminders so users don’t miss a dose. The program can also notify a caregiver if a dose is missed. It gives its users the ability to track medical appointments, track their symptoms, and maintain a list of health care contacts and measurements. It also has a drug interaction checker where users can enter multiple medications to see if they are safe to take at the same time.
Caring Village, which was founded in 2015, has an appointment calendar, a to-do list, and a wellness journal where users can keep track of their loved one’s symptoms and moods, and even upload a photo. Caregivers can assign tasks through the app, create a care plan, and receive reminders to take medication. The app also comes with an AI assistant called Julia that can answer caregiving questions.
In 2022, Bret Koncak, based on his experiences with his two sons who have complex needs, cocreated Mejo, a web-based caregiver app. Users enter an individual’s medical history, which is then consolidated into a one-page summary that can be shared with caregivers, doctors, and therapists.
“A lot of people think that caregiving begins and ends with interactions with the health care system, but a lot of it is about what happens between care visits,” says Koncak. “That's what we're focused on.” For $6 a month or $60 a year, the premium version of Mejo gives users access to daily journaling, which they can share with other caregivers, so everyone stays on the same page without having to catch up verbally.
For now, information in Mejo is entered manually, but Koncak says his team is looking into ways to incorporate AI to help users come up with appropriate questions to ask during medical appointments.
Brett Rowell, whose son Briggs has cerebral palsy, is creating an app called Briggzy, so he and his wife, who work different hours, can more easily hand off their son’s care. Briggzy is currently in the testing phase, and Rowell hopes to launch it to a wider community in 2027.
“My wife took [our son] to most of the appointments because I worked 8 to 5 and she was off during that time,” said Rowell. “So the questionnaires alone, I don't know how to answer half of them unless I have Briggzy. My goal was to bring her mind into a shared space for me, so that way I can be helpful.”
Nasha Fitter, who has a daughter with a rare disease, launched Citizen Health in 2024 with cofounder Farid Vij to collect medical records for patients and store them in a secure portal. “With the users’ consent, we can extract information from those medical records, deidentify it, harmonize it, and start to pull an understanding of diseases through that,” says Fitter. “And then we feed that understanding back to patients so they would get a better sense of the trajectory of their child’s disease.” Citizen Health works with patient advocacy groups to support their research on drug development.
Six months ago, the company launched Ari, an AI “health teammate” that lets caregivers and patients track their loved one's care and symptoms by texting with it. Ari, currently in beta, can also access medical records, patient portals, and Google Calendar events, including specific appointment dates and surgeries. Ari notices caregiver patterns, such as whether they take medication at different times of the day and how that might impact symptoms. It prepares patients and caregivers for appointments by summarizing past medical information and providing appropriate questions to ask medical professionals. And it can help navigate insurance and government benefits.
Right now, Ari is only available for people with rare diseases, but the goal is to make it available and useful to all caregivers and patients.
Trying to Lighten the Load
I. Glenn Cohen, a bioethics and health law researcher and professor at Harvard Law School, is optimistic about AI in the health space overall. “For example, I think it will empower many patients to prep for questions they might want to ask their doctor before going in to see them.”
But he says that users should go into the process with their eyes open to understand the risks and what you're getting out of it, especially if a product is free or cheap.
Most of these devices are not medical devices, says Cohen. “As such, the FDA has not reviewed them, so their safety and efficacy remain a question mark, or it's the company's word for it that you have to take.”
The health information patients and caregivers plug into these AI tools is not protected by federal HIPAA statutes because the information is typically not coming from a covered entity. Instead, it comes from a person or from data collection at home. “If your privacy is important and you care about how the information is used, in some cases, all you can rely on is the contractual promises,” Cohen says. “They typically have language that absolves [the companies] from responsibility in many instances.”
He also warns that the information collected may not be only for the person receiving care, but may also include information about parents or other caregivers.
While I love the idea of keeping my son’s information all in one place so I can keep track of patterns, update his doctors without feeling emotionally drained, and easily hand off his caregiving needs to my husband, making sure we update the app regularly will be the key to actually seeing those benefits.
Denise M. Brown, CEO and founder of the Caregiving Years Training Academy, has seen many apps come and go because she says they can be tedious to maintain, especially when caregivers are already overloaded.
“We have to upload data to the app (care plans, schedules, tasks), and that’s a lot of work,” Brown says. “A physician, visiting nurse, therapist, or hospital discharge planner won’t log into the app to provide updates, which ends up falling back on the caregiver.”
At the end of the day, the need for caregiver apps is great, and many developers in this community, many of whom are caregivers themselves, are trying to do something to lessen the load.
“The technology and apps can open the door for broader seamless integration of care—and hopefully less stress on you as the caregiver,” says Nicole Howell, director of direct care workforce development at the National Council on Aging. But she says the final solution [to the overall caregiver crisis] will be something that not one family, not one caregiver can solve.
“It has to be all hands at the wheel. It has to be government. It has to be private. It has to be family members speaking up, saying the hard truth so we get the best of American ingenuity to move this to where we need to be.”

John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families, who during three decades in the U.S. Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died on Friday (November 6, 2026) at his home in Washington, the Washington Post reported. He was 89.
His family did not provide a cause, the newspaper added.
Mr. Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his five six-year terms representing West Virginia in the Senate after two terms as Governor of the poor coal-mining State.
Mr. Rockefeller voted in 2002 in favour of the Republican Bush’s measure authorising the Iraq war, which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate intelligence committee, accused Mr. Bush of taking the nation to war on “false premises.”
He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty that included his uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller.
Initiatives in public office
New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.
When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, fight poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping the programme created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps States provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.
Mr. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.
In the debate over Mr. Obama’s measure, Mr. Rockefeller unsuccessfully sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.
“Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Mr. Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would not seek a sixth Senate term.
On the Iraq war
Before the Iraq invasion, Mr. Bush’s administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the al Qaeda network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the U.S.
“If I had known then what I know now, I would have voted against it,” Mr. Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure.
“I think the intelligence was shaped,” he continued. “And I think the interpretation of the intelligence was shaped. You had a president who we now know was determined to go to war.”
‘Fundamentally misleading’
A report from the intelligence committee issued in 2008, when he served as its chairman, asserted that Mr. Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and other leading officials exaggerated intelligence findings and ignored disputes within U.S. intelligence circles about Iraq’s weapons and the hotly disputed ties to al Qaeda.
The report rejected pre-war statements by Mr. Bush and Cheney that Iraq might give al Qaeda weapons of mass destruction.
“Representing to the American people that the two had an operational partnership and posed a single, indistinguishable threat was fundamentally misleading and led the nation to war on false premises,” Mr. Rockefeller said as the report was released.
During his Senate tenure, he also headed the Commerce, Science, and Transportation and Veterans Affairs committees.
Wealthy family
Mr. Rockefeller was born on June 18, 1937, weeks after the death of his great-grandfather, who had been America’s richest man.
The Rockefeller name came with high expectations. His father was a famous philanthropist. His uncle Nelson served as U.S. vice president, as well as Governor of New York. His uncle David Rockefeller headed Chase Manhattan Bank and uncle Winthrop Rockefeller was governor of Arkansas.
He was elected to West Virginia’s legislature in 1966 before age 30, then elected West Virginia’s Secretary of State in 1968.
He lost a bid to become Governor in 1972, then served as a college president before being elected Governor in 1976. Mr. Rockefeller, who became one of the wealthiest members of the U.S. Congress, spent millions of dollars of his own money to bankroll his successful campaign for the US Senate in 1984.
Mr. Rockefeller sometimes found himself overshadowed by his State’s other senator, Robert Byrd, who died in 2010 at age 92 as the longest-serving member of Congress in U.S. history.
He usually backed his State’s coal and steel industries but angered coal executives in 2012 by fighting Republican efforts to prevent regulation of emissions from coal-fired power plants.
He was married to public television executive Sharon Percy Rockefeller, with whom he had four children.

What do dark circles under a child’s eyes indicate?
Dark circles under a child’s eyes may not always be due to lack of sleep. Genetics, allergies and nasal congestion can also play a role. Paediatricians explain the causes and when parents should seek medical advice
Dark circles alone need not be a cause for concern if the child is otherwise healthy. Parents should, however, consult a paediatrician if the discolouration persists or is accompanied by other symptoms |Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: File Photo
A child may wake up after a full night’s sleep and still have dark circles under the eyes. For some children, this may simply be a family trait. In others, it could be associated with allergies, persistent nasal congestion or skin conditions. Dark circles, also referred to as periorbital hyperpigmentation, are not a condition in themselves. While parents may immediately associate dark circles with inadequate sleep or nutritional deficiencies, their causes can be more varied.

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, one of his most powerful and politically aggressive aides, would be his next White House chief of staff following disastrous results for Republicans in the midterm elections.
Miller, whose titles until now were deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, has orchestrated the most polarizing policies of Trump’s second term—most notably a brutal crackdown on immigration that has claimed the lives of US citizens.
Trump made the change public in a statement on his Truth Social platform, writing that Miller would take over from Susie Wiles on Monday—less than a week after Republicans lost the House and Senate in a searing rebuke of Trump’s policy agenda.
In recent days, Trump has privately blamed Wiles for the worst Republican midterm performance in decades, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday, the sources say.
Trump broadly considered three candidates to replace Wiles, the sources say: special envoy Steve Witkoff, director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, and Miller.
But with the looming threat of congressional investigations starting next year, Trump settled on Miller, seemingly because of his zeal in defending the president and his deep loyalty. Miller has been with Trump since his first campaign and stood by him through his political exile in 2021.
Miller had made his interest for the job known inside the West Wing for weeks, ever since Wiles weathered a series of negative stories before the midterms that suggested her job was at risk, the sources say.
In recent months, Trump also started cutting Wiles out of certain decisions, which contributed to the sense among her detractors that she was on shaky ground, sources say. For instance, Trump reportedly hired Katie Zacharia as press secretary without consulting Wiles, though the White House pushed back on the claim.
With Wiles’ departure, White House aides were bracing for further personnel changes. Among other names, Wiles’ deputies James Blair, who put together the GOP midterm strategy, and Richard Walters are seen as vulnerable to being fired by Miller unless they resign first, sources say.
The changing of the guard also is likely to bring respite to defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has had a strained relationship with Wiles as of late but is seen as ideologically aligned with Miller, sources say.
Hegseth and Miller worked closely last year when the Trump administration began a campaign of strikes against boats around Venezuela. Miller, who also leads the Homeland Security Council within the White House, orchestrated the campaign through the Pentagon.
Wiles leaves the White House as arguably the most successful chief of staff to Trump, who infamously cycled through chiefs in his first term. By comparison, Wiles kept Trump’s confidence from the start of his second presidential campaign in 2021.
Still, Wiles weathered a number of challenges in recent months. She underwent a successful course of chemotherapy, but also faced accusations that her daughter had received lucrative contracts in part because of the family’s connection to the president. (The White House and Wiles’ daughter’s firm pushed back on these claims.)
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” Wiles wrote on X. “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

The Bombay High Court has refused to discharge Vishal Ingle and held that Section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita can apply when the complainant is a transgender who identifies as a woman. Justice Mehroz Pathan passed the order on November 3.
The judge rejected the argument that Section 75 cannot apply because the complainant is a transgender and not a woman. The judge said the complainant identifies as a woman and has taken medicines for hormone changes.
The FIR contains allegations against the applicant of outraging the modesty of the complainant. The complainant identifies as a woman and has undergone treatment for hormone changes. The judge said the FIR contains allegations against the applicant of outraging the modesty of the complainant, who identifies as a woman after hormone therapy. The judge said Section 75 appears to be made out.
The judge said allegations of assault and outraging the modesty of a woman can be sustained when the victim is a transgender who identifies as a woman.
Mr. Ingle served as an Agniveer. The police registered an offence under Section 75 and Section 296 of the BNS and under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.
The judge rejected the argument that Section 18(D) of the Act of 2019 is not made out because the complainant did not have a certificate of identity under the Act. The judge said Section 2(k) shows a person may identify as a transgender even without a certificate of identity. Section 5 provides a route to apply to the District Magistrate for a certificate.
The complainant received a certificate of identity on February 12, 2026. The assault took place on October 28, 2025 and October 30, 2025. The judge said the absence of a certificate at the time of the offence does not bar use of the Act of 2019. The judge said the FIR shows Section 18(D) was invoked and the allegations attract the provisions invoked against the applicant.
The judge refused to discharge the accused.

Update | November 5, 19:43 After the story was published, RapidClaims founder and CEO Dushyant Mishra said the startup is not in talks with WestBridge Capital to raise any funding round. He also said that the $200 Mn valuation figure is “incorrect”. Original | October 5, 18:22 AI-powered SaaS startup RapidClaims is in talks to raise around $30 Mn in a funding round led by WestBridge Capital at a valuation of about $200 Mn, sources told Inc42. The round is expected to be its Series B, with existing investors Accel and Together Fund likely to participate, the sources added. RapidClaims did not respond to questions sent by Inc42, while WestBridge Capital declined to comment. Founded in 2023 by Dushyant Mishra, Abhinay Vyas, and Jot Sarup Singh, RapidClaims builds AI-powered revenue cycle management (RCM) software that helps healthcare providers automate medical coding, improve clinical documentation, prevent insurance claim denials, and recover outstanding payments. The startup primarily caters to healthcare providers in the US, helping them address billing errors, rejected claims, and delays in reimbursements. Automating Healthcare Revenue Workflows RapidClaims’ products include RapidCode for medical coding, RapidVBC for clinical documentation and risk adjustment, and RapidRecovery for managing denied claims, automating appeals, and detecting underpayments. The platform integrates with healthcare providers’ existing electronic health record systems. It serves physician groups, hospitals, health systems, federally qualified health centres (FQHCs), and ambulatory surgery centres, among other healthcare organisations. The startup is also developing inpatient coding capabilities with design partners, extending its automation tools to coding for hospital admissions. In April 2025, RapidClaims raised $8 Mn in a Series A round led by Accel, with participation from Together Fund. It also disclosed that it had previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding. RapidClaims had earmarked the Series A proceeds for expanding its go-to-market efforts, strengthening its technology and product capabilities, and growing its sales and marketing teams. At the time, the startup said it had grown sixfold over the preceding four months and served a double-digit client base. It was also looking to expand its presence among FQHCs, physician groups, outpatient facilities, and ambulatory surgery centres. Investors Bet On Automation The proposed fundraise comes amid increasing investor interest in startups looking to automate healthcare administration and insurance workflows. In October, Confido Health raised $12.5 Mn in a Series A extension led by Z47, taking its total Series A funding to $22.5 Mn. The startup develops AI agents for tasks including appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills, and payment collection. Meanwhile, Consint.AI raised ₹22 Cr to expand internationally and develop its AI capabilities for fraud detection and claims processing. Its products automate claims processing, digitise documents, and standardise healthcare records.

Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.
High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.
Fairtrade research suggests that during the previous El Niño cycle, productivity across its farmers and workers dropped by 13% in the Dominican Republic, 22% in Ecuador, and 6% in Peru compared with the year before. The El Niño event in 1983 – one of the strongest ever recorded – affected 15% of total planted banana area in Ecuador, with a reduction in exports of 36%.
Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, a climate and environment lead at Fairtrade, says this El Niño is expected to lead to more extreme weather, including heavy rainfall and strong winds and “we expect the impacts for producers to be more severe” than in the 23-24 cycle.
Evidence is mounting to fuel those fears. Exports from the Colombian Caribbean region fell 32% to $122m (£91m) between July and September this year, according to the Association of Banana Growers of Magdalena and La Guajira, as reported by the trade publication Fruitnet.
It said that in September alone, shipments were down 42% year on year, with earnings close to halving to $40m from $70m.
“Given the risks threatening the continuity of banana production, we are calling on international markets to foster commercial conditions that recognise actual production costs and contribute to the sector’s sustainability,” the association said.
It said that climate-related productivity losses and a decline in earnings from exports made worse by currency issues was “undermining the economic sustainability of the industry”.
Ever Antonio Flores Muños, a worker at the Agrosiete banana producer in Colombia, told Fairtrade: “Over the past 10 years the climate has changed a lot. It’s been getting much hotter … it’s really intense. Some places have had losses due to the climate, flooding, strong winds. It’s going to affect all of us – our workers, colleagues – everything will be at great risk, and our wages will decrease.”
Fairtrade is calling for legislation in the UK to tackle unfair trading practices, such as low or late payments to farmers and contracts which push risk down the supply chain, so that producers can invest more into improving their crops’ resilience to severe weather and more likelihood of pests and diseases. Worker health is also expected to be affected by more extreme weather.
While some businesses, including Sainsbury’s, the Co-op and Waitrose, have taken voluntary steps by sourcing only Faitrade bananas, which guarantee a minimum price, it says there is more work to do.
Eleanor Harrison, the chief executive of Fairtade, said: “The UK’s banana supply depends on the people growing our bananas having the resources they need to adapt to climate change, and to invest in their future. Fair prices, climate resilience and decent work go hand in hand.”
While bananas are becoming harder and more expensive to produce, supermarket prices have remained unchanged for almost 40 years despite rising costs for fertiliser, fuel and labour.
Caoimhe Buckley, the chief corporate affairs officer at the large supplier Fyffes, said: “The long-term sustainability of the banana sector … cannot be separated from purchasing practices. The price of bananas in the supermarket needs to recognise the real and sustainable cost of production, including labour and decent wages, environmental management, human-rights due diligence and the investment necessary to adapt to climate change.”
Research by the Ethical Trading Initiative found that prices paid to suppliers in 2026 did not even cover basic production costs for 66.7% of them.
It said producers need more help to adapt or mitigate climatic changes, which could mean suitable land for banana cultivation could shrink by an average of 61% across Latin America and the Caribbean by 2050, according to research for the Inter-American Development Bank published in 2020.

The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options.
Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
You can get a temporary break from the $200 price hike that hit both Air sizes this summer.
If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99.
Apple 13-inch MacBook Air (M5)
Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people.
If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases.

Missiles target Kyiv and wound 5 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
Drone and missile explosions wounded at least nine people across Ukraine Saturday, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States
KYIV, Ukraine -- Drone and missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.
“The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It’s very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren’t sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. “I’m old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?”
Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 816-meter-long (892-yard-long) Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city’s heating and water supply systems.”
In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by “launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure.”
Later, he said that Moscow was stepping up strikes to build pressure on Ukraine ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression,” he wrote in an online post.
The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, of which only four were shot down due to a lack of Patriot interceptors.
Zelenskyy also said that Russia had used North Korean-made ballistic missiles to strike energy facilities, citing preliminary findings from investigations at impact sites.
The barrage involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said.
“When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv — a city of millions — and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone,” Zelenskyy said. He urged greater U.S. support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine’s Energy Ministry said Saturday’s missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.
It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.
“She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.”
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.
The head of Russia’s southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged “civilian infrastructure” and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.
The head of Russia’s Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol’s Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.
